title: Open ultrasound foundation model for robust segmentation and clinical measurement across heterogeneous settings
comment: The PDF includes the Supplementary Information
summary: Ultrasound is the most widely deployed imaging modality worldwide, yet clinical AI remains fragmented into narrow single-task models that fail when device, operator, or anatomy changes. Here we present SonoCorpus, an open resource unifying 456,963 images and 1,626,085 expert masks from 53 public datasets spanning 24 clinical applications and 17 countries, and SonoBase, an interactive segmentation foundation model pretrained on it. Across fifteen evaluation datasets introducing new organs, devices, operators, and geographies, SonoBase outperforms SAM2, MedSAM2, and the concept-promptable MedSAM3 on every dataset and matches per-dataset specialist models trained on the same data; on fully external data it exceeds the accuracy these baselines achieve on their own in-distribution benchmarks. Ejection fraction derived from its segmentations falls within inter-observer variability (6.63\% error), with fewer misclassifications at the defibrillator-candidacy threshold than either promptable baseline (13\% versus 18--42\%); fetal head-circumference (1.81~mm) and gestational-age (1.2 days) errors fall below inter-observer variability. Where a baseline fails outright, one in four test cases, SonoBase recovers a usable segmentation in 81\% of them, including on handheld probes operated by minimally trained users in two low- and middle-income countries (Sierra Leone and Tanzania). Five labeled examples can help the model adapt to a new setting, and the identical training protocol transfers well to newer models such as SAM3, locating the advantage in ultrasound-specific pretraining rather than any single architecture. To ensure reproducibility and enable the community to build on SonoBase as a platform, we release all checkpoints, optimizer states, data-split indices, deduplication hashes, and starter code.

AI.tldr: SonoCorpus is a large-scale ultrasound dataset (456,963 images, 1.6M masks from 53 datasets, 24 applications, 17 countries) used to pretrain SonoBase, a segmentation foundation model that generalizes across new devices, operators, and anatomies, outperforming SAM2, MedSAM2, and MedSAM3 while matching specialist models.
AI.motivation: Clinical ultrasound AI is fragmented into narrow single-task models that fail when device, operator, or anatomy changes. There is a need for a generalizable foundation model that works across diverse clinical settings, including low-resource environments.
AI.method: Created SonoCorpus by unifying 53 public datasets (456,963 images, 1,626,085 expert masks). Pretrained SonoBase segmentation foundation model on this corpus. Evaluated on 15 datasets with domain shifts (new organs, devices, operators, geographies). Tested few-shot adaptation with 5 labeled examples and transfer to newer architectures (SAM3).
AI.result: SonoBase outperforms SAM2, MedSAM2, and MedSAM3 on all 15 evaluation datasets and matches per-dataset specialist models. On fully external data, it exceeds baseline accuracy on their own in-distribution benchmarks. Ejection fraction error (6.63%) within inter-observer variability. Fetal head circumference error 1.81mm, gestational age error 1.2 days—both below inter-observer variability. When baselines fail (25% of cases), SonoBase recovers 81% of segmentations. Works with handheld probes in Sierra Leone and Tanzania. Five labeled examples enable adaptation to new settings. Ultrasound-specific pretraining is key advantage.
AI.conclusion: SonoBase demonstrates that a well-pretrained foundation model can achieve robust, generalizable performance across diverse ultrasound settings, matching specialist models while outperforming generalist baselines. The key advantage lies in ultrasound-specific pretraining rather than architecture choice. The released resources (checkpoints, code, data splits) enable community building on this platform.

title: RAUL: Reference-Assisted Ureteroscopy Localization for Skill Assessment
summary: Objective: Incomplete navigation of anatomy during ureteroscopic kidney stone surgeries can contribute to repeat interventions. While skilled surgeons have lower reintervention rates, there are no objective metrics to quantify scope-navigation performance to evaluate when a trainee becomes skilled. This work aims to recover ureteroscope trajectories from endoscopic video and derive navigation metrics to quantify differences in skill. Methods: We propose RAUL, a reference-assisted reconstruction framework for recovering ureteroscope trajectories from ureteroscope videos only in phantoms. For each phantom, we use a slow, high-quality reference exploration video to generate a reference reconstruction. We localize subsequent exploration videos against this reference. We evaluate localization accuracy against electromagnetically tracked scope pose. We compute navigation metrics from phantom exploration trajectories to compare surgical residents across experience levels. Results: The proposed reference-assisted framework achieves a mean translation root mean square error of $0.5 \pm 0.1$ mm across 9 phantoms. Compared to standard Structure-from-Motion (SfM), the proposed pipeline increases frame-wise localization coverage from $50.5 \pm 14.9\%$ to $86.1 \pm 7.2\%$ of all video frames. The reconstructed trajectories revealed significant differences between high- and low-experience trainees in established navigation metrics. Conclusion: RAUL enables substantially more complete recovery of ureteroscope trajectories from videos compared to standard SfM pipelines, enabling trajectory-based skill assessment without additional tracking equipment. Significance: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first use of video-only recovery of ureteroscope trajectories without external tracking sensors for skill assessment, supporting scalable automated assessment of ureteroscopy navigation skill.

AI.tldr: RAUL is a reference-assisted reconstruction framework that recovers ureteroscope trajectories from endoscopic videos alone, enabling objective quantification of surgical navigation skill without external tracking equipment. The method achieves 0.5mm translation accuracy and significantly outperforms standard Structure-from-Motion pipelines.
AI.motivation: Incomplete navigation of anatomy during ureteroscopic kidney stone surgeries leads to repeat interventions. While skilled surgeons have lower reintervention rates, there are no objective metrics to quantify scope-navigation performance to evaluate trainee competency. Current methods lack a way to objectively assess when a trainee becomes skilled.
AI.method: The proposed RAUL framework uses a slow, high-quality reference exploration video to generate a reference reconstruction for each phantom. Subsequent exploration videos are then localized against this reference. Localization accuracy was evaluated against electromagnetically tracked scope pose. Navigation metrics were computed from phantom exploration trajectories to compare surgical residents across experience levels.
AI.result: The framework achieves a mean translation RMSE of 0.5 ± 0.1 mm across 9 phantoms. Compared to standard SfM, RAUL increases frame-wise localization coverage from 50.5 ± 14.9% to 86.1 ± 7.2% of all video frames. The reconstructed trajectories revealed significant differences between high- and low-experience trainees in established navigation metrics.
AI.conclusion: RAUL enables substantially more complete recovery of ureteroscope trajectories from videos compared to standard SfM pipelines, enabling trajectory-based skill assessment without additional tracking equipment. This represents the first use of video-only recovery of ureteroscope trajectories without external tracking sensors for skill assessment, supporting scalable automated assessment of ureteroscopy navigation skill.

title: Can Vision-Language Models Judge Olympic Diving? From Reasoning to Scores in Zero-Shot Action Quality Assessment
summary: Automated action quality assessment (AQA) in Olympic sports remains a challenging task due to the complexity of human motion and the subjectivity inherent in expert judging. This work evaluates the capability of open-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to perform zero-shot action quality assessment on Olympic diving videos using the AQA-7 benchmark dataset. In this regard, a regression-based framework is pro-posed to leverage both the semantic reasoning and phase-level sub-scores generated by the VLMs, combining TF-IDF vectorization, dimensionality reduction, and ensemble learning to predict final competition scores. Experimental results show that standalone VLMs achieve moderate Spearman correlations below 0.32, while the proposed ensemble regression framework substantially improves performance in the reported evaluation, reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.67 with a four-model configuration. Textual reasoning features con-sistently outperformed raw numerical sub-scores, highlighting the richness of VLM-generated explanations for action quality analysis. These findings suggest that VLMs hold strong potential as assistive tools for explainable and semi-automated sports performance evaluation. The code is publicly available on GitHub https://github.com/hvelesaca/olympic diving judge vlm

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the capability of open-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to perform zero-shot action quality assessment on Olympic diving videos using the AQA-7 benchmark dataset. The proposed ensemble regression framework combines VLM-generated semantic reasoning and phase-level sub-scores with TF-IDF vectorization, dimensionality reduction, and ensemble learning to predict final competition scores.
AI.motivation: Automated action quality assessment in Olympic sports is challenging due to the complexity of human motion and subjectivity in expert judging. This work aims to leverage VLMs' semantic reasoning capabilities to address this problem.
AI.method: A regression-based framework combining: (1) VLMs for zero-shot action quality assessment on diving videos, (2) TF-IDF vectorization of VLM-generated textual reasoning, (3) dimensionality reduction, and (4) ensemble learning to predict final competition scores.
AI.result: Standalone VLMs achieved moderate Spearman correlations below 0.32. The proposed ensemble regression framework substantially improved performance, reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.67 with a four-model configuration. Textual reasoning features consistently outperformed raw numerical sub-scores.
AI.conclusion: VLMs hold strong potential as assistive tools for explainable and semi-automated sports performance evaluation. The combination of semantic reasoning features with ensemble learning significantly improves AQA performance compared to standalone VLM approaches.

title: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection with promptable segmentation
summary: Three-dimensional object detection for autonomous driving is dominated by detectors trained on large corpora of human-annotated 3D boxes. Such a detector learns a fixed category list, and everything outside it is invisible. This paper asks whether the task can be solved training-free and open-vocabulary. A promptable segmentation model (SAM3), queried with class names as text prompts, supplies instance masks in the vehicle's six surround-view cameras, and the masks are turned into metric 3D boxes using the geometry of the scene. The core is a controlled three-stage comparison on nuScenes in which 2D detection is held fixed and only the source of 3D geometry changes. Geometry predicted from images alone reaches 0.183 mean average precision (mAP) under the official protocol; fitting boxes from raw LiDAR points inside the same masks with training-free rules reaches 0.298 mAP / 0.348 nuScenes detection score (NDS) at zero labeling cost; borrowing supervised box geometry at inference time lifts the same detections to 0.413 mAP / 0.555 NDS, which locates the pipeline's largest deficit in measurement precision rather than 2D detection, while class confusion and confidence calibration survive that substitution. Reversing the direction, a three-state camera-witness rule built from the same masks improves a supervised LiDAR-only detector from 0.596 to 0.630 mAP, roughly half the gain of fully supervised camera fusion, with no training. A coverage analysis shows that SAM3 finds 84% of in-range objects with a correctly named mask; the classes that fail in the official metric are misnamed or geometrically unforgiving, not unseen.

AI.tldr: This paper explores training-free, open-vocabulary 3D object detection for autonomous driving using SAM3 (a promptable segmentation model) with text prompts to generate instance masks from surround-view cameras, then converting masks to metric 3D boxes using scene geometry. The approach achieves 0.298 mAP / 0.348 NDS with training-free LiDAR box fitting, and 0.413 mAP / 0.555 NDS when borrowing supervised box geometry, identifying measurement precision as the main bottleneck rather than 2D detection.
AI.motivation: Current 3D object detectors are trained on large corpora of human-annotated 3D boxes with fixed category lists, making everything outside that list invisible. This paper investigates whether the task can be solved in a training-free and open-vocabulary manner.
AI.method: The method uses SAM3 (a promptable segmentation model) queried with class names as text prompts to supply instance masks in six surround-view cameras. These masks are then converted into metric 3D boxes using scene geometry. A controlled three-stage comparison on nuScenes varies the source of 3D geometry while holding 2D detection fixed: (1) geometry predicted from images alone, (2) fitting boxes from raw LiDAR points inside masks using training-free rules, and (3) borrowing supervised box geometry at inference time. Additionally, a three-state camera-witness rule is built from masks to improve a supervised LiDAR-only detector.
AI.result: Image-based geometry alone achieves 0.183 mAP. Training-free LiDAR box fitting inside masks reaches 0.298 mAP / 0.348 NDS at zero labeling cost. Borrowing supervised box geometry at inference lifts this to 0.413 mAP / 0.555 NDS, revealing the largest deficit is in measurement precision rather than 2D detection. The camera-witness rule improves a supervised LiDAR-only detector from 0.596 to 0.630 mAP, roughly half the gain of fully supervised camera fusion. SAM3 finds 84% of in-range objects with correctly named masks; failures are due to misnamed classes or geometric challenges, not unseen categories.
AI.conclusion: The main bottleneck in this training-free pipeline is measurement precision rather than 2D detection capability. SAM3 can find 84% of in-range objects when given correct class names. The approach demonstrates that open-vocabulary 3D detection is feasible without training, though measurement precision remains challenging. The camera-witness rule provides significant improvement to supervised LiDAR detectors without any training.

title: A State-Space Model of Figured-Bass Realization: Local Constraints, Coupled Voices, and Polynomial-Time Solvability
summary: Figured-bass realization can be described as a sequence of choices constrained both within each sonority and between successive sonorities. This paper gives an explicit mathematical model of a restricted, examination-style four-part realization problem. Pitch spelling, range, chord membership, doubling, omission, spacing, crossing, overlap, melodic motion, consecutive perfect intervals, and selected resolution requirements are expressed as predicates. We distinguish hard constraints from optional preference costs. Four labeled notes are represented visually as the vertices of a quadrilateral and computationally as one ordered voicing state. Legal progressions become paths through a layered graph. We prove that feasibility and minimum-cost realization are polynomial-time problems for a fixed number of voices with explicit finite note domains and fixed local rules. For fixed ranges, a fixed note alphabet, and adjacent-event rules, the number of graph operations is linear in the number of events. Worked two-, four-, and eight-beat examples illustrate legality, optimization, and the failure of a greedy choice. The result concerns the stated formal model; it is not a claim that every musical judgment is captured by local predicates.

title: Regularized Emphatic Temporal-Difference Learning: Stability under Constant Stepsizes
summary: Emphatic temporal-difference learning (ETD) stabilizes the expected off-policy TD update and changes its projection geometry, but neither property determines constant-stepsize sampled dynamics. We construct an ergodic two-state counterexample in which the ETD mean map contracts while the sampled product has a positive top Lyapunov exponent. Regenerative-cycle analysis separates this sign from the infinite variance of the follow-on trace. We introduce regularized emphatic TD (RETD), a normalized first-order post-shock repair that leaves the trace and importance ratios unchanged, stores the emphatic TD signal in a leaky scalar state, and releases a delayed correction. RETD's raw equilibrium is an affine shift of the ETD equilibrium; single- and two-regularization readouts recover the ETD fixed point exactly. We prove almost-sure convergence for harmonic diminishing stepsizes and a conditional constant-stepsize moment-contraction result from a Markovian random-product bound. RETD has certified negative exponents on the two-state construction and one Baird point, whereas the positive Baird ETD sign remains numerical. Paired 10,000-run experiments validate both separations, fixed-point recovery, a nonmonotone stability region, and task dependence. RETD changes post-shock dynamics; it does not reduce the shared follow-on-trace variance.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a fundamental limitation of Emphatic Temporal-Difference Learning (ETD): while ETD stabilizes expected off-policy TD updates, it fails to ensure stability in sampled (finite-sample) dynamics. The authors introduce Regularized ETD (RETD), which modifies the post-shock dynamics to achieve almost-sure convergence with diminishing stepsizes and moment-contraction with constant stepsizes, while exactly recovering the ETD fixed point through regularization readouts.
AI.motivation: ETD was designed to stabilize expected off-policy TD learning by changing projection geometry. However, the authors discovered that this expected-value stability does not guarantee sampled-dynamics stability. They constructed an ergodic two-state counterexample where ETD's mean map contracts but the sampled product exhibits a positive top Lyapunov exponent (indicating instability), stemming from infinite variance of the follow-on trace. This reveals a critical gap between theoretical expected updates and practical constant-stepsize behavior.
AI.method: The authors develop RETD using three key mechanisms: (1) normalized first-order post-shock repair that preserves the trace and importance ratios, (2) a leaky scalar state storing the emphatic TD signal, and (3) a delayed correction release. They employ regenerative-cycle analysis to separate the sign of the Lyapunov exponent from infinite trace variance. The analysis uses Markovian random-product bounds to prove almost-sure convergence for harmonic diminishing stepsizes and conditional moment-contraction for constant stepsizes.
AI.result: Theoretical results: (i) Almost-sure convergence for harmonic diminishing stepsizes; (ii) Conditional constant-stepsize moment-contraction; (iii) RETD achieves certified negative exponents on the two-state counterexample and one Baird counterexample; (iv) The raw equilibrium is an affine shift of ETD equilibrium, and single/two-regularization readouts recover the ETD fixed point exactly. Experimental validation: 10,000-run experiments confirm separation (positive vs negative exponents), fixed-point recovery, nonmonotone stability region, and task dependence. Importantly, RETD changes post-shock dynamics but does not reduce the shared follow-on-trace variance.
AI.conclusion: The paper resolves a fundamental limitation in off-policy RL theory by showing that expected stability does not imply sampled stability. RETD successfully bridges this gap through normalized post-shock repair, achieving both theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical stability, while preserving the original ETD fixed points through regularization. The key insight is that variance reduction in the follow-on trace is not necessary for stability—modifying post-shock dynamics is sufficient. This work advances understanding of off-policy learning stability and provides a practical algorithm with proven convergence properties.

title: Generative Query Suggestion via Intent Coverage and Query-Level Credit Assignment
summary: Generative query suggestion aims to enhance user engagement by anticipating user intents and recommending relevant follow-up queries. A central challenge is to generate slates whose individual queries are useful while the slate covers distinct intents. We propose an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization. First, intent-aware diversity modeling constructs intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage. Second, query-level credit assignment routes individual quality signals to the corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate. Experiments on a large-scale production dataset, including online A/B testing and offline evaluation, show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization to generate query slates that balance individual query usefulness with intent diversity. The approach uses intent-aware diversity modeling for supervised fine-tuning and query-level credit assignment for signal routing.
AI.motivation: The core challenge in generative query suggestion is generating slates where individual queries are useful while ensuring the slate covers distinct user intents. This addresses the trade-off between query-level quality and slate-level diversity.
AI.method: The framework employs dual-stage optimization: (1) Intent-aware diversity modeling constructs intent-aligned SFT data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage; (2) Query-level credit assignment routes individual quality signals to corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate.
AI.result: Experiments on a large-scale production dataset with both online A/B testing and offline evaluation show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully balances individual query usefulness with slate-level diversity through dual-stage optimization, demonstrating practical value in production environments.

title: From Models to Systems: A Comprehensive Survey of Efficient Multimodal Learning
summary: The rapid expansion of multimodal models has surfaced formidable bottlenecks in computation, memory, and deployment, catalyzing the rise of Efficient Multimodal Learning (EML) as a pivotal research frontier. Despite intensive progress, a cohesive understanding of what, how, and where efficiency is manifested across the learning stack remains fragmented. This survey systematizes the EML landscape by introducing the first structured, model-to-system taxonomy. We distill insights from over 300 seminal works into three hierarchical levels--model, algorithm, and system--addressing architectural parsimony, execution refinement, and hardware-aware orchestration, respectively. Moving beyond a purely categorical review, we offer a methodological synthesis of the vertical synergies between these layers, elucidating how cross-layer co-design contributes to the fundamental "Efficiency-Utility-Privacy" trade-off. Through an integrative case study of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), we trace the field's evolutionary trajectory from initial structural adjustments to modern full-stack resource orchestration. Furthermore, we provide a holistic discussion and application-specific optimization blueprints for diverse domains and posit a paradigm shift toward self-regulating intelligence, where efficiency is an intrinsic, emergent property of the model's fundamental design rather than a post-hoc constraint. Finally, we present open challenges and future directions that will define the trajectory of EML research. This survey establishes a structured framework for multimodal systems that are not only high-performing and generalizable but natively efficient and ready for ubiquitous deployment. A continuously updated version is available at https://github.com/pwang322/Efficient-Multimodal-Learning-Survey.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey systematizing Efficient Multimodal Learning (EML) research through a novel model-to-system taxonomy, covering over 300 works across three hierarchical levels (model, algorithm, system) and tracing the evolution of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
AI.motivation: The rapid expansion of multimodal models has created significant bottlenecks in computation, memory, and deployment, making EML a critical research frontier. Existing understanding of efficiency across the learning stack remains fragmented, lacking a cohesive framework.
AI.method: The survey introduces the first structured, model-to-system taxonomy, organizing over 300 seminal works into three hierarchical levels: (1) model level - architectural parsimony, (2) algorithm level - execution refinement, and (3) system level - hardware-aware orchestration. It provides methodological synthesis of vertical synergies between layers and examines the Efficiency-Utility-Privacy trade-off through an integrative case study of MLLMs.
AI.result: The survey establishes a structured framework for understanding EML, traces the evolutionary trajectory of MLLMs from structural adjustments to full-stack resource orchestration, and provides application-specific optimization blueprints for diverse domains.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes a paradigm shift toward self-regulating intelligence where efficiency becomes an intrinsic, emergent property of the model's design rather than a post-hoc constraint. It identifies open challenges and future directions for EML research, aiming to enable multimodal systems that are high-performing, generalizable, and natively efficient for ubiquitous deployment.

title: FootprintRAG: Visual Analytics for Evidence Context Refinement in RAG-based Scientific Literature Exploration
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly used to ground large language model (LLM) outputs in scientific literature. However, in open-ended literature exploration, the evidence context used for generation is often produced through hidden retrieval, reranking, assessment, and filtering steps. Users may receive retrieval summaries without knowing how the system constructed the evidence context, which evidence units were retained or discarded, or whether potentially useful evidence was excluded before synthesis. We present FootprintRAG, an LLM-agent-powered visual analytics system for evidence context refinement in RAG-based scientific literature exploration. The core idea is to treat the RAG evidence context as an explicit, inspectable, and revisable analytical object before generation. FootprintRAG parses scientific literature into text and figure evidence units, expands an initial query into parallel query variants, retrieves and assesses evidence across iterative rounds, and surfaces ERS-ranked supplementary candidates from the corpus-level evidence space. Through coordinated views, the system connects retrieval trajectories, evidence-state revision, and provenance-aware summary generation into a user-steerable workflow. We evaluate FootprintRAG through two case studies, a user study, and a workflow-level comparison with representative RAG systems. The results show that FootprintRAG helps users compare retrieval directions, revise candidate evidence, recover potentially overlooked evidence, and trace generated summaries back to supporting evidence units. FootprintRAG is available at https://github.com/meteorshowering/FootprintRAGVA.git.

AI.tldr: FootprintRAG is a visual analytics system that makes the otherwise hidden RAG evidence context explicit, inspectable, and revisable before generation. It parses scientific literature into text and figure evidence units, expands queries into parallel variants, retrieves and assesses evidence iteratively, and surfaces supplementary candidates through ERS-ranking. The system enables users to compare retrieval directions, revise candidate evidence, recover overlooked evidence, and trace generated summaries back to source evidence.
AI.motivation: In open-ended literature exploration using RAG, the evidence context used for generation is produced through hidden retrieval, reranking, assessment, and filtering steps. Users receive retrieval summaries without knowing how the system constructed the evidence context, which evidence units were retained or discarded, or whether potentially useful evidence was excluded before synthesis. This lack of transparency and controllability limits users' ability to trust and effectively use RAG outputs.
AI.method: FootprintRAG uses an LLM-agent-powered approach with several key components: (1) Parsing scientific literature into text and figure evidence units; (2) Expanding initial queries into parallel query variants; (3) Retrieving and assessing evidence across iterative rounds; (4) Surfacing ERS-ranked supplementary candidates from corpus-level evidence space. The system provides coordinated views connecting retrieval trajectories, evidence-state revision, and provenance-aware summary generation into a user-steerable workflow.
AI.result: Evaluation through two case studies, a user study, and workflow-level comparison with representative RAG systems shows that FootprintRAG helps users: (1) Compare retrieval directions; (2) Revise candidate evidence; (3) Recover potentially overlooked evidence; (4) Trace generated summaries back to supporting evidence units.
AI.conclusion: FootprintRAG addresses the transparency and controllability issues in RAG-based literature exploration by treating the evidence context as an explicit analytical object. The system enables users to steer the retrieval process, inspect evidence selection decisions, and understand the provenance of generated summaries, ultimately improving trust and effectiveness in scientific literature exploration.

title: Code-as-Auditor: Executable Compliance Reasoning via Regulation-to-Code
comment: 12 pages. Accepted at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '26), November 7-11, 2026, Rome, Italy
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted for compliance and legal reasoning tasks, yet their outputs often lack explicit grounding in legal logic and evidence. We present Code-as-Auditor, an LLM-based framework that extends the model's reasoning capability toward structured and evidence-grounded compliance assessment. The framework translates regulatory information into (1) formalized checklists and executable decision trees, encoding regulations and conditions as interpretable code structures. During inference, each checklist item is (2) dynamically expanded into factual and counterfactual questions, guiding the model to reason over case-specific evidence and potential violations. This process establishes a reasoning pipeline that proceeds from evidence identification, through rule application, to final decision-making, while a self-verification loop improves the logical consistency of the generated code and the traceability of outcomes. Experiments on privacy and data protection scenarios demonstrate that Code-as-Auditor delivers more accurate and evidence-backed evaluations, enabling automated compliance regulation checking grounded in explicit regulatory criteria.

AI.tldr: Code-as-Auditor is an LLM-based framework that enhances compliance assessment by translating regulations into executable code structures (checklists and decision trees), dynamically generating factual/counterfactual questions for evidence-based reasoning, and incorporating self-verification for logical consistency. Experiments show improved accuracy in privacy and data protection compliance checking.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for compliance and legal reasoning tasks, but their outputs lack explicit grounding in legal logic and evidence, making them unreliable for critical compliance assessment.
AI.method: The framework translates regulatory information into: (1) formalized checklists and executable decision trees encoding regulations as interpretable code; (2) dynamically expands checklist items into factual and counterfactual questions during inference to reason over case-specific evidence; (3) establishes a reasoning pipeline from evidence identification through rule application to final decision-making; (4) includes a self-verification loop for logical consistency and traceability.
AI.result: Experiments on privacy and data protection scenarios demonstrate more accurate and evidence-backed evaluations, enabling automated compliance regulation checking grounded in explicit regulatory criteria.
AI.conclusion: Code-as-Auditor successfully extends LLM reasoning capability toward structured and evidence-grounded compliance assessment, improving accuracy and traceability in automated regulatory compliance checking.

title: LinePilot Digitizer: Line-Plot Recovery with Manual and Automatic Calibration
summary: Recovering numerical series from line plots requires accurate axis calibration and reliable curve extraction. We present LinePilot Digitizer (LinePilot), which combines continuous color-based curve recovery with three calibration modes: LinePilot (standard), LinePilot (enhanced), and LinePilot (OCR). We also introduce DigitizerBench, the first dedicated benchmark for systematically evaluating digitizer performance, using an orthogonal design spanning signal, rendering, and plot-structure factors with complementary automatic and human-guided evaluations. We evaluate performance using failure-penalized capped normalized root-mean-square error (FPC-NRMSE), which assigns unit loss to missing, unusable, or catastrophically inaccurate outputs. On DigitizerBench-Full, LinePilot (OCR) achieves the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.672) and highest trusted usability (38.2%) among the tested automatic pipelines. On DigitizerBench-Lite, LinePilot (enhanced) achieves the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.081), 100% output success, and highest trusted usability (93.3%). The orthogonal benchmark design further enables factor analysis to identify the factors that most significantly affect digitizer performance. Together, the three calibration modes provide a practical trade-off between automation, user control, and accuracy within a shared curve-recovery workflow.

AI.tldr: LinePilot Digitizer recovers numerical data from line plots through color-based curve extraction with three calibration modes. DigitizerBench, the first dedicated benchmark for digitizers, evaluates performance using FPC-NRMSE. LinePilot (OCR) achieves lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.672) on DigitizerBench-Full, while LinePilot (enhanced) achieves 0.081 on DigitizerBench-Lite with 100% success rate.
AI.motivation: Recovering numerical data from line plots is challenging due to the need for accurate axis calibration and reliable curve extraction. Existing tools lack systematic evaluation benchmarks, making it difficult to compare performance across different methods.
AI.method: LinePilot combines continuous color-based curve recovery with three calibration modes: standard, enhanced, and OCR. The authors introduce DigitizerBench, using an orthogonal design across signal, rendering, and plot-structure factors with both automatic and human-guided evaluations. Performance is measured using failure-penalized capped normalized root-mean-square error (FPC-NRMSE).
AI.result: On DigitizerBench-Full, LinePilot (OCR) achieves lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.672) and highest trusted usability (38.2%). On DigitizerBench-Lite, LinePilot (enhanced) achieves lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.081), 100% output success, and highest trusted usability (93.3%). Factor analysis identifies key factors affecting digitizer performance.
AI.conclusion: The three calibration modes provide practical trade-offs between automation, user control, and accuracy within a shared curve-recovery workflow, enabling users to choose appropriate modes based on their needs.

title: A Cross-Lingual Acoustic Disease-Alignment Framework for Respiratory Health Assessment from Spontaneous Speech
summary: Spontaneous speech offers a scalable, noninvasive signal for respiratory health assessment, yet interpretable models that generalize across languages remain challenging because disease-related acoustic changes are confounded by language-specific phonetic variation. We present CL-DAF, a Cross-Lingual Disease-Alignment Framework that identifies acoustic dimensions whose disease effects remain consistent across languages. Using 201 English and 75 newly collected Bangla speakers, we construct a common 272-dimensional acoustic representation and quantify disease alignment using signed rank-biserial effects and the Language Invariance Score. We first show that spontaneous Bangla speech separates COPD from controls (AUC 0.85); however, 133 features reverse their disease direction across languages and the full representation transfers poorly (AUC 0.49 from Bangla to English). CL-DAF isolates 26 disease-aligned features that raise AUCs to 0.825 and 0.722 from English to Bangla and Bangla to English, respectively. These findings provide a foundation for multilingual clinical speech models emphasizing pathology over language-dependent variation.

AI.tldr: CL-DAF is a Cross-Lingual Disease-Alignment Framework that identifies language-invariant acoustic features for respiratory health assessment from spontaneous speech. Using 201 English and 75 Bangla speakers, it isolates 26 disease-aligned features that achieve cross-lingual transfer AUCs of 0.825 (English→Bangla) and 0.722 (Bangla→English), outperforming the full 272-feature representation which transfers poorly (AUC 0.49).
AI.motivation: Spontaneous speech offers a scalable, noninvasive signal for respiratory health assessment, but interpretable models that generalize across languages remain challenging because disease-related acoustic changes are confounded by language-specific phonetic variation.
AI.method: Using 201 English and 75 newly collected Bangla speakers, construct a common 272-dimensional acoustic representation and quantify disease alignment using signed rank-biserial effects and the Language Invariance Score. The framework identifies acoustic dimensions whose disease effects remain consistent across languages.
AI.result: Bangla speech separates COPD from controls (AUC 0.85); however, 133 features reverse their disease direction across languages and the full representation transfers poorly (AUC 0.49 from Bangla to English). CL-DAF isolates 26 disease-aligned features that raise AUCs to 0.825 and 0.722 from English to Bangla and Bangla to English, respectively.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide a foundation for multilingual clinical speech models emphasizing pathology over language-dependent variation.

title: BioPhys-Bridge: A Benchmark for Interdisciplinary Scientific Reasoning in Physics-Grounded Biological Research
comment: Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 2026, 11 pages, 3 figures
summary: Language models face unique challenges in analyzing interdisciplinary scientific research literature. In biophysics research, faithful answers require grounding observed data in source evidence, interpreting it through a quantitative physics model, and linking it to a biological mechanism. To address this challenge, we introduce BioPhys-Bridge, a novel benchmark dataset for evidence-grounded scientific reasoning over biophysical literature. Each case contains evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next decisions as grounding targets for question answering (QA) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The initial release contains 500 cases, 1,517 agent-facing tasks, and covers six biological domains and nine physical model families, including three sparse families reserved for future expansion. We enforce strict quality gates for all cases in schema, evidence-integrity, quantitative-grounding, source-license, duplicate, unit-normalization, with domain expert review and annotation for 81 cases. Preliminary evaluations show that DeepSeek-V4-Flash obtain the highest evidence-ID $F_1$ score (0.360), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.316) and GPT-4o-mini (0.294). BioPhys-Bridge is an interdisciplinary benchmark for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design with complex, multi-step scientific reasoning. Future works will increase the size and complexity of the dataset and perform comprehensive evaluations. Code and data are available in the GitHub repository and on Hugging Face.

AI.tldr: BioPhys-Bridge is a benchmark dataset for evaluating language models' evidence-grounded scientific reasoning over biophysical literature, containing 500 cases with 1,517 tasks across six biological domains and nine physical model families. The best model (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) achieved an evidence-ID F1 score of 0.360.
AI.motivation: Language models face unique challenges in analyzing interdisciplinary scientific research literature, particularly in biophysics where faithful answers require grounding data in source evidence, interpreting it through quantitative physics models, and linking it to biological mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors created a benchmark dataset with evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next decisions as grounding targets. They enforced strict quality gates including schema validation, evidence-integrity, quantitative-grounding, source-license verification, duplicate checking, and unit-normalization, with domain expert review for 81 cases.
AI.result: Preliminary evaluations showed DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieved the highest evidence-ID F1 score (0.360), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.316) and GPT-4o-mini (0.294). The benchmark covers six biological domains and nine physical model families, with three sparse families reserved for future expansion.
AI.conclusion: BioPhys-Bridge serves as an interdisciplinary benchmark for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design with complex, multi-step scientific reasoning. Future work will increase dataset size and complexity and perform comprehensive evaluations.

title: Layer-wise Curriculum Learning for Efficient LLM Compression
comment: Accepted by the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) 2026
summary: In this paper, we introduce layer-wise curriculum learning for efficient LLM compression. The proposed method facilitates the knowledge transfer from the teacher model to the student model, utilizing a curriculum learning approach that begins with easier optimization tasks and progressively tackles harder ones. In order to adopt the layer-wise learning in LLM compression, we partition the whole model into multiple segments consisting of layers, thereby enabling more computationally efficient knowledge transfer for LLMs. Based on our theoretical analysis of cumulative error phenomenon, layer-wise curriculum learning accelerates convergence while stabilizing the knowledge transfer process. In addition, we present a feature caching method with a multi-threading strategy to efficiently address feature misalignment across layers, maximizing GPU utilization. Consequently, our method exhibits advanced model compression performance, as well as high computational efficiency in terms of minimized memory usage and short training hours. Experiments on multiple datasets show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing GPU memory usage and training hours by more than 50\% on BERT and GPT-2. Moreover, it outperforms the other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models under the same training hours, with a lower GPU memory footprint.

AI.tldr: A layer-wise curriculum learning method for LLM compression that partitions models into segments and uses curriculum learning (easy-to-hard) along with feature caching to achieve SOTA performance while reducing GPU memory and training time by over 50%.
AI.motivation: The cumulative error phenomenon in layer-wise knowledge transfer causes convergence issues and instability. Current LLM compression methods face challenges in efficient knowledge transfer from teacher to student models while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: Layer-wise curriculum learning with: (1) Partitioning whole model into multiple segments of layers for efficient knowledge transfer; (2) Curriculum learning approach progressing from easier to harder optimization tasks; (3) Feature caching with multi-threading strategy to address feature misalignment and maximize GPU utilization.
AI.result: Achieves SOTA performance on multiple datasets with >50% reduction in GPU memory usage and training hours on BERT and GPT-2. Outperforms other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models under same training hours with lower GPU memory footprint.
AI.conclusion: The proposed layer-wise curriculum learning achieves SOTA model compression performance while reducing GPU memory usage and training hours by over 50% on BERT and GPT-2, and outperforms other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models with lower memory footprint.

title: Trigger Timing, Deadline Readiness, and Event-Aligned Accounting for Dynamic Ad Insertion
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables; 11-page supplement in ancillary files. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22774143
summary: Dynamic ad insertion comparisons can conflate trigger, reach, readiness, playback, billability and measurement even when the accounting is arithmetically correct. We separate these events with an observed-event ledger, a candidate-invariant reference deadline and pod-level contribution accounting. The deadline rule is fixed before candidate assignment and tests whether an admissible transition state remains valid, not whether preparation merely finished earlier. A restricted monotone-playback representation states when media-position summaries suffice; a counterexample shows why they fail over a wider path class. An offline synthetic study exercises the definitions over nine short-lifetime conditions informative for the readiness comparison and nine long-lifetime conditions serving as analytic controls. Across 45,000 shared scripts, two trigger policies share imposed playback paths, latency draws and hypothetical value and cost coefficients. Playhead summaries substantially misclassify reach events in the nonmonotone mixtures, yet neither shortcut reverses the contribution contrast in this grid, because some errors cancel under the shared design. Replacing validity at the deadline with completion by the deadline reverses the comparison in three of the nine informative conditions, all at one of the three latency settings. Scoring readiness at actual viewer arrival rather than at the reference deadline shifts pause-path readiness but changes no contribution sign. These outcomes are consequences of the event definitions applied to established misclassification mechanisms. Conservative bounds retain uncertainty when records are missing, and the artifact records code, seeds, event histories and checking procedures. The evidence is synthetic, uses no commercial telemetry, and ranks neither server-side nor server-guided insertion.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses conflation problems in dynamic ad insertion comparisons by proposing event ledger separation and deadline-based validity testing. Synthetic experiments reveal that playhead summaries misclassify reach events but errors cancel under shared designs, while deadline definition changes can reverse comparisons in certain conditions.
AI.motivation: Dynamic ad insertion (DAI) comparisons often conflate distinct events (trigger, reach, readiness, playback, billability, measurement) even when calculations are arithmetically correct, leading to misleading comparisons between ad insertion policies.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) an observed-event ledger to separate events, (2) a candidate-invariant reference deadline with a deadline rule that tests validity of admissible transition states (not merely if preparation finished), (3) pod-level contribution accounting, and (4) a restricted monotone-playback representation. They conduct an offline synthetic study with 45,000 shared scripts across 9 short-lifetime conditions and 9 long-lifetime conditions, testing two trigger policies with shared playback paths, latency draws, and hypothetical value/cost coefficients.
AI.result: Playhead summaries substantially misclassify reach events in nonmonotone mixtures, but neither shortcut reverses the contribution contrast in the tested grid due to error cancellation under shared design. Replacing validity-at-deadline with completion-by-deadline reverses the comparison in 3 of 9 informative conditions at one latency setting. Scoring readiness at actual viewer arrival rather than the reference deadline shifts pause-path readiness but changes no contribution sign.
AI.conclusion: Outcomes are consequences of event definitions applied to established misclassification mechanisms. Conservative bounds retain uncertainty with missing records. The evidence is synthetic, uses no commercial telemetry, and ranks neither server-side nor server-guided insertion.

title: DELUGE: Decomposed Entropy-coded Live Unstructured Geometry Exchange for Real-time Particle Streaming
comment: 11 pages + supplement 3 pages. Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG), to be presented at IEEE ISMAR 2026
summary: Particle-based physics simulations, including fluids, smoke, and granular media, are fundamental to visual realism in immersive VR and AR. With the growing adoption of social VR and digital twins, demand is increasing for shared experiences in which multiple users interact with the same simulation in real time. Realizing such experiences requires low-latency streaming of large-scale particle data from a server to each client, yet existing point cloud compression methods such as G-PCC (TMC13) and Draco assume static geometric structures; when applied to dynamic particle streaming, their encoding latency exceeds the frame period, failing to meet real-time delivery requirements. We propose DELUGE, a streaming compression architecture that exploits the temporal coherence and velocity predictability inherent in physics simulation particles, achieving sub-frame-latency encoding and decoding through three complementary techniques. Evaluation on dynamic point cloud datasets demonstrates that DELUGE achieves approximately $20\times$ faster decoding than G-PCC (TMC13) and $6\times$ faster encoding than Draco. We further build end-to-end client implementations for both web browsers and Apple Vision Pro, and confirm through a within-participants perceptual quality evaluation and a two-person collaborative task study on Vision Pro that the proposed method supports real-time collaborative experiences with hand-tracked fluid interaction.

AI.tldr: DELUGE is a real-time streaming compression architecture for dynamic particle physics simulations in VR/AR, achieving sub-frame-latency encoding/decoding by exploiting temporal coherence and velocity predictability. It delivers ~20x faster decoding than G-PCC and ~6x faster encoding than Draco, enabling real-time collaborative experiences on web browsers and Apple Vision Pro.
AI.motivation: Social VR and digital twins require multiple users to interact with the same particle simulation in real time. Existing point cloud compression methods (G-PCC, Draco) assume static geometric structures and have encoding latency exceeding frame periods, making them unsuitable for dynamic particle streaming in real-time applications.
AI.method: DELUGE uses three complementary techniques: (1) exploiting temporal coherence in physics simulations, (2) leveraging velocity predictability of particles, and (3) optimizing for sub-frame-latency encoding/decoding. Implementation was done for web browsers and Apple Vision Pro, with evaluation via perceptual quality assessment and two-person collaborative task studies.
AI.result: DELUGE achieves approximately 20× faster decoding than G-PCC (TMC13) and 6× faster encoding than Draco. End-to-end implementations on web browsers and Apple Vision Pro confirm real-time collaborative experiences with hand-tracked fluid interaction.
AI.conclusion: DELUGE enables real-time collaborative VR/AR experiences with dynamic particle simulations by providing low-latency compression suitable for streaming large-scale particle data. The approach successfully supports two-person collaborative tasks with hand-tracked fluid interaction on Apple Vision Pro.

title: DeltaSelect: Affordable A/B Testing for Coding Agents
summary: Coding-agent benchmarks are built for broad and comprehensive comparisons, not frequent development decisions. Individual runs vary, full suites are expensive, and the benchmark harness may differ from the harness used in practice. In a resampling analysis of DeepSWE's published trials, only 19.5% of tasks (22 of 113) had a fifth-percentile Pearson correlation of at least 0.50 with full-benchmark performance. The paper presents DeltaSelect, an open-source method that identifies tasks whose one-run results consistently track full-benchmark performance using Pearson correlation, maps fractional verifier results to a common score using linear regression, and selects a fixed task set within a dollar budget. DeltaSelect is intended for repeated baseline-versus-candidate comparisons during development, not model rankings. In a gpt-5.6-luna low-reasoning case study, DeltaSelect was used to revise custom skills and instructions. Across 13 evaluations, the recorded cost was USD 27.86 at rates published August 16, 2026. The adopted version cost 58.1% less than the initial version (USD 1.75 versus USD 4.18; p=0.008), while the calibrated score was higher (42.36% versus 36.46%; published-analog variance p=0.326).

AI.tldr: This paper presents DeltaSelect, an open-source method for selecting a subset of coding-agent benchmark tasks that consistently track full-benchmark performance, enabling cost-effective repeated comparisons during development. In a case study using gpt-5.6-luna, the method reduced costs by 58.1% while improving calibrated scores.
AI.motivation: Coding-agent benchmarks are designed for broad comparisons but are impractical for frequent development decisions due to high cost, run-to-run variance, and harness differences. The authors identified that only 19.5% of DeepSWE tasks (22/113) had reliable correlation with full-benchmark performance, necessitating a method to identify consistently tracking tasks.
AI.method: DeltaSelect uses three components: (1) Pearson correlation to identify tasks whose one-run results consistently track full-benchmark performance, (2) linear regression to map fractional verifier results to a common score, and (3) budget-constrained task set selection within a dollar budget. The method is designed for baseline-versus-candidate comparisons during development, not model rankings.
AI.result: In a gpt-5.6-luna low-reasoning case study across 13 evaluations (total cost USD 27.86), the adopted version cost 58.1% less than the initial version (USD 1.75 vs USD 4.18; p=0.008) while achieving a higher calibrated score (42.36% vs 36.46%). The difference in calibrated scores was not statistically significant (published-analog variance p=0.326).
AI.conclusion: DeltaSelect enables cost-effective repeated comparisons during coding agent development. The method successfully reduced evaluation costs by over half while improving performance scores, demonstrating its utility for development-stage decisions. However, the calibrated score improvement was not statistically significant, suggesting further validation may be needed.

title: Riemannian--Lorentz Fusion of Vision Transformers and State-Space Models
summary: Scaling deep learning faces critical bottlenecks: data exhaustion, exponential training costs, and resource concentration. Model merging combines pre-trained checkpoints without gradient descent, offering orders-of-magnitude savings versus retraining. Combining independently trained vision models is difficult when their architectures and parameter shapes differ. Existing weight-space merging methods generally assume aligned, shape-compatible checkpoints, whereas a Vision Transformer (ViT) and a state-space model (SSM) implement token mixing with different operators. We study a hybrid Heterogeneous merging setting that retains both architectures while aligning parameter groups by semantic role. Our proposed Riemannian--Lorentz Parameter Fusion (RLPF) method projects aligned groups to common coordinates, lifts selected coordinates to the Lorentz hyperboloid model of hyperbolic space, computes a regularized geodesic barycenter, and decodes the result into the two branches. A learned gate then combines branch logits for each input. Component groups use fixed curvature values, with normalization parameters treated as Euclidean. In the results available in this manuscript, the fine-tuned system obtains 82.37\% on CIFAR-10, 75.04\% on Oxford-IIIT Pet, and 78.58\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K; the corresponding best-parent accuracies are 76.54\%, 71.42\%, and 76.42\%. On ImageNet-1K, the reported pre-fine-tuning initialization reaches 77.80\%. These results support further study of geometry-aware heterogeneous fusion, but not a training-free single-checkpoint merge: RLPF is a two-branch hybrid whose gate and reported final models are trained.

AI.tldr: RLPF is a geometry-aware method for merging heterogeneous vision models (ViT and SSM) with different architectures by projecting parameters to hyperbolic space, computing geodesic barycenters, and using a learned gate for final predictions. The method achieves 82.37% on CIFAR-10, 75.04% on Oxford-IIIT Pet, and 78.58% on ImageNet-1K, outperforming parent models but requires fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Deep learning scaling faces data exhaustion, exponential costs, and resource concentration. Model merging offers efficiency but existing methods assume aligned architectures. The challenge is combining heterogeneous models (ViT and SSM) with different parameter shapes and token mixing operators.
AI.method: RLPF projects aligned parameter groups to common coordinates, lifts selected coordinates to the Lorentz hyperboloid model of hyperbolic space, computes a regularized geodesic barycenter, and decodes into two branches. A learned gate combines branch logits for each input. Normalization parameters are treated as Euclidean with fixed curvature values.
AI.result: Fine-tuned RLPF achieves 82.37% on CIFAR-10, 75.04% on Oxford-IIIT Pet, and 78.58% top-1 on ImageNet-1K, outperforming best parent models (76.54%, 71.42%, 76.42%). Pre-fine-tuning initialization reaches 77.80% on ImageNet.
AI.conclusion: Results support further study of geometry-aware heterogeneous fusion. However, RLPF is not training-free—it requires fine-tuning of the gate and final models. The method demonstrates that hyperbolic geometry can effectively merge heterogeneous vision models, achieving performance gains over both parent models.

title: CoRELoop: Parameter-Efficient Controlled Recurrent Refinement for Audio Deepfake Detection
summary: Generalizing to unseen attacks remains challenging for audio deepfake detectors, and collecting training data covering all potential attacks is impractical. We explore recurrent refinement in an already-trained SSL-based detector without additional data or changes to its original parameters. However, directly recycling encoder outputs as inputs degrades detection in our diagnostic. We propose CoReLoop, which makes this reuse effective by adapting recurrent inputs to the frozen encoder, controlling state updates, and aligning refined outputs with the frozen classifier. By training only lightweight refinement modules and loop-specific low-rank adapters on the original data, CoReLoop enables additional refinement while preserving the detector's original first-pass prediction. On 14 cross-domain test sets, the 24-layer model reduces pooled equal error rate (EER) from 4.85% to 3.74% with two passes, with approximately 10M trainable parameters out of 598M. To selectively apply this refinement, an optional halting head chooses the depth for each utterance, achieving 3.73% pooled EER with an average of 1.18 passes.

AI.tldr: CoReLoop enables an already-trained SSL-based audio deepfake detector to generalize better to unseen attacks through recurrent refinement, using only lightweight trainable modules (∼10M parameters) while keeping the original 598M-parameter model frozen.
AI.motivation: Audio deepfake detectors struggle to generalize to unseen attacks, and collecting training data covering all potential attacks is impractical. The authors explored recurrent refinement in an SSL-based detector but found that directly recycling encoder outputs as inputs degrades detection performance.
AI.method: CoReLoop adapts recurrent inputs to the frozen encoder, controls state updates, and aligns refined outputs with the frozen classifier. It trains only lightweight refinement modules and loop-specific low-rank adapters on original data, enabling additional refinement while preserving the detector's original first-pass prediction. An optional halting head selectively applies refinement by choosing the depth for each utterance.
AI.result: On 14 cross-domain test sets, the 24-layer model reduces pooled equal error rate (EER) from 4.85% to 3.74% with two passes, using approximately 10M trainable parameters out of 598M. With the halting head, it achieves 3.73% pooled EER with an average of 1.18 passes.
AI.conclusion: CoReLoop successfully enables additional refinement in a frozen SSL-based detector with minimal trainable parameters, improving generalization to unseen attacks while maintaining the original first-pass prediction capability.

title: What Do We Expect from LLMs? Mapping the Design of LLM Benchmarks
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Data and code: https://github.com/xxcg322/LLM-Bench-Map
summary: Benchmarks are central to how progress in large language models (LLMs) is assessed and communicated. Yet model rankings alone reveal little about how evaluation requirements themselves are changing. The expanding variety of benchmarks offers another perspective: what researchers expect LLMs to do, and what they count as successful performance. We systematically map 14,767 papers introducing or updating evaluation resources from arXiv submissions between January 2022 and August 2026. Using staged screening and automated full-text coding, we examine changes in target systems and domains, evaluation materials and conditions, and scoring mechanisms. The collection shows growing emphasis on action, interaction, and professional applications, while established and newer design elements frequently coexist. Model participation also develops unevenly: LLM-based scoring grows within both agent and non-agent groups, whereas model-generated materials show no comparable sustained increase in recent cohorts. These findings illuminate how public research translates capability expectations into concrete tests and criteria for success. As AI participates in constructing tests, performing tasks, and judging responses, they also raise a question: does expanding evaluation provide more independent evidence, or risk reproducing the preferences and blind spots of its participating models?

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 14,767 arXiv papers on LLM evaluation resources from 2022-2026, revealing trends in benchmarks and evaluation criteria. It finds growing emphasis on action, interaction, and professional applications, with LLM-based scoring increasing while model-generated materials show no sustained growth. The study raises concerns about AI's expanding role in test construction and evaluation.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand how evaluation requirements for LLMs are changing over time, beyond simple model rankings. The researchers aim to uncover what researchers expect LLMs to do and what constitutes success, by examining the evolving landscape of benchmarks and evaluation resources.
AI.method: The researchers systematically mapped 14,767 arXiv papers introducing or updating evaluation resources from January 2022 to August 2026. They used staged screening and automated full-text coding to examine changes in: (1) target systems and domains, (2) evaluation materials and conditions, and (3) scoring mechanisms.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) Growing emphasis on action, interaction, and professional applications in evaluation benchmarks; (2) Established and newer design elements frequently coexist; (3) LLM-based scoring grows within both agent and non-agent groups; (4) Model-generated materials show no comparable sustained increase in recent cohorts.
AI.conclusion: The study illuminates how public research translates capability expectations into concrete tests and criteria for success. It raises a critical question: as AI participates in constructing tests, performing tasks, and judging responses, does expanding evaluation provide more independent evidence, or risk reproducing the preferences and blind spots of its participating models?

title: Block Parallelism For Efficient Distributed Long-Context Diffusion Language Model Training
summary: Block diffusion language models (BDLMs) combine autoregressive dependencies across blocks with parallel denoising within blocks, but long-context training is constrained by distributed attention communication and activation memory. Conventional context parallelism (CP) shards the combined clean-plus-corrupted sequence by position, communicating shared clean K/V together with block-specific corrupted K/V and their gradients. We observe that the BDLM objective separates over target blocks. We introduce block parallelism (BP), a new distributed parallelism dimension that assigns each corrupted-block computation to one rank. To scale BP to long contexts, we introduce context-sharded block parallelism (CSBP), which also shards the shared clean sequence across those ranks. CSBP keeps corrupted K/V and gradients local, avoids replicated clean prefixes, and preserves BDLM training semantics. On 16 H200 GPUs at 256K context, CSBP improves throughput over the best baseline by 1.18-1.45x for supervised fine-tuning and 1.27-1.33x for conversion of autoregressive models to BDLMs, while matching or reducing peak HBM. Full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K. On eight H100 GPUs, CSBP accelerates DFlash2 speculative-decoder training by 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M. In matched 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates at every trained checkpoint on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite. Code: https://github.com/ScalingIntelligence/Turbo-dLLM

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Context-Sharded Block Parallelism (CSBP), a new distributed training paradigm for block diffusion language models (BDLMs) that addresses long-context training bottlenecks. CSBP shards both the corrupted blocks and the shared clean sequence across GPU ranks, keeping local computation and gradients while enabling efficient scaling to 256K-1M context lengths.
AI.motivation: Long-context training for BDLMs is constrained by two key limitations: (1) distributed attention communication overhead and (2) activation memory requirements. Conventional context parallelism (CP) shards the combined clean-plus-corrupted sequence by position, requiring communication of shared clean K/V along with block-specific corrupted K/V and their gradients. This creates scalability issues at very long context lengths.
AI.method: The key insight is that the BDLM objective separates over target blocks. The paper introduces block parallelism (BP) as a new distributed parallelism dimension that assigns each corrupted-block computation to one rank. To scale BP to long contexts, CSBP extends this by also sharding the shared clean sequence across ranks. This keeps corrupted K/V and gradients local, avoids replicated clean prefixes, and preserves BDLM training semantics.
AI.result: On 16 H200 GPUs at 256K context: 1.18-1.45x throughput improvement for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and 1.27-1.33x for conversion of autoregressive models to BDLMs, while matching or reducing peak HBM. Full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K. On eight H100 GPUs: 2.48x acceleration at 512K and 7.59x at 1M for DFlash2 speculative-decoder training. In matched 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates at every trained checkpoint on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite.
AI.conclusion: CSBP represents a significant advancement in distributed training for block diffusion language models, enabling efficient scaling to 1M+ context lengths while improving both throughput and model quality. The technique achieves substantial speedups across various training scenarios (SFT, model conversion, speculative decoding) while maintaining or reducing memory consumption, making it practical for training large-scale BDLMs on long-context tasks.

title: Printing the Underdetermined: Materializing Multi-solutionness in Figurative Paintings
summary: Figurative paintings are often approached as if they depict a single recoverable 3D scene: viewers infer depth and occlusion, and reconstruction pipelines attempt to converge to one stable model. We instead foreground multi-solutionness, the non-uniqueness of 3D configurations compatible with a single painted image, and propose a workflow that keeps this non-uniqueness visible and material. Multi-solutionness arises from two sources: unobserved content, where backsides and occluded volumes admit multiple plausible completions, and observed cues, where perspective, shading, and occlusion still underconstrain geometry. When additional views are synthesized by a video generative model without explicit 3D constraints, small frame-level drifts become inevitable rather than exceptional. Our pipeline samples multiple camera-orbit multi-view video sequences from one painting, reconstructs each sequence with 3D Gaussian Splatting into a point-based Gaussian scene representation where density halos and ghosting expose unresolved degrees of freedom, and fabricates these representations as physical artifacts using DreamPrinting. By treating multiple compatible interpretations as explicit outputs rather than residual error, we provide a computational framework for spatial readings of figurative painting that can be inspected, compared, and discussed in both digital and physical form.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the assumption that figurative paintings depict a single recoverable 3D scene, instead proposing that multiple valid 3D interpretations are possible. The authors present a pipeline that generates multiple camera-orbit video sequences from a painting, reconstructs each using 3D Gaussian Splatting, and fabricates physical artifacts via DreamPrinting, treating multiple interpretations as explicit outputs rather than errors.
AI.motivation: Current computational approaches to figurative paintings assume a single recoverable 3D scene, treating ambiguity as noise to be eliminated. The authors argue this misses the fundamental multi-solutionness inherent in paintings - the non-uniqueness of 3D configurations compatible with a single image. This non-uniqueness arises from both unobserved content (occluded volumes, back sides) and observed cues that underconstrain geometry (perspective, shading, occlusion).
AI.method: The proposed workflow: (1) Sample multiple camera-orbit multi-view video sequences from one painting using a video generative model without explicit 3D constraints; (2) Reconstruct each sequence using 3D Gaussian Splatting into point-based Gaussian scene representations where density halos and ghosting expose unresolved degrees of freedom; (3) Fabricate these representations as physical artifacts using DreamPrinting. The key is keeping multi-solutionness visible and material throughout the pipeline.
AI.result: The pipeline produces multiple compatible 3D interpretations of a single painting that can be inspected, compared, and discussed in both digital and physical form. The 3D Gaussian Splatting representation with density halos and ghosting exposes unresolved degrees of freedom, making ambiguity explicit rather than hidden.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a computational framework for spatial readings of figurative painting that foregrounds ambiguity as a feature rather than a bug. By treating multiple compatible interpretations as explicit outputs rather than residual error, it enables new ways of analyzing and discussing the spatial possibilities in paintings. The physical fabrication via DreamPrinting allows tangible engagement with these multiple interpretations.

title: BA-TRACE: Boundary-Aware Trace Reconstruction for Scenario-Based Evaluation of Mixed AUTOSAR Adaptive and ROS 2 Vehicular Embedded Systems
summary: Modern vehicular embedded systems increasingly combine ROS 2-based autonomous-driving stacks with AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform (AUTOSAR AP). Such mixed stacks make scenario-based evaluation hard to interpret because execution paths cross DDS-SOME/IP middleware boundaries between ROS 2 and AUTOSAR AP. Existing simulators and tracing tools execute scenarios or collect platform-local traces but cannot reconstruct cross-domain data flows. This paper presents BA-TRACE, a boundary-aware trace reconstruction framework for scenario-based evaluation of mixed AUTOSAR AP and ROS 2 vehicular embedded systems. BA-TRACE combines ROS 2 trace events, AUTOSAR ara::log events, ARXML-derived structural dependencies, and bridge-level instrumentation to reconstruct an end-to-end execution graph across the DDS-SOME/IP boundary. A case study with an AWSIM/OpenSCENARIO-based object-detection and braking scenario shows that BA-TRACE reconstructs the expected cross-platform path and exposes boundary-specific latency such as point-cloud transfer overhead. The reconstructed topology is used as evidence of traceability, not as proof of behavioral correctness or safety.

AI.tldr: BA-TRACE is a framework for reconstructing end-to-end execution graphs across DDS-SOME/IP boundaries between ROS 2 and AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform in vehicular embedded systems, enabling scenario-based evaluation of mixed stacks that was previously difficult due to cross-domain data flow complexity.
AI.motivation: The increasing combination of ROS 2-based autonomous-driving stacks with AUTOSAR AP in modern vehicular embedded systems creates evaluation challenges. Existing simulators and tracing tools cannot reconstruct cross-domain data flows when execution paths cross DDS-SOME/IP middleware boundaries, making scenario-based evaluation hard to interpret.
AI.method: BA-TRACE combines four key data sources: (1) ROS 2 trace events, (2) AUTOSAR ara::log events, (3) ARXML-derived structural dependencies, and (4) bridge-level instrumentation. These are integrated to reconstruct an end-to-end execution graph across the DDS-SOME/IP boundary.
AI.result: The case study using AWSIM/OpenSCENARIO-based object-detection and braking scenario demonstrates that BA-TRACE successfully reconstructs the expected cross-platform path and exposes boundary-specific latency such as point-cloud transfer overhead.
AI.conclusion: The reconstructed topology serves as evidence of traceability for cross-domain analysis but is explicitly not intended as proof of behavioral correctness or safety. The paper focuses on enabling better interpretation of scenario-based evaluations rather than verifying system safety.

title: WZPlanner: Safe End-to-End Path Planning for Autonomous Driving in Work Zones
summary: Work zones alter lane geometry through temporary traffic controls and closures that may be absent from on-board maps, challenging autonomous vehicle (AV) perception and planning. Generalization is also limited by scarce public datasets with structured geometric supervision. We present WorkZonePlan, a dataset comprising 149K+ synthetic and 5K+ real-world multimodal samples with 3D annotations for lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectory options. It also provides 76 closed-loop CARLA scenarios replayed under three weather conditions, yielding 228 Bench2Drive-format evaluation routes. We introduce WAVE (Work-zone-focused AV data generation in Virtual and rEal Environments), a semi-automated pipeline for creating the dataset, and BoundaryFormer (BF), a transformer-based model that jointly predicts lane and work zone boundary polynomials and driving trajectories. BF uses slot attention for boundary prediction. Ablations show that a separate trajectory decoder using boundary slot features substantially improves trajectory prediction over a slot-attention-only approach. Building on this finding, BF++ offers Camera and Camera+LiDAR variants with metric ground-plane encoding, typed boundary/trajectory queries, long-range point anchors, image-space curve refinement, and conservative gated LiDAR fusion. On the 211 routes common to all four models at the evaluation freeze, BF++-Camera and BF++-Camera+LiDAR achieve Driving Scores of 63.0 and 64.4, respectively, compared with 59.3 for SimLingo and 26.1 for TransFuser++ (TF++). BF++ is 40 times smaller than SimLingo and more than 10 times smaller than TF++, while achieving higher Driving Scores. These results support jointly predicting lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectories as a promising direction toward safer AV operation in work zones. Code and dataset: https://github.com/Nishad-Sahu/WZPlanner.

AI.tldr: WorkZonePlan is a dataset addressing AV perception challenges in work zones, featuring 149K+ synthetic and 5K+ real-world multimodal samples with 3D annotations. BoundaryFormer (BF) and BF++ are transformer-based models that jointly predict lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectories. BF++ achieves Driving Scores of 63.0 (Camera) and 64.4 (Camera+LiDAR), outperforming SimLingo (59.3) and TransFuser++ (26.1) while being 40x smaller than SimLingo.
AI.motivation: Work zones alter lane geometry through temporary traffic controls absent from on-board maps, challenging AV perception and planning. Limited public datasets with structured geometric supervision hinder generalization. This work addresses the lack of dedicated datasets and models for safe AV operation in work zones.
AI.method: WAVE pipeline was developed for semi-automated dataset creation.
