AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive experience retrieval framework for repository-level program repair that addresses three key limitations in existing memory-augmented methods: imbalanced episodic memory across repositories, non-monotonic relationship between memory volume and repair success, and phase-misaligned memory accumulation. The framework employs coverage-aware retrieval, quality-aware selection, and stage-aware routing to improve repair performance, particularly for under-covered repositories.
AI.motivation: Current memory-augmented repository-level program repair methods suffer from three critical limitations: (1) episodic memory is highly imbalanced across repositories, leaving low-resource repositories with insufficient support; (2) more memory does not monotonically improve repair success, indicating that relevance, quality, and redundancy matter more than raw volume; (3) memory accumulation is phase-misaligned with repositories having many reproduction experiences but few patch or refinement experiences.
AI.method: The proposed framework introduces three key components: (1) Coverage-aware retrieval, which falls back to cross-repository or repair-type-based memories when same-repository memory is insufficient; (2) Quality-aware selection, which ranks memories by relevance, historical utility, specificity, and redundancy; (3) Stage-aware routing, which separates and retrieves memories for distinct repair stages (reproduction, localization, patch generation, patch refinement, and validation).
AI.result: Evaluated on SWE-Bench-Lite and SWE-Bench-Verified, the framework improves repair performance on under-covered repositories, reduces noisy memory retrieval, and better supports failed-to-fixed patch refinement. The key insight is that the success of memory-augmented repair depends on retrieving the right experiences for the right repair context, not merely accumulating more experiences.
AI.conclusion: The key to effective memory-augmented program repair is not simply accumulating more experiences, but retrieving the right experiences for the right repair context. This requires addressing memory imbalance, prioritizing quality over quantity, and aligning memory retrieval with specific repair phases.

title: ParticleSplat: Self-supervised Object-centric Latent Particle Splatting
summary: We present ParticleSplat, a self-supervised object-centric learning method that decomposes scenes into a set of latent ''particles'' representing semantic entities through feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting. Building on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, which represents images as a set of particles with attributes such as position, scale, and visual appearance, we address a key limitation of DLP: its inherently 2D nature, which prevents explicit 3D spatial and geometric reasoning that are critical for downstream tasks such as robotic manipulation. Leveraging the structural similarity between latent particles and 3D Gaussian primitives, we introduce a 3D latent particle space trained with a novel view synthesis objective. Our model jointly encodes multiple views with camera poses into a shared 3D object-centric latent space, then transforms particles into particle-aligned 3D Gaussians whose composition reconstructs the full scene. On simulated and real-world datasets, we show that this formulation inherently learns object masks without supervision and supports controllable 3D scene editing, such as moving objects by modifying particles in the latent space. We further establish that the learned 3D representation improves downstream performance on robotic manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: ParticleSplat is a self-supervised object-centric learning method that decomposes scenes into 3D latent particles using feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressing the 2D limitation of the prior Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework to enable explicit 3D spatial and geometric reasoning.
AI.motivation: The key limitation of DLP is its inherently 2D nature, which prevents explicit 3D spatial and geometric reasoning that are critical for downstream tasks such as robotic manipulation.
AI.method: The method introduces a 3D latent particle space trained with a novel view synthesis objective. It jointly encodes multiple views with camera poses into a shared 3D object-centric latent space, then transforms particles into particle-aligned 3D Gaussians whose composition reconstructs the full scene.
AI.result: The formulation inherently learns object masks without supervision and supports controllable 3D scene editing, such as moving objects by modifying particles in the latent space. The learned 3D representation improves downstream performance on robotic manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: ParticleSplat successfully enables 3D object-centric representation learning through latent particles and 3D Gaussian Splatting, achieving unsupervised object mask learning, controllable 3D scene editing, and improved performance on robotic manipulation downstream tasks.

title: MAGS: Multi-agent Auto-formalization Guarantees Safety for Agentic Outputs
summary: LLM coding agents now generate complex programs at a scale that makes thorough human review increasingly difficult, raising the risk of safety and security failures. Common approaches, including fuzz testing, static analysis, and LLM-as-a-Verifier, can detect many failures but struggle to cover all possible edge cases. Formal verification addresses this by providing machine-checkable guarantees over specified properties, but traditionally demands substantial manual specification and proof engineering. We introduce a unified multi-agent framework, MAGS, that generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees, using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation where safety properties can be mechanically checked. MAGS formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, translates generated code into Dafny, repairs violations using verifier feedback, and compiles verified programs back into executable code. We evaluate MAGS on 100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, and 20 robotic-arm tasks. Across all 220 examples, it achieves a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations further show strong performance across all three domains, while revealing failures when the auto-formalized semantics do not fully capture the target behavior.

AI.tldr: MAGS is a unified multi-agent framework that generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation. It formalizes human-audited APIs, translates generated code into Dafny, repairs violations using verifier feedback, and compiles verified programs back to executable code. Achieved 100% success rate across 220 examples including CUDA kernels, terminal scripts, and robotic-arm tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents generate complex programs at scale that are difficult to thoroughly review, raising safety and security risks. Existing approaches like fuzz testing, static analysis, and LLM-as-a-Verifier struggle to cover all edge cases. Traditional formal verification requires substantial manual specification and proof engineering.
AI.method: MAGS uses a multi-agent framework with Dafny as intermediate representation: (1) Formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, (2) Translates generated code into Dafny, (3) Repairs violations using verifier feedback, (4) Compiles verified programs back into executable code.
AI.result: Across all 220 examples (100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, 20 robotic-arm tasks), MAGS achieves 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations show strong performance, though some failures occur when auto-formalized semantics don't fully capture target behavior.
AI.conclusion: MAGS demonstrates that formal verification can be integrated into LLM code generation workflows to provide machine-checkable safety guarantees. The approach is effective across diverse domains but requires careful formalization of specifications to avoid semantic gaps between formal and intended behavior.

title: How to Guide Your Language Flow
summary: We introduce a new method to guide flow matching models. Our approach, which we call probe guidance, uses the frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to construct a guidance signal. This works using a similar principle as autoguidance, but eliminates the need for an additional forward pass at inference time and provides a reliable path to ensure that the weak and strong model share similar dynamics. We apply and benchmark this method on continuous diffusion language models, where probe guidance sets a new state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation. When applied to a 1.7B diffusion language model, probe guidance consistently improves on multiple choice question answering benchmarks. Using our probes, we study the traditional autoguidance setting where the strong model is a weak checkpoint, and find that the weak model must come from a low-entropy region of training. These findings both provide a practical way to improve diffusion language models and shed light on the actual mechanism behind autoguidance, which is currently poorly understood.

AI.tldr: Probe guidance is a new method that uses frozen internal states of diffusion models to construct guidance signals, improving continuous diffusion language models without additional inference-time forward passes. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation and improves QA benchmarks for 1.7B models.
AI.motivation: Current autoguidance methods require additional forward passes at inference time, making them inefficient. There is also a need to understand the mechanism behind autoguidance and ensure weak and strong models share similar dynamics.
AI.method: Probe guidance uses frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to construct a guidance signal. It applies to continuous diffusion language models, eliminating the need for an additional forward pass at inference time while ensuring weak and strong models share similar dynamics.
AI.result: Probe guidance sets a new state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation. When applied to a 1.7B diffusion language model, it consistently improves on multiple choice question answering benchmarks. The study also finds that for autoguidance, the weak model must come from a low-entropy region of training.
AI.conclusion: Probe guidance provides a practical and efficient method to improve diffusion language models while also shedding light on the actual mechanism behind autoguidance, which was previously poorly understood.

title: SplashSplat: Reconstructing Splashing Liquids from Real-World Multi-View Videos
comment: 18 pages (11 main + 7 supplementary), 14 figures, 12 tables. Project page: https://niko-creater.github.io/splashsplat-web/
summary: A splash lives for a fraction of a second: sheets tear into ligaments and droplets, appearance is view-dependent and nearly textureless, and little persists long enough to track. Reconstruction research has consequently focused on smoke, synthetic liquids, or gently deforming surfaces. To our knowledge, no synchronized multi-view dataset of splashing liquids exists. We therefore introduce a benchmark of 20 real scenes, from coherent streams to violent splashes, captured by seven synchronized, calibrated 4K cameras at 60 fps, with manually refined per-view liquid and container masks and fixed evaluation splits. We further present SplashSplat, built on a single principle: impose physical structure only where the observations can constrain it. Per-frame liquid SDFs fused from the masks provide the geometry, level-set transport between consecutive SDFs yields a coarse velocity field, and Lagrangian carriers advected along this flow, corrected against each new observation and reseeded where coverage is lost, decode local Gaussians for differentiable rendering. SplashSplat outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian splatting methods on our real captures and on a synthetic benchmark, with physically more plausible motion and a lower training cost. The same representation supports temporal interpolation and style transfer without re-optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first synchronized multi-view dataset of real splashing liquids (20 scenes, 7 cameras, 4K 60fps) and presents SplashSplat, a novel 3D reconstruction method that combines Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for geometry, level-set transport for velocity estimation, and Lagrangian carriers with local Gaussians for differentiable rendering. The method outperforms existing dynamic Gaussian splatting approaches on both real and synthetic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Splash phenomena are extremely challenging to capture and reconstruct because they are short-lived, view-dependent, nearly textureless, and difficult to track. Existing reconstruction research has focused on smoke, synthetic liquids, or gently deforming surfaces. There is no existing dataset of real splashing liquids, which limits research progress in this area.
AI.method: SplashSplat is built on the principle of imposing physical structure only where observations can constrain it. The method consists of: (1) Per-frame liquid SDFs fused from multi-view masks to provide geometry; (2) Level-set transport between consecutive SDFs to yield a coarse velocity field; (3) Lagrangian carriers advected along this flow, corrected against new observations and reseeded where coverage is lost; (4) Local Gaussians decoded for differentiable rendering.
AI.result: SplashSplat outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian splatting methods on the authors' real captures and on a synthetic benchmark. It achieves physically more plausible motion and lower training cost. The same representation supports temporal interpolation and style transfer without re-optimization.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first benchmark dataset for real splash reconstruction and demonstrates that the proposed SplashSplat method can effectively reconstruct dynamic liquid splashes with physically plausible motion, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining lower computational cost.

title: CodeTransBenchmark: Evaluating LLM-based Code Translation and Repair Across Programming Languages
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) pre-trained on expansive text and code corpora have revealed promising code generation abilities and have attracted increasing attention in code translation. In this work, we investigate the effectiveness of LLMs in code translation and translation error repair. First, we present CodeTransBenchmark, a framework for evaluating LLM-based translation and repair and devise a post-processing strategy to extract code from inconsistent LLM outputs. Then, we discuss an empirical study evaluates eight models on three datasets and 12 language pairs, in which we categorize incorrect translations by errors to identify weaknesses of existing LLMs. Our work shows that while LLMs specifically trained for multi-lingual coding, like Codestral, correctly translate the majority of code, most general-purpose models struggle with the syntactic rules of the target language. The analysis of erroneous translations reveals the substantial impact of the interrelationship between involved programming languages and training data on the effectiveness. We show that a general post-processing approach must tolerate inconsistencies and leverage the predictability of LLM answers. Further, we show that iterative translation repair via automated feedback significantly improves translation accuracy. While our combined findings highlight the potential of LLMs to automate code translation, an effective deployment of LLM-based code translation in practice would require models with larger context windows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CodeTransBenchmark, a framework for evaluating LLM-based code translation and repair, testing eight models across three datasets and 12 language pairs. The study finds that specialized coding LLMs (e.g., Codestral) outperform general-purpose models, and that iterative translation repair with automated feedback significantly improves accuracy.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to investigate the effectiveness of Large Language Models in code translation and translation error repair, an area gaining attention due to the promising code generation abilities of LLMs pre-trained on text and code corpora.
AI.method: The researchers: (1) Developed CodeTransBenchmark, a framework for evaluating LLM-based translation and repair; (2) Devised a post-processing strategy to extract code from inconsistent LLM outputs; (3) Conducted an empirical study evaluating eight models on three datasets and 12 language pairs; (4) Categorized incorrect translations by error types to identify weaknesses of existing LLMs; (5) Tested iterative translation repair via automated feedback.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) LLMs specifically trained for multi-lingual coding (like Codestral) correctly translate the majority of code; (2) Most general-purpose models struggle with syntactic rules of the target language; (3) The interrelationship between involved programming languages and training data significantly impacts translation effectiveness; (4) A general post-processing approach must tolerate inconsistencies and leverage predictability of LLM answers; (5) Iterative translation repair via automated feedback significantly improves translation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: While LLMs show potential to automate code translation, effective deployment in practice requires models with larger context windows. The study highlights the importance of specialized coding LLMs and the value of iterative repair mechanisms for improving translation accuracy.

title: SCOUT: Sim-to-Real Text-Based Person Retrieval by Embedding-Space Prediction over Frozen Video Features
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on AI City Challenge (Track 4). Code and annotations: https://github.com/abtraore/SCOUT-ECCV
summary: Text-based person retrieval under a sim-to-real gap (synthetic training data, a real-image gallery) is usually tackled with costly fine-tuned cross-encoders. We ask whether a frozen-encoder system can compete. We present SCOUT, which casts cross-modal retrieval as prediction in embedding space. A trainable predictor maps the patch tokens of a frozen video encoder into the embedding space of a frozen text encoder under a bidirectional InfoNCE objective, and no encoder is fine-tuned in the base model. The video encoder is V-JEPA, the text encoder is EmbeddingGemma, and the predictor is initialized from a Qwen3.5-0.8B decoder. We make three findings. First, the best frozen text encoder is simply the one whose geometry best matches the video features. A training-free alignment score ranks three candidate text encoders in the same order as their retrieval accuracy on our held-out split (Spearman $ρ= 1.0$); a fourth, LLM-based encoder shows the rule is metric-dependent, holding for a neighborhood-overlap score ($ρ= 0.8$) but not for a linear probe ($ρ= -0.2$). Second, two precision-targeted levers, parameter-efficient ExPLoRA adaptation of the video encoder and a training-free attribute-decomposed reranker built on a vision-language model, improve the top-rank precision that otherwise limits the frozen system, adding 2.2 points of leaderboard R@1. Third, a local-versus-public calibration study explains which interventions transfer to the real domain. On AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4 the full retrieve-fuse-rerank system reaches 84.25 mAP@10 on the final leaderboard, while a single frozen model submitted alone reaches 60.63. Our trained components cost about 95 GPU-hours. CMP, the dataset authors' fine-tuned cross-encoder that trains for sixteen GPU-days, is one fusion member of the full system, not an alternative. Code and annotations: https://github.com/abtraore/SCOUT-ECCV

AI.tldr: SCOUT is a frozen-encoder system for text-based person retrieval under sim-to-real gap that maps patch tokens from a frozen video encoder (V-JEPA) into the embedding space of a frozen text encoder (EmbeddingGemma) using a trainable predictor (Qwen3.5-0.8B), without fine-tuning any encoder in the base model.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether a frozen-encoder system can compete with costly fine-tuned cross-encoders for text-based person retrieval under sim-to-real gap (synthetic training data, real-image gallery).
AI.method: 1) Trainable predictor maps video patch tokens into text embedding space under bidirectional InfoNCE objective; 2) Training-free alignment score selects best text encoder based on geometry matching; 3) ExPLoRA adaptation for video encoder and training-free attribute-decomposed reranker using vision-language model for precision improvement; 4) Local-versus-public calibration study for domain transfer.
AI.result: Full system achieves 84.25 mAP@10 on AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4 leaderboard; single frozen model reaches 60.63 mAP@10; training-free alignment score shows Spearman ρ=1.0 for ranking text encoders; ExPLoRA and reranker add 2.2 points R@1; trained components cost ~95 GPU-hours vs. 16 GPU-days for CMP fine-tuned cross-encoder.
AI.conclusion: Frozen-encoder systems can compete with fine-tuned cross-encoders for text-based person retrieval; text encoder selection should be geometry-based; precision-targeted levers (ExPLoRA + reranker) improve top-rank precision; domain transfer depends on local-versus-public calibration. The full system uses CMP as a fusion member, not as an alternative.

title: Closed-World Resolution Against Tool Hallucination in LLM Agents
summary: Tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents fail in a way no tool-selection or tool-security method addresses: they call tools that do not exist and pass arguments no schema declares. Existing defenses either pick the right tool (selection) or constrain what an agent may do with real tools (gating), both of which presuppose the emitted call refers to a real tool at all. We show this is a structural blind spot: a hallucinated call is by construction not a decision any gate made, so no gate can reject it. This paper is primarily a measurement and benchmark study. We give a five-class taxonomy of tool hallucination (H1-H5) and, as a reference point, the Resolution Rung: a training-free, closed-world resolver (registry membership plus a signature check) whose interest is where it must sit, not what it computes. We prove hallucination defense must precede any causal gate, and characterize the one irreducible residue (borrowed arguments schema-indistinguishable from a valid call). Across ten hosted models under two invocation surfaces we measure 322 genuine hallucinations; fabricated-tool calls concentrate on the unconstrained raw-JSON surface (34 vs. 3), and model scale does not help (a 675B model matches a 7-8B one). We then extend to the Model Context Protocol, where merging several servers into one namespace creates hallucination surfaces a single registry cannot express (a second taxonomy, M1-M5); on the live MCP surface we measure 154 hallucinations, including from frontier models that were clean on the single-registry surface, because collisions and shadowing are structural to the merge. We release the versioned Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) so any resolver is comparable across submissions.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and addresses a critical structural blind spot in tool-augmented LLM agents: they call tools that do not exist (hallucinated tools) with arguments that match no schema. Existing defenses (tool-selection or gating methods) presuppose the tool exists, so they cannot detect these hallucinations. The authors provide a taxonomy of tool hallucination types (H1-H5), propose a training-free resolver (Resolution Rung), prove that hallucination defense must precede gating, and measure 322 hallucinations across 10 models on 2 surfaces, plus 154 on the live MCP surface.
AI.motivation: To address a fundamental gap in LLM agent security: existing defenses assume tools exist, but agents can call completely fabricated tools. This hallucinated tool call problem is structural and not addressed by any existing method.
AI.method: 1) Develop a five-class taxonomy (H1-H5) of tool hallucination types; 2) Propose Resolution Rung as a training-free resolver with registry membership plus signature check; 3) Prove theoretically that hallucination defense must precede causal gates; 4) Empirically measure across 10 hosted models under 2 invocation surfaces (raw-JSON and MCP); 5) Extend analysis to Model Context Protocol with second taxonomy (M1-M5) addressing namespace merging issues.
AI.result: Key findings: 322 genuine hallucinations measured across models; fabricated-tool calls concentrate on unconstrained raw-JSON surface (34 vs. 3); model scale does not help (675B matches 7-8B models); on live MCP surface, 154 hallucinations measured including from frontier models previously clean on single-registry surface, due to structural collisions and shadowing from namespace merging.
AI.conclusion: Tool hallucination is a structural problem requiring defense before any gating mechanism. The Resolution Rung provides a reference point. The Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) enables comparable evaluation across resolvers. The problem extends to multi-server contexts like MCP where namespace merging creates hallucination surfaces a single registry cannot express.

title: Smart Insole Human Activity Recognition for Continuous Monitoring in Elderly Care
summary: Falls in older adults are often preceded by changes in mobility, balance, and postural transitions. This paper presents a wireless smart insole platform and machine-learning workflow for recognizing sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking from plantar-pressure and inertial signals. Each insole integrates 16 active pressure-sensing locations and a six-dimensional IMU stream consisting of tri-axial acceleration and angular velocity. Data were collected from 15 healthy adults at 80~Hz and segmented into overlapping windows. Window length and candidate model families were first screened with stratified 10-fold cross-validation; the primary performance estimate was then obtained with participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group cross-validation, ensuring that all windows from a participant remained in a single fold. Under this protocol, Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.954 and 0.959 for the left and right feet, respectively, and 0.980 with bilateral sensing. A compact 1D-CNN evaluated with the same participant-independent folds did not significantly outperform HGB ($p=0.0625$). The results show that low-profile footwear sensing can infer activity state from pressure and IMU measurements for participants unseen during training, establishing a basis for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care.

AI.tldr: A wireless smart insole system with 16 pressure sensors and a 6D IMU per foot, combined with machine learning (HGB/1D-CNN), can accurately classify sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking with macro-F1 scores up to 0.980 using bilateral sensing, enabling fall prevention monitoring for elderly adults.
AI.motivation: Falls in older adults are preceded by changes in mobility, balance, and postural transitions. Early detection of unstable walking patterns could enable timely fall prevention interventions, but requires continuous monitoring of plantar pressure and inertial signals during daily activities.
AI.method: The study used a wireless smart insole platform with 16 active pressure sensors and a six-dimensional IMU (tri-axial acceleration + angular velocity) per insole. Data from 15 healthy adults were collected at 80 Hz and segmented into overlapping windows. Window length and model families were screened using stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with final performance evaluated using participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group cross-validation (ensuring all windows from one participant stayed in a single fold). Two models were compared: Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) and a compact 1D-CNN.
AI.result: HGB achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.954 (left foot), 0.959 (right foot), and 0.980 with bilateral sensing. The 1D-CNN did not significantly outperform HGB (p=0.0625). The participant-independent validation confirms the models generalize to unseen individuals.
AI.conclusion: Low-profile footwear sensing with pressure and IMU measurements can reliably infer activity states (sitting, standing, walking, unstable walking) for participants not seen during training. This establishes a practical foundation for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care applications.

title: Evaluating Package-Level Scoping Strategies for Repository-Level Code Completion in Pharo
summary:
Source code is organized in repositories, packages, and projects, yet token-level completion engines rarely exploit this structure. Pharo provides a semantic completion engine based on ordered, lazy heuristics that retrieve and rank candidates. Its default strategy follows language semantics and scoping rules, but ignores package structure and dependencies. Consequently, classes from the same package or project, and classes used by them, receive no special priority.
  We introduce and evaluate three package-aware heuristics: Lateral Packages, Direct Package Dependencies, and Two-Level Package Dependencies. Our benchmark covers method call sites from 219 packages, including 4,535 classes and 35,972 methods across major Pharo projects such as Iceberg, Moose, Roassal, Seaside, and Spec. We assess class-name and method-name completion and ask whether explicit package dependencies can provide a lightweight structural signal for improving candidate ranking without introducing a new learning model.
  The Direct Package Dependencies heuristic produced the strongest results. For 3-character prefixes, Mean Reciprocal Rank increased from 0.20 to 0.44 for class-name completion and from 0.10 to 0.41 for method-name completion. These findings show that package-aware strategies provide more accurate and relevant suggestions than the default Semantics-Based strategy on the evaluated projects. Based on the improvement in class-name completion, the Pharo Industrial Consortium adopted the Direct Package Dependencies heuristic for Pharo 13.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the limitation of token-level completion engines in Pharo that ignore package structure and dependencies. The authors propose three package-aware heuristics (Lateral Packages, Direct Package Dependencies, and Two-Level Package Dependencies) to improve candidate ranking. Evaluation on 219 packages from major Pharo projects showed the Direct Package Dependencies heuristic significantly improved Mean Reciprocal Rank, leading to its adoption in Pharo 13.
AI.motivation: Current semantic completion engines in Pharo follow language semantics and scoping rules but ignore package structure and dependencies. Classes from the same package or project, and classes used by them, receive no special priority, resulting in less relevant completion suggestions.
AI.method: The authors introduced three package-aware heuristics: (1) Lateral Packages - prioritizes classes from the same package, (2) Direct Package Dependencies - prioritizes classes from directly dependent packages, (3) Two-Level Package Dependencies - extends to transitive dependencies. They benchmarked method call sites from 219 packages containing 4,535 classes and 35,972 methods across major Pharo projects (Iceberg, Moose, Roassal, Seaside, Spec) and evaluated both class-name and method-name completion.
AI.result: The Direct Package Dependencies heuristic produced the strongest results. For 3-character prefixes, Mean Reciprocal Rank increased from 0.20 to 0.44 for class-name completion (120% improvement) and from 0.10 to 0.41 for method-name completion (310% improvement).
AI.conclusion: Package-aware strategies provide more accurate and relevant suggestions than the default Semantics-Based strategy. The Direct Package Dependencies heuristic was adopted by the Pharo Industrial Consortium for Pharo 13, demonstrating that explicit package dependencies can provide a lightweight structural signal for improving candidate ranking without introducing a new learning model.

title: AMB3R-SLAM: Kilometer-scale SLAM with Hierarchical Backend
summary: We present AMB3R-SLAM, a real-time monocular SLAM system capable of reconstructing kilometer-scale trajectories over 10k frames on a single consumer-grade GPU. Our model couples a lightweight front-end for low-latency online tracking with a hierarchical backend that progressively enforces local, mid-level, and global consistency. By avoiding bundle adjustment that relies on the static world assumption, our system naturally handles complex dynamic scenes out of the box. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be extended to leverage stereo, RGB-D, and LiDAR as additional inputs. AMB3R-SLAM achieves strong camera tracking performance across 9 datasets, reducing the absolute trajectory error (ATE) of previous state-of-the-art methods on VBR and Oxford Spires by over 70%. With additional LiDAR input, our model further reduces ATE to sub-meter level on KITTI and VBR datasets.

AI.tldr: AMB3R-SLAM is a real-time monocular SLAM system that can reconstruct kilometer-scale trajectories over 10k frames on a single consumer-grade GPU. It uses a lightweight front-end for low-latency tracking coupled with a hierarchical backend enforcing local, mid-level, and global consistency. The system handles dynamic scenes without relying on the static world assumption and can be extended to leverage stereo, RGB-D, and LiDAR inputs.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of existing SLAM systems that struggle with kilometer-scale trajectories, require expensive hardware, rely on static world assumptions (making them unsuitable for dynamic scenes), and have limited extensibility to different sensor modalities.
AI.method: Couples a lightweight front-end for low-latency online tracking with a hierarchical backend that progressively enforces local, mid-level, and global consistency. Avoids bundle adjustment that relies on the static world assumption, enabling natural handling of complex dynamic scenes. Extensible to multiple sensor inputs (stereo, RGB-D, LiDAR).
AI.result: Achieves strong camera tracking performance across 9 datasets. Reduces absolute trajectory error (ATE) of previous state-of-the-art methods on VBR and Oxford Spires by over 70%. With additional LiDAR input, reduces ATE to sub-meter level on KITTI and VBR datasets.
AI.conclusion: AMB3R-SLAM demonstrates a robust, scalable, and extensible SLAM system that handles dynamic scenes effectively while maintaining real-time performance on consumer-grade hardware, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.

title: The syntax and semantics of goals
comment: To appear in Topics in Cognitive Science, special issue on Goal-Centric Perspectives in Cognitive Science
summary: In both cognitive science and computer science, goals are conceptualized as cognitive states that flexibly combine with world knowledge to organize and specify purposeful behavior. In this way, goals are compositional representations whose content relates to rational behavior. We here draw attention to goals as representations and their content because it highlights a parallel with other areas in cognitive science - in particular, the syntax-semantics interface in linguistics and logic - while also foregrounding foundational questions about the expressivity, design, and efficiency of different goal representations. For example, goals are typically taken as fixed and imposing constraints on desirable behaviors, but we can also identify constraints on goal representations themselves, such as whether a particular goal language is sufficiently expressive to capture behaviors of interest, or whether different goal representations capture the same behavior. Here, we synthesize work that aims to characterize the properties of different goal representations and suggest these are points of a broader design space. We close by discussing how distinguishing the form and meaning of goals can elucidate the implicit assumptions we make about goals, inform the study of interactions between higher-level cognition and motivation, and isolate axes of variation for different conceptions of goals.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses goals as cognitive representations that flexibly combine with world knowledge to organize purposeful behavior. It draws parallels between goals in cognitive/computer science and the syntax-semantics interface in linguistics and logic, focusing on foundational questions about the expressivity, design, and efficiency of different goal representations.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to draw attention to goals as representations and their content, highlighting a parallel with linguistics and logic while foregrounding foundational questions about goal representations themselves - specifically their expressivity, design, and efficiency.
AI.method: The paper synthesizes work characterizing properties of different goal representations, treating different goal representations as points in a broader design space.
AI.result: The authors identify goals as points in a broader design space, showing how different goal representations can capture behaviors of interest and the constraints on these representations.
AI.conclusion: Distinguishing the form and meaning of goals can elucidate implicit assumptions about goals, inform the study of interactions between higher-level cognition and motivation, and isolate axes of variation for different conceptions of goals.

title: Stiefel Attention: When the Geometry of Transformer Projection Matrices Dominates Optimizer Choice---and When It Does Not
summary: The query and key projections $\WQ,\WK$ in attention are almost always trained by Euclidean optimizers with no constraint on their geometry. We constrain them to the Stiefel manifold and optimize them there with a Riemannian Adam that carries one scalar second moment per frame, caps its step by a trust region, and retracts polarly. Four propositions prove this update is steepest descent in the embedded metric, independent of gradient scale, well conditioned, and exactly $\mathrm{O}(d)$-equivariant, each certified numerically in \texttt{float64}. A fifth supplies the mechanism: weight decay has \emph{identically zero} Riemannian gradient on $\St(d,r)$, since $W = W I_r$ lies in the normal space, so the learned attention geometry survives the collapse cycles that decay drives through the rest of the model. On modular arithmetic grokking, a single run holds $97.0\%$ validation accuracy at epoch 20\,000 against the baseline's $61.1\%$---an unstable endpoint we report as evidence for the mechanism rather than as an effect size. On CIFAR-10 patches the same rule gains $\mathbf{+8.98}$\,pp over 12 paired starts ($t{=}60.6$, $12/12$), and the gap widens with data rather than eroding. The step rule earns this: a fixed-step Riemannian update is degree one in the gradient, so it moves $24$--$40\times$ less per step than an identically shaped AdamW matrix---its frames barely leave their initialization, and freezing them outright costs only $0.28$\,pp. An ablation credits the whole gain to making the step scale free, and nothing measurable to the projector or to equivariance. A negative result sharpens the account: gauge removal cannot motivate the method, because a direction along which the loss is invariant carries no gradient at all.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes constraining attention projections (WQ, WK) to the Stiefel manifold using a Riemannian Adam optimizer. The key finding is that weight decay has zero Riemannian gradient on this manifold, preserving learned attention geometry. The method achieves significant improvements on grokking (97.0% vs 61.1%) and CIFAR-10 (+8.98pp), with the gain attributed to scale-free steps rather than the projector or equivariance.
AI.motivation: The authors observe that query and key projections (WQ, WK) in attention mechanisms are typically trained with Euclidean optimizers without any geometric constraints. They propose constraining these projections to the Stiefel manifold to preserve the attention geometry during training, particularly to survive the collapse cycles that weight decay drives through the rest of the model.
AI.method: The method involves constraining WQ and WK to the Stiefel manifold and optimizing with a custom Riemannian Adam optimizer that: (1) carries one scalar second moment per frame, (2) caps its step by a trust region, and (3) retracts polarly. The key mechanism discovered is that weight decay has identically zero Riemannian gradient on St(d,r), meaning the learned attention geometry survives weight decay cycles.
AI.result: Four propositions prove the update is: steepest descent in the embedded metric, independent of gradient scale, well conditioned, and exactly O(d)-equivariant. On modular arithmetic grokking, the method achieves 97.0% validation accuracy at epoch 20,000 vs baseline's 61.1%. On CIFAR-10 patches, it gains +8.98pp over 12 paired starts (t=60.6, 12/12). The step rule moves 24-40x less per step than identically shaped AdamW, and freezing the projections entirely costs only 0.28pp.
AI.conclusion: The ablation credits the whole gain to making the step scale free, and nothing measurable to the projector or equivariance. A negative result shows that gauge removal cannot motivate the method since a direction along which the loss is invariant carries no gradient at all.

title: Towards a Characterization of Microservice Architectures Generated by Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for software design tasks, yet little is known about the structure and coherence of the architectures they produce. In particular, how LLMs behave in Architecture-to-Architecture transformations remains insufficiently understood. This study empirically characterizes how LLMs generate microservice architectures from natural language descriptions of modular monoliths, focusing on structural and descriptive properties rather than architectural correctness. We conduct controlled experiments on two modular monolith systems, comparing zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies using GPT-based models from OpenAI and models from DeepSeek. Generated architectures are represented in a standardized CSV format and evaluated using normalized metrics capturing service granularity, inter-service communication patterns, communication density, service isolation, and responsibility descriptiveness. The results reveal systematic differences driven primarily by prompting strategy rather than model provider. Few-shot prompting consistently produces finer-grained decompositions with lower communication density and more detailed responsibility descriptions, whereas zero-shot prompting favors coarser and more tightly connected architectures. Rather than assessing architectural quality, this study provides an empirical baseline for understanding LLM behavior in text-driven Architecture-to-Architecture transformations, informing future research on generative design workflows and hybrid architectural reasoning in early-stage software modernization.

AI.tldr: This study empirically investigates how LLMs generate microservice architectures from natural language descriptions of modular monoliths, comparing zero-shot vs few-shot prompting strategies across OpenAI GPT and DeepSeek models. The key finding is that prompting strategy has a greater impact than model provider: few-shot prompting produces finer-grained, loosely-coupled architectures with detailed descriptions, while zero-shot favors coarser, tightly-connected designs.
AI.motivation: Despite the increasing use of LLMs for software design tasks, there is limited understanding of the structural and coherence properties of architectures they produce, particularly in Architecture-to-Architecture transformations. This gap hinders the effective use of LLMs in generative design workflows and software modernization.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on two modular monolith systems were conducted. The study compared zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies using GPT-based models from OpenAI and models from DeepSeek. Generated architectures were represented in a standardized CSV format and evaluated using five normalized metrics: service granularity, inter-service communication patterns, communication density, service isolation, and responsibility descriptiveness.
AI.result: The results reveal systematic differences driven primarily by prompting strategy rather than model provider. Few-shot prompting consistently produces finer-grained decompositions with lower communication density and more detailed responsibility descriptions, whereas zero-shot prompting favors coarser and more tightly connected architectures.
AI.conclusion: This study provides an empirical baseline for understanding LLM behavior in text-driven Architecture-to-Architecture transformations, rather than assessing architectural correctness. The findings inform future research on generative design workflows and hybrid architectural reasoning in early-stage software modernization.

title: PerSeM: Persistent Semantic Memory for Long-Horizon Open-Vocabulary UAV Mapping
summary: Open-vocabulary segmentation enables rich semantic perception for UAVs, but frame-wise predictions can remain temporally inconsistent across repeated observations and changing viewpoints. We present PerSeM, a training-free persistent semantic memory framework for long-horizon open-vocabulary UAV mapping. PerSeM associates frame-wise semantic observations with persistent world-space voxels and constructs a majority-based semantic memory, which is conservatively refined through history-preserving spatial refinement, trust-aware replay, and context-guided verification. Experiments on the Forest and UAVScenes benchmarks show that persistent 3D memory provides substantial gains in semantic correctness and temporal stability over frame-wise predictions. Beyond this strong persistent-memory baseline, PerSeM provides consistent additional improvements, improving both semantic accuracy and temporal stability across all five evaluated UAVScenes sequences. Analysis using regions identified independently of the final PerSeM predictions further shows that these gains are concentrated in semantically difficult and temporally unstable regions, where majority-based memory is most likely to remain uncertain. These results demonstrate that persistent 3D aggregation provides a strong foundation for long-horizon semantic mapping, while conservative refinement of uncertain memory states can provide additional improvements without retraining or additional neural-network inference.

AI.tldr: PerSeM is a training-free persistent semantic memory framework for long-horizon open-vocabulary UAV mapping that associates frame-wise semantic observations with persistent world-space voxels, using majority-based memory with conservative refinement through history-preserving spatial refinement, trust-aware replay, and context-guided verification.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary segmentation enables rich semantic perception for UAVs, but frame-wise predictions can remain temporally inconsistent across repeated observations and changing viewpoints. The key problem is maintaining semantic consistency over time for long-horizon UAV mapping tasks.
AI.method: PerSeM associates frame-wise semantic observations with persistent world-space voxels and constructs a majority-based semantic memory. This memory is conservatively refined through three mechanisms: (1) history-preserving spatial refinement, (2) trust-aware replay, and (3) context-guided verification. The approach is training-free and does not require retraining or additional neural-network inference.
AI.result: Experiments on the Forest and UAVScenes benchmarks show that persistent 3D memory provides substantial gains in semantic correctness and temporal stability over frame-wise predictions. PerSeM provides consistent additional improvements across all five evaluated UAVScenes sequences in both semantic accuracy and temporal stability. Gains are concentrated in semantically difficult and temporally unstable regions where majority-based memory is most likely to remain uncertain.
AI.conclusion: Persistent 3D aggregation provides a strong foundation for long-horizon semantic mapping. Conservative refinement of uncertain memory states can provide additional improvements without retraining or additional neural-network inference, making PerSeM a practical solution for real-world UAV applications.

title: Compositional Reasoning in Language Models under Reinforcement Learning Post-Training
summary: Compositional reasoning is critical for real-world problem solving: since training data is necessarily limited, models must generalize by composing learned skills in new ways. While post-training methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially improved the reasoning abilities of language models (LMs), their effects on compositional reasoning remain less well understood. We propose a dependency-graph framework to formalize compositional reasoning, yielding three levels of compositionality with increasing complexity. Empirically, we instantiate this framework with data-structure tasks, which provide deterministic reward computation and clear compositional structure. We find a consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry: decomposed-skill training does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, whereas composed-task training transfers more readily back to decomposed tasks. We provide theoretical explanation for this asymmetry, and further evaluate compositional generalization under length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to tasks requiring unseen skills. Finally, we present a pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks, showing preliminary evidence that the decomposed-to-composed asymmetry can extend to practical settings.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how post-training methods (like RL) affect compositional reasoning in language models. Using a dependency-graph framework with three compositionality levels, the study discovers a key asymmetry: training on decomposed skills fails to transfer to composed tasks, but training on composed tasks transfers well to decomposed ones. This finding is supported by theoretical analysis and experiments across length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and unseen skills transfer, with preliminary evidence from real-world tool-calling benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Training data is limited, so models must generalize by composing learned skills in new ways. While post-training methods like RL have improved reasoning abilities, their specific effects on compositional reasoning remain unclear. This gap motivated the researchers to formally study compositional reasoning and understand how different training approaches affect generalization.
AI.method: The researchers proposed a dependency-graph framework to formalize compositional reasoning with three levels of increasing complexity. They instantiated this framework using data-structure tasks, which offer deterministic rewards and clear compositional structure. They conducted experiments examining length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to unseen skills, plus a pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks.
AI.result: A consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry was found: decomposed-skill training does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, whereas composed-task training transfers more readily back to decomposed tasks. This asymmetry was also observed in preliminary real-world tool-calling benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The study provides both empirical evidence and theoretical explanation for the decomposed-to-composed asymmetry in compositional reasoning. This asymmetry appears to extend to practical settings, suggesting that training on composed tasks may be more effective for developing generalizable compositional reasoning skills than training on decomposed skills alone.

title: Machine-Learning Assessment of the Predictive Value of Inflammatory Biomarkers for Cognitive Impairment in an Older Hispanic Adult Cohort
summary: Small clinical tabular datasets require interpretable machine learning because deep learning is often impractical and ensemble models can be difficult to inspect. A key pitfall is that statistical significance does not necessarily imply predictive utility. Using data from the Panama Aging Research Initiative--Health Disparities (PARI-HD) cohort (n=165), we implemented a leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes (BNB/CNB) classifier. Within every training fold, each continuous predictor was reduced to a supervised chi-square-derived state, while income entered the model through a categorical likelihood. All data-dependent steps were performed within repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats. The demographic baseline achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.630 +/- 0.017. I-309 (CCL1) was the dominant incremental feature, increasing AUC by 0.110, with paired DeLong tests yielding p<0.05 in 100% of repeats. In the pre-specified primary analysis, I-309 produced a fixed-partition DeLong p=0.0018, with robustness assessed across 200 random partitions, where the median p-value was 0.0011. Within the exploratory family of 18 candidate markers, I-309 achieved a Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q=0.032 on the frozen partition and satisfied q<0.05 in 85% of random partitions, whereas no other marker demonstrated reliable incremental predictive value. Because the fitted model is an inspectable table of thresholds and class-conditional probabilities, these results identify I-309/CCL1 as an interpretable candidate feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment, pending external validation.

AI.tldr: This study addresses interpretable machine learning for small clinical tabular datasets, using a leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes classifier to predict cognitive impairment in 165 participants from the Panama Aging Research Initiative. The analysis identified I-309 (CCL1) as a significant incremental predictor, increasing AUC by 0.110 with robust statistical significance across multiple validation approaches.
AI.motivation: Small clinical tabular datasets require interpretable machine learning because deep learning is impractical and ensemble models are difficult to inspect. A key pitfall is that statistical significance does not necessarily imply predictive utility. The study aimed to identify interpretable features for cognitive impairment prediction while avoiding data leakage.
AI.method: A leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes (BNB/CNB) classifier was implemented. Within every training fold, continuous predictors were reduced to supervised chi-square-derived states, while income entered as categorical likelihood. All data-dependent steps were performed within repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats. Statistical significance was assessed using paired DeLong tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 200 random partitions.
AI.result: The demographic baseline achieved ROC-AUC of 0.630 ± 0.017. I-309 (CCL1) was the dominant incremental feature, increasing AUC by 0.110. Paired DeLong tests yielded p<0.05 in 100% of repeats. In the primary analysis, I-309 produced fixed-partition DeLong p=0.0018, with median p-value of 0.0011 across 200 random partitions. Among 18 candidate markers, I-309 achieved Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q=0.032 on the frozen partition and satisfied q<0.05 in 85% of random partitions. No other marker demonstrated reliable incremental predictive value.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies I-309/CCL1 as an interpretable candidate feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment, pending external validation. The inspectable model (table of thresholds and class-conditional probabilities) provides a transparent approach suitable for small clinical datasets where interpretability is crucial.

title: Assessing the Construct Validity of Object-Oriented, Class-Level Code Quality Metrics
comment: Accepted to the ESEIW 2026 ESEM - Technical Track
summary: Background: Code quality metrics are intended to measure latent properties of software source code. Although numerous code metrics have been proposed and used, their construct validity is rarely evaluated. Thus, the extent to which code metrics actually measure what they claim to measure is often unclear. Aim: Drawing from modern measurement theory, we investigate the construct validity of common class-level, object-oriented code quality metrics by identifying their factor structure using Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA). The metrics were extracted from the Apache Maven project by three software tools: Designite, JHawk, and Understand. The factor structure was later verified using Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) on 22 randomly selected open source projects meeting a predetermined eligibility criteria. Results: 24 code quality metrics that correspond to six constructs: Cohesion, In-Coupling, Out-Coupling, Size, Sub-Inheritance (related to subclasses), and Sup-Inheritance (related to superclasses) were revealed in the underlying factor structure. Ten metrics did not correspond to any known dimension of software quality and were removed in the EFA. Ten additional metrics exhibited low loadings in the CFA, suggesting their removal from the final measurement model. Size, Cohesion, Inheritance, and Coupling were the constructs retained, with subcategories identified for Inheritance and Coupling. Conclusions: Our results strongly support the construct validity of 24 code quality metrics. Coupling and Inheritance are revealed as multidimensional constructs, since they require measuring two different concepts, revealed as sub-categories in our analysis, and Complexity may be better explored in a multilevel model. Overall, our study demonstrates the value of applying modern measurement theory and latent variable modeling in validating software code quality metrics.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the construct validity of object-oriented code quality metrics using Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA). Researchers analyzed metrics from Apache Maven projects and 22 open-source projects, identifying 24 valid metrics across six constructs: Cohesion, In-Coupling, Out-Coupling, Size, Sub-Inheritance, and Sup-Inheritance.
AI.motivation: Code quality metrics are widely used to measure software properties, but their construct validity is rarely evaluated. It remains unclear whether these metrics actually measure what they claim to measure. This study addresses this gap by applying modern measurement theory to validate common class-level, object-oriented code quality metrics.
AI.method: The study used three software tools (Designite, JHawk, and Understand) to extract code metrics from Apache Maven projects. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) was conducted to identify the underlying factor structure. The factor structure was then verified using Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) on 22 randomly selected open-source projects meeting eligibility criteria.
AI.result: The analysis revealed 24 code quality metrics corresponding to six constructs: Cohesion, In-Coupling, Out-Coupling, Size, Sub-Inheritance (related to subclasses), and Sup-Inheritance (related to superclasses). Ten metrics were removed in EFA due to no known dimension association, and ten additional metrics showed low loadings in CFA, resulting in their removal from the final model. Size, Cohesion, Inheritance, and Coupling were retained as constructs, with subcategories identified for Inheritance and Coupling.
AI.conclusion: The results strongly support the construct validity of 24 code quality metrics. Coupling and Inheritance emerged as multidimensional constructs requiring separate measurements. The study demonstrates the value of applying modern measurement theory and latent variable modeling in validating software code quality metrics, while suggesting Complexity may be better explored in multilevel models.

title: A Multi-Modal Generative Model for Tomato Disease Leaves Understanding
comment: In submission to Computers and Electronics in Agriculture Journal
summary: Artificial intelligence for plant disease analysis has advanced from task-specific classifiers to multi-modal models capable of jointly interpreting visual and textual information. However, practical deployment in precision agriculture remains limited because most existing approaches treat disease understanding as isolated prediction tasks, failing to capture the complementary relationships among symptom recognition, severity assessment, and question-driven diagnostic reasoning. In tomato pathology, accurate interpretation of diseased leaves requires more than label prediction; it demands integrating visual symptoms with semantic context to support a comprehensive and explainable understanding. Here, we present SOLAR, a multimodal generative model that understands tomato disease spanning six question-answering tasks. SOLAR learns to align visual features with task-aware language representations by Fusion Expert module based on mixture-of-expert, enabling it to generate contextually relevant answers across diverse diagnostic tasks. By formulating tomato disease analysis as a generative Visual Question Answering (VQA) task, SOLAR provides a flexible framework that supports multi-task inference within a single model while improving performance and cross-task knowledge sharing. We evaluate SOLAR on $41,677$ images, including $216,209$ Question-Answering (QA) pairs to understand tomato leaf disease under both closed and open-ended QA settings. Experimental results show that SOLAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art vision-only, vision-language, and task-specific models across all tasks, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and multimodal reasoning. These findings highlight the potential of generative multimodal modeling as an effective direction for understanding of plant disease. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/EnalisUs/SOLAR.

AI.tldr: SOLAR is a multimodal generative model for comprehensive tomato disease understanding that formulates disease analysis as a Visual Question Answering task, supporting six QA tasks within a single model through a Fusion Expert module based on mixture-of-expert.
AI.motivation: Existing AI approaches for plant disease analysis treat disease understanding as isolated prediction tasks, failing to capture complementary relationships among symptom recognition, severity assessment, and diagnostic reasoning. Practical deployment is limited because current methods lack the ability to integrate visual symptoms with semantic context for comprehensive and explainable understanding.
AI.method: SOLAR learns to align visual features with task-aware language representations using a Fusion Expert module based on mixture-of-expert. The model formulates tomato disease analysis as a generative Visual Question Answering (VQA) task, enabling multi-task inference within a single model and cross-task knowledge sharing.
AI.result: Evaluated on 41,677 images with 216,209 QA pairs under both closed and open-ended QA settings, SOLAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art vision-only, vision-language, and task-specific models across all tasks, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Generative multimodal modeling represents an effective direction for plant disease understanding, offering a flexible framework that supports diverse diagnostic tasks within a single model while improving performance through cross-task knowledge sharing.

title: Safety Beyond the Interface: Detecting Harm via Latent States in Large Language Models
summary: Autonomous systems increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) yet the safety infrastructure surrounding these models introduces latency and compute overhead. This limits utility in resource-constrained, time-critical deployments. Existing external guardrail models remain blind to the model's internal workings, creating a fundamental assurance gap. We ask: does the model already know when the content is harmful? We extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts. Evaluated on WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0, our probes achieve F1 scores of 99%, 83%, and 84%, respectively competitive with 1000x larger guard models while cutting latency and compute costs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) trained on internal activations of LLaMA-3.1-8B to detect harmful prompts, achieving high F1 scores (99%, 83%, 84%) on three benchmarks while significantly reducing latency and compute costs compared to external guardrail models.
AI.motivation: Existing external guardrail models for LLM safety introduce latency and compute overhead, and remain blind to the model's internal workings, creating an assurance gap. The core question is whether the model itself already knows when content is harmful - if so, internal activations could be leveraged for efficient safety detection.
AI.method: The authors extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts. They evaluate on three datasets: WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0.
AI.result: The probes achieve F1 scores of 99% on WildJailbreak, 83% on Beavertails, and 84% on AEGIS 2.0. These results are competitive with guard models that are approximately 1000x larger, while significantly reducing latency and compute costs.
AI.conclusion: The model already knows when content is harmful - internal representations can be effectively used for safety detection. This approach offers a more efficient alternative to external guardrails, leveraging the model's own knowledge for harm detection with minimal overhead.

title: FCx: An algorithm for finding Feasible Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Counterfactual (CF) explanations identify changes that alter an input's classification. While existing methods produce realistic and low-cost CFs, they often fail to ensure feasibility, by suggesting non-constructive modifications or incompatible with future changes (e.g., changing an individual's race to secure a job offer). We introduce a refinement of CF explanations that explicitly enforces feasibility. Our approach is the first to efficiently generate CFs that are realistic, low-cost and feasible. We accommodate both hard feasible constraints, specified by domain knowledge users, and soft feasible constraints, inferred automatically via causal inference from the dataset. Our method, Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx), is based on a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) optimized with a multi-factor loss function. We measure the cost of a change based on the absolute change in values (proximity) as well as the number of features changed (sparsity) while realism is measured based on the LOF for density estimation, guaranteeing that CFs reside in densely populated regions. Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that our approach matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx), a method that addresses the feasibility problem in counterfactual explanations by using a modified VAE with multi-factor loss. It handles both hard constraints (domain knowledge) and soft constraints (causal inference) to generate CFs that are realistic, low-cost, and feasible.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods fail to ensure feasibility - they may suggest non-constructive modifications or changes incompatible with future changes (e.g., changing an individual's race). The authors identify this as a critical gap since unrealistic CFs are not actionable in practice.
AI.method: FCx uses a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) optimized with a multi-factor loss function. It incorporates: (1) hard feasible constraints specified by domain knowledge users, (2) soft feasible constraints inferred automatically via causal inference from the dataset. Cost is measured by proximity (absolute change in values) and sparsity (number of features changed). Realism is measured using Local Outlier Factor (LOF) for density estimation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that FCx matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.
AI.conclusion: FCx is the first method to efficiently generate counterfactual explanations that are simultaneously realistic, low-cost, and feasible. It successfully handles both user-specified hard constraints and automatically inferred soft constraints through causal inference.

title: Spotlights: Discovering Improvement Opportunities in Software Repositories
summary: Coding agents and evolutionary code-search systems can improve implementations once a target and evaluation criterion have been specified. Applying these methods to an existing software repository raises an earlier question: which implementation choices are worth investigating for a high-level engineering objective? We introduce \emph{optimization-opportunity discovery}, the repository-level task of identifying candidate source regions, explaining how they relate to the objective, and proposing possible changes. The task takes as input a repository, an engineering objective, and optional runtime evidence such as offline telemetry observations or profiles. It does not require the user to specify a defect, bottleneck, or code location. We present \emph{Spotlights}, a system that performs this task through logical repository mapping, successive agent reviews, and optional research linking candidates to relevant techniques. We evaluate Spotlights across model serving, document retrieval, blockchain ordering, and document processing. Across three cases, it recovers seven of nine expert-selected targets. In the reliability study, 70\% of the top ten candidates meet the stated correctness and severity thresholds. Across five repeated retrieval runs, 73.6\% of candidate occurrences have a matching source region in all five runs. Spotlights also rediscovers the target of a withheld retrieval optimization and connects it to a relevant tiling technique. In an implementation study, a discovered change reduces end-to-end page-processing runtime by 10.6\% while preserving measured output quality. These results establish optimization-opportunity discovery as a distinct and empirically evaluable step between a broad engineering objective and subsequent implementation and validation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces optimization-opportunity discovery - a repository-level task that identifies candidate source regions, explains their relationship to a high-level engineering objective, and proposes possible changes. The authors present Spotlights, a system that performs this task through logical repository mapping, successive agent reviews, and optional research linking candidates to relevant techniques.
AI.motivation: Current coding agents and evolutionary code-search systems require a specific target and evaluation criterion, but the earlier question of which implementation choices are worth investigating for a high-level engineering objective remains unaddressed. The motivation is to fill this gap by automatically discovering optimization opportunities in existing software repositories without requiring users to specify defects, bottlenecks, or code locations.
AI.method: Spotlights uses logical repository mapping, successive agent reviews, and optional research linking candidates to relevant techniques. The system takes as input a repository, an engineering objective, and optional runtime evidence (e.g., offline telemetry or profiles). It was evaluated across four domains: model serving, document retrieval, blockchain ordering, and document processing.
AI.result: Across three cases, Spotlights recovers seven of nine expert-selected targets. In the reliability study, 70% of the top ten candidates meet the stated correctness and severity thresholds. Across five repeated retrieval runs, 73.6% of candidate occurrences have a matching source region in all five runs. It also rediscovers the target of a withheld retrieval optimization and connects it to a relevant tiling technique. In an implementation study, a discovered change reduces end-to-end page-processing runtime by 10.6% while preserving measured output quality.
AI.conclusion: Optimization-opportunity discovery is established as a distinct and empirically evaluable step between a broad engineering objective and subsequent implementation and validation. This represents a new frontier in automated software optimization where systems can proactively identify worth-investigating implementation choices without explicit defect specifications.

title: Selective Cotton Boll Localization for Robotic Harvesting: Evaluation of Deep Learning Vision Models Under Field Conditions
summary: This study developed and evaluated a deep-learning-based perception framework for selective robotic cotton picking. The dataset contained 1,008 annotated field images collected using three cameras under varying natural lighting and weather conditions. Object-detection models from the YOLOv8 through YOLOv13 families were evaluated using their default configurations, while segmentation performance was assessed using YOLOv8-seg, YOLOv11-seg, YOLOv12-seg, the Segment Anything Model (SAM), SAMv2.1, FastSAM, and Grounded-SAM with the Recognize Anything Model (RAM). Among the detection models, GELAN-s achieved the most favorable balance between mean average precision (mAP) and inference speed, obtaining an mAP of 86.1%, precision of 81.6%, recall of 76.6%, and an F1-score of 79.0%, with an average inference time of 42.3 ms per image. Among the direct segmentation models, YOLOv12-m-seg provided the most favorable balance between AP@0.5 and FPS, achieving a segmentation AP@0.5 of 83.7% with an inference time of 20.4 ms per image. In the detection-prompted segmentation approach, bounding-box prompts generated by GELAN-s improved the localization of cotton bolls for SAM and SAMv2.1, while SAMv2.1 Tiny consistently outperformed FastSAM and Grounded-SAM with RAM. In the area-based evaluation against manually annotated segmentation masks, YOLOv12-m-seg achieved an $R^2$ value of 0.966, compared with 0.860 for GELAN-s + SAMv2.1 Tiny. Field experiments conducted using a UR5e robotic manipulator, a custom end-effector, and a ZED2i stereo camera further validated the effectiveness of the YOLOv12-m-seg model for real-time cotton boll detection, segmentation, and selective picking under varying confidence levels. These results demonstrate that YOLOv12-m-seg provides an efficient perception model for robotic cotton harvesting and has strong potential for field deployment.

AI.tldr: This study developed a deep learning perception framework for selective robotic cotton picking, evaluating YOLOv8-13 detection models and various segmentation models on 1,008 field images. YOLOv12-m-seg achieved the best segmentation performance with AP@0.5 of 83.7% and 20.4ms inference time, while GELAN-s was the best detection model with mAP 86.1%. Field validation using a UR5e robotic manipulator confirmed YOLOv12-m-seg's suitability for real-time robotic cotton harvesting.
AI.motivation: The research addresses the need for efficient perception systems in agricultural robotics, specifically for selective cotton picking. Manual cotton harvesting is labor-intensive, and existing robotic solutions lack reliable real-time detection and segmentation of cotton bolls under varying field conditions (natural lighting, weather).
AI.method: The study evaluated multiple detection models (YOLOv8-YOLOv13 families) using default configurations and segmentation models (YOLOv8-seg, YOLOv11-seg, YOLOv12-seg, SAM, SAMv2.1, FastSAM, Grounded-SAM with RAM). Dataset: 1,008 annotated field images from 3 cameras under varying conditions. Field validation used UR5e robotic manipulator, custom end-effector, and ZED2i stereo camera. Evaluation metrics included mAP, precision, recall, F1-score, AP@0.5, FPS, and R² for area-based segmentation comparison.
AI.result: Best detection: GELAN-s achieved mAP 86.1%, precision 81.6%, recall 76.6%, F1 79.0%, with 42.3ms inference. Best direct segmentation: YOLOv12-m-seg achieved AP@0.5 83.7% with 20.4ms inference. In detection-prompted segmentation, GELAN-s + SAMv2.1 Tiny performed best. Area-based evaluation: YOLOv12-m-seg achieved R²=0.966 vs 0.860 for GELAN-s + SAMv2.1 Tiny. Field experiments validated YOLOv12-m-seg for real-time detection, segmentation, and selective picking under varying confidence levels.
AI.conclusion: YOLOv12-m-seg provides the most efficient perception model for robotic cotton harvesting, offering the best balance between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. It demonstrates strong potential for field deployment in real-time selective cotton picking applications.

title: QVAC Genesis III: A Large-Scale, High-Quality Open Synthetic STEM Corpus for Efficient Language Model Pre-Training
summary: High-quality pre-training data is a critical bottleneck for educational and STEM-specific language models targeting edge AI and on-device deployment where token budgets are tightly constrained. While major organizations train ever-larger models on private corpora, the open ecosystem lacks STEM-focused synthetic datasets that deliver high per-token learning value efficiently for small models. To address this gap, we introduce QVAC Genesis III, a 191.43B-token, STEM-focused multi-domain synthetic corpus covering 19 domains across several difficulty levels and different educational styles. QVAC Genesis III is built via a dual generation strategy that performs targeted teacher distillation using a weak edge-scale student model as signal: the student's failures are converted into corrective explanations, while its successes are expanded into contrastive option-level reasoning over all answer choices. We further introduce an LLM-as-a-parser evaluation protocol that extracts final answers from free-form outputs and tracks both accuracy and answer validity. To validate the effectiveness of our QVAC Genesis III data, we conduct controlled from-scratch ablations with 1.7B-parameter models, showing that models trained with QVAC Genesis III consistently outperform both models trained with the open-source synthetic corpus Cosmopedia-v2 and the publicly released Cosmo-1B model across ARC, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU STEM benchmarks, achieving up to +28.57% on ARC-E and +21.35% on ARC-C, while reaching a Valid Answer Rate of up to 99.45%.

AI.tldr: QVAC Genesis III is a 191.43B-token STEM-focused synthetic corpus designed for training small language models (1.7B parameters) for edge AI deployment.
