Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers typically rely on predefined objectives, limiting their ability to adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical hybrid large language model (LLM)- multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture organized as a dual-loop structure. Specifically, an outer adaptation loop employs LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, and reconfigure objectives and resource priorities, while an inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game. A logistics-monitoring case study illustrates how the proposed framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies. Finally, we discuss key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical hybrid LLM-MARL architecture with dual-loop structure to enable autonomous adaptation of low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) for heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems. The outer loop uses LLM for game orchestration while the inner loop executes decentralized MARL policies.
AI.motivation: The coexistence of heterogeneous services in LAWNs creates strong coupling among mobility, connectivity, and shared resources, forming a dynamic non-cooperative game. Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers cannot adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities due to their reliance on predefined objectives.
AI.method: The proposed framework employs a hierarchical hybrid LLM-MARL architecture organized as a dual-loop structure: (1) Outer adaptation loop uses LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, and reconfigure objectives and resource priorities; (2) Inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game.
AI.result: A logistics-monitoring case study demonstrates that the framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LLM-MARL framework enables autonomous adaptation in LAWNs. Key challenges remain in achieving scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs for real-world deployment.

title: Compressed Active Subspaces for Scalable Bayesian Inference
summary: Active subspace methods provide a framework for quantifying predictive uncertainty in high-dimensional models by identifying and performing inference along parameter directions that have the greatest influence on the model output. However, the construction of active subspaces requires storing many full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes prohibitive as model size increases. We address this limitation by proposing Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS), a scalable approach that first maps the model parameters to a compressed space using a structured isometric embedding and then constructs the active subspace within this reduced parameterization. Our approach substantially reduces the memory required for active subspace construction and enables Bayesian inference for large models where standard active subspace methods become impractical. We demonstrate the scalability of CAS on neural networks of increasing size while maintaining predictive performance and robust uncertainty estimates.

AI.tldr: Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS) is a scalable method for quantifying predictive uncertainty in high-dimensional models by compressing parameters via structured isometric embedding before constructing active subspaces, reducing memory requirements and enabling Bayesian inference for large neural networks.
AI.motivation: Standard active subspace methods require storing many full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes prohibitive as model size increases, limiting their applicability to large models.
AI.method: CAS first maps model parameters to a compressed space using a structured isometric embedding, then constructs the active subspace within this reduced parameterization, substantially reducing memory requirements.
AI.result: CAS maintains predictive performance and robust uncertainty estimates while demonstrating scalability on neural networks of increasing size.
AI.conclusion: CAS enables Bayesian inference for large models where standard active subspace methods become impractical, offering a practical solution for uncertainty quantification in high-dimensional settings.

title: An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents
summary: Coding harnesses shape how autonomous coding agents translate model capabilities into long-horizon software-engineering performance, yet existing work typically evaluates harnesses as monolithic systems, leaving the effectiveness of individual components unclear. To enable component-level comparisons, we study this question with a lightweight coding harness whose execution loop is fixed while three components are varied: planning, action space, and context management. Across four models evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, we evaluate 176 matched settings spanning five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space. We find that: (1) Context management becomes increasingly valuable as the context-window budget tightens, with most of its benefit coming from preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Staging rule-based elision before LLM-based summarization provides the strongest overall efficiency among the context-management strategies, whereas making elided content recoverable adds machinery that models rarely use and yields no accuracy gain. (3) Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy. (4) Predefined tools improve performance for models with weaker bash proficiency, whereas bash-capable models can operate effectively with a bash-only interface and achieve substantially lower cost, especially on command-line-centric tasks. Trajectory-level analysis explains these effects: context management extends execution trajectories without substantially altering agent behavior, planning changes where trajectories stop, and the action space changes the granularity at which code is written. These findings inform model- and budget-aware harness design and provide a modular framework for evaluating future harness components.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates individual components of coding harnesses (planning, action space, context management) for autonomous coding agents by evaluating 176 settings across 4 models on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, revealing that context management prevents overflow failures, rule-based elision outperforms LLM summarization, planning serves different roles for weak vs. strong models, and predefined tools help weaker models while bash-capable models achieve lower cost.
AI.motivation: Existing work evaluates coding harnesses as monolithic systems, making it unclear how individual components contribute to performance. This limits understanding of what works and why, hindering optimal harness design for different models and budgets.
AI.method: The authors used a lightweight coding harness with fixed execution loop while varying three components independently: planning, action space, and context management. They evaluated 4 models across 176 matched settings, testing 5 context-management strategies, 4 context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Context management is most valuable under tight budget constraints, primarily preventing overflow failures; (2) Rule-based elision before LLM summarization outperforms other strategies, while making elided content recoverable adds unused machinery; (3) Planning shifts from accuracy scaffold (weaker models) to cost saver (stronger models) with minimal accuracy impact; (4) Predefined tools help models with weak bash proficiency, while bash-capable models achieve lower cost with bash-only interface. Trajectory analysis shows context management extends execution without changing behavior, planning changes termination points, and action space changes code granularity.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a modular framework for evaluating harness components and inform model- and budget-aware harness design. Researchers should consider model capabilities and budget constraints when selecting harness configurations.

title: Understanding and Exploiting Diagonal Attention Sparsity in Autoregressive Image Generation
summary: Autoregressive image generation has emerged as a paradigm for multimodal AI systems due to its compatibility with transformer-based LLM serving infrastructures. However, generating thousands of visual tokens per request makes decoding increasingly bottlenecked by KV cache accesses during attention computation. Sparse attention is particularly attractive for this workload because many visual generation applications tolerate moderate quality degradation in exchange for improved performance and efficiency. While sparse attention has been extensively explored for text-based LLM inference, it remains unclear whether its sparsity assumptions generalize effectively to autoregressive image generation. We present the first systematic characterization of attention sparsity in autoregressive image generation across diverse workloads and representative open-source models. Our analysis reveals several distinguishing properties, including a pronounced prefill-decode asymmetry, strong attention concentration on prompt and local tokens, and a unique diagonal attention sparsity pattern arising from the spatial locality of visual tokens. Motivated by these observations, we propose a diagonal-aware sparse attention mechanism that selectively skips KV entries along the diagonal attention direction within a recent window. Implemented on top of a GPU-based serving system using FlexGen, FlashAttention-2, and custom kernels, our approach achieves up to 3.1x throughput and 1.19x latency improvements with less than 2% quality degradation compared to dense inference.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic analysis of attention sparsity in autoregressive image generation, discovering unique patterns like prefill-decode asymmetry and diagonal sparsity. Based on these findings, the authors propose a diagonal-aware sparse attention mechanism that achieves up to 3.1x throughput improvement with less than 2% quality degradation.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive image generation creates thousands of visual tokens per request, making KV cache accesses during attention computation a major performance bottleneck. While sparse attention has been explored for text-based LLMs, it was unclear whether its assumptions generalize to autoregressive image generation workloads.
AI.method:
1) Systematic characterization of attention sparsity across diverse workloads and open-source models
2) Discovery of three key properties: prefill-decode asymmetry, attention concentration on prompt/local tokens, and diagonal attention sparsity pattern
3) Proposal of diagonal-aware sparse attention that selectively skips KV entries along the diagonal direction within a recent window
4) Implementation on GPU-based serving system using FlexGen, FlashAttention-2, and custom kernels
AI.result: Up to 3.1x throughput improvement and 1.19x latency improvement with less than 2% quality degradation compared to dense inference.
AI.conclusion: Sparse attention can be effectively applied to autoregressive image generation when designed with awareness of the unique diagonal sparsity pattern and prefill-decode asymmetry, enabling significant efficiency gains while maintaining acceptable quality.

title: Continual Enterprise World Model Discovery in Dynamic Systems
summary: In an enterprise system, updating one field can set another, create a record, or start an approval. These effects are produced by business rules that are not built into the platform but written by each organization and revised over time. An agent working in such a system cannot predict the result of its own actions without knowing these rules. We study continual enterprise world model discovery, where an agent starts without knowledge of these business rules and discovers them by interacting with records and observing the outcomes. From those observations it builds a world model, which it revises as the rules change. To evaluate this, we introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, built on a live ServiceNow environment with nine tables, 25 hidden rules and 600 evaluation actions. It presents four versions of the same enterprise world, with the tables and records held fixed while a rule is modified, then added, then removed, so that discovery, revision, extension and retirement are each tested in turn. Our Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) builds such a model and carries it from one world to the next. It predicts the effects of the hidden rules more accurately than looking them up for each question, the approach taken by prior work, by up to 8.98 IoU points, and it answers from its own model without querying the running system.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem of an AI agent working in enterprise systems (like ServiceNow) that contain hidden business rules written by organizations. These rules can update fields, create records, or trigger approvals. The authors propose a Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) that learns these business rules through interaction and maintains a world model that adapts as rules change over time.
AI.motivation: In enterprise systems, business rules are not built into the platform but written by each organization and revised over time. An agent cannot predict the result of its actions without knowing these rules. Prior work simply looked up rules for each question, which is inefficient. The authors aim to build a model that can discover, revise, extend, and retire rules as the enterprise world evolves.
AI.method: The authors introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, a benchmark built on a live ServiceNow environment with 9 tables, 25 hidden rules, and 600 evaluation actions. The benchmark has four versions of the same enterprise world where tables and records are fixed but rules are modified, added, or removed to test discovery, revision, extension, and retirement. Their Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) builds a world model by interacting with records, observing outcomes, and carrying the model from one world to the next.
AI.result: CDA predicts the effects of hidden rules more accurately than the lookup approach (used by prior work) by up to 8.98 IoU (Intersection over Union) points. It also answers questions from its own model without querying the running system.
AI.conclusion: The Continual Discovery Agent successfully discovers and maintains a world model of enterprise business rules through continual interaction. It outperforms prior lookup-based approaches and can adapt to rule changes (modifications, additions, and removals) while maintaining accuracy without requiring constant system queries.

title: FedFIbOS: Fisher Importance based Optimal Submodelling for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
summary: Heterogeneous federated learning requires clients with diverse computational capacities to collaboratively train a global model, where each client trains a capacity-constrained submodel. Existing methods select submodel parameters using heuristic importance measures---most prominently parameter magnitude---without theoretical justification for why these measures support convergence. We identify a fundamental gap: existing parameter selection criteria lack theoretical grounding in the convergence framework, partial client participation introduces additional estimation effects in the Fisher scores. We propose \textbf{FedFIbOS}: Fisher Importance-based Optimal Submodelling for heterogeneous federated learning, using Fisher Information in a principled criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error. %We formally establish when magnitude selection is equivalent to Fisher selection fail under non-IID heterogeneous federated learning. We theoretically formulate submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate and show that the raw Fisher top-$k$ rule implemented by FedFIbOS solves this surrogate under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition. The resulting method retains the convergence structure of the underlying masked federated optimization bound. Fisher scores are efficiently estimated from empirical diagonal Fisher information using squared gradients, enabling stable and adaptive parameter selection without additional optimization overhead. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings show FedFIbOS achieves ${\approx}10\%$ higher accuracy than the state of the art, with improvements becoming more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: FedFIbOS is a novel method for heterogeneous federated learning that uses Fisher Information for principled submodel parameter selection. It addresses the lack of theoretical justification in existing magnitude-based selection methods by deriving a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate. The method achieves approximately 10% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art approaches on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under non-IID settings, with improvements more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that existing parameter selection criteria in heterogeneous federated learning (e.g., magnitude-based selection) lack theoretical grounding in convergence frameworks. Additionally, partial client participation introduces estimation effects in Fisher scores. There was no principled criterion for selecting submodel parameters that could guarantee convergence.
AI.method: FedFIbOS uses Fisher Information as a principled selection criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error. The method: (1) Formulates submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate; (2) Shows the raw Fisher top-k rule solves this surrogate under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition; (3) Retains convergence structure of underlying masked federated optimization bound; (4) Efficiently estimates Fisher scores from empirical diagonal Fisher information using squared gradients, enabling stable and adaptive parameter selection without additional optimization overhead.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings show FedFIbOS achieves approximately 10% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods. The improvements become more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in challenging heterogeneous federated learning scenarios.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a theoretically grounded framework for submodel selection in heterogeneous federated learning using Fisher Information. The Fisher-based criterion is proven to solve a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate under specific conditions, and the method maintains convergence properties while significantly outperforming existing approaches, particularly in non-IID heterogeneous settings.

title: GAPrompt++: Multi-Granular Geometry-Aware Point Cloud Prompt for 3D Vision Model
summary: Pre-trained 3D vision models have substantially advanced point cloud analysis, yet adapting them to downstream tasks via full fine-tuning is computationally expensive and storage-intensive. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) offers a promising alternative by reducing both adaptation cost and storage burden. However, existing prompting-based approaches ignore the intrinsic geometric structures of point clouds, thereby limiting their adaptation capability. This limitation stems from their inability to encode both fine-grained geometric cues and coarse-grained structural semantics, as well as failing to propagate such information effectively through the model hierarchy. To address these challenges, we propose GAPrompt++, a multi-granular geometry-aware prompting method that provides richer geometric guidance for efficient 3D task adaptation. Specifically, we introduce a Point Shift Prompter that extracts multi-granular geometric features across different scales, enabling instance-specific geometric adjustments during adaptation. Next, a Keypoint Prompter adaptively generates point-level prompts to highlight local geometric saliency and fine-grained structural details. Furthermore, a Prompt Propagation mechanism injects these multi-granular geometric cues throughout the feature extraction hierarchy, strengthening the ability to capture essential geometric characteristics. Extensive experiments show that GAPrompt++ achieves state-of-the-art performance among prompting-based PEFT methods and even surpasses full fine-tuning across diverse benchmarks, while requiring less than 2\% trainable parameters. In addition, to address the saturation of existing evaluation datasets, we construct two more challenging benchmarks derived from 3D Gaussian Splatting and Multi-View Stereo reconstruction, offering diverse and realistic point cloud scenarios to promote future research.

AI.tldr: GAPrompt++ is a multi-granular geometry-aware prompting method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pre-trained 3D vision models on point cloud analysis tasks. It addresses the limitation of existing prompting-based approaches that ignore intrinsic geometric structures of point clouds.
AI.motivation: Existing prompting-based PEFT methods for 3D vision models ignore the intrinsic geometric structures of point clouds, limiting their adaptation capability. They cannot encode both fine-grained geometric cues and coarse-grained structural semantics, nor effectively propagate such information through the model hierarchy. Additionally, full fine-tuning is computationally expensive and storage-intensive.
AI.method: GAPrompt++ introduces three key components: (1) Point Shift Prompter - extracts multi-granular geometric features across different scales for instance-specific geometric adjustments; (2) Keypoint Prompter - generates point-level prompts to highlight local geometric saliency and fine-grained structural details; (3) Prompt Propagation mechanism - injects multi-granular geometric cues throughout the feature extraction hierarchy.
AI.result: GAPrompt++ achieves state-of-the-art performance among prompting-based PEFT methods and even surpasses full fine-tuning across diverse benchmarks, while requiring less than 2% trainable parameters. The authors also construct two new challenging benchmarks derived from 3D Gaussian Splatting and Multi-View Stereo reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: GAPrompt++ demonstrates that geometry-aware prompting can effectively adapt pre-trained 3D vision models with minimal parameters, outperforming both existing prompting methods and full fine-tuning. The new benchmarks address dataset saturation issues and provide diverse, realistic point cloud scenarios for future research.

title: SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership
comment: COLM 2026 Learning from Situated and Embodied Interaction Workshop
summary: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer not only what people need in the moment, but also how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. We introduce SimLife, a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Built on SimLife, SimLife-BP evaluates long-context pattern understanding: the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from weeks or months of everyday observations. The benchmark contains 106 episodes averaging 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days, and 1,439 question-answer pairs. Each task probes direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under different levels of rule hints. Evaluating frontier models and architectures, we find that current models often achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change. These findings suggest that long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents, while SimLife opens a broader space for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

AI.tldr: SimLife is a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with rich visual observations, action logs, and synthetic dialogues. SimLife-BP benchmark evaluates long-context pattern understanding (inferring latent behavioral rules from weeks/months of observations). Current models fail at comprehensive rule understanding, relying on frequency-based heuristics rather than causal reasoning.
AI.motivation: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer what people need, how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. This necessitates long-context pattern understanding capabilities.
AI.method: Built SimLife platform with visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Created SimLife-BP benchmark with 106 episodes (avg 15.49 hours, 38.57 in-game days) and 1,439 QA pairs testing direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under different rule hint levels.
AI.result: Current frontier models achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change.
AI.conclusion: Long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents. SimLife opens possibilities for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

title: SeetaPsych v1.0: An Open-source Computer Vision Toolkit for Behavior-based Psychological Measurement
summary: Automated visual analysis opens new avenues for behavior--based psychological measurement. Nevertheless, existing technological modules are typically scattered across task specific systems with heterogeneous interfaces and disparate deployment requirements. In this work, we present SeetaPsych v1.0, an open source, unified and extensible computer vision toolkit designed to extract psychologically relevant signals from facial images and/or face based videos. The current release encompasses four major core modules aiming at behavior--based physiological perception: unified face based emotion analysis (simultaneous facial expression recognition, facial action unit detection, and valence--arousal estimation), camera based heart rate estimation, screen point--of--gaze estimation, and scene gaze following. A suite of auxiliary preprocessing modules for human centric visual analysis is also included, comprising face detection, facial landmark detection, and head detection. These functionalities are encapsulated within a modular Pipeline/Runner architecture that automatically resolves attribute dependencies, constructs computation graphs, and support intermediate result sharing among modules. SeetaPsych provides standardized Python APIs to facilitate reproducible, large scale analyses, alongside an interactive WebUI for rapid, code--free method evaluation. Overall, SeetaPsych offers an integrated and accessible visual measurement platform for research in psychology, behavioral science, human computer interaction, and related fields.

AI.tldr: SeetaPsych v1.0 is an open-source, unified computer vision toolkit for extracting psychologically relevant signals from facial images and videos. It provides four core modules for emotion analysis, heart rate estimation, gaze tracking, and scene gaze following, along with preprocessing utilities, all within a modular Pipeline/Runner architecture with Python APIs and WebUI.
AI.motivation: Existing technological modules for visual behavior analysis are scattered across task-specific systems with heterogeneous interfaces and disparate deployment requirements, creating barriers for researchers in psychology and behavioral science.
AI.method: Developed a unified, extensible toolkit (SeetaPsych v1.0) with four major core modules: (1) unified face-based emotion analysis (simultaneous facial expression recognition, facial action unit detection, and valence-arousal estimation), (2) camera-based heart rate estimation, (3) screen point-of-gaze estimation, and (4) scene gaze following. Auxiliary preprocessing modules include face detection, facial landmark detection, and head detection. The system uses a modular Pipeline/Runner architecture that automatically resolves attribute dependencies, constructs computation graphs, and supports intermediate result sharing.
AI.result: SeetaPsych provides standardized Python APIs for reproducible, large-scale analyses and an interactive WebUI for code-free method evaluation. The toolkit integrates multiple psychological measurement capabilities into a single accessible platform.
AI.conclusion: SeetaPsych offers an integrated and accessible visual measurement platform for research in psychology, behavioral science, human-computer interaction, and related fields, addressing the fragmentation problem in existing behavioral analysis tools.

title: From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into vehicle voice assistants. But linking natural-language requests to vehicle functions creates a safety-critical authorization problem. Before executing a command, the system must choose whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger an emergency response, or make no tool call. To our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. We introduce a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy. We evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. Alignment ranges from 40.1% for Llama 3.2 3B to 89.1% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. The API-based models score between 83.2% and 89.1%, with no statistically significant differences among them. Even these models produce two to three False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios, and persistent errors remain in confirmation and manual-control decisions. A controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation increases alignment to 40.1% under the structured authorization policy, versus 28.2-29.2% under schema-only and generic-safety baselines, but it does not eliminate False Executes. Structured LLM decisions are therefore insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism, and deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

AI.tldr: A benchmark study evaluating LLM decision-making for vehicle voice assistants, focusing on pre-action authorization decisions across 202 scenarios. The study finds that even the best models (89.1% alignment) still produce dangerous false executions, concluding that LLMs alone cannot serve as safety mechanisms and require an independent enforcement layer.
AI.motivation: Prior evaluations of LLMs in vehicle voice assistants do not isolate the critical pre-action decision (authorization) across multiple factors: speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. This gap is safety-critical since executing wrong commands could cause harm.
AI.method: Created a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy. Evaluated two local open-weight models (Llama 3.2 3B and one other) and three API-based LLMs (including Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview). Used Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. Performed controlled ablation on Llama 3.2 3B comparing structured authorization policy vs schema-only and generic-safety baselines.
AI.result: Alignment ranged from 40.1% (Llama 3.2 3B) to 89.1% (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview). API-based models scored 83.2-89.1% with no statistically significant differences. Even top models produced 2-3 False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios. Persistent errors remained in confirmation and manual-control decisions. Structured policy ablation increased alignment to 40.1% (vs 28.2-29.2% for baselines) but did not eliminate False Executes.
AI.conclusion: Structured LLM decisions are insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism for vehicle control. Deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function. LLMs can assist but cannot replace explicit authorization checks.

title: A Policy Profile for Croissant: Refusal as a Property of the Dataset
comment: 23 pages. Reference implementation and conformance corpus archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22018156 and doi:10.5281/zenodo.22016112
summary: Croissant is the de facto machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets: JSON-LD over schema.org. Since version 1.1 it also carries data use conditions, recommending DUO and ODRL for them. What no version specifies is how any of them is evaluated: no decision procedure, no bound on evaluation cost, no outcome for a condition an implementation cannot evaluate, no record of what was checked, and nothing on composition with caller-side authority. We supply that half. An additive profile lets a dataset declare the operations it admits and the conditions under which it admits them, over a closed set of five operators whose decision procedure is given in full, so a gate decides from the descriptor alone and records what it checked. Two corpora evaluate it and their evidence is kept apart. Three descriptors that gated a real nf-core pipeline give the deployment result: decisions from a profile document match the gate's native descriptor record for record, stripping the layer leaves a valid Croissant document, and the added cost is 11.7 $μ$s against a 119 $μ$s decision. A corpus generated from the profile's grammar gives the breadth, covering every operator, refusal class and conformance clause. Across its valid cases, 552 complete decision records agree three ways -- native descriptor, profile terms, and the same policy as ODRL in usageInfo. The carrier is therefore not the contribution; the evaluation semantics is. Finally, caller-bound and data-bound policies range over non-overlapping state spaces, so neither permit set contains the other.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the missing evaluation semantics in Croissant, the de facto machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets. While Croissant (v1.1+) recommends DUO and ODRL for data use conditions, it lacks decision procedures, evaluation bounds, and outcome handling for unevaluable conditions. The authors propose an additive profile with a closed set of five operators and complete decision procedure, enabling gates to decide from descriptors alone and record checks.
AI.motivation: Croissant lacks evaluation semantics for data use conditions—it specifies what conditions to check but not how to evaluate them, with no decision procedure, cost bounds, handling of unevaluable conditions, or record of what was checked. This gap prevents reliable automated policy enforcement.
AI.method: The authors designed an additive profile over Croissant allowing datasets to declare admitted operations and conditions using five operators with a complete decision procedure. They evaluated using two corpora: (1) three real nf-core pipeline descriptors providing deployment results, and (2) a grammar-generated corpus covering all operators, refusal classes, and conformance clauses. 552 complete decision records were compared across native descriptor, profile terms, and ODRL usageInfo.
AI.result: Decisions from the profile document match the gate's native descriptor record for record. Stripping the profile layer leaves a valid Croissant document. Added cost is 11.7 μs against a 119 μs decision. Across valid cases, 552 decision records agree three ways (native descriptor, profile terms, and ODRL usageInfo). Caller-bound and data-bound policies range over non-overlapping state spaces, so neither permit set contains the other.
AI.conclusion: The evaluation semantics (not the carrier format) is the contribution. The profile enables decidable, recordable, and efficient policy evaluation while maintaining Croissant compatibility. The non-overlapping state spaces of caller-bound and data-bound policies suggest they must be handled separately in policy systems.

title: Recency Forcing: Bridging the Long-Horizon Gap in Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Autoregressive (AR) video generation degrades over long horizons due to an overlooked train-inference discrepancy we term KV eviction mismatch: models train on short clips where all context frames reside in the KV cache, but at inference, memory constraints force distant frames to be evicted from the KV cache - removing context the model was conditioned on. Rather than simulating eviction via context truncation - which discards temporal information the model still needs and degrades motion coherence - we keep the context but while progressively reducing the influence of distant frames, making their eventual eviction negligible. To guide this design, we introduce the positional response $R( Δ, \, t_{\text{denoise}})$, a perturbation-based sensitivity measure revealing that context influence decays steeply with temporal distance and varies systematically across denoising steps. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Recency Forcing, which applies a non-positive, timestep-dependent bias, termed Temporal Response Bias (TRB), on pre-softmax attention logits derived directly from $R$, closing the train-inference gap without modifying context length or training objectives. We further introduce Biased Attention Reparameterization (BAR), an exact reformulation that moves the bias outside the softmax, making TRB a standard FlashAttention call at zero overhead. Recency Forcing operates in both training-free mode and training-based mode. Experiments on VBench and VBench-Long demonstrate state-of-the-art long-horizon generation quality at no additional inference cost.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses a fundamental train-inference discrepancy in autoregressive video generation called "KV eviction mismatch." When models train on short clips all context fits in KV cache, but at inference memory constraints force distant frames to be evicted, degrading generation quality. The authors propose Recency Forcing, which progressively reduces influence of distant frames using a Temporal Response Bias (TRB) derived from a new positional sensitivity measure R(Δ, t_denoise). They also introduce BAR (Biased Attention Reparameterization) for zero-overhead implementation.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video generation degrades over long horizons due to a train-inference discrepancy: models train on short clips where all context frames remain in KV cache, but at inference memory constraints force distant frames to be evicted - removing context the model was trained on. Previous approaches simulate eviction via context truncation, which discards temporal information needed for motion coherence.
AI.method: 1) Introduce positional response R(Δ, t_denoise) - a perturbation-based sensitivity measure revealing that context influence decays steeply with temporal distance and varies across denoising steps. 2) Propose Recency Forcing - applies non-positive, timestep-dependent bias (TRB) on pre-softmax attention logits derived from R. 3) Introduce Biased Attention Reparameterization (BAR) - reformulates bias outside softmax for standard FlashAttention call at zero overhead. Operates in both training-free and training-based modes.
AI.result: State-of-the-art long-horizon generation quality on VBench and VBench-Long at no additional inference cost.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Recency Forcing method effectively closes the train-inference gap in autoregressive video generation by progressively reducing distant frame influence rather than discarding them entirely. The KV eviction mismatch is a fundamental issue that this work identifies and addresses through a principled approach based on positional sensitivity analysis. BAR enables zero-overhead implementation while maintaining compatibility with FlashAttention.

title: Reach or Solve? Attributing Agentic RL Gains with Checkpoint Handoffs
summary: Reinforcement learning now trains language-model agents that act over dozens of steps in live environments. The gains are large, and they are read as better decision-making. An agent in a closed loop writes its own inputs. Each observation follows from its own earlier actions, so the states it meets late in an episode are partly of its own making. An SFT checkpoint and an RL checkpoint are then scored from different states, even on identical tasks. Endpoint success mixes two changes: where the agent arrives, and what it does once it is there. Restricting the comparison to states both policies reach does not separate them. That restriction selects on an outcome, and in our data it flips the sign of the effect. We introduce checkpoint handoff, an evaluation protocol that clones a state one released checkpoint reached and hands it to another, with no retraining. Crossing a reacher role and a solver role over SFT and RL splits an endpoint gain into REACH and SOLVE. REACH is how often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success. SOLVE is how often it finishes from an identical cloned state. Across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines, the reacher by solver interaction is positive in all five conditions. An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction. Handoff asks only that one checkpoint's history can be replayed under another, so long-horizon evaluation can report arrival and completion beside endpoint success.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a methodological issue in evaluating reinforcement learning (RL) trained language model agents: endpoint success metrics conflate two distinct abilities—reaching good states (REACH) and solving from those states (SOLVE). The authors introduce "checkpoint handoff," an evaluation protocol that clones states between checkpoints to isolate these components, revealing that the interaction between reacher and solver roles is consistently positive across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of RL-trained language agents uses endpoint success, which conflates two separate capabilities: where the agent arrives and what it does once there. This makes it impossible to disentangle whether RL improves navigation/arrival or problem-solving abilities. The authors note that restricting comparisons to states both policies reach "selects on an outcome" and can even flip the sign of the effect, making proper evaluation impossible.
AI.method: The authors introduce "checkpoint handoff" - an evaluation protocol that clones a state one checkpoint reached and hands it to another checkpoint without retraining. They split endpoint performance into two components: (1) REACH - how often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success, and (2) SOLVE - how often it finishes from an identical cloned state. They test this across two benchmarks (ALFWorld) and two independently released pipelines, crossing a reacher role and solver role over SFT and RL checkpoints.
AI.result: Across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines, the reacher × solver interaction is positive in all five conditions. An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both REACH and SOLVE terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that checkpoint handoff is a valuable evaluation protocol that allows long-horizon evaluation to report arrival and completion separately from endpoint success. The method requires only that one checkpoint's history can be replayed under another, making it practical for evaluating RL-trained language agents. The consistent positive interaction across conditions suggests RL improves both navigation and problem-solving capabilities, rather than just one.

title: CoRe: Coherence and Relational Alignment for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP 2026)
summary: Direct forecasting has become a standard paradigm for multivariate time-series forecasting because it predicts the full future horizon in a single pass. However, its training objective is often still decomposed into pointwise errors such as MSE. Such objectives provide stable supervision, but they do not explicitly preserve the structure of the future trajectory: temporal coherence within each variable and relational consistency across variables can both be weakened. We propose CoRe, a model-agnostic learning objective for direct multivariate forecasting. CoRe replaces pointwise supervision with two output-space constraints: a frequency coherence loss that aligns predicted and target spectra, and a low-rank relational graph loss that matches sampled pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. The resulting objective introduces no trainable parameters and can be applied to existing forecasting backbones by changing only the loss. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that CoRe improves strong baselines, compares favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings overall consistently.

AI.tldr: CoRe proposes a model-agnostic learning objective for direct multivariate time-series forecasting that replaces pointwise supervision (like MSE) with two output-space constraints: frequency coherence loss and low-rank relational graph loss, to preserve temporal coherence within variables and relational consistency across variables.
AI.motivation: Current direct forecasting methods use pointwise errors (MSE) which fail to preserve the structure of future trajectories - specifically temporal coherence within each variable and relational consistency across variables. The training objective does not explicitly maintain the holistic structure of the future horizon.
AI.method: CoRe introduces two output-space constraints: (1) Frequency coherence loss that aligns predicted and target spectra in the frequency domain, and (2) Low-rank relational graph loss that matches sampled pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. The method is model-agnostic with no trainable parameters, applied by changing only the loss function.
AI.result: Experiments on standard benchmarks show that CoRe improves strong baselines, compares favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings.
AI.conclusion: CoRe provides a generally effective improvement for multivariate time-series forecasting by explicitly preserving trajectory structure through frequency and relational constraints, without requiring architectural changes to existing forecasting models.

title: Federated Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserving Kidney Stone Detection
summary: Recent innovations in deep learning have significantly enhanced the diagnosis of medical images, although they are based on the use of centralized data storage that pose severe threats to patient privacy and medical data security. To address this issue, this research proposes a Federated Learning (FL) model that is coupled with an optimized YOLOv8 network to detect the kidney stones on a computed tomography (CT) image and at the same time, protect privacy of the patients. The suggested system can help various medical organizations to jointly train a common model without exchanging the information about the patients. This is to ensure that data protection laws like GDPR and HIPAA are adhered to. The residual feature fusion and DropBlock regularization among other architectural improvements are also included in YOLOv8 to enhance detection robustness and minimize overfitting. Experimental analysis carried out on a distributed CT dataset demonstrated that the federated YOLOv8 model has a mAP at 50 of 0.733 and is able to keep the data confidential. Moreover, its lean design facilitates fast edge deployment and real-time inference across a clinical setting. Altogether, these findings indicate that Federated Learning is a safe and efficient solution to AI-assisted diagnosis in contemporary healthcare when combined with the use of sophisticated object detection models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a privacy-preserving Federated Learning system combined with an optimized YOLOv8 network for automatic kidney stone detection in CT images, achieving mAP@50 of 0.733 while keeping patient data confidential and complying with data protection regulations.
AI.motivation: The motivation addresses a critical challenge in medical AI: while deep learning has improved medical image diagnosis, traditional centralized data storage poses severe threats to patient privacy and data security. There is a need for AI systems that can train on distributed medical data without exposing sensitive patient information, while complying with regulations like GDPR and HIPAA.
AI.method: The proposed method combines Federated Learning (FL) with an optimized YOLOv8 network. The YOLOv8 architecture is enhanced with residual feature fusion and DropBlock regularization to improve detection robustness and reduce overfitting. The FL framework enables multiple medical organizations to jointly train a model without sharing patient data.
AI.result: Experimental results on a distributed CT dataset demonstrate that the federated YOLOv8 model achieves a mAP@50 of 0.733 while maintaining data confidentiality. The lean design enables fast edge deployment and real-time inference suitable for clinical settings.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that Federated Learning combined with sophisticated object detection models like YOLOv8 provides a safe and efficient solution for AI-assisted diagnosis in modern healthcare, effectively balancing diagnostic accuracy with privacy protection requirements.

title: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
summary: Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To evaluate ScientistTwo's capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result, ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/

AI.tldr: ScientistTwo is a fully autonomous multi-agent AI framework that can independently conduct scientific research - from problem formulation to hypothesis generation, experimentation, methodology refinement, and peer-review validation. It aims to be an autonomous scientific pioneer that can push the frontiers of human discovery.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to achieve the ultimate vision of AI in science: problem-driven autonomous research where given a fundamental challenge, the AI can independently navigate the scientific landscape, identify theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expand the knowledge frontier.
AI.method: ScientistTwo is a multi-agent framework that coordinates specialized agents to: (1) establish state-of-the-art baselines, (2) formulate novel hypotheses, (3) orchestrate end-to-end discovery cycles, (4) conduct experiments with diverse datasets and metrics, (5) perform automated ablation studies for methodology refinement, and (6) validate findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine.
AI.result: ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents.
AI.conclusion: ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. It demonstrates the feasibility of fully autonomous AI-driven scientific research.

title: Conservation Buys Stability and Factoring Buys Counterfactuals in Physical World Models
summary: A learned simulator can reproduce its training conditions accurately yet fail in two distinct ways once those conditions change. Over long rollouts, small errors accumulate until the trajectory drifts away from physically plausible behavior; under an intervention on a physical parameter, the model may continue to follow the law seen during training rather than the intervened one. We show that these two failures require different structural remedies. Evolving a learned energy with a symplectic integrator preserves the geometry of the conservative dynamics and keeps rollouts bounded and physically meaningful for up to $100\times$ the training horizon, while equal-capacity predictors, an energy-regularized predictor, and a tuned neural ODE diverge. By contrast, encoding the physical coupling through an explicit linear factorization enables the model to follow a never-seen sign of that coupling, whereas an unrestricted parameterization remains locked to the training law. Crucially, the two mechanisms are separable: removing the structure responsible for long-horizon stability leaves counterfactual transfer intact, while removing the factorized coupling destroys counterfactual transfer without eliminating stability. This double dissociation, established with matched controls that remove or replace one structural component at a time, persists beyond the headline three-body system and remains visible when the physical state must be inferred from pixels rather than provided directly. The result is a concrete design principle for physical world models: long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization arise from distinct structural commitments, and each can be imposed deliberately without requiring the other.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses two distinct failure modes in learned physics simulators: (1) error accumulation over long rollouts causing physically implausible behavior, and (2) inability to generalize to changed physical laws under intervention. The key insight is that these require separate structural remedies: symplectic integration with learned energy for long-horizon stability, and linear factorization for counterfactual transfer. These mechanisms are demonstrably separable (double dissociation).
AI.motivation: Learned simulators can accurately reproduce training conditions but fail in two distinct ways when conditions change: (1) over long rollouts, small errors accumulate causing drift from physically plausible behavior, and (2) under intervention on physical parameters, the model follows the training law rather than the intervened one. This raises the question of whether these failures require different structural remedies.
AI.method: The study uses matched controls to isolate the effect of each structural component: (1) A learned energy function with symplectic integrator to preserve conservative dynamics geometry, (2) Linear factorization to encode physical coupling explicitly. The experiments use the three-body system as the primary testbed, with additional tests using pixel-based state inference.
AI.result: Symplectic integration with learned energy maintains bounded, physically meaningful rollouts for up to 100× the training horizon, while equal-capacity predictors, energy-regularized predictors, and neural ODEs all diverge. Linear factorization enables the model to follow never-seen signs of physical coupling, whereas unrestricted parameterizations remain locked to training laws. A key finding is the double dissociation: removing symplectic structure eliminates long-horizon stability but preserves counterfactual transfer, while removing factorized coupling destroys transfer without eliminating stability.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization arise from distinct structural commitments in learned physical world models. Each can be imposed deliberately without requiring the other. This provides a concrete design principle: use symplectic integrators with learned energy for temporal stability, and linear factorization for interventional generalization.

title: Region-Level Policy Optimization for Fine-grained MLLM Perception
summary: Fine-grained visual perception in MLLMs is commonly improved by raising the resolution, but the added visual tokens inflate vision-encoding and language-model prefilling costs. We show that the two operations underlying fine-grained perception, localizing the region of interest (RoI) and recognizing its content, have different resolution requirements. In a controlled diagnostic, localization tolerates roughly 3 to 4 times stronger token compression than recognition, which motivates localizing from a coarse view and concentrating resolution on the selected evidence. Decoding coordinates with the MLLM can be trained end-to-end from answers, but costs a full model pass per query and depends on grounding ability. A lightweight proposal network distilled from the model's attention is fast, but inherits the noise of its attention targets. The RoI from the proposal network reaches the answer through a discrete region choice, so its faithfulness to the answer cannot supervise the network. We therefore optimize the proposal network with region-level reinforcement learning, which we call Vision-RL2. It treats coherent regions as actions, and a frozen MLLM reader scores each one by how its removal changes the answer likelihood. Complementary subtractive and additive objectives suppress distracting proposals and recover missing evidence, updating only the predictor without region annotations, response sampling, or reasoning trajectories. The refined proposal further enables a sparse encoding that magnifies evidence and excludes background tokens. Across six fine-grained benchmarks and four MLLM backbones, Vision-RL2 improves accuracy over the base model at every token budget and surpasses its largest-budget accuracy with about 4 times fewer visual tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/YuHengsss/VisionRL2 .

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Vision-RL2, a region-level reinforcement learning method that optimizes a lightweight proposal network for fine-grained visual perception in Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs). It enables localizing regions of interest from coarse views while concentrating resolution on selected evidence, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with 4x fewer visual tokens.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained visual perception in MLLMs typically requires higher resolution, which increases visual token costs for encoding and language model prefilling. The authors observe that localization and recognition have different resolution requirements - localization can tolerate 3-4x stronger token compression than recognition. This motivates a strategy of localizing from coarse views and focusing resolution on selected evidence.
AI.method: The paper proposes Vision-RL2 with three key components: 1) A lightweight proposal network distilled from the model's attention for fast region selection; 2) Region-level reinforcement learning that treats coherent regions as actions, where a frozen MLLM scores each region by how its removal changes answer likelihood; 3) Complementary subtractive and additive objectives to suppress distracting proposals and recover missing evidence. The refined proposals enable sparse encoding that magnifies evidence while excluding background tokens.
AI.result: Vision-RL2 improves accuracy over the base model at every token budget across six fine-grained benchmarks and four MLLM backbones. It surpasses the largest-budget accuracy with approximately 4 times fewer visual tokens.
AI.conclusion: The method successfully addresses the token-efficiency challenge in fine-grained visual perception by decoupling localization from recognition resolution requirements. Region-level reinforcement learning effectively trains the proposal network without region annotations, response sampling, or reasoning trajectories, achieving superior accuracy with significantly reduced computational costs.

title: Replan, Repair, or Edit? A Unified Empirical Evaluation of Travel Agents for Itinerary Revision under Resource Disruptions
summary: Travel-planning agents generate itineraries that may become infeasible after acceptance because of flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, or attraction closures. Revising these itineraries involves full replanning, classical plan repair, and LLM-based travel-agent revision, whose differing task formulations and evaluation protocols hinder comparison. We conduct a systematic empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: 500 single-disruption cases, including feasible and infeasible instances, and 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. We compare LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and an iTIMO local-revision adapter across effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost. LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest observed compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched that configuration's single-disruption overall success, while preserving substantially more of the accepted itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, the evaluated LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference, and the iTIMO adapter consumed substantially more tokens. The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic empirical comparison of three approaches for revising infeasible travel itineraries: LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and iTIMO local-revision adapter. The study uses 500 single-disruption and 200 compound-disruption cases to evaluate effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost.
AI.motivation: Travel-planning agents generate itineraries that may become infeasible after acceptance due to disruptions (flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, attraction closures). Existing revision methods (full replanning, classical plan repair, LLM-based revision) have different task formulations and evaluation protocols, making comparison difficult. This study aims to provide systematic empirical comparison to guide practical implementation.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a systematic empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: (1) 500 single-disruption cases with feasible and infeasible instances, and (2) 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. They compared three approaches: LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and iTIMO local-revision adapter across three dimensions: effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost.
AI.result: LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched LLM-Z3's single-disruption success rate while preserving substantially more of the original itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference, and iTIMO consumed substantially more tokens.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within evaluated settings. Key trade-offs include: full replanning maximizes feasibility recovery but changes more of the original itinerary; hierarchical and local repair methods preserve more commitments but may have lower success rates on complex disruptions.

title: Opinion Dynamics-based Coalition Formation for Federated Learning in Heterogeneous IoT Systems
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving, on-device training across heterogeneous Internet-of-Things (IoT) deployments such as smart-city water-metering networks, where each smart meter observes a household-specific consumption time series. Under such statistical heterogeneity, the standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) aggregation averages dissimilar local models into a single global model that may fail to capture client-specific patterns. We address this by forming client coalitions directly in the local-weight space and aggregating at the coalition level. Extending a prior weight-driven coalition-formation scheme, we model coalition formation as a Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process acting on the local weights, and develop variants of the HK interaction based on Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria. The framework is applied to short-term water-consumption forecasting with local Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models and evaluated against FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAvg with Euclidean-distance or cosine-similarity coalition formation. Experiments on a real smart-metering dataset of water consumption show that the proposed HK-based coalition formation produces stable, endogenous coalition structures within at most ten inner iterations, incurs no additional client-side computation or communication compared to FedAvg, and reduces the average MAE by up to 54% relative to FedAvg, 39% relative to FedProx, and 24% relative to Per-FedAvg, while achieving the highest global accuracy (83-85%).

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of statistical heterogeneity in federated learning for IoT deployments (smart-city water-metering networks) by proposing a coalition-formation approach using Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion dynamics. The method forms client coalitions in local-weight space and aggregates at the coalition level, achieving up to 54% MAE reduction compared to FedAvg and 83-85% global accuracy.
AI.motivation: Federated Averaging (FedAvg) fails under statistical heterogeneity because it averages dissimilar local models into a single global model that cannot capture client-specific patterns. This is particularly problematic in IoT deployments like smart-city water-metering networks where each smart meter observes household-specific consumption patterns.
AI.method: The paper extends a prior weight-driven coalition-formation scheme by modeling coalition formation as a Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process acting on local weights. Two variants are developed based on Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria. The framework is applied to short-term water-consumption forecasting using local Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models.
AI.result: The proposed HK-based coalition formation produces stable, endogenous coalition structures within at most ten inner iterations. It incurs no additional client-side computation or communication compared to FedAvg. The average MAE is reduced by up to 54% relative to FedAvg, 39% relative to FedProx, and 24% relative to Per-FedAvg, while achieving the highest global accuracy (83-85%).
AI.conclusion: The HK-based coalition formation approach effectively addresses statistical heterogeneity in federated learning for IoT applications. It provides a practical solution that maintains communication efficiency while significantly improving forecasting accuracy for water consumption prediction.

title: STAR: Structure-aware Test-time Adaptation for diffusion-based light field Reconstruction
summary: Light field (LF) reconstruction from limited and noisy focal stack (FS) measurements is a highly ill-posed inverse problem. Although the LF-to-FS imaging geometry is fixed for a given optical setup, LF spatial-angular structure---including within-view spatial details, cross-view angular dependencies, and disparity across views---varies across scenes. Consequently, a fixed pre-trained prior may not optimally capture the spatial-angular structure of each test LF. We propose Structure-aware Test-time Adaptation for diffusion-based light field Reconstruction (STAR), the first test-time adaptation framework for reconstructing an LF from FS. For each test LF, STAR freezes a pre-trained diffusion prior and fits three lightweight adapters to the observed FS to jointly adapt the three components of the LF's spatial-angular structure. STAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both two- and three-focal-sheet settings, with shorter inference times than those with test-time parameter updates.

AI.tldr: STAR is the first test-time adaptation framework for reconstructing light fields (LF) from focal stack (FS) measurements. It uses three lightweight adapters to adapt a pre-trained diffusion prior to the specific spatial-angular structure of each test LF, outperforming state-of-the-art methods with faster inference times.
AI.motivation: Light field reconstruction from limited and noisy focal stack measurements is a highly ill-posed inverse problem. Existing methods use fixed pre-trained priors that cannot optimally capture the varying spatial-angular structure (within-view spatial details, cross-view angular dependencies, and disparity across views) of different test light fields.
AI.method: The proposed STAR framework freezes a pre-trained diffusion prior and fits three lightweight adapters to the observed FS measurements. These adapters jointly adapt the three components of the LF's spatial-angular structure: within-view spatial details, cross-view angular dependencies, and disparity across views.
AI.result: STAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both two- and three-focal-sheet settings while achieving shorter inference times than methods with test-time parameter updates.
AI.conclusion: This work introduces the first test-time adaptation framework for LF reconstruction from FS, demonstrating that adapting to each test sample's unique structure significantly improves reconstruction quality while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks but exhibit systematic inefficiency: they often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches based on uniform length penalties or rigid routing incur an efficiency tax, trading reduced computation on easy instances for accuracy loss on hard instances. We formulate efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem and propose When2Think, a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that dynamically allocates computation based on problem difficulty. Our method introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that leverages pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. When2Think encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances, thereby learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think). Experiments on mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: on AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model, and on AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

AI.tldr: When2Think is a post-training framework that enables Large Reasoning Models to dynamically allocate computation based on problem difficulty, learning when to use quick direct answering (System 1/NoThink) versus extended reasoning (System 2/Think).
AI.motivation: Large Reasoning Models suffer from systematic inefficiency: they overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches using uniform length penalties or rigid routing trade accuracy loss on hard instances for reduced computation on easy ones, creating an undesirable efficiency tax.
AI.method: The paper proposes Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that uses pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. The method encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances.
AI.result: On AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model. On AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: When2Think successfully learns instance-adaptive computation allocation, achieving improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs by dynamically deciding when to engage System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think) reasoning based on problem difficulty.

title: Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling: A Specification and Design Guide for Contrast-Based Multi-Armed Bandits
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables in the main text; 2 figures and 3 tables in the supplement. Reference implementation at https://github.com/sulgik/orts
summary: Batched multi-armed bandits update on a service's own schedule, and the usual implementation carries each arm's absolute reward rate from one update to the next. When the shared level moves between batches, that memory goes stale even though the comparisons between arms may not have. Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS) instead carries the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and fits the common level afresh in every batch, marginalizing it out. This paper specifies that update, places it inside a Bayesian bandit agent with two controls, decay for how much past evidence survives an update and aggressiveness for how sharply belief becomes allocation, and evaluates it against absolute-rate memory. Across 86 public A/B series the level varies about twenty-five times more than the contrast. In prespecified synthetic environments a moving level costs absolute-rate memory five times the regret and leaves the best arm below a majority of traffic in 7 of 20 runs, against none for OR-TS. In a policy simulation built from 71 real experiments, where the contrasts are too small to resolve, expected-click differences stay within 0.1% for 58 of them, yet contrast memory still ends on the better arm more than twice as often. Where the contrasts themselves move, the bet fails, and that case is reported too.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS), a novel approach for batched multi-armed bandits that addresses the problem of stale memory when the shared reward level changes between batches. OR-TS carries the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts rather than absolute reward rates, fitting the common level fresh in each batch. The method is evaluated against standard absolute-rate memory across 86 public A/B series, synthetic environments, and a policy simulation from 71 real experiments.
AI.motivation: The standard implementation of batched multi-armed bandits carries each arm's absolute reward rate from one update to the next. When the shared level (common baseline) moves between batches, this memory becomes stale, even though the comparisons between arms may still be valid. This problem leads to significant regret when the underlying reward level is non-stationary.
AI.method: The paper proposes Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS), which carries the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts instead of absolute rates. This approach fits the common level afresh in every batch and marginalizes it out. The method is implemented in a Bayesian bandit agent with two controls: (1) decay - controlling how much past evidence survives an update, and (2) aggressiveness - controlling how sharply belief becomes allocation. Evaluation is performed across 86 public A/B series, synthetic environments with moving levels, and a policy simulation built from 71 real experiments.
AI.result: In synthetic environments with a moving level, absolute-rate memory incurs five times the regret compared to OR-TS, and the best arm falls below a majority of traffic in 7 out of 20 runs (vs. none for OR-TS). Across 86 public A/B series, the level varies about twenty-five times more than the contrast. In the policy simulation from 71 real experiments (where contrasts are too small to resolve), expected-click differences stay within 0.1% for 58 experiments, yet contrast memory still ends on the better arm more than twice as often as absolute-rate memory.
AI.conclusion: OR-TS significantly outperforms absolute-rate memory when the shared reward level moves between batches, reducing regret by up to 5x. However, when the contrasts themselves move (not just the level), the method fails.
