Tested 5 geometric and learned localization systems under native sensing configurations.
AI.result: Stock checkpoints (official released weights) perform near zero on SlugTrails (max 0.004 R@1m30°). Fine-tuning on SlugTrails improves every trainable family on all tasks (e.g., F³Loc: 0.0→0.141 single-frame, 0.03→0.66 sequential). Cross-dataset generalization on LaMAR also improves (F³Loc sequential R@1m: 0.048→0.143, UnLoc: 0.063→0.127). Train-from-scratch underperforms fine-tuning from stock weights, indicating localization is limited by data rather than architecture.
AI.conclusion: Floor plan localization is currently limited by indoor data availability rather than architecture. Fine-tuning on large-scale benchmarks like SlugTrails enables effective transfer to new environments. The dataset, protocols, and tools are released publicly.

title: MetaRTL: Meta-path Attention Enhanced Relational Table Learning
summary: Relational table learning has gained increasing attention with the widespread use of relational databases. Existing methods typically rely on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, leading to high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases. We propose MetaRTL, a two-stage framework for scalable and expressive relational table learning. In the first stage, MetaRTL obtains initial table embeddings via lightweight pre-training. In the second stage, it performs non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module, MetaAttn. By shifting computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation, MetaRTL captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: MetaRTL is a two-stage framework for relational table learning that combines lightweight pre-training for initial embeddings with non-parametric message passing and attention-based meta-path aggregation, achieving scalable and expressive performance on relational databases.
AI.motivation: Existing relational table learning methods rely on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, which suffer from high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases, necessitating a more efficient approach.
AI.method: MetaRTL employs a two-stage framework: (1) lightweight pre-training to obtain initial table embeddings, and (2) non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module called MetaAttn.
AI.result: Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of MetaRTL.
AI.conclusion: MetaRTL successfully captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency by shifting computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation, offering a scalable solution for relational table learning.

title: AURA: Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis for Email Threat Detection
summary: Email spam and phishing attacks remain a critical security threat. Adversaries increasingly exploit large language models to craft contextually convincing malicious messages, and existing spam detection systems often struggle to keep pace. Generalization across diverse and evolving attack scenarios is limited, which reduces effectiveness once these systems are deployed in practice. This paper introduces Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis (AURA), a multimodal email threat detection system that analyzes both the content of an email and its embedded URLs. AURA is built around two layers: the first quantifies prediction uncertainty from a URL classifier, and only ambiguous messages are escalated to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis. The system is evaluated on eight heterogeneous training corpora together with two held-out real-world corpora spanning a decade of adversarial campaigns. AURA reaches a macro F1-score of 0.9858 in-distribution, and on NazPhish-Eval and GuenterTrap-Eval it maintains 0.9502 and 0.9436, respectively, which is evidence of robust generalization under genuine distribution shift.

AI.tldr: AURA (Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis) is a multimodal email threat detection system that uses a two-layer architecture: first quantifying prediction uncertainty from a URL classifier, then escalating ambiguous messages to a fine-tuned transformer for semantic analysis. It achieves 0.9858 macro F1 in-distribution and maintains robust performance (0.9502 and 0.9436) on two held-out real-world corpora, demonstrating strong generalization under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Email spam and phishing attacks remain a critical security threat. Adversaries increasingly exploit large language models to craft contextually convincing malicious messages, and existing spam detection systems struggle to keep pace. Current systems have limited generalization across diverse and evolving attack scenarios, reducing effectiveness when deployed in practice.
AI.method: AURA employs a two-layer multimodal architecture: (1) A URL classifier quantifies prediction uncertainty for each email's embedded URLs; (2) Only ambiguous messages (those with high uncertainty) are escalated to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis. The system was evaluated on eight heterogeneous training corpora combined with two held-out real-world corpora spanning a decade of adversarial campaigns.
AI.result: AURA achieves a macro F1-score of 0.9858 in-distribution. On the held-out NazPhish-Eval corpus, it maintains 0.9502 F1-score, and on GuenterTrap-Eval it achieves 0.9436 F1-score, demonstrating robust generalization under genuine distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: The two-layer uncertainty-routed approach effectively handles the challenge of generalization across diverse and evolving attack scenarios. By using uncertainty quantification to selectively route ambiguous cases to more computationally expensive semantic analysis, AURA maintains high detection performance while adapting to novel adversarial campaigns that differ from training data.

title: A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents
comment: Preprint of a manuscript completed in November, 2025
summary: LLM-based GUI agents increasingly act on behalf of users in digital environments that were designed with human users in mind. These graphical user interfaces were designed to support, but also deliberately steer, the behaviour and decisions of users. While behavioural biases in the textual outputs of LLMs are well-documented, far less is known about how such influence operates when models act as agents that perceive interfaces and execute decisions---and, in particular, whether the reasoning capabilities increasingly built into these agents make them more robust to it. Drawing on Dual-Process Theory, we empirically investigate whether LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges, and how their reasoning configuration moderates this susceptibility. In a randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and a total of 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers, we found that agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Crucially, the reasoning configuration moderated these effects in opposing directions, reducing susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening it to reflective social influence nudges. Extensive reasoning therefore did not make agents more robust but redirected the route through which choice architecture takes effect. Exploratory analysis further showed this redirection to be systematically structured by model scale. Beyond establishing nudge susceptibility as a behavioural property of agentic AI, the study positions interface design as a governance concern for organizations that delegate decisions to autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to digital nudges (both automatic Type 1 and reflective Type 2), and how reasoning configuration moderates this susceptibility. Through a large-scale experiment with 3,600 agents and 21,600 simulations across six frontier models, researchers found that agents are vulnerable to both nudge types, but reasoning configuration has opposing effects: reducing susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening susceptibility to reflective social influence nudges.
AI.motivation: While behavioral biases in LLM textual outputs are well-documented, little is known about how influence operates when models act as agents that perceive interfaces and execute decisions. The researchers wanted to determine whether increasingly built-in reasoning capabilities make agents more robust to digital nudges, given that GUIs were designed to steer human behavior.
AI.method: A randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and a total of 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers. The study drew on Dual-Process Theory to examine susceptibility to automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges, and how reasoning configuration moderates this susceptibility.
AI.result: Agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Crucially, reasoning configuration moderated these effects in opposing directions: it reduced susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening susceptibility to reflective social influence nudges. This redirection was systematically structured by model scale.
AI.conclusion: Extensive reasoning does not make agents more robust to nudges but redirects the route through which choice architecture takes effect. The study establishes nudge susceptibility as a behavioral property of agentic AI and positions interface design as a governance concern for organizations delegating decisions to autonomous agents.

title: Uni-LaDiR: Latent Diffusion Unifies Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Multimodal reasoning requires models to draw on information from multiple modalities throughout the reasoning process. Yet existing methods often concatenate modality-specific thought tokens in a single sequence, leaving the model to bridge representational differences as it reasons across modalities. We introduce Uni-LaDiR (Unified Latent Diffusion Reasoner), a framework that brings these thoughts into a shared latent space for reasoning. A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens, trained to preserve the information needed for later reasoning steps and the final answer or action. Because the same context can support multiple valid next steps, we use diffusion to predict the next block of thought tokens from the input and preceding blocks. Jointly training the encoder and diffusion reasoner with shared model weights encourages thought tokens to be both useful for the task and predictable from the available context. At inference, the model generates these tokens without teacher observations. Across eleven vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks and two vision-language-action (VLA) suites, Uni-LaDiR achieves relative gains over the strongest evaluated baselines of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Uni-LaDiR introduces a unified latent space approach for multimodal reasoning, where thought tokens from different modalities are mapped into a shared representation space. It uses a diffusion model to predict next thought tokens and achieves significant improvements across 11 VLM benchmarks and 2 VLA suites.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal reasoning methods concatenate modality-specific thought tokens in a single sequence, forcing the model to bridge representational differences between modalities without explicit alignment. This creates a gap in how reasoning across modalities is handled.
AI.method: 1) Unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens, trained to preserve information needed for reasoning and final answers. 2) Diffusion model predicts next block of thought tokens from input and preceding blocks (addressing multiple valid next steps). 3) Joint training of encoder and diffusion reasoner with shared model weights encourages thought tokens to be both useful and predictable.
AI.result: Relative gains over strongest baselines: 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks (11 VLM benchmarks) and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks (2 VLA suites).
AI.conclusion: Uni-LaDiR successfully bridges representational differences across modalities through a unified latent space with diffusion-based reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multimodal reasoning and robotic manipulation tasks.

title: Constraint-Safe Graph-Context Scoring for Stable Point-Feature Labels Under Text-Width and Accessibility-Inspired Profiles
summary: Point-feature label placement on interactive maps must reconcile geometric validity, display yield, local placement utility, and stability across camera motion. Accessibility and multilingual requirements further change label dimensions, yet algorithmic evaluations often collapse these concerns into overlap counts. We present LABELSENSE-Pilot, a reproducible prototype that generates eight compass candidates per feature, scores candidates with a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries, adds a previous-placement bonus, and selects a layout through mixed-integer optimization. The executed scorer is deliberately not described as a graph transformer. Every returned layout is checked for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance. Experiments use 2,500 airport coordinates and names spanning 155 countries, with country-grouped splits and generated density, camera, text-suffix, preference, and enlarged-font stressors. Across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot displayed 85.62 percent of labels with 2.09 percent flicker and zero collisions. Versus a handcrafted-utility integer program, LABELSENSE-Pilot sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display while reducing flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, whereas standard geometry reevaluated at 1.5x violated 52.57 percent of selected placements. These results establish an auditable engineering trade-off, not human accessibility, multilingual usability, or preference. Official recent baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission.

AI.tldr: LABELSENSE-Pilot is a reproducible prototype for point-feature label placement on interactive maps that uses an MLP scorer over graph-context summaries combined with mixed-integer optimization. Across 2,500 airport coordinates from 155 countries, it achieves 85.62% display rate with only 2.09% flicker and zero collisions, while enlarged-box-aware layouts eliminate proxy violations entirely.
AI.motivation: Point-feature label placement on interactive maps must balance geometric validity, display yield, local placement utility, and stability across camera motion. Accessibility and multilingual requirements further affect label dimensions, yet existing algorithms often oversimplify these concerns into overlap counts alone.
AI.method: The system generates eight compass candidates per feature, scores each using a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries, adds a previous-placement bonus for stability, and selects the final layout through mixed-integer optimization. All layouts are validated for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance.
AI.result: LABELSENSE-Pilot displayed 85.62% of labels with 2.09% flicker and zero collisions. Compared to a handcrafted-utility integer program, it sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display but reduced flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, whereas standard geometry at 1.5x scale violated 52.57% of selected placements.
AI.conclusion: The results establish an auditable engineering trade-off for label placement. However, the paper explicitly notes that human accessibility, multilingual usability, and preference assessments remain as future work, requiring official baselines and participant evidence before submission.

title: Online Adaptive Kernel Mixing for Gaussian Process Decision Making
comment: 35 pages, 9 figures. Accepted as a full paper at IFIP Performance 2026
summary: Gaussian Processes (GPs) are widely used as surrogates for black-box functions in sequential decision-making problems such as Bayesian optimization (BO), level set estimation (LSE), and Bayesian active learning (BAL). GP performance critically depends on kernels, and standard kernels can lead to suboptimal decisions under misspecification. To address this, we introduce HACK GPs (Hedge Adaptive Cumulative Kernels), a method that views kernel selection as an online learning with expert advice problem. HACK treats each candidate kernel as a GP "expert" and updates a distribution over experts online using AdaHedge, based on a loss received as a proxy for their ability to fit the function and align with the task objective. We provide two variants of HACK: (i) Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and (ii) categorical sampling. We establish general guarantees showing that, under a loss-gap condition, the weight concentrates on the best kernel and the resulting acquisition function is close to that of the best expert. Empirically, we observe robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL compared to standard kernels such as Squared Exponential and Matern-5/2, as well as simple ensemble baselines.

AI.tldr: HACK GPs addresses kernel misspecification in Gaussian Processes by framing kernel selection as an online learning problem with expert advice. The method treats candidate kernels as experts and uses AdaHedge to update weights, providing two variants: Mixture of Gaussians and categorical sampling. Theoretical guarantees ensure weight concentration on the best kernel under loss-gap conditions, with empirical validation across Bayesian optimization, level set estimation, and Bayesian active learning.
AI.motivation: Gaussian Processes are widely used as surrogates in sequential decision-making problems like Bayesian optimization, level set estimation, and Bayesian active learning. However, GP performance critically depends on kernel selection, and standard kernels can lead to suboptimal decisions when the kernel is misspecified (i.e., does not match the true underlying function structure).
AI.method: The paper proposes HACK GPs (Hedge Adaptive Cumulative Kernels), which views kernel selection as an online learning with expert advice problem. Each candidate kernel is treated as a GP "expert," and a distribution over experts is updated online using AdaHedge. The loss function serves as a proxy for the expert's ability to fit the function and align with the task objective. Two variants are provided: (i) Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and (ii) categorical sampling.
AI.result: Theoretically, under a loss-gap condition, the method ensures that weights concentrate on the best kernel and the resulting acquisition function is close to that of the best expert. Empirically, HACK GPs demonstrate robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL tasks compared to standard kernels (Squared Exponential and Matern-5/2) and simple ensemble baselines.
AI.conclusion: HACK GPs provides a principled approach to kernel selection that adapts to the data and task objective. By leveraging online learning with expert advice, the method achieves robust performance across multiple sequential decision-making paradigms without requiring prior knowledge of the optimal kernel.

title: CitySTAR: Structured and Topology-Aware Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Urban 3D Grounding
summary: 3D grounding aims to localize target entities in complex scenes from natural language and plays a fundamental role in embodied perception and spatial reasoning. However, existing approaches mostly rely on feature similarity or direct matching, making it difficult to connect natural-language intent with the implicit semantic and geometric structures hidden in billion-scale urban point clouds. We reformulate city-scale 3D grounding as structured constraint reasoning, where description semantics are organized into computable cross-modal constraints over open-vocabulary 3D entities, attributes, and spatial relations. We present CitySTAR, a training-free framework for reasoning-driven urban 3D grounding. CitySTAR lifts raw billion-scale urban point clouds into a query-ready scene graph of open-vocabulary 3D instances, with CodeLLM-driven tools supplying multimodal evidence for node attributes and 3D spatial relations. It then models target-context topology with paired hypergraphs and performs bidirectional topology verification for structural disambiguation. Finally, a Reflective Cross-modal Grounding module integrates topology consistency and candidate-centered 2D visual evidence to make decisions over a metric-aware 3D context graph. To further support this setting, we introduce CitySTAR-3D, an enhanced benchmark that improves semantic coverage, instance completeness, bounding-box fidelity, and spatial-relation complexity in city-scale 3D grounding. Extensive experiments show that CitySTAR consistently improves open-world urban 3D grounding while maintaining strong interpretability and generalization.

AI.tldr: CitySTAR is a training-free framework for reasoning-driven urban 3D grounding that transforms billion-scale urban point clouds into query-ready scene graphs and uses structured constraint reasoning with paired hypergraphs and bidirectional topology verification to accurately localize target entities from natural language descriptions.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D grounding approaches rely on feature similarity or direct matching, which struggle to connect natural-language intent with implicit semantic and geometric structures in large-scale urban point clouds.
AI.method: 1) Lift raw point clouds into query-ready scene graphs of open-vocabulary 3D instances using CodeLLM-driven tools for multimodal evidence on node attributes and 3D spatial relations; 2) Model target-context topology with paired hypergraphs and perform bidirectional topology verification for structural disambiguation; 3) Integrate topology consistency and candidate-centered 2D visual evidence via Reflective Cross-modal Grounding module over metric-aware 3D context graph.
AI.result: CitySTAR consistently improves open-world urban 3D grounding while maintaining strong interpretability and generalization.
AI.conclusion: The structured constraint reasoning paradigm outperforms direct matching approaches, and the introduced CitySTAR-3D benchmark provides improved semantic coverage, instance completeness, bounding-box fidelity, and spatial-relation complexity for city-scale 3D grounding evaluation.

title: Reproducibility is not construct validity: LLM measurement of institutionally situated communication
summary: High annotation reproducibility does not necessarily imply that an LLM-inferred measure captures the construct it is intended to measure. We test this distinction using a dataset from the European Commission's AI Act consultation, linking structured survey responses to free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders. LLM annotations of consultation submissions are highly reproducible (intraclass correlations > 0.99), yet show limited convergence with survey-reported measures of the nominal construct they were intended to approximate. Divergence between survey-and LLM-inferred text-based measures varies systematically across stakeholder groups: business associations express greater concern about AI risks in text-based consultations than in survey responses ({g} = +1.0), whereas public authorities and several nonbusiness groups show smaller or negative divergences. Divergences between scores suggest positive spatial autocorrelation across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036), indicating that stakeholders from neighboring countries tend toward more similar text-based stances towards AI safety concerns. Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remain strongly associated with support for explainability across all divergence levels. These results demonstrate that LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence and motivate validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when LLMs are used as measurement instruments.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether high reproducibility of LLM annotations guarantees that the measured construct is valid. Using European Commission's AI Act consultation data, the study finds that while LLM annotations are highly reproducible (ICC > 0.99), they show limited convergence with survey-reported measures. Divergences vary systematically across stakeholder groups, with business associations showing the largest divergence (g = +1.0). Spatial autocorrelation exists across European countries, yet survey concerns remain associated with explainability support regardless of divergence levels.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to challenge the assumption that high annotation reproducibility from LLMs automatically means valid measurement. The authors argue that reproducibility does not guarantee construct validity - LLM annotations may be consistent but not actually measure what they intend to measure.
AI.method: The study links structured survey responses to free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders in the European Commission's AI Act consultation. LLM annotations were used to analyze consultation submissions, and their results were compared with survey-reported measures. Intraclass correlations (ICC) were used to assess reproducibility. Effect sizes (Cohen's g) measured divergence between text-based and survey-based measures. Moran's I tested spatial autocorrelation across European countries.
AI.result: LLM annotations showed extremely high reproducibility (ICC > 0.99), yet demonstrated limited convergence with survey-reported measures. Business associations expressed greater AI risk concern in text-based consultations than in surveys (g = +1.0), while public authorities and nonbusiness groups showed smaller or negative divergences. Positive spatial autocorrelation was found across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036). Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remained strongly associated with support for explainability across all divergence levels.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct validity. This motivates the need for validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when using LLMs as measurement instruments. The key takeaway is that researchers should not equate high reproducibility with valid measurement.

title: REARL: A Closed-loop Autonomous Driving Simulation Enhancement Framework with Real Traffic Data and Large Language Models
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Corresponding author: Yiwen Sun. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 62503015)
summary: Accurate simulation is crucial for autonomous driving development, yet capturing real-world traffic complexity remains challenging. Existing simulators that rely on predefined rules or static data playback struggle with dynamic traffic. CRITICAL uses real traffic data and a large language model (LLM) to adjust the initial simulation configuration, but the simulated distribution still diverges from real traffic as the rollout evolves. We propose REARL, a closed-loop simulation enhancement framework that integrates real traffic data with LLMs. Real traffic data are clustered, and each cluster center is used as a representative scenario that provides typical real-world traffic patterns for the LLM. A timed sliding-window detector then monitors discrepancies in vehicle speed distribution and mean spacing between pairs of vehicles. If a metric exceeds a threshold, the LLM adjusts vehicle decision-making; otherwise the existing controller is kept. The LLM also selects a matching real vehicle from a traffic snapshot and modulates the simulated vehicle with reference to that real action. In a controlled HighD highway setting, compared with the CRITICAL baseline and a PPO-based learning baseline, REARL reduces the Hellinger distance for speed distributions to 0.3067 and the MAPE for mean spacing to 0.8371, while achieving a time headway (THW) of 22.8575 and a lane change rate of 0.0708.

AI.tldr: REARL is a closed-loop simulation framework that integrates real traffic data with large language models to enhance autonomous driving simulation accuracy. It uses clustering to create representative scenarios and a sliding-window detector to monitor traffic distribution discrepancies, enabling LLM-based adjustments to vehicle decision-making in real-time.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving simulators rely on predefined rules or static data playback, which struggle to capture real-world traffic complexity and dynamic interactions. Prior work (CRITICAL) uses LLM to adjust initial simulation configuration but experiences distribution divergence as simulation evolves. A closed-loop approach is needed to continuously align simulated traffic with real-world patterns.
AI.method: REARL employs three key components: (1) Real traffic data clustering where cluster centers represent typical real-world traffic patterns; (2) A timed sliding-window detector monitoring discrepancies in vehicle speed distribution and mean spacing between vehicle pairs; (3) LLM-based adjustment mechanism that modifies vehicle decision-making when metrics exceed thresholds, and selects matching real vehicles from traffic snapshots to modulate simulated vehicle behavior.
AI.result: In controlled HighD highway setting, REARL achieved: Hellinger distance for speed distributions = 0.3067, MAPE for mean spacing = 0.8371, time headway (THW) = 22.8575, and lane change rate = 0.0708, outperforming CRITICAL baseline and PPO-based learning baseline.
AI.conclusion: The closed-loop framework REARL effectively bridges the sim-to-real gap by continuously monitoring traffic distribution discrepancies and leveraging LLM to adapt vehicle behaviors in real-time. This approach significantly improves simulation fidelity for autonomous driving development.

title: DirtyMoCap: Robust Motion Capture from Unconstrained Markers
summary: Optical motion capture delivers high-fidelity human motion, but its reliance on strict marker layouts and clean trajectories severely limits its real-world applicability. In practice, tracking systems frequently output unconstrained markers: sparse, noisy, and unordered point clouds with unknown or varying configurations. To bridge the gap between corrupted raw markers and parametric human models, we introduce DirtyMoCap, a robust, marker-layout-free framework. Our core insight is to map unordered marker observations to a fixed set of "proxy anchors" comprising skeletal joints and body surface points, which serve as a stable intermediate representation. We first initialize and track these anchors over long sequences using a recurrent sliding-window architecture. Then, a custom differentiable Gauss-Newton solver fits the SMPL-H model to the tracked anchors to recover full-body pose, translation, and shape. By explicitly deriving geometric residuals, our solver learns adaptive observation confidence, smoothness, and prior weights end-to-end, adapting dynamically to the reliability of the input data. Extensive experiments on diverse, noisy marker configurations demonstrate that DirtyMoCap successfully generalizes across arbitrary layouts using only a single trained model. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art configuration-specific baselines in both joint and vertex reconstruction accuracy, while our custom CUDA solver achieves up to a 100x speedup over standard PyTorch implementations. We further apply DirtyMoCap to heterogeneous raw optical MoCap recordings of traditional Chinese martial arts, yielding a Kung Fu motion dataset of temporally coherent SMPL-H reconstructions. Code and data are available at https://wanglongzju.github.io/DirtyMoCap-Project-Page.

AI.tldr: DirtyMoCap addresses the challenge of reconstructing human motion from corrupted, sparse, noisy, and unordered marker observations in optical motion capture systems. It uses a marker-layout-free framework that maps observations to proxy anchors and employs a differentiable Gauss-Newton solver to fit the SMPL-H model.
AI.motivation: Optical motion capture requires strict marker layouts and clean trajectories, severely limiting real-world applicability. Real-world tracking systems output unconstrained markers: sparse, noisy, unordered point clouds with unknown configurations. There was a need for a robust solution that bridges corrupted raw markers and parametric human models.
AI.method: 1) Map unordered marker observations to fixed "proxy anchors" (skeletal joints and body surface points) as stable intermediate representation. 2) Initialize and track anchors over long sequences using recurrent sliding-window architecture. 3) Custom differentiable Gauss-Newton solver fits SMPL-H model to tracked anchors, deriving geometric residuals explicitly. 4) Solver learns adaptive observation confidence, smoothness, and prior weights end-to-end, adapting to input data reliability.
AI.result: Successfully generalizes across arbitrary marker layouts using a single trained model. Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art configuration-specific baselines in both joint and vertex reconstruction accuracy. Custom CUDA solver achieves up to 100x speedup over standard PyTorch implementations. Applied to heterogeneous raw optical MoCap recordings of traditional Chinese martial arts, yielding a Kung Fu motion dataset with temporally coherent SMPL-H reconstructions.
AI.conclusion: DirtyMoCap provides a robust, marker-layout-free solution for optical motion capture that can handle corrupted real-world data. The approach successfully generalizes across arbitrary marker configurations with a single model, significantly outperforms existing methods, and enables new applications like reconstructing historical motion data (Chinese martial arts).

title: Physical knowledge on historical data matters more than enforcing physical constraints on the forecast
summary: Time series forecasting has seen signicant advancements with the emergence of new deep learning models. However, forecasting time series in applications involving physical processes remains a major challenge. Despite the apparition of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINN), recent models do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which are important for domain experts to understand the target behavior. To this end, we propose a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) which predicts, along the target, unobservable variables on both historic data and forecast target. This approach enhances the model robustness and results interpretation using domain knowledge. Our method is easily adaptable to any physical model using several equations, each having its own set of unobservable variables, to describe it-self. As a case study, we incorporate physical equations used for groundwater levels predictions by the physical model called Gardenia. This model uses transfers equations between reservoirs, optimized with data assimilation, to simulate the evolution of groundwater levels. Evaluation includes several well known neural network models and the Gardenia model compared on twelve real world datasets. In addition, we study the impact of each component through an ablation study. Our model outperforms other models on ve out of the twelve datasets and our ablation study underlines the importance of having a physical background in our time series forecasting task. Finally, the coherence of the physical variables predicted by our neural network is assessed by a domain expert.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) that predicts both target variables and unobservable intermediate physical variables in time series forecasting. The method incorporates domain knowledge from physical models (specifically groundwater level prediction using the Gardenia model) to enhance robustness and interpretability. PIRNN outperforms baseline models on 5 out of 12 real-world datasets, and ablation studies confirm the importance of physical background in the model.
AI.motivation: Time series forecasting with deep learning has advanced, but forecasting physical processes remains challenging. Existing models like PINNs do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which are important for domain experts to understand target behavior. This work aims to address this gap by predicting unobservable variables alongside the target.
AI.method: The authors propose a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) that predicts both the target and unobservable variables on historic data and forecasts. The method incorporates physical equations (transfer equations between reservoirs from the Gardenia model) and uses data assimilation. It is adaptable to any physical model using multiple equations with their own unobservable variables.
AI.result: PIRNN outperforms other models (neural networks and the Gardenia physical model) on 5 out of 12 real-world groundwater datasets. The ablation study demonstrates the importance of having physical background in time series forecasting. Domain expert validation confirms the coherence of predicted physical variables.
AI.conclusion: The PIRNN approach enhances model robustness and results interpretation by incorporating domain knowledge through physical equations. The method is flexible and adaptable to various physical models. The study confirms that integrating physical background significantly improves time series forecasting for physical processes.

title: Digital Twins for Opinion Dynamics: A Generative LLM Framework for Social Networks
summary: The study of opinion dynamics in social networks is one of the key challenges in computational social science with direct relevance to understanding political polarization, misinformation, and health responses. Current approaches focus on simplified mathematical models that ignore linguistic and contextual factors related to belief updates or use Large Language Model (LLM)-based simulations that have not been validated against real data. We present a framework based on the concept of a digital twin to simulate opinion dynamics in social networks. The approach fills the gap by cloning a real-world Twitter network, assigns a set of attributes for agents (such as persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, and influence), and employs Mistral-7B to perform opinion update based on memory and social exposure. To evaluate the proposed approach, we validate it against two real Twitter datasets (COVID-19 discourse and U.S elections 2020). The results show that the capability of the proposed framework reproduces opinion trajectories and reduces individual prediction error by more than 50% compared to the best-performing classical baseline (Mistral-7B achieves Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = 0.150 and 0.121 on the COVID-19 and US Election 2020 datasets, respectively). We observe similar improvements in structural alignment (Delta_r = 0.120 and 0.180) and polarization dynamics (Delta_Var = 0.106 and 0.115) on the two datasets, respectively. Additionally, the ablation studies confirm that agent attributes, memory, and social exposure all contribute to the framework's predictive fidelity in reproducing opinion trajectories, with agent attributes being the most critical contributor. Overall, our results demonstrate that grounding Mistral-7B within empirically cloned interaction networks produces a realistic simulation framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a digital twin-based framework to simulate opinion dynamics in social networks by cloning real Twitter networks and using Mistral-7B for opinion updates. The framework is validated against COVID-19 and US Election 2020 Twitter datasets, achieving over 50% reduction in prediction error compared to classical baselines.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to opinion dynamics either oversimplify by ignoring linguistic/contextual factors or use unvalidated LLM-based simulations. There is a gap between realistic social network modeling and data-driven validation.
AI.method: Digital twin framework: (1) Clone real Twitter network, (2) Assign agent attributes (persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, influence), (3) Use Mistral-7B for opinion updates based on memory and social exposure. Validated on COVID-19 and US Election 2020 datasets.
AI.result: Mistral-7B achieves MAE = 0.150 (COVID-19) and 0.121 (US Election 2020). Structural alignment: Delta_r = 0.120 and 0.180. Polarization dynamics: Delta_Var = 0.106 and 0.115. Ablation studies confirm agent attributes are most critical, followed by memory and social exposure.
AI.conclusion: Grounding Mistral-7B within empirically cloned interaction networks produces a realistic simulation framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics, with over 50% improvement over classical baselines.

title: Enhanced Knowledge Distillation for Detection Transformer via Teacher Prediction Refinement
summary: Detection Transformers (DETRs) achieve strong performance in object detection but remain challenging to deploy on edge devices due to their high computational cost. Existing DETR distillation methods mainly focus on aligning distillation points, while largely overlooking the quality of the teacher's supervision itself. We observe that due to stage-wise non-monotonic prediction behavior in DETRs, well-localized or correctly classified predictions from earlier stages may degrade in later ones, and some negative predictions become increasingly overconfident. As a result, relying solely on the current stage's predictions yields inaccurate and inconsistent supervision. To address this issue, we propose Teacher Prediction Refinement Distillation (TPRD), a plug-and-play module that refines teacher predictions before distillation by exploiting stage-wise prediction information. TPRD improves supervision quality through Positive Prediction Correction (PPC), which corrects degraded positive predictions by restoring more accurate ones from earlier stages, ensuring reliable localization and classification signals, and Negative Prediction Suppression (NPS) suppresses the influence of overconfident negatives, preventing them from providing misleading supervision to the student. To preserve informative dark knowledge, we further introduce Maximum Dark Knowledge Preservation (MDKP), which selectively refines target-class logits while retaining non-target relations. Extensive experiments on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method. Our code is available at https://github.com/xingyitong1/TPRD.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TPRD (Teacher Prediction Refinement Distillation), a plug-and-play distillation module for DETRs that improves supervision quality by addressing stage-wise non-monotonic prediction behavior, where well-localized predictions may degrade in later stages and negative predictions become overconfident.
AI.motivation: DETRs achieve strong detection performance but are computationally expensive for edge deployment. Existing distillation methods focus on aligning distillation points while neglecting the quality of teacher's supervision. The key insight is that due to stage-wise non-monotonic prediction behavior in DETRs, predictions can degrade in later stages and negative predictions become overconfident, leading to inaccurate and inconsistent supervision.
AI.method: TPRD introduces three components: (1) Positive Prediction Correction (PPC) - restores more accurate predictions from earlier stages to correct degraded positive predictions; (2) Negative Prediction Suppression (NPS) - suppresses overconfident negative predictions to prevent misleading supervision; (3) Maximum Dark Knowledge Preservation (MDKP) - selectively refines target-class logits while retaining non-target class relationships for informative dark knowledge.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed TPRD method.
AI.conclusion: TPRD successfully improves distillation supervision quality for DETRs by addressing prediction degradation and overconfidence issues, providing a plug-and-play solution that enhances student model performance while maintaining computational efficiency for edge deployment.

title: TRACE: Accountable Agentic Retrieval for Source Discovery in Digital Archives
summary: Historical archives pose a difficult retrieval problem for retrievalaugmented generation systems: documents are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous across genres and sources, and require strong source traceability for scholarly and institutional use. We introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. The system was developed in the context of DECIDON, an interdisciplinary project on the circulation of political discourse between parliamentary debates and the press during the French Third Republic, involving digitised historical collections and institutional use cases. The prototype is currently deployed internally within the project and accessible to 24 researchers across six partner institutions. We evaluate TRACE on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1,752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, with documents derived from Biblioth{è}que nationale de France digitised collections. TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. At approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration, TRACE also remains economically feasible for heritage institutions, laboratories or companies that cannot rely on costly local GPU infrastructure. These results suggest that, for large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a training-free agentic retrieval framework for historical archives, achieving R@10=0.856 and MRR=0.653 on French historical questions, outperforming multiple RAG baselines at ~$0.02 per query.
AI.motivation: Historical archives pose difficult retrieval challenges due to OCR-degraded documents, heterogeneous sources, and need for source traceability. Existing RAG systems struggle with these domain-specific requirements.
AI.method: TRACE is a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. It was developed for the DECIDON project on French Third Republic political discourse circulation between parliamentary debates and press.
AI.result: TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653 on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic benchmark (1,752 French historical questions over 1887 parliamentary debates and newspapers from BnF collections), outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. Cost is approximately $0.02 per question.
AI.conclusion: For large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches. The system is deployed internally for 24 researchers across six partner institutions.

title: Amortizing Physics-Informed Neural Solvers via Graph Hypernetworks
comment: Accepted at the Learning on Graphs Conference (LoG), 2026
summary: Amortizing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across related PDEs requires describing each equation to a reusable solver. Coefficient vectors encode numerical parameters in predefined slots, leaving operator and cross-field assignments implicit. We make these relationships explicit in an operator graph, with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals and coefficients retained as term attributes. A graph hypernetwork generates diagonal codes that initialize a meta-trained factorized PINN for each target equation. Meta-training and target-specific adaptation use governing equations and prescribed conditions without solution labels. We compare coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning by solution accuracy within a fixed adaptation budget. In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction problems, both term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy, with similar performance. In two-field Fisher-KPP, meta-training sees uncoupled and one-way systems; after 3,000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, the graph's mean final error is 35.7% below the term set and 67.7% below the coefficient vector. In a fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model, the coefficient vector performs best. These results support extending coefficient conditioning with explicit equation relationships for physics-based solver adaptation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an operator graph framework to explicitly represent PDE relationships for amortizing PINNs across related equations. A graph hypernetwork generates initialization codes for meta-trained factorized PINNs, showing improved adaptation to unseen PDEs compared to coefficient-vector and term-set approaches.
AI.motivation: Current coefficient-vector approaches for amortizing PINNs across related PDEs leave operator and cross-field relationships implicit, limiting transferability to new equations. The authors seek to make these relationships explicit to improve meta-learning performance.
AI.method: The authors represent PDEs as operator graphs with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals, with coefficients as term attributes. A graph hypernetwork generates diagonal initialization codes for a meta-trained factorized PINN. They compare three conditioning methods: coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning.
AI.result: In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction problems, both term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy. In two-field Fisher-KPP, after 3000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, the graph approach achieves 35.7% lower error than term-set and 67.7% lower than coefficient-vector. However, in a fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model, the coefficient vector performs best.
AI.conclusion: Explicit equation relationships via operator graphs can significantly improve physics-based solver adaptation for related PDEs, though performance varies by problem structure. The approach shows promise for extending coefficient conditioning with explicit equation relationships.

title: Beyond the Foreground: FOV-Aware Polyp Image Synthesis via Lesion-Guided Adaptive Mucosal Context Propagation
summary: Synthetic image and mask pairs can alleviate scarce colonoscopy annotations, but realistic synthesis requires preserving the supplied lesion while generating compatible mucosa. Existing foreground-guided methods treat all non-foreground pixels as background and rely mainly on local integration. Directly applying them to colonoscopy causes two problems: non-mucosal black regions contaminate generated tissue, and local reasoning produces inconsistent mucosal texture and illumination. We propose LAMP, the first foreground-guided framework for polyp image synthesis based on lesion-guided adaptive mucosal context propagation. LAMP explicitly separates the lesion, valid mucosa, and camera exterior using a field-of-view (FOV) mask. Lesion-to-Mucosa cross-attention extracts lesion appearance conditions for valid-mucosa locations, while FOV-constrained multidirectional Vision Receptance Weighted Key Value propagates them over legal tissue support. An adaptive gate then controls their residual fusion into the diffusion U-Net. Extensive experiments on five polyp datasets demonstrate that LAMP substantially outperforms existing methods in overall generation quality and consistently improves five downstream segmentation models. Our code will be released at https://github.com/wangtong627/LAMP.

AI.tldr: LAMP is the first foreground-guided framework for polyp image synthesis that addresses two key problems in existing methods: non-mucosal black region contamination and inconsistent mucosal texture/illumination. It uses lesion-guided adaptive mucosal context propagation with FOV masking, cross-attention, and multidirectional propagation to generate high-quality synthetic polyp images that improve downstream segmentation models.
AI.motivation: Synthetic image generation can alleviate scarce colonoscopy annotations, but existing foreground-guided methods treat all non-foreground pixels as background and rely on local integration, causing two problems when applied to colonoscopy: (1) non-mucosal black regions contaminate generated tissue, and (2) local reasoning produces inconsistent mucosal texture and illumination.
AI.method: LAMP proposes lesion-guided adaptive mucosal context propagation with three key components: (1) FOV mask to explicitly separate lesion, valid mucosa, and camera exterior; (2) Lesion-to-Mucosa cross-attention to extract lesion appearance conditions for valid-mucosa locations; (3) FOV-constrained multidirectional Vision Receptance Weighted Key Value to propagate conditions over legal tissue support; (4) Adaptive gate controlling residual fusion into diffusion U-Net.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on five polyp datasets demonstrate that LAMP substantially outperforms existing methods in overall generation quality and consistently improves five downstream segmentation models.
AI.conclusion: LAMP provides an effective solution for polyp image synthesis in colonoscopy, successfully addressing the limitations of prior foreground-guided methods by explicitly handling non-mucosal regions and enabling consistent mucosal texture generation through adaptive context propagation.

title: From "Who Is This User?" to "What Does This Purchase Mean?": A Deployed Pipeline for Semantic User Profiling at Bank Scale
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, IEEE International Conference on Data Mining 2026 (ICDM)
summary: Per-user LLM inference on transaction histories binds the inference budget linearly to user count, which becomes prohibitive at applied scale. We re-cast attribute inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern. The pipeline runs in three phases: Resolve abstracts item names with optional web grounding, Profile infers attributes for each frequent pattern, and Tag clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. In Profile, a single LLM call per pattern emits predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates. Because inference runs over patterns rather than users, the budget grows with the pattern count rather than the user count. On the public Open e-commerce corpus, the database is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM that reads each user's raw history directly in AUC across the evaluated attributes, and the prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users. The pipeline is deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling on the order of tens of millions of users, with close to a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets versus a per-user pipeline. The code is publicly available on https://github.com/CyberAgentAILab/profiling-agent-open-ecommerce.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a cost-effective LLM-based attribute inference pipeline for transaction data that shifts inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern, achieving near-identical accuracy while reducing inference targets by ~1000x.
AI.motivation: Per-user LLM inference on transaction histories scales poorly - the inference budget grows linearly with user count, making it prohibitive at applied scale (tens of millions of users).
AI.method: Three-phase pipeline: (1) Resolve - abstracts item names with optional web grounding; (2) Profile - single LLM call per pattern emits categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates; (3) Tag - clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. Inference runs over patterns rather than users.
AI.result: On the public Open e-commerce corpus, the database achieves statistically indistinguishable AUC from an LLM reading each user's raw history directly across evaluated attributes. Prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users. Deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling tens of millions of users, achieving close to three-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets.
AI.conclusion: The pattern-based approach maintains accuracy while transforming scalability from O(users) to O(patterns), making LLM-based user profiling practical at production scale.

title: One Intervention per Component is Enough: Towards Identifiability in Linear Stochastic Dynamics from Steady State
summary: We study the problem of recovering the parameters of a multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process from steady-state observational and interventional data. In many applications, such as large-scale gene perturbation experiments, only stationary "snapshot" measurements are available, making standard stochastic differential equation estimation methods that rely on time-series trajectories inapplicable. We first establish an identifiability result: one intervention per strongly connected component (SCC) of the drift graph suffices to recover all OU process parameters generically up to a global scaling factor. This holds provided that the SCC condensation graph is connected with a single root and certain spectral nondegeneracy assumptions hold. We propose a recursive learning algorithm that orders SCCs topologically and, for each component, isolates its marginal dynamics and solves a linear system derived from the steady-state moment equations, leveraging parameters recovered for upstream components. Building on this theoretical foundation, we propose a regularized least-squares estimator that jointly minimizes residuals of the steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data. Experimental results validate our theoretical findings in recovering parameters of the underlying OU process.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses parameter recovery of multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes from steady-state snapshot data (observational and interventional), which is common in large-scale gene perturbation experiments. The key theoretical contribution shows that one intervention per strongly connected component suffices for identifiability. A recursive learning algorithm and regularized least-squares estimator are proposed based on steady-state moment equations.
AI.motivation: Standard SDE estimation methods require time-series trajectories, but many applications (e.g., large-scale gene perturbation experiments) only provide stationary "snapshot" measurements, making traditional methods inapplicable. This motivates the need for parameter estimation methods that work with steady-state data.
AI.method: 1) Theoretical identifiability analysis: establishing that one intervention per SCC of the drift graph suffices (under conditions: SCC condensation graph connected with single root, spectral nondegeneracy). 2) Recursive learning algorithm: topological ordering of SCCs, isolating marginal dynamics, solving linear systems from steady-state moment equations using upstream parameters. 3) Regularized least-squares estimator: jointly minimizes residuals of steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data.
AI.result: Theoretical findings are validated experimentally - the method successfully recovers parameters of the underlying OU process from steady-state data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables parameter recovery of multivariate OU processes from snapshot data, which was previously considered infeasible. The identifiability condition (one intervention per SCC) is both necessary and sufficient under the stated assumptions. The recursive algorithm and regularized estimator provide practical tools for implementation.

title: An Event Preserving Velocity Invariant Representation for Event Cameras
comment: @inproceedings{ikura2026event, title={An Event Preserving Velocity Invariant Representation for Event Cameras}, author={Ikura, Mikihiro and Gava, Luna and Wu, Jiahang and Glover, Arren and Bartolozzi, Chiara}, year={2026}, booktitle={ECCV 2026 Workshop-Event-Based Multimodal Vision: From Imaging to Perception and Understanding} }
summary: Event cameras provide low-latency, high temporal resolution perception for real-time vision tasks such as robotics.The novel circuitry (i.e. asynchronous, independent pixels) that enables these advantages also introduces new algorithmic challenges. Velocity-invariant representations alleviate missing observations under slow motion and motion blur under fast motion, but most discard temporal information by converting events into image-like representations. We propose Set of Centre Active Receptive Fields (SCARF), a real-time velocity-invariant representation that preserves raw events while consistently handling fast motion, stationary scenes, and independently moving objects. SCARF achieves state-of-the-art performance in both computational efficiency and representation quality.

AI.tldr: SCARF is a novel real-time velocity-invariant representation for event cameras that preserves raw events while handling various motion scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance in computational efficiency and representation quality.
AI.motivation: Event cameras offer low-latency, high temporal resolution perception but introduce algorithmic challenges. Existing velocity-invariant representations alleviate motion issues but discard temporal information by converting events into image-like representations.
AI.method: The paper proposes Set of Centre Active Receptive Fields (SCARF), a real-time velocity-invariant representation that preserves raw events while consistently handling fast motion, stationary scenes, and independently moving objects.
AI.result: SCARF achieves state-of-the-art performance in both computational efficiency and representation quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SCARF representation successfully addresses the limitations of existing approaches by maintaining temporal information while effectively handling various motion conditions in event camera applications.

title: Beyond Depth Truncation: Controlled Evaluation of Depth Utilization in Recursive Language Models
summary:
Depth-recurrent language models iteratively apply a small layer stack, decoupling per-token compute from distinct parameter count. To determine whether such a model genuinely utilizes its depth, both recurrence and layer-pruning literatures rely on a shared evaluation: truncating depth at inference time, plotting quality against retained depth fraction, and reading off the slope. While cheap and training-free, this metric suffers from an unexamined flaw: it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that alters multiple model properties simultaneously. Depth truncation concurrently reduces the number of block applications, decreases the volume of distinct computation performed, and pushes the readout head onto an out-of-distribution residual stream. The observed slope conflates all three factors, yet is conventionally interpreted as reflecting solely the second.
  We propose the Depth Control Protocol (DCP), a diagnostic suite that disentangles these three quantities. DCP comprises three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, a negative control applying the identical interventions to dense transformers to ensure the effect is not an artifact of the measurement protocol, and a controlled training intervention to verify causality. The linchpin control, running the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration, is strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures, since in a dense network repeating a layer yields an entirely different model rather than the same model in an alternative configuration.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a flaw in how depth-recurrent language models are evaluated: current methods truncate depth and measure quality slope, but this conflates three distinct factors (block applications, distinct computation, and residual stream position). The authors propose the Depth Control Protocol (DCP) - a diagnostic suite with positive controls, negative controls, and a training intervention to disentangle these factors.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of depth-recurrent language models relies on truncating depth at inference time and measuring the quality slope against retained depth. However, this method suffers from an unexamined flaw: it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that alters multiple model properties simultaneously - the number of block applications, the volume of distinct computation, and the position of the readout head in the residual stream. The observed slope conflates all three factors, yet is conventionally interpreted as reflecting solely the distinct computation.
AI.method: The authors propose the Depth Control Protocol (DCP), a diagnostic suite comprising: (1) three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, (2) a negative control applying identical interventions to dense transformers to ensure the effect is not an artifact, and (3) a controlled training intervention to verify causality. The linchpin control runs the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration, which is strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures.
AI.result: The abstract does not present experimental results; it describes the proposed methodology (DCP) and its components.
AI.conclusion: The DCP provides a framework to disentangle the three confounded factors in depth evaluation. The key insight is that the linchpin control (running full block applications with single distinct iteration) is only realizable in weight-sharing architectures, as repeating a layer in dense networks yields a different model rather than an alternative configuration of the same model.

title: Graph-Based Stochastic Power-UCT: Monte-Carlo Graph Search with Power Mean Estimation
summary: Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) duplicates the same state when it is reached through different trajectories, which can waste simulations in stochastic MDPs. We introduce Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT), which shares states reached at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for states reached at different depths. This design applies to general stochastic MDPs, including problems with cycles. We prove that for a fixed planning horizon, the root estimate converges to the finite-horizon value at rate $O(n^{-1/2})$, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. We also study two full-state variants: GS-Power-UCT-F, which stores one node per physical state to increase sample sharing but may mix values from different remaining horizons, and GS-Power-UCT-F$^+$, which uses an adaptive horizon to control this bias. The latter converges to $V^{\star}(s_0)$, the optimal infinite-horizon discounted value at the root state $s_0$, when the remaining cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.

AI.tldr: GS-Power-UCT is a graph-based MCTS algorithm that shares states at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for different depths, addressing the state duplication problem in tree-based MCTS for stochastic MDPs. It achieves O(n^{-1/2}) convergence rate for finite-horizon problems and includes variants (GS-Power-UCT-F and GS-Power-UCT-F+) for full-state sharing with adaptive horizon control.
AI.motivation: Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search duplicates the same state when reached through different trajectories, which wastes simulations in stochastic MDPs. This inefficiency is particularly problematic in problems with cycles or stochastic transitions.
AI.method: Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT) shares states reached at the same planning depth while maintaining separate values for states at different depths. Two variants are proposed: GS-Power-UCT-F (one node per physical state for maximum sample sharing) and GS-Power-UCT-F+ (adaptive horizon to control bias from mixing different remaining horizons).
AI.result: For fixed planning horizon, root estimate converges to finite-horizon value at O(n^{-1/2}) rate, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. GS-Power-UCT-F+ converges to V*(s0), the optimal infinite-horizon discounted value, when the remaining cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: GS-Power-UCT provides a theoretically sound and empirically effective solution for improving sample efficiency in stochastic MDPs. The adaptive horizon variant (GS-Power-UCT-F+) successfully balances sample sharing with bias control, achieving convergence to optimal infinite-horizon values.

title: QCPruner: Query-Conditioned Population Coverage for Visual Token Pruning
summary: The high visual-token load in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) motivates training-free pruning to reduce later-layer computation, but under a fixed budget, pruning must preserve query-relevant evidence while avoiding redundancy. Existing methods rank tokens, diversify selected subsets, or optimize coverage without using a shared per-visual query utility to weight both visual targets and candidate representatives. We introduce QCPruner, which makes both roles query-conditioned through bilateral utility weighting. Using keyword-matched query anchors, QCPruner fuses two cross-modal cues into utility and applies it to both visual targets and candidate representatives within visual-affinity-based coverage. The resulting nonnegative facility-location objective is monotone and submodular, retains the standard (1-1/e) greedy guarantee, and requires no model training or parameter updates. Across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-Video, and Qwen2.5-VL, QCPruner achieves the highest average relative performance among evaluated complete-system pruning methods at every reported token budget. At 32 of 576 tokens on LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 96.1% of unpruned performance, versus 93.9% for the strongest evaluated baseline. At 256 of 1296 tokens on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the corresponding values are 96.7% and 92.5%.

AI.tldr: QCPruner is a training-free visual token pruning method for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that uses query-conditioned bilateral utility weighting to simultaneously evaluate visual targets and candidate representatives. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple MLLM benchmarks while maintaining a theoretical (1-1/e) approximation guarantee.
AI.motivation: The high visual-token load in MLLMs creates computational overhead, especially in later layers. Existing pruning methods either rank tokens, diversify subsets, or optimize coverage, but they fail to use a shared per-visual query utility to weight both visual targets and candidate representatives jointly. This limitation leads to suboptimal retention of query-relevant evidence and redundancy issues.
AI.method: QCPruner introduces query-conditioned bilateral utility weighting using keyword-matched query anchors. It fuses two cross-modal cues into a unified utility metric applied to both visual targets and candidate representatives within a visual-affinity-based coverage framework. The method yields a nonnegative facility-location objective that is monotone and submodular, preserving the standard (1-1/e) greedy approximation guarantee. No model training or parameter updates are required.
AI.result: Across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-Video, and Qwen2.5-VL, QCPruner achieves the highest average relative performance among evaluated complete-system pruning methods at every token budget. At 32/576 tokens on LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 96.1% performance (vs 93.9% best baseline). At 256/1296 tokens on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it retains 96.7% (vs 92.5% baseline).
AI.conclusion: QCPruner demonstrates that query-conditioned bilateral utility weighting effectively addresses the visual token pruning problem in MLLMs. By jointly optimizing visual target and representative selection through a unified utility metric, it achieves superior performance across diverse models and benchmarks while maintaining theoretical guarantees and requiring no training.

title: MaSCoD: A Multi-Agent Framework for Structural-Context-Guided Candidate Causal Graph Generation
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to causal discovery, but candidate-graph generation rarely treats premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. We propose MaSCoD, a multi-agent framework that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. We evaluate MaSCoD on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs using GPT-5.4 as the primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication. MaSCoD exhibits a dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority. Across all six dataset-backbone settings, Full, which supplies structural hypotheses before direct-edge judgment, achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than No Phase 1, which instead constructs them within the judgment procedure, while also increasing false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention over all evaluated baselines was observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o, rather than uniformly across settings. Partial ablations showed that supplying both information components did not always outperform supplying only one. For GPT-5.4, stage-wise analysis showed that the Full-No Phase 1 retention gap was already present after direct-edge judgment, while reconciliation introduced additional reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs. These findings support structural pre-organization as an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control and motivate evaluating context construction jointly with its utilization in judgment.

AI.tldr: MaSCoD is a multi-agent framework for LLM-based causal discovery that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment to control for premature omission of causal relations. It outperforms baseline approaches in Recall and F1 but increases false-positive rates, with performance varying across datasets and backbones.
AI.motivation: Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to causal discovery, but candidate-graph generation rarely treats premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. This paper addresses the problem of omission control in LLM-based causal discovery.
AI.method: MaSCoD, a multi-agent framework that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. The framework includes a "Full" approach that supplies structural hypotheses before direct-edge judgment, and a "No Phase 1" approach that constructs them within the judgment procedure. Evaluation on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs datasets using GPT-5.4 and GPT-4o.
AI.result: Full achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than No Phase 1 across all six dataset-backbone settings, but also increased false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention over baselines was observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o, but not uniformly across settings. Supplying both information components did not always outperform supplying only one. Stage-wise analysis showed the retention gap was present after direct-edge judgment, while reconciliation introduced additional reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs.
AI.conclusion: Structural pre-organization should be treated as an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control in LLM-based causal discovery. Context construction should be evaluated jointly with its utilization in judgment. The framework shows dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority.

title: CellRFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling
summary: Predicting cellular responses to perturbations supports the study of gene function, disease mechanisms, and therapeutic strategies. Despite advances in single-cell perturbation modeling, existing models typically optimize surrogate losses that do not directly reflect the biological criteria used for evaluation, so better data fitting need not yield better biological predictions. To address this mismatch, we introduce \textbf{CellRFT}, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that uses biological evaluation as direct training feedback. CellRFT uses policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable evaluations of generated cell populations and integrates multiple biological rewards through hierarchical reward aggregation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate CellRFT's applicability across different pretrained models and effectiveness in improving perturbation prediction, reveal that optimizing one biological criterion can help or hinder others, and show that complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those directly optimized, offering a way to probe how biological metrics shape model behavior, with the potential to inform evaluation design. Code will be made available.

AI.tldr: CellRFT is a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that optimizes perturbation prediction models directly using biological evaluation criteria as training feedback, rather than relying on surrogate losses that may not align with downstream biological goals.
AI.motivation: Current single-cell perturbation models are optimized using surrogate losses that do not directly reflect the biological criteria used for evaluation, meaning better data fitting does not necessarily translate to better biological predictions.
AI.method: CellRFT uses policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable evaluations of generated cell populations and integrates multiple biological rewards through hierarchical reward aggregation. It was tested across different pretrained models.
AI.result: The method demonstrates effectiveness in improving perturbation prediction, reveals trade-offs between biological criteria (optimizing one can help or hinder others), and shows that complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those directly optimized.
AI.conclusion: CellRFT offers a way to probe how biological metrics shape model behavior and has potential to inform evaluation design for perturbation modeling, with implications for studying gene function, disease mechanisms, and therapeutic strategies.

title: AVTrace: Diagnosing Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning in Omni Models
