summary: Omni models can describe video content, but can they locate events in time, preserve event order, and judge audio-visual synchronization? We introduce AVTrace (Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning Assessment and Capability Evaluation), a silver-standard diagnostic suite spanning onset and span grounding, synchronization, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, and event-conditioned comprehension. It contains 34,114 training examples and category-balanced development and test splits of 3,500 and 7,000 examples. We evaluate five open omni models under their respective input configurations using reference-blind response normalization followed by deterministic scoring. All five off-the-shelf systems score below the test split's majority-label baseline of 0.556 on synchronization verification, and obtain low scores on chain parsing and event-conditioned grounding and comprehension. Development-set perturbations reveal task-dependent sensitivity in Qwen3-Omni-30B to modality removal and changes in visual input processing, without isolating their underlying causes. Parameter-efficient temporal post-training improves Gemma4-E4B-it on several benchmark metrics. On three external image benchmarks, task metrics change modestly, including some degradations, while teacher-forcing perplexity decreases. Together, these findings show that semantic reference-text overlap should not be treated as a proxy for temporal localization, and that AVTrace can identify task-specific weaknesses while providing a testbed for temporal post-training.

AI.tldr: AVTrace is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating omni models on audio-visual temporal reasoning tasks, revealing that current models score below baselines on synchronization and temporal reasoning tasks, while semantic overlap is not a valid proxy for temporal localization.
AI.motivation: Current omni models can describe video content but lack evaluation of their ability to locate events in time, preserve event order, and judge audio-visual synchronization. Existing benchmarks do not adequately assess these temporal reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: The authors introduced AVTrace (Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning Assessment and Capability Evaluation), a silver-standard diagnostic suite with 34,114 training examples and balanced dev/test splits (3,500/7,000 examples). They evaluated five open omni models using reference-blind response normalization and deterministic scoring across six task types: onset/span grounding, synchronization, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, and event-conditioned comprehension.
AI.result: All five off-the-shelf models scored below the majority-label baseline (0.556) on synchronization verification, with low scores on chain parsing and event-conditioned grounding/comprehension. Qwen3-Omni-30B showed task-dependent sensitivity to modality removal and visual input changes. Parameter-efficient temporal post-training improved Gemma4-E4B-it on several metrics. External image benchmarks showed modest changes including some degradations.
AI.conclusion: Semantic reference-text overlap should not be treated as a proxy for temporal localization. AVTrace can identify task-specific weaknesses in omni models while providing a testbed for temporal post-training improvements.

title: Not All AI Agents Are Equal: Characterizing Resource and Performance Dynamics
summary: LLM-based AI agents process user requests through iterative reasoning and tool execution, often involving the invocation of remote LLM APIs with local tool containers. This execution model can make the optimization of agent serving difficult because latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks inter-mix across requests. However, the current agent ecosystem runs without much consideration of resource dynamics, which results in significant waste of the precious resources. This paper analyzes the resource inter-mix of AI agents for three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. To this end, we characterize the latency with respect to the resource dynamics of processing multiple requests and tasks concurrently. Our measurements show that agents have a wide range of behaviors depending on tasks, so that even the same tool can differ substantially in resource dynamics. We also find that running multiple requests concurrently exposes task-dependent bottlenecks in resource dynamics such as CPU, disk I/O, and memory. Furthermore, we uncover that faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. Based on these observations, we demonstrate new optimization opportunities that exploit the resource dynamics of tasks: CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation. Our results show that the latency of CPU-sensitive agent tasks improves $\sim$5.4$\times$, and the average latency across multiple tasks is reduced $\sim$32% compared to native agents.

title: Past, Future, All at Once: Mitigating Stability-Plasticity Dilemma via Post-hoc JANUS Rectification
summary: Fine-tuning foundation models on new tasks inevitably suffer from catastrophic forgetting. While existing works attempt to mitigate this on the basis of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, they adopted an overly restrictive Subspace Orthogonality condition. In this paper, we introduce a purely post-hoc and tuning-agnostic weight rectification framework that achieves Parameter Space Orthogonality, which is the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance to the first order. By projecting parameter updates into the JAcobian NUll Space (JANUS), our method significantly recovers compromised historical knowledge without interfering with the underlying fine-tuning process. To overcome the local validity of the Jacobian approximation, we further propose a Multi-step Adaptive Rectification mechanism that utilizes the JANUS shift to dynamically verify the valid trust region and adjust step sizes. Coupled with our proposed ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level singular value decomposition compression techniques, JANUS also achieves great temporal and spatial efficiency. Experiments demonstrate that JANUS seamlessly integrates with various fine-tuning methods, significantly mitigating the stability-plasticity dilemma by recovering historical knowledge while preserving downstream task adaptation.

AI.tldr: JANUS is a post-hoc, tuning-agnostic weight rectification framework that mitigates catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuned foundation models by projecting parameter updates into the Jacobian Null Space, achieving Parameter Space Orthogonality - the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical knowledge.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning foundation models on new tasks inevitably causes catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods rely on overly restrictive Subspace Orthogonality conditions, which inadequately address this problem.
AI.method: The paper proposes projecting parameter updates into the JAcobian NUll Space (JANUS) to achieve Parameter Space Orthogonality. This is combined with: (1) Multi-step Adaptive Rectification for dynamic trust region verification and step size adjustment, (2) Ghost projection, (3) Ghost orientation comparison, and (4) Sequence-level SVD compression for temporal and spatial efficiency.
AI.result: JANUS significantly recovers compromised historical knowledge without interfering with the fine-tuning process. It seamlessly integrates with various fine-tuning methods and mitigates the stability-plasticity dilemma by preserving downstream task adaptation while recovering historical knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Parameter Space Orthogonality is the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance to the first order. JANUS provides an effective post-hoc solution that achieves this condition through Jacobian Null Space projection, outperforming restrictive Subspace Orthogonality approaches.

title: GRF-Recon: Global Ray-Field Optimization for Long-Sequence Feed-forward Reconstruction
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026 as a Spotlight presentation
summary: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction provides an efficient paradigm for scene modeling from image sequences. Scaling these models to large monocular scenarios are constrained by excessive GPU memory footprint, degraded local geometry, and long-term trajectory drift. Existing chunk-based optimization strategies provide limited geometric constraints and fail to maintain global consistency over extended trajectories. We present a unified framework for stable and scalable feed-forward 3D reconstruction from long monocular sequences. Our approach builds on coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment augmented by lightweight geometric prior injection. Distilling monocular geometric cues into the feed-forward backbone via LoRA adaptation improves depth accuracy on fine structures while preserving inference efficiency. We introduce a hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization that leverages high-frequency geometric features to guide local point-cloud refinement and enforce consistent inter-frame ray constraints. Unlike prior chunk-based methods, this establishes strong cross-frame geometric coupling while maintaining scalability. Finally, an efficient trajectory stitching strategy with joint ray-error optimization explicitly reduces accumulated drift. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves competitive trajectory accuracy compared with representative SLAM systems, while maintaining globally consistent 3D reconstruction in large-scale scenarios.

AI.tldr: A unified framework for stable and scalable feed-forward 3D reconstruction from long monocular sequences, addressing GPU memory constraints, local geometry degradation, and trajectory drift through trajectory alignment, LoRA-based geometric prior injection, hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization, and drift reduction via trajectory stitching.
AI.motivation: Existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods struggle with scaling to large monocular scenarios due to excessive GPU memory consumption, degraded local geometry quality, and long-term trajectory drift. Current chunk-based optimization strategies provide limited geometric constraints and fail to maintain global consistency over extended trajectories.
AI.method: The proposed approach integrates three key components: (1) Coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment with lightweight geometric prior injection; (2) LoRA adaptation to distill monocular geometric cues into the feed-forward backbone for improved depth accuracy on fine structures while maintaining inference efficiency; (3) Hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization leveraging high-frequency geometric features for local point-cloud refinement and inter-frame ray constraint enforcement; (4) Efficient trajectory stitching strategy with joint ray-error optimization for accumulated drift reduction.
AI.result: The approach achieves competitive trajectory accuracy compared with representative SLAM systems while maintaining globally consistent 3D reconstruction in large-scale scenarios.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates that feed-forward 3D reconstruction can be scaled to large monocular sequences with stable performance and global consistency, bridging the gap between efficient feed-forward paradigms and traditional SLAM systems in terms of trajectory accuracy and reconstruction quality.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Agentic AI for Networked Low-Altitude UAVs
comment: Agentic AI, neuro-symbolic AI, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), autonomous decision-making, networked UAV systems
summary: Networked low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) need reliable and adaptive decision-making capabilities to operate under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity, while many existing agentic systems remain limited by hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization. This article investigates neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework for combining neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction to support more reliable and adaptive UAV autonomy. We first examine its capability foundations in data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, and zero-shot transfer, and then develop a reference architecture integrating task and goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification and metacognition, skill execution and network interaction, and shared knowledge and memory. An urban fire-inspection case implemented in LAESim illustrates how a UAV can coordinate sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuse a verified image-delivery skill, and satisfy explicit evidence conditions before completing the mission. The results illustrate the potential of NSAAI to support reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAV systems. We further discuss key research directions in uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework to enhance reliability and adaptability in networked low-altitude UAV operations, addressing challenges like uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity. It integrates neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction through a reference architecture with task management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification, skill execution, and shared memory. A fire-inspection case study demonstrates the approach's capability in coordinating sensing under connectivity constraints while maintaining evidence-grounded decision-making.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic systems for UAV autonomy suffer from hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization. Networked UAVs need reliable, adaptive decision-making under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity. The authors aim to address these limitations by proposing a neuro-symbolic approach that combines neural and symbolic AI strengths.
AI.method: The paper develops a reference architecture integrating: (1) task and goal management, (2) neuro-symbolic planning, (3) verification and metacognition, (4) skill execution and network interaction, and (5) shared knowledge and memory. The approach is evaluated through an urban fire-inspection case implemented in LAESim, demonstrating UAV coordination under intermittent connectivity and verified skill reuse.
AI.result: The case study shows that NSAAI can support reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAV systems. The UAV successfully coordinated sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reused a verified image-delivery skill, and satisfied explicit evidence conditions before mission completion.
AI.conclusion: NSAAI shows promise for enhancing UAV autonomy through its integration of neural and symbolic reasoning. Key research directions include uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation. The framework addresses critical limitations of existing agentic systems while enabling reliable, adaptive UAV operations in complex environments.

title: EPIG-Tree: Compute-Optimal Branching for Gradient-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reward-based reinforcement learning for language models, exemplified by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), collapses an entire stochastic trajectory into a single scalar reward. This is clean and scalable, but it explores and allocates reward inefficiently: a trajectory may contain many causal decisions, recovery attempts, and environment-randomness events, yet every token or action inherits one trajectory-level advantage. We study tree-based rollout construction as a compute-allocation problem for policy-gradient estimation. Our central claim is that branches should be placed not where the policy is merely uncertain, but where an additional branch most reduces uncertainty about the policy gradient per unit of compute. From a law-of-total-variance decomposition of the local policy-gradient random variable, we derive two allocation laws: new branches reduce decision uncertainty, while repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The resulting EPIG-Tree score allocates branches using the already computed rollouts. It estimates occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty, along with a suffix law $n_e \propto w_e \|\nabla_θ\log π(a_e|h_e)\| σ_e / \sqrt{c_e}$. Empirically, EPIG reduces gradient MSE in cloned-state control, winning in all nine dense continuous-control environments of a 13-environment sweep and recovering the reference gradient direction near-perfectly, and it improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration relative to entropy branching. In online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO, while branch placement is secondary to token-level credit assignment. In online multi-turn Wordle, EPIG attains the highest final win rate (0.850), overtaking flat GRPO, which saturates early at 0.790, and entropy branching as training proceeds, confirming that the gradient-estimation advantage transfers to a stateful, large-action setting.

AI.tldr: EPIG-Tree is a tree-based rollout method for RL in language models that allocates computation branches where they most reduce gradient uncertainty per unit of compute, using two derived allocation laws: decision uncertainty reduction via new branches and continuation uncertainty reduction via suffix rollouts.
AI.motivation: Current reward-based RL methods (like GRPO) collapse entire trajectories into single scalar rewards, treating all tokens/actions as having the same trajectory-level advantage. This is inefficient because trajectories contain multiple causal decisions, recovery attempts, and randomness events that warrant different credit assignment.
AI.method: The paper models tree-based rollout construction as a compute-allocation problem for policy-gradient estimation. From a law-of-total-variance decomposition of the local policy-gradient random variable, two allocation laws are derived: (1) new branches reduce decision uncertainty, and (2) repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The EPIG-Tree score estimates occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty with a suffix law: n_e ∝ w_e ||∇_θ log π(a_e|h_e)|| σ_e / √c_e.
AI.result: EPIG reduces gradient MSE in cloned-state control (wins all 9 dense continuous-control environments), recovers reference gradient direction near-perfectly, improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration vs entropy branching. In online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO. In online multi-turn Wordle, EPIG achieves highest final win rate (0.850) vs flat GRPO (0.790) and entropy branching.
AI.conclusion: The key insight is that branch placement should target gradient uncertainty reduction rather than policy uncertainty. The gradient-estimation advantage transfers to stateful, large-action settings (Wordle), while token-level credit assignment matters more than branch placement in single-turn math. Tree-structured credit assignment outperforms flat reward aggregation.

title: Astronex-World 1.0: Real-Time Interactive World Model Foundation
comment: Technical report. 25 pages, 13 figures, 10 tables. Project page: https://world.astronex.com.cn ; Code: https://github.com/Astronex-Robotics/Astronex-World ; Weights: https://huggingface.co/Astronex-Lab/Astronex-World
summary: We present Astronex-World 1.0, an open controllable video world-model foundation. Given a text prompt (text-to-video) or an initial observation (image-to-video), the model predicts future visual states under frame-aligned camera trajectories, continuous actions, and an embodiment identifier, and accepts text events inserted at a specified position of a rollout. The family provides a bidirectional model for full-context generation and a causal model with block-causal attention and cross-block KV caching for persistent generation, both built on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B prior. PRoPE injects camera intrinsics and extrinsics, while a 64-dimensional action stream modulates every Transformer layer. A five-stage training path develops bidirectional camera and action control, converts the backbone to block-causal generation, distills a few-step student, restores mixed-domain dynamics, and applies asymmetric DMD/DMD2 distribution matching. The causal model generates 832x480 video at 24 fps. All five training stages run on two NVIDIA L20 48 GB GPUs, and the causal model streams in real time on one. It scores 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full. On Full, this 5B model is above the 13.6B LongCat-Video and the 14B Helios, within one point of the 22B LTX-2.3, and above YUME 1.5, which is post-trained from the same 5B prior on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The reserved action input and output interfaces allow post-training for embodied intelligence and autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: Astronex-World 1.0 is an open-source controllable video world-model foundation (5B parameters) built on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, supporting text-to-video and image-to-video generation with camera trajectory control, continuous action modulation, and text event insertion. It achieves 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full, competitive with much larger models while running in real-time on a single NVIDIA L20 GPU.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to create an open, controllable video world model that enables precise camera and action control for embodied intelligence and autonomous driving applications. Existing video generation models lack fine-grained control over camera parameters and actions, limiting their utility for simulation and planning tasks.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) PRoPE for injecting camera intrinsics and extrinsics; (2) A 64-dimensional action stream modulating every Transformer layer; (3) Two model variants - bidirectional for full-context generation and causal with block-causal attention and cross-block KV caching for persistent generation; (4) A five-stage training pipeline: bidirectional control development, block-causal conversion, few-step distillation, mixed-domain dynamics restoration, and asymmetric DMD/DMD2 distribution matching.
AI.result: The causal model generates 832x480 video at 24 fps. It scores 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full. On Full, this 5B model outperforms the 13.6B LongCat-Video and 14B Helios, is within one point of the 22B LTX-2.3, and exceeds YUME 1.5 (post-trained from the same 5B prior). All five training stages run on two NVIDIA L20 48 GB GPUs, and the causal model streams in real-time on one GPU.
AI.conclusion: Astronex-World 1.0 demonstrates that a 5B-parameter model can achieve competitive performance with models 2-4x its size through careful architecture design and training. The open, controllable nature with reserved action interfaces makes it suitable for post-training in embodied intelligence and autonomous driving domains.

title: Customizable and Jointly Optimized Route Planning: A Deep Architecture Enabling Differentiable Shortest-Path Search
summary: With the widespread use of online navigation and ride-hailing services, achieving optimal route planning for diverse user preferences has recently attracted increasing attention. Classic graph algorithms for pathfinding use heuristic cost functions to define edge weight, thus providing no optimality guarantee of route quality. Prior data-driven approaches equating ground truth of the optimal route with user trajectory, which is however moderately influenced by the navigation service, suffers from the feedback loop problem. To address these issues, we propose a deep architecture that is able to jointly optimize cost functions and route-ranking model towards any route preference. First, we run a multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect the set of Pareto optimal routes, deeming it as the complete candidate set. Exploiting the property of such a set, we design a neural network structure that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Second, we define route preference as a task of constrained optimization of route attributes, and propose a novel loss function that optimizes a single-objective variable, with other variables strictly under constraints. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The results show that our architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deep learning architecture for route planning that jointly optimizes cost functions and route-ranking models to generate personalized routes based on diverse user preferences, addressing limitations of classic graph algorithms and prior data-driven approaches that suffer from feedback loop problems.
AI.motivation: Classic graph algorithms use heuristic cost functions without optimality guarantees, while prior data-driven approaches equate optimal routes with user trajectories, which are influenced by navigation services themselves, creating a feedback loop problem. There is a need for a method that can generate high-quality, customizable routes for diverse user preferences.
AI.method: 1) Run multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect Pareto optimal routes as the complete candidate set; 2) Design a neural network that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner; 3) Define route preference as constrained optimization of route attributes and propose a novel loss function optimizing a single-objective variable while keeping other variables strictly under constraints.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that the proposed architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed deep architecture successfully addresses the limitations of traditional route planning methods by providing an end-to-end differentiable solution that can generate high-quality, personalized routes based on diverse user preferences while maintaining optimality guarantees through Pareto optimal route collection.

title: Dynamic Generalized Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport
summary: Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT) extends classical optimal transport by introducing structure-aware transport cost. This is particularly relevant for spatial transcriptomics, where dynamical reconstruction should preserve tissue structure in addition to matching expression patterns. While static formulations have been widely used for such structure-aware alignment, a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories is still missing. We introduce Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation (TP-DATE), a theoretical and computational framework to generalize GW-OT dynamically in a simulation-free manner. We formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions and prove the static dynamic equivalence. We further develop travelling-pair flow matching, which allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes their interactions into a single vector field. On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.

AI.tldr: TP-DATE is a computational framework that generalizes Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT) to a dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories in spatial transcriptomics, preserving tissue structure while matching expression patterns.
AI.motivation: Static GW-OT formulations have been used for structure-aware alignment in spatial transcriptomics, but they cannot reconstruct continuous trajectories. A general dynamic formulation was missing, limiting the ability to model dynamical reconstruction that preserves tissue structure in addition to matching expression patterns.
AI.method: TP-DATE introduces: (1) A broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) formulated through path actions; (2) Proof of static-dynamic equivalence; (3) Travelling-pair flow matching that allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes interactions into a single vector field. The approach is simulation-free.
AI.result: On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: TP-DATE provides a theoretical and computational framework that successfully generalizes GW-OT dynamically, enabling better preservation of spatial structure and improved continuous trajectory reconstruction in spatial transcriptomics analysis.

title: A Free Lunch? Adapting PP-OCRv6 for Historical Text Recognition
summary: Despite impressive reported scores, large vision-language models have seen limited practical uptake in historical automatic text recognition because of their computational cost, dependence on large-scale pretraining, and hallucination. Historical ATR therefore continues to rely largely on compact CRNN line recognizers, which are visually grounded and trainable on modest data. Lightweight recurrence-free recognizers promise the accuracy of larger models with the practical advantages of CRNNs, yet have not been comprehensively evaluated on historical writing. We adapt PP-OCRv6, a recent compact text recognizer without strong language modeling, for historical line recognition and compare it with a conventional CRNN across generalized pretraining, domain-specific training, corpus-level fine-tuning, and manuscript-specific few-shot adaptation on multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script material. While PP-OCRv6 does not consistently outperform the baseline when trained from scratch, heterogeneous pretraining produces markedly better generalization. Comparisons with the Qwen3.5-based Medusa recognizer further show that fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform a large VLM tailored towards historical Latin-script HTR.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates PP-OCRv6, a lightweight recurrence-free text recognizer, against conventional CRNN models for historical automatic text recognition (ATR) across multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script materials. The study finds that heterogeneous pretraining significantly improves generalization, and fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform large vision-language models like Qwen3.5-based Medusa for historical Latin-script HTR.
AI.motivation: Large vision-language models have high computational costs, require large-scale pretraining, and suffer from hallucination issues, limiting their practical adoption in historical ATR. The field continues to rely on compact CRNN models. This work investigates whether lightweight recurrence-free recognizers can achieve accuracy comparable to larger models while maintaining practical advantages.
AI.method: The authors adapted PP-OCRv6 (a compact text recognizer without strong language modeling) for historical line recognition and compared it with conventional CRNN across four training scenarios: generalized pretraining, domain-specific training, corpus-level fine-tuning, and manuscript-specific few-shot adaptation. Evaluation was performed on multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script material. Additional comparison was made with the Qwen3.5-based Medusa recognizer.
AI.result: PP-OCRv6 does not consistently outperform the baseline when trained from scratch. However, heterogeneous pretraining produces markedly better generalization. Fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform a large VLM (Qwen3.5-based Medusa) tailored towards historical Latin-script HTR.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight recurrence-free recognizers like PP-OCRv6, when properly pretrained, can achieve competitive or superior performance compared to large VLMs for historical text recognition, offering a more practical alternative with better computational efficiency.

title: E-AVI: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Assessment for Automated Video Interviews
summary: Automated video interview assessment integrates verbal content, acoustic delivery, and visual behavior, yet numerical predictions alone provide limited inspectable support. We present E-AVI, an evidence-grounded framework that extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring. A shared evidence pool further supports natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering. On RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses characterize the predictive contribution, grounding, and practical utility of the evidence pathway. Together, these results demonstrate that our proposed E-AVI framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

AI.tldr: E-AVI is an evidence-grounded framework for automated video interview assessment that provides timestamped multimodal evidence and supports natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering, outperforming baselines while offering inspectable support for assessment.
AI.motivation: Current automated video interview assessment systems provide numerical predictions without inspectable support, limiting interpretability and practical utility for feedback and analysis.
AI.method: E-AVI extracts timestamped multimodal evidence (verbal content, acoustic delivery, visual behavior) and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings. A shared evidence pool supports natural-language feedback and QA. Evaluated via ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses.
AI.result: E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation on RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset. The evidence pathway demonstrates predictive contribution, grounding, and practical utility.
AI.conclusion: E-AVI improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis, bridging the gap between accuracy and interpretability in automated interview assessment.

title: Correct Now, Insufficient Later: Auditing Update Sufficiency in Context Compression
comment: 20 pages, 9 tables, 2 figures. Code and reproducibility materials to be released separately
summary: A memory can answer a current query correctly while discarding distinctions required by a later update. We investigate this failure with a paired-history audit: two histories have the same current answer, receive a shared future update, and require different subsequent answers. A pilot evaluates 24 history pairs across six synthetic mechanisms, 12 memory conditions, two repeats, and two model backends. A deterministic frontier selector obtains strict reveal accuracy of 96/96 on DeepSeek and 82/96 on GLM; a structured writer obtains 62 successes with one unresolved outcome and 56/96. The configured four-outcome joint contrast has finite-sample identification intervals of [0.521, 0.542] and [0.292, 0.313], not confidence intervals. A record-level audit distinguishes retained-state adequacy, response delivery, and answer-schema compliance without changing those original scores. It finds 26 and 25 well-formed but semantically wrong structured reveal memories, while all 14 GLM frontier reveal failures contain correct values in the wrong wrapper. Tombstone removal produces 16/16 exact replay failures in the targeted mechanism. Identifier renaming then exposes a separate flaw: original frontier late-reference adequacy falls from 8/8 to 94/320 transformed instances. We provide and test a label-equivariant repair, but it preserves only 2/8 original late-reference answers: eliminating a naming shortcut does not solve unknown future relevance. These results support a scoped evaluation methodology and reproducible failure analysis, not general superiority of the repaired algorithm. Paid pilot evidence, retrospective diagnostics, and new offline tests are reported separately; no independent held-out or natural-task validation is claimed.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memory failures in AI systems where current correct answers discard distinctions needed for future updates. The authors propose a paired-history audit methodology and test it across multiple mechanisms, memory conditions, and model backends (DeepSeek and GLM). Results reveal significant failures in memory recall, particularly with identifier renaming and tombstone removal, suggesting the need for scoped evaluation rather than general algorithmic superiority claims.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that memory systems can correctly answer current queries while losing information necessary for future updates - a fundamental failure mode where correct present answers sacrifice future adaptability. This "forgotten relevance" issue requires new evaluation paradigms beyond standard accuracy metrics.
AI.method: The authors employ a paired-history audit: two histories share the same current answer but receive a shared future update requiring different subsequent answers. They evaluate 24 history pairs across 6 synthetic mechanisms, 12 memory conditions, 2 repeats, and 2 model backends (DeepSeek and GLM). Methods include deterministic frontier selector, structured writer, four-outcome joint contrast with finite-sample identification intervals, record-level audit, tombstone removal, and identifier renaming tests.
AI.result: Deterministic frontier selector achieved 96/96 on DeepSeek but 82/96 on GLM. Structured writer obtained 62 successes with one unresolved outcome and 56/96. Identification intervals were [0.521, 0.542] and [0.292, 0.313]. Record-level audit found 26 and 25 well-formed but semantically wrong structured reveal memories, with all 14 GLM frontier reveal failures containing correct values in wrong wrappers. Tombstone removal produced 16/16 exact replay failures. Identifier renaming reduced late-reference adequacy from 8/8 to 94/320. The label-equivariant repair preserved only 2/8 original late-reference answers.
AI.conclusion: The study supports a scoped evaluation methodology and reproducible failure analysis rather than general superiority of any repaired algorithm. The authors acknowledge no independent held-out or natural-task validation, with paid pilot evidence and retrospective diagnostics reported separately. Key insight: eliminating naming shortcuts does not solve unknown future relevance problems.

title: PointEvent: Rethinking Event-based Tiny Object Detection via Serialized Motion Evidence Accumulation
summary: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, yet distant targets generate sparse and fragmented events that are easily overwhelmed by clutter and ego-motion. Existing methods mainly rely on dense event representations or local sparse spatiotemporal modeling, resulting in redundant computation or fragmented modeling of motion continuity across distant asynchronous events. To address this limitation, we introduce serialized motion evidence accumulation, which treats motion continuity as an ordered evidence propagation process. Specifically, the same event stream is organized into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths through the latent complementary serializations. Based on this principle, we propose PointEvent, a lightweight event-wise state-space framework that alternates serialized scans across the complementary orders, progressively consolidating fragmented motion evidence beyond fixed local neighborhoods. A high-resolution event branch preserves fine-grained target responses, while compact context modulation suppresses interference. Experiments demonstrate that PointEvent achieves SOTA with the fewest parameters and fastest measured inference among the compared methods. Code: https://github.com/wzz-z/PointEvent

AI.tldr: PointEvent is a lightweight event-wise state-space framework for tiny UAV detection using event cameras. It addresses the challenge of sparse and fragmented events from distant targets by introducing serialized motion evidence accumulation, which organizes events into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths through latent complementary serializations.
AI.motivation: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, but distant targets generate sparse and fragmented events that are easily overwhelmed by clutter and ego-motion. Existing methods rely on dense event representations or local sparse spatiotemporal modeling, resulting in either redundant computation or fragmented modeling of motion continuity across distant asynchronous events.
AI.method: The proposed method introduces serialized motion evidence accumulation, treating motion continuity as an ordered evidence propagation process. The same event stream is organized into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths through latent complementary serializations. PointEvent alternates serialized scans across complementary orders, progressively consolidating fragmented motion evidence beyond fixed local neighborhoods. A high-resolution event branch preserves fine-grained target responses, while compact context modulation suppresses interference.
AI.result: PointEvent achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with the fewest parameters and fastest measured inference among compared methods.
AI.conclusion: The serialized motion evidence accumulation approach effectively addresses the sparsity and fragmentation challenges in tiny UAV detection with event cameras. By modeling motion continuity as an ordered evidence propagation process and using complementary spatiotemporal paths, PointEvent achieves superior performance with minimal computational resources, making it suitable for deployment on tiny UAVs.

title: Geopolitical Divisions Across Languages in Large Language Models
summary: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots for news and explanations of world events. But do they receive the same political answers when they ask in different languages? Here we show that the language of a question can change how the same AI systems assess the war in Ukraine. We ask GPT, Claude and Gemini to evaluate twenty statements about the war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. When we group responses by countries' official languages, they follow a pattern resembling worldwide political divisions: relatively more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favourable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in United Nations votes, and less aid to Ukraine. The broad pattern recurs across all three models and remains when individual statement pairs are removed. Our findings suggest a possible route through which information warfare may shape the text used to train AI models, which may in turn spread geopolitical biases.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether AI chatbots (GPT, Claude, Gemini) provide different political answers when asked about the war in Ukraine in different languages. Testing 20 statements across 112 languages (67,200 responses), the researchers found that language choice affects the political leaning of responses, with patterns correlating to countries' official languages and their geopolitical positions toward Russia/Ukraine.
AI.motivation: The research addresses growing concerns about AI chatbots being used for news and world event explanations, while investigating whether language of inquiry influences the political answers provided - potentially revealing systemic biases in AI systems.
AI.method: The researchers asked GPT, Claude, and Gemini to evaluate 20 statements about the war in Ukraine in 112 different languages, collecting 67,200 total responses. They grouped responses by countries' official languages and correlated them with public opinion data, UN voting records, and aid to Ukraine.
AI.result: The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses varied across languages. When grouped by official languages, responses correlated with geopolitical positions: countries with more favorable views of Russia, less UN support for Ukraine, and less aid to Ukraine received more Russia-leaning AI responses. This pattern appeared across all three models and remained consistent when individual statement pairs were removed.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest a potential pathway for information warfare to influence AI training data, which may in turn propagate geopolitical biases through AI systems. The language-dependent responses indicate that AI models may absorb and reflect existing political divisions present in their training data.

title: Evaluating Explanation Methods by the Predictors They Induce
summary: Explanations of machine learning models are usually judged by criteria that are hard to compare. We propose a simpler test: if an explanation really describes how a model uses its features, it should be possible to rebuild the model's predictions from it. We turn each explanation into a predictor by reading each feature's effect and adding them up, and measure how well that predictor reproduces the model on unseen data. Nothing is fitted, so the score reflects the explanation itself. The test applies to any explanation that can be written as a function of the features; we demonstrate it on partial dependence plots (PDP), accumulated local effects (ALE), SHAP and LIME. We prove that summing partial dependence curves gives the best possible additive summary of a model when its features are independent, and that this fails when they are dependent. Across 13 real datasets and 9 synthetic designs and four model families, which method scores best depends entirely on feature dependence: where features are independent SHAP is slightly worse than PDP, exactly as the theory predicts; on dependent real data SHAP leads. Some widely used quality metrics even prefer a damaged explanation to an intact one.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a new test for evaluating machine learning model explanations: whether an explanation can be used to rebuild the model's predictions by summing feature effects. They apply this test to PDP, ALE, SHAP, and LIME across multiple datasets and model families.
AI.motivation: Existing criteria for evaluating explanations are hard to compare. The authors seek a simpler, more objective test that directly measures whether an explanation truly describes how a model uses its features.
AI.method: The authors turn each explanation into a predictor by reading each feature's effect and adding them up, then measure how well this predictor reproduces the model on unseen data. They prove theoretical results about when additive explanations work (independent features) and fail (dependent features). They test across 13 real datasets, 9 synthetic designs, and 4 model families.
AI.result: Summing partial dependence curves gives the best additive summary when features are independent, but fails with dependent features. On independent features, SHAP is slightly worse than PDP (as theory predicts); on dependent real data, SHAP leads. Some widely used quality metrics even prefer damaged explanations to intact ones.
AI.conclusion: Which explanation method scores best depends entirely on feature dependence. The proposed reconstruction test provides a simple, objective way to evaluate explanations that directly measures their explanatory power.

title: G^2RA-NET: Graph-based Cross-Slice Relation Modeling with Attention Gating for Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Medical image segmentation supports quantitative clinical analysis and computer-aided diagnosis. Recent methods for medical image segmentation have improved both local feature representation and volumetric context modeling. However, existing methods still strug- gle to efficiently model cross-slice relations in anisotropic volumet- ric images, limiting segmentation consistency and accuracy. This pa- per proposes G^2RA-Net, a medical image segmentation framework that combines graph-based cross-slice relation modeling with atten- tion gating. Graph-Based Slice Relationship Modeling (GSRM) cap- tures anatomical dependencies across consecutive slices by repre- senting each slice as a graph node and propagating semantic con- text through graph message passing. The Cross-Slice Attention Gate (CSAG) then selects relevant neighboring context and emphasizes target anatomical regions through attention-guided feature modula- tion. Experiments on brain MRI and abdominal CT datasets demon- strate that G^2RA-Net outperforms representative methods in seg- mentation accuracy and boundary quality. Ablation studies further validate the proposed design.

AI.tldr: G²RA-Net is a medical image segmentation framework that addresses the challenge of modeling cross-slice relations in anisotropic volumetric images by combining graph-based representation with attention gating mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing medical image segmentation methods struggle to efficiently model cross-slice relations in anisotropic volumetric images, which limits segmentation consistency and accuracy. The motivation is to improve both local feature representation and volumetric context modeling while specifically addressing the cross-slice relationship modeling problem.
AI.method: The paper proposes G²RA-Net with two key components: (1) Graph-Based Slice Relationship Modeling (GSRM) - represents each slice as a graph node and captures anatomical dependencies across consecutive slices through graph message passing for semantic context propagation; (2) Cross-Slice Attention Gate (CSAG) - uses attention-guided feature modulation to select relevant neighboring context and emphasize target anatomical regions.
AI.result: Experiments on brain MRI and abdominal CT datasets demonstrate that G²RA-Net outperforms representative methods in segmentation accuracy and boundary quality. Ablation studies validate the proposed design.
AI.conclusion: The combination of graph-based cross-slice relation modeling with attention gating effectively improves medical image segmentation performance, particularly for anisotropic volumetric images where cross-slice relationships are challenging to capture.

title: FedeRICo: Federated Region-Influenced Coupling for Traffic Flow Prediction
summary: Urban traffic forecasting often relies on information distributed across stakeholders who may be unable to share raw data due to privacy or commercial constraints, motivating federated spatial-temporal approaches. In such federated settings, each client observes traffic over a distinct sensor subgraph with its own spatial topology and temporal dynamics, leading to significant heterogeneity across clients. Existing federated spatial-temporal methods typically rely on model parameter aggregation and provide limited mechanisms for recovering spatial dependencies across client boundaries. This introduces two key limitations. Specifically, parameter aggregation across heterogeneous graph domains tends to dilute client-specific representations, while road network partitioning breaks the propagation of traffic dynamics across client boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose FedeRICo, a federated traffic forecasting framework that combines gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication. FedeRICo employs a dual-branch forecasting architecture in which a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure, while a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. The global branch is coordinated through gradient alignment across all clients, enabling collaborative optimisation without destructive parameter interference. To recover cross-client spatial dependencies, boundary messages are extracted through a trend-residual decomposition that suppresses periodic structure and communicates only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients. Experiments across four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.

AI.tldr: FedeRICo is a federated learning framework for urban traffic forecasting that addresses client heterogeneity and cross-client spatial dependency recovery through dual-branch architecture (global + private residual), gradient alignment collaboration, and boundary-aware residual communication using trend-residual decomposition.
AI.motivation: Urban traffic forecasting requires data across multiple stakeholders who cannot share raw data due to privacy/commercial constraints. Existing federated methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) parameter aggregation dilutes client-specific representations in heterogeneous graph domains, and (2) road network partitioning breaks traffic dynamics propagation across client boundaries.
AI.method: FedeRICo employs three key mechanisms: (1) Dual-branch forecasting architecture with a globally guided branch for transferable forecasting structure and a private residual branch for client-specific corrections with boundary residual signals; (2) Gradient alignment across all clients for collaborative optimization without destructive parameter interference; (3) Boundary message extraction through trend-residual decomposition that suppresses periodic structure and communicates transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients.
AI.result: Experiments across four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.
AI.conclusion: FedeRICo successfully addresses the heterogeneity and cross-client dependency challenges in federated traffic forecasting by combining gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication, achieving superior forecasting performance while preserving privacy and client-specific characteristics.

title: MATCH: Model-Aware Tool Learning with Curriculum Scheduling and Hierarchically Gated Rewards
summary: Tool learning enables large language models (LLMs) to use external tools for tasks beyond parametric knowledge. Reinforcement learning can optimize tool-call behavior from feedback, but current methods still face two problems: fixed-threshold curricula can become misaligned with the policy's evolving capability boundary, and additive rewards can leak argument-level credit when the predicted tool is wrong. To address these problems, we propose MATCH, a closed-loop framework for model-aware tool learning with curriculum scheduling and hierarchically gated rewards. Model-Aware Curriculum Learning (MACL) maintains reward-derived sample difficulty that co-evolves with the policy, and each epoch selects samples near the current capability boundary together with a top-k pool of harder cases. Hierarchical Tool-call Gated Reward (HTGR) scores tool name, argument key, and argument value as a gated chain, granting credit at each level only when prerequisites hold. The same HTGR rewards drive both GRPO updates and MACL's difficulty refresh, closing the loop between policy optimization and sample scheduling. On API-Bank and BFCL V3, MATCH reaches 72.19% and 62.87% overall accuracy, outperforming the main supervised and RL-based baselines. Backbone experiments further show consistent improvements across four backbones from two model families.

AI.tldr: MATCH is a closed-loop framework for optimizing tool learning in LLMs through model-aware curriculum scheduling and hierarchically gated rewards, addressing misaligned curricula and reward credit leakage issues.
AI.motivation: Current reinforcement learning methods for tool learning face two key problems: (1) fixed-threshold curricula become misaligned with the policy's evolving capability boundary, and (2) additive rewards leak argument-level credit when the predicted tool is wrong.
AI.method: MATCH employs two components: (1) Model-Aware Curriculum Learning (MACL) that maintains reward-derived sample difficulty co-evolving with the policy, selecting samples near the capability boundary plus top-k harder cases; (2) Hierarchical Tool-call Gated Reward (HTGR) that scores tool name, argument key, and argument value as a gated chain, granting credit only when prerequisites hold. The same HTGR rewards drive both GRPO updates and MACL's difficulty refresh, creating a closed loop.
AI.result: MATCH achieves 72.19% overall accuracy on API-Bank and 62.87% on BFCL V3, outperforming supervised and RL-based baselines. Consistent improvements are observed across four backbones from two model families.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MATCH framework effectively addresses curriculum misalignment and reward credit leakage in tool learning through its closed-loop design, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods on benchmark datasets.

title: A Smaller Transformer in Your Transformer
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the 37th British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC 2026)
summary: Recent findings indicate that Vision Transformers settle into locally similar computational phases, implying a level of depthwise computational redundancy. However, existing methods to exploit this redundancy either fail to reduce inference compute or severely degrade model expressivity. In this work, we formalise a unified view of block redundancy that decouples the geometry from specific surrogate interventions. We then introduce Transformer-Within-Transformer (TWT), a post-hoc method that fuses contiguous groups of redundant layers into a single learned surrogate layer. TWT reduces parameter count and inference compute while remaining competitive with original models using half the depth on natural images, and in several downstream histopathology settings, TWT matches or even improves on the original baseline.

AI.tldr: TWT (Transformer-Within-Transformer) is a post-hoc method that reduces Vision Transformer depth by fusing contiguous redundant layers into single learned surrogate layers, achieving parameter and compute reduction while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.motivation: Vision Transformers exhibit depthwise computational redundancy, settling into locally similar computational phases. Existing methods to exploit this redundancy either fail to reduce inference compute or severely degrade model expressivity.
AI.method: Formalizes a unified view of block redundancy that decouples geometry from surrogate interventions. TWT fuses contiguous groups of redundant layers into a single learned surrogate layer as a post-hoc modification.
AI.result: TWT reduces parameter count and inference compute while remaining competitive with original models using half the depth on natural images. In downstream histopathology settings, TWT matches or even improves on the original baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TWT method effectively addresses depthwise computational redundancy in Vision Transformers, enabling significant depth reduction without substantial performance degradation, and even showing improvements in specific domains like histopathology.

title: Can Data Attribution Filter Out Subliminal Learning? Not Reliably
summary: Subliminal learning allows language models to transmit behavioral traits through training data with no obvious semantic relationship to those traits, undermining content-based data filtering as a safety intervention. Training data attribution offers an alternative: it identifies the training examples responsible for a given model behavior, independent of their semantic content, and so may apply in exactly the cases where semantic inspection fails. We evaluate three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, a contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC) across three models, comparing them against divergence tokens, a strong baseline previously shown to localize subliminal learning (albeit one that requires access to counterfactual teacher models). Filtering at the token level, EK-FAC mitigates a significant part of the effect, the other methods provide little benefit, and all mostly fall short of divergence tokens. Filtering entire samples is less effective for every method, though EK-FAC often gives a stronger signal than divergence tokens in this setting. Success is inconsistent across methods and settings: variants that work well for some model-preference combinations fail for others, and we do not identify a consistent explanation for these differences. Our results suggest that gradient-based attribution can identify data responsible for subliminal learning in some settings, but that some approximations are more reliable than others.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, contrastive GradCos, and EK-FAC) against divergence tokens for identifying training data responsible for subliminal learning in language models. EK-FAC shows some effectiveness at token-level filtering, but overall results are inconsistent across models and settings.
AI.motivation: Subliminal learning allows language models to acquire behavioral traits from training data with no semantic relationship to those traits, undermining content-based data filtering as a safety intervention. The authors seek to evaluate training data attribution as an alternative approach that can identify responsible training examples regardless of semantic content.
AI.method: The authors evaluated three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC) across three models, comparing them against divergence tokens as a baseline. They tested both token-level and sample-level filtering approaches.
AI.result: At token-level filtering, EK-FAC mitigates a significant portion of the subliminal learning effect, while other methods provide little benefit and mostly fall short of divergence tokens. At sample-level filtering, all methods are less effective, though EK-FAC often provides a stronger signal than divergence tokens. Results are inconsistent across model-preference combinations with no consistent explanation for these differences.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-based attribution can identify data responsible for subliminal learning in some settings, but some approximations (particularly EK-FAC) are more reliable than others. The inconsistency across methods and settings suggests that further research is needed to develop more reliable attribution techniques for this safety-critical application.

title: SETTer: Sparse-Encoder Transformer for Long-term Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
summary: Long-term multivariate time series plays a significant role in many application areas such as power systems, trading, etc. However, their accurate prediction is quite difficult for conventional forecasting methods as they often exhibit high dimensionality and complex relationships. Recent works show that transformer-based approaches are quite effective for long-term forecasting thanks to their attention mechanism. However, in the presence of complex high-dimensional inputs, they show evidence of oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity. To this end, this paper introduces SETTer, a transformer-based model that addresses these challenges by incorporating novel techniques for decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking. The proposed techniques enable SETTer to effectively capture the dominant short- and long-term patterns across the temporal and channel dimensions. In addition, we enrich the model layers with simple explainable structures that indicate the discriminative pattern of SETTer. We show that with a single-layer transformer architecture, SETTer can effectively model long-term dependencies in the presence of varying data complexities. Extensive experiments on real-word benchmark datasets for long-term multivariate time series forecasting demonstrate that SETTer outperforms state-of-the-art models in 88% of the scenarios.

AI.tldr: SETTer is a transformer-based model for long-term multivariate time series forecasting that addresses oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity issues in existing transformers through decoupled self-attention, hybrid masking, and explainable structures.
AI.motivation: Long-term multivariate time series prediction is challenging due to high dimensionality and complex relationships. While transformer-based approaches are effective for long-term forecasting, they suffer from oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity when handling complex high-dimensional inputs.
AI.method: The paper proposes SETTer with three novel techniques: (1) Decoupled self-attention to capture patterns across temporal and channel dimensions separately, (2) Hybrid masking to enable effective modeling of dominant short- and long-term patterns, and (3) Enriched model layers with simple explainable structures for discriminative pattern identification. The model uses a single-layer transformer architecture.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world benchmark datasets show that SETTer outperforms state-of-the-art models in 88% of the scenarios for long-term multivariate time series forecasting.
AI.conclusion: SETTer effectively addresses the limitations of existing transformer-based approaches for long-term time series forecasting, achieving superior performance across diverse datasets while maintaining interpretability through its explainable structures.

title: AnyviewMeter: Adapting Robotic Reward Models with Camera Geometry and Multi-View Attention
summary: Robotic reward models evaluate task execution from visual observations, but their predictions can change with camera viewpoint and occlusion even when the underlying task state is unchanged. Adapting a pretrained reward model to a local task therefore requires accounting for how that task is observed. We introduce AnyviewMeter, a geometry-conditioned adaptation framework for robotic reward models that represent task progress as a scalar reward signal. It combines low-rank fine-tuning with token-aligned Plucker rays and synchronous block attention: ray conditioning incorporates camera geometry into visual features and attention queries and keys, while block attention fuses synchronized views inside the pretrained decoder. The framework supports both single-view reward prediction and joint multi-view evaluation through parameter-efficient adaptation of a pretrained Robometer model. On PickCube, single-view adaptation improves progress prediction in every camera group and reduces mean absolute error under a changed field of view by approximately 21% relative to RGB fine-tuning. Across simulated manipulation tasks, joint multi-view prediction reduces progress error by 41-69% compared with averaging single-view RGB predictions and improves temporal ordering in approximately 88% of task-camera groups. On real tasks with fixed and wrist-mounted cameras, mean absolute error decreases by approximately 21% relative to averaged RGB fine-tuning. These results support camera geometry and joint visual evidence as useful components of task-specific robotic reward adaptation.

AI.tldr: AnyviewMeter is a geometry-conditioned adaptation framework for robotic reward models that addresses viewpoint and occlusion sensitivity by combining low-rank fine-tuning with token-aligned Plucker rays and synchronous block attention. It supports both single-view and joint multi-view reward prediction through parameter-efficient adaptation of a pretrained Robometer model.
AI.motivation: Robotic reward models evaluate task execution from visual observations, but their predictions can change with camera viewpoint and occlusion even when the underlying task state remains unchanged. Adapting a pretrained reward model to a local task requires accounting for how that task is observed.
AI.method: The framework combines three key components: (1) Low-rank fine-tuning for parameter-efficient adaptation; (2) Token-aligned Plucker rays for camera geometry conditioning - incorporating geometry into visual features and attention queries/keys; (3) Synchronous block attention - fusing synchronized views inside the pretrained decoder. The method supports both single-view reward prediction and joint multi-view evaluation.
AI.result: On PickCube, single-view adaptation improved progress prediction in every camera group and reduced mean absolute error by ~21% under changed field of view. Across simulated manipulation tasks, joint multi-view prediction reduced progress error by 41-69% compared with averaging single-view RGB predictions and improved temporal ordering in ~88% of task-camera groups. On real tasks with fixed and wrist-mounted cameras, MAE decreased by ~21% relative to averaged RGB fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Camera geometry and joint visual evidence are useful components of task-specific robotic reward adaptation. The proposed AnyviewMeter framework effectively addresses viewpoint and occlusion sensitivity through geometry-conditioned adaptation.

title: DART: Distillation-Aware Reparameterization for Training-Free LoRA Reuse in Few-Step Video Diffusion Models
summary: Step distillation reduces the cost of video generation, but reusing a LoRA trained for a longer trajectory can alter its functional effect or degrade target quality. Static parameter compatibility offers one perspective on this problem; our observations show that similar measured geometry can coexist with different adapter behavior under a shortened denoising schedule. We propose DART, a training-free method that combines low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration using forward evaluations and no source training videos. On a four-step Wan2.2 target, DART-F improves the joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and changes macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349. Component analysis shows that calibration accounts for most of the quality improvement, while coordinate transport provides complementary gains when combined with calibration. Adapter-level results reveal positive functional effects for some adapters and strong attenuation with reduced negative functional effects for others. Evaluations on two additional targets show the same aggregate trend. These results motivate evaluating distilled-model LoRA reuse jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, without assuming recovery for every adapter.

AI.tldr: DART is a training-free method that addresses LoRA adaptation problems when reusing adapters trained for longer video generation trajectories on shortened (distilled) denoising schedules. It combines low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration to improve quality and functional retention without requiring source training videos.
AI.motivation: Step distillation reduces video generation costs, but reusing LoRAs trained for longer trajectories on shorter schedules causes functional alteration or quality degradation. Current approaches assume static parameter compatibility, but the authors observe that similar geometry can coexist with different adapter behaviors under shortened schedules.
AI.method: DART combines two components: (1) Low-rank coordinate transport for parameter alignment, and (2) Target-schedule response calibration using forward evaluations. The method is training-free and requires no source training videos. The method was evaluated on Wan2.2 with a four-step target schedule.
AI.result: On Wan2.2 four-step target: DART-F improved joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and changed macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349. Component analysis showed calibration accounts for most quality improvement while coordinate transport provides complementary gains when combined. Adapter-level results reveal positive functional effects for some adapters and strong attenuation with reduced negative effects for others. Same aggregate trend observed on two additional targets.
AI.conclusion: The results motivate evaluating distilled-model LoRA reuse jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, rather than assuming recovery for every adapter. The method successfully improves both quality and functional retention without requiring source training data.

title: CARE-VI: Conservative Adaptive Reliability Estimation for Value Improvement in Off-Policy Actor-Critic Learning
summary: Reliable temporal-difference targets are central to off-policy actor-critic learning. Direct value improvement refines the next-state target with alternative actions, but the reliability of this refinement depends on how candidate actions are ranked, reviewed, and weighted. Noisy rankings may force premature candidate commitment, reusing selection scores may bias target valuation, and fixed enhancement weights may amplify weak evidence. To address these risks, we develop Conservative Adaptive Ranking and Screening (CARS), which retains an ordered candidate prefix within a preset budget and narrows it only when the observed boundary gap exceeds a disagreement-scaled uncertainty radius. Selector-Evaluator Value Assessment (SEVA) uses selector critics to order candidates and a separately parameterized evaluator critic to review the selected value, then caps the reviewed value at the selector reference. Dynamic Adaptive Risk-aware Enhancement (DARE) then regulates each residual correction using candidate reliability, the gap between selector and evaluator signals, and a finite stage factor. Together, CARS, SEVA, and DARE form CARE-VI, an evidence-regulated target construction framework that preserves the backbone interfaces for critic regression and actor updates. The analysis bounds the CARS boundary error, the SEVA selected-value overestimation, and the one-sided deviation of the DARE residual displacement from its population counterpart, and establishes fixed-policy recovery after the finite-stage perturbation ends. Experiments with SAC, TD3, and TD7 on four MuJoCo tasks show that CARE-VI achieves the highest mean return in all twelve settings. Grouped ablations and scalar diagnostics support the roles of the three components in improving target reliability.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CARE-VI, an evidence-regulated target construction framework for off-policy actor-critic learning that addresses three key risks in temporal-difference target computation: noisy rankings causing premature candidate commitment, selection score reuse biasing target valuation, and fixed weights amplifying weak evidence. The framework combines CARS (Conservative Adaptive Ranking and Screening), SEVA (Selector-Evaluator Value Assessment), and DARE (Dynamic Adaptive Risk-aware Enhancement) to improve target reliability through adaptive ranking, dual-critic review, and risk-aware residual regulation.
AI.motivation: Off-policy actor-critic methods rely on reliable temporal-difference targets for learning, but three risks undermine this reliability: (1) Noisy rankings may force premature candidate commitment, (2) reusing selection scores may bias target valuation, and (3) fixed enhancement weights may amplify weak evidence. These issues degrade the quality of value estimates and hinder learning performance.
AI.method: The paper develops three complementary components: (1) CARS retains an ordered candidate prefix within a preset budget and narrows it only when the observed boundary gap exceeds a disagreement-scaled uncertainty radius; (2) SEVA uses selector critics to order candidates and a separately parameterized evaluator critic to review selected values, capping the reviewed value at the selector reference; (3) DARE regulates each residual correction using candidate reliability, the gap between selector and evaluator signals, and a finite stage factor. Together, these form CARE-VI, preserving backbone interfaces for critic regression and actor updates.
AI.result: Experiments with SAC, TD3, and TD7 on four MuJoCo tasks show that CARE-VI achieves the highest mean return in all twelve settings (3 algorithms × 4 environments). Grouped ablations and scalar diagnostics confirm the individual contributions of CARS, SEVA, and DARE in improving target reliability.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides theoretical bounds on CARS boundary error, SEVA selected-value overestimation, and the one-sided deviation of DARE residual displacement from its population counterpart. The framework establishes fixed-policy recovery after finite-stage perturbation ends. The three components work synergistically: CARS provides conservative candidate selection, SEVA offers dual-critic review to prevent overestimation, and DARE implements risk-aware enhancement, together significantly improving off-policy actor-critic learning performance.

title: Cross-Modal Attention Acts as a Frequency Filter: Why Verbose Prompts Improve Robustness in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are fragile under image corruption. We find that the wording of the question affects VLMs in two opposite ways. Verbose questions make VLMs substantially more robust---e.g., rephrasing "Is there a cat?" into "Please look carefully and answer: is there a cat?". Conversely, VLMs become more fragile under corruption when the question is semantically complex or finer-grained, e.g., "what colour is the cup left of the chair?" instead of "is there a cup?". Both effects stem from question-conditioned cross-modal attention, which induces a spectral filter over image patches: verbose questions broaden its frequency support, while fine-grained questions concentrate it onto fewer visual scales. The model's answer drifts most when this filter and the corruption sit on the same spatial frequencies. We test the filter view on Qwen3-VL and LLaVA-OneVision across GQA and CLEVR; verbose paraphrasing reduces drift variance by 70--81% on the 8B models. The practical recipe---pad the prompt---further yields measurable gains in accuracy, even under image corruption.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that question wording affects VLM robustness to image corruption in opposite ways: verbose questions (e.g., "Please look carefully and answer: is there a cat?") improve robustness, while fine-grained questions (e.g., "what colour is the cup left of the chair?") increase fragility. Both effects are explained by question-conditioned cross-modal attention acting as a spectral filter over image patches.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models are fragile under image corruption, but the underlying mechanism is not well understood. This work investigates how the wording of questions affects VLM robustness.
AI.method: The authors analyze question-conditioned cross-modal attention as a spectral filter over image patches, examining how verbose vs. fine-grained questions affect the frequency support of this filter. They test this filter view on Qwen3-VL and LLaVA-OneVision across GQA and CLEVR datasets, and propose a practical recipe of padding the prompt.
AI.result: Verbose paraphrasing reduces drift variance by 70-81% on 8B models. The practical recipe of padding the prompt yields measurable gains in accuracy even under image corruption.
