AI.conclusion: The conclusion demonstrates that collaborative sample-complexity speedups are achievable in federated reinforcement learning even in the presence of adversarial agents, with near-optimal finite-time rates and minimal communication requirements. This makes the approach practical for federated learning scenarios where communication is the major bottleneck.

title: Scene-Q: Confidence-Aware Coarse-to-Fine Querying of 3D Scenes with Selective VLM Reasoning
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IROS 2026
summary: Indoor mobile robots require open-vocabulary scene understanding that grounds natural-language queries in a consistent 3D map. Many existing systems ultimately rely on cosine-similarity retrieval with contrastive image--text encoders, which is efficient but brittle when labels are near-synonymous or multiple similar instances appear. We present Scene-Q, a confidence-aware coarse-to-fine querying framework that normalizes encoder scores with temperature scaling and selectively invokes a reasoning VLM only for low-confidence cases. High-confidence queries are answered by fast retrieval, while ambiguous ones are reranked over a small top-K candidate set using the original multi-view images and instance bounding boxes, enabling context-aware disambiguation at low cost. Scene-Q improves open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation on ScanNet200 and natural-language 3D instance retrieval on real-world reconstructions, with the largest gains on spatial and relational queries while keeping a substantial fraction of queries on the fast path.

AI.tldr: Scene-Q is a confidence-aware coarse-to-fine querying framework for indoor mobile robots that combines fast contrastive retrieval with selective VLM reasoning for ambiguous cases, improving open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding.
AI.motivation: Indoor mobile robots require open-vocabulary scene understanding to ground natural-language queries in 3D maps. Existing cosine-similarity retrieval with contrastive image-text encoders is efficient but brittle when labels are near-synonymous or multiple similar instances appear.
AI.method: Scene-Q normalizes encoder scores with temperature scaling and selectively invokes a reasoning Vision-Language Model (VLM) only for low-confidence cases. High-confidence queries are answered by fast retrieval, while ambiguous queries are reranked over a small top-K candidate set using multi-view images and instance bounding boxes for context-aware disambiguation.
AI.result: Scene-Q improves open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation on ScanNet200 and natural-language 3D instance retrieval on real-world reconstructions, with the largest gains on spatial and relational queries while maintaining a substantial fraction of queries on the fast path.
AI.conclusion: The coarse-to-fine approach successfully balances efficiency (fast retrieval for high-confidence cases) and accuracy (VLM reasoning for ambiguous cases), achieving state-of-the-art performance on open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding tasks.

title: Perception, Layout, and Validation: Calibrated Confidence for Reliable Straight-Through Processing of Financial Documents
summary: Straight-through processing (STP) on extracted key-value fields from financial documents without human review requires a calibrated probability together with a bounded guarantee on the residual error of the auto-approved tier. The emergence of modern Vision Language Models (VLMs) provides an out-of-the-box capability for extracting the key-values, but their verbalized confidence signals are unreliable and weakly track field correctness. This paper introduces a decomposed confidence layer along three interpretable channels, including perception, layout, and validation. Together with a final conformal risk control, the score can be used for reliable STP of financial documents. The method is validated on three public datasets covering real invoices, synthetic invoices, and ad-buy forms, using two different VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite). Our decomposed score consistently improves the separation of correct from incorrect extractions, substantially raising the AUROC from 0.54-0.74 for VLM verbalized signals to 0.90-0.99 with contributions from all three designed channels. Crucially for industrial deployment, this enables usable STP. The native VLM confidence signals could clear only 0.1%-7.0% of fields under risk control at a target error of <10%. In contrast, the proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while holding the empirical error of the accepted tier at or below the target.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of unreliable confidence signals from Vision Language Models (VLMs) when extracting key-value fields from financial documents. The authors propose a decomposed confidence layer with three interpretable channels (perception, layout, validation) combined with conformal risk control to enable reliable Straight-Through Processing (STP) without human review.
AI.motivation: Modern VLMs can extract key-values from financial documents but their verbalized confidence signals are unreliable and weakly correlate with field correctness. This prevents automated STP as there is no calibrated probability with bounded guarantee on residual error for the auto-approved tier.
AI.method: The proposed method introduces a decomposed confidence layer with three interpretable channels: (1) Perception channel - assesses visual understanding quality, (2) Layout channel - evaluates spatial structure recognition, (3) Validation channel - checks semantic consistency. These are combined with a final conformal risk control mechanism to provide reliable probability estimates with bounded error guarantees.
AI.result: The method was validated on three public datasets (real invoices, synthetic invoices, ad-buy forms) using two VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite). Results show: (1) AUROC improved from 0.54-0.74 (VLM verbalized signals) to 0.90-0.99 (proposed method); (2) STP approval rate increased from 0.1%-7.0% to 49-72% while maintaining error rate below 10% target.
AI.conclusion: The decomposed confidence score with three channels consistently improves separation of correct from incorrect extractions across all datasets and VLM families. This enables practical industrial deployment of STP for financial document processing, with the proposed method clearing 49-72% of fields under risk control compared to only 0.1-7.0% using native VLM confidence signals.

title: When Does Retrieval Help Time-Series Forecasting?
summary: Retrieval plug-ins supply a deep forecaster with information its lookback window cannot carry. Published evaluations report consistent gains, and each credits its own mechanism. We show that the benefit belongs instead to the operating point: the relation between window length $S$ and dominant seasonal period $L$, an axis the standard protocol never varies. Stratifying the evaluation by that relation exposes the regime. At $S{=}12$, a simple control that repeats the last observed period beats the six standard backbones, in aggregate, on four of seven benchmarks by $8\%$ to $44\%$ of MSE. It beats the strongest plug-in we run on ETTm1 and matches it on ECL. It is worse by up to $25\%$ on the three datasets whose training-split spectra lack a concentrated, shared period. A controlled synthetic sweep of horizon, period, and window shows the benefit boundary tracks the period (correlation $+0.71$), not the horizon ($-0.23$). A paired control with no phase to recover nearly erases the effect, consistent with phase starvation. Zero-shot pretraining does not escape it: a foundation model trails trained backbones by $22\%$ to $50\%$ on the periodic benchmarks. Within our instrument, exact lookup matches graph diffusion: the payoff is consulting the record, not the machinery on top. Two interpretable statistics, a trend test and a staleness rate, predict the sign of the per-cell benefit at $0.76$ accuracy under leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, a suggestive margin over the $0.69$ majority rule, where a 22-feature stack manages $0.57$. We propose no new plug-in. The contribution is the regime map, the protocol that reveals it, and two statistics that screen it before deployment. Code: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/retrieval-regime.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the prevailing assumption that retrieval plugins improve deep time series forecasters through sophisticated mechanisms. Instead, the authors demonstrate that the performance gains come from the operating point—the relationship between lookback window length (S) and dominant seasonal period (L). A simple control that repeats the last observed period beats six standard backbones and even strong retrieval plugins on periodic benchmarks, but fails on datasets without clear seasonal patterns. The key insight is "phase starvation": the benefit tracks the seasonal period (correlation +0.71), not the horizon. Two interpretable statistics (trend test and staleness rate) can predict when retrieval will help.
AI.motivation: Current literature credits retrieval plugins' benefits to their sophisticated mechanisms (graph diffusion, exact lookup, etc.). However, the authors noticed that standard evaluation protocols never vary the relationship between window length (S) and seasonal period (L), which could be the true source of improvement. This paper aims to disentangle whether gains come from the retrieval mechanism itself or from this operating point.
AI.method: The authors conducted a series of controlled experiments: (1) Stratified evaluation by the S-L relationship across 7 benchmarks; (2) A simple control that repeats the last observed period as baseline; (3) Synthetic sweep varying horizon, period, and window; (4) Paired control with no phase to recover; (5) Evaluation of a foundation model under zero-shot setting; (6) Development of two interpretable statistics (trend test and staleness rate) to predict benefit sign; (7) Leave-one-dataset-out evaluation to test prediction accuracy.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) At S=12, the simple repeat control beats six backbones on 4/7 benchmarks by 8-44% MSE, beats the strongest plugin on ETTm1, and matches on ECL; (2) Benefit is worse by up to 25% on datasets lacking concentrated shared period; (3) Benefit boundary tracks period (correlation +0.71), not horizon (-0.23); (4) Paired control with no phase nearly erases the effect, confirming phase starvation; (5) Foundation model trails trained backbones by 22-50% on periodic benchmarks; (6) Exact lookup matches graph diffusion; (7) Two statistics predict benefit sign at 0.76 accuracy vs 0.69 majority rule.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is not a new retrieval plugin but: (1) A regime map showing when retrieval helps; (2) A protocol that reveals the true source of gains; (3) Two statistics (trend test and staleness rate) that can screen retrieval benefits before deployment. The core insight is that the payoff comes from consulting the historical record, not the sophisticated machinery on top. This challenges the field to reconsider evaluation protocols and focus on identifying when periodic patterns exist before deploying retrieval mechanisms.

title: SAGE-Yoga: Multi-Cue Learning for Yoga Pose Classification and Joint-Level Correction
summary: Automated yoga analysis requires both accurate pose classification and interpretable feedback on pose execution. However, existing methods often rely on a single visual prediction, struggle to distinguish visually similar poses, and treat pose classification and correction as separate tasks. To address these limitations, we propose SAGE-Yoga, a unified coarse-to-fine framework for yoga pose classification and joint-level correction from a single RGB image. Inspired by how yoga instructors assess posture using multiple complementary cues, SAGE-Yoga first employs a bagging-based ensemble of complementary visual backbones to generate a ranked set of candidate pose classes. Additionally, a margin-based gating mechanism preserves confident visual predictions while invoking geometric verification only for ambiguous cases. Moreover, once the final pose class is determined, SAGE-Yoga retrieves a medoid reference pose and compares the observed joint angles with class-specific distributions to identify misaligned joints. Finally, these deviations are translated into actionable corrective feedback. Empirically, experiments on the Yoga-82 dataset show that the visual ensemble achieves 89.0% Top-1 accuracy, while the complete framework improves performance to 90.7% Top-1 accuracy and 90.1% Macro-F1. These results demonstrate that combining complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification improves fine-grained pose classification while enabling interpretable, joint-level correction.

AI.tldr: SAGE-Yoga is a unified coarse-to-fine framework combining visual ensemble prediction with geometric verification for yoga pose classification (90.7% Top-1 accuracy) and joint-level corrective feedback from single RGB images.
AI.motivation: Existing yoga analysis methods rely on single visual predictions, struggle to distinguish visually similar poses, and treat pose classification and correction as separate tasks, lacking interpretable feedback on pose execution.
AI.method: SAGE-Yoga employs: (1) bagging-based ensemble of complementary visual backbones for ranked candidate poses; (2) margin-based gating mechanism preserving confident predictions while invoking geometric verification for ambiguous cases; (3) medoid reference pose comparison with class-specific joint angle distributions for misalignment detection; (4) translation of deviations into actionable corrective feedback.
AI.result: On Yoga-82 dataset: visual ensemble achieves 89.0% Top-1 accuracy; complete framework improves to 90.7% Top-1 accuracy and 90.1% Macro-F1. Combines complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification for improved fine-grained classification and interpretable joint-level correction.
AI.conclusion: Combining complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification improves fine-grained yoga pose classification while enabling interpretable, joint-level correction—bridging the gap between classification accuracy and actionable feedback for yoga instruction.

title: MTVA-Bench: Evaluating the Language Model Inside Cascaded Voice Agents
summary: Generally, most voice agents are cascaded systems, i.e., an ASR model transcribes the caller's audio, a language model reads the transcript and decides what to say and which backend tools to call, and a TTS model speaks the reply. Nearly all of the decision making happens in the language model, but existing evaluations measure it either too broadly or too narrowly. End-to-end voice benchmarks score the full pipeline, so recognition errors and model errors mix into a single number. LLM benchmarks isolate the model but they do not evaluate what makes real phone calls hard, such as transcription issues, caller's voice being split across messages and the requirement that replies follow the language and script specified. We introduce the Multi-Turn Voice Agent Benchmark (MTVA-Bench), which evaluates the language model on the same conditions it faces inside a cascaded system. The caller is played by an LLM following a set of rubrics and tool calls are answered by a mock backend which responds to the arguments the model actually sent. The benchmark contains 49 agents working across 490 reviewed scenarios and supports 7 languages. Scoring is a combination of deterministic checks on tool calls with two LLM judges, one that scores scenario specific rules and one that grades conversation quality without access to the task. Both judges must cite specific messages from the transcript. Task and conversation scores are weighted equally, since a call can complete its task and still go badly for the caller. In a seven-model study, six of the models select the correct tool within 6.4 points of one another, but their overall scores span 24.4 points. Most of the gap comes from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and what the model says around its tool calls.

AI.tldr: MTVA-Bench is a benchmark designed to evaluate language models within cascaded voice agent systems, addressing the gap between end-to-end benchmarks (too broad, mixing errors) and LLM benchmarks (too narrow, missing real-world challenges like transcription issues and call flow dynamics). The benchmark features 49 agents across 490 scenarios in 7 languages, using deterministic checks on tool calls plus two LLM judges for task-specific rules and conversation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of voice agents are inadequate: end-to-end benchmarks mix recognition and model errors into one score, while LLM benchmarks don't capture real phone call challenges like transcription issues, voice splitting across messages, and script/language compliance. The authors needed a way to evaluate the language model's decision-making in the same conditions it faces in production cascaded systems.
AI.method: MTVA-Bench evaluates LLM decision-making under cascaded system conditions using: (1) an LLM to play the caller following rubrics, (2) a mock backend that responds to actual model-sent arguments, (3) 49 agents across 490 reviewed scenarios in 7 languages. Scoring combines deterministic tool call checks with two LLM judges—one scoring scenario-specific rules, one grading conversation quality without task access. Both judges must cite specific transcript messages. Task and conversation scores are equally weighted.
AI.result: In a seven-model study, six models performed within 6.4 points of each other on correct tool selection, but overall scores spanned 24.4 points. The performance gap stemmed primarily from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and model behavior around tool calls—not tool selection itself.
AI.conclusion: Tool selection is not the differentiator in voice agent performance; rather, the gap comes from how models handle argument values, action sequencing, rule compliance, and conversational behavior around tool calls. MTVA-Bench provides a more realistic evaluation by testing LLMs under the same conditions they face in production cascaded voice systems, revealing that subtle implementation differences in model behavior can significantly impact overall performance.

title: SoftTri: Smooth Triangular Membership Functions for Adaptive Fuzzy Inference Systems
summary: Triangular membership functions (MFs) are widely used in fuzzy systems because of their interpretability, low parameterization complexity, and strong locality properties. However, their inherent nondifferentiability at knot points limits the effectiveness of gradient-based optimization in adaptive neuro-fuzzy architectures, often necessitating subgradient approximations or heuristic smoothing techniques. In this paper, we propose \emph{SoftTri}, a differentiable triangular membership function constructed using a smooth soft-hinge mechanism inspired by Swish-type activations. The proposed formulation preserves the geometric structure and localized behavior of classical triangular MFs while providing $C^\infty$ smoothness with respect to both the input variable and the membership parameters $(a,b,c)$ for any finite sharpness parameter $β>0$. Closed-form analytical gradients are derived to enable efficient and fully differentiable backpropagation-based learning. SoftTri is integrated into a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy neural network with grid-partitioned rules and evaluated on multiple one-dimensional and two-dimensional nonlinear approximation benchmarks as well as a real-world regression task using the Airfoil Self-Noise dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that SoftTri consistently improves optimization stability and approximation accuracy compared with classical triangular membership functions, while achieving performance comparable to or better than Gaussian MFs under identical rule structures and training settings. The proposed approach provides an effective compromise between interpretability and differentiable optimization in modern neuro-fuzzy learning systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SoftTri, a differentiable triangular membership function that addresses the nondifferentiability limitation of classical triangular MFs in neuro-fuzzy systems. It uses a smooth soft-hinge mechanism inspired by Swish-type activations to preserve the geometric structure of triangular MFs while providing C∞ smoothness and enabling efficient backpropagation.
AI.motivation: Triangular membership functions are widely used in fuzzy systems due to their interpretability and low complexity, but their inherent nondifferentiability at knot points limits the effectiveness of gradient-based optimization in adaptive neuro-fuzzy architectures. This necessitates subgradient approximations or heuristic smoothing techniques.
AI.method: The proposed SoftTri uses a smooth soft-hinge mechanism inspired by Swish-type activations to construct a differentiable triangular membership function. Closed-form analytical gradients are derived for efficient backpropagation. SoftTri is integrated into a Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy neural network with grid-partitioned rules.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that SoftTri consistently improves optimization stability and approximation accuracy compared with classical triangular membership functions, while achieving performance comparable to or better than Gaussian MFs under identical rule structures and training settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides an effective compromise between interpretability and differentiable optimization in modern neuro-fuzzy learning systems, making it a valuable contribution to adaptive neuro-fuzzy architectures.

title: Distance to Class Prototypes: Active Learning for Object Detection
summary: Deploying a deep object detector in a new setting is limited less by architecture than by the cost of annotating data from that setting. Active learning lowers the cost by choosing which images to label, and the choice is only as good as the signal used to score an unlabeled image. That signal is usually the class posterior, which is cheap but poorly calibrated, or the disagreement across several models or several stochastic passes, which is better but multiplies inference over a pool far larger than the labeled set. We propose a signal richer than the posterior yet still read from one forward pass of one network. A supervised contrastive term added to the training objective shapes a per-object embedding space in which distance encodes class membership, and an unlabeled detection is scored by how far it lies from the region occupied by its predicted category, weighted by its confidence. The criterion needs no ensemble, no auxiliary predictor and no repeated inference, and its entire cost is 2.89M parameters, an increase of 8.3% over a bare detector. On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO it beats the posterior of the same detector in every round in which a selection is made, by up to 1.08% mAP50 against run to run deviations of 0.02% to 0.18%, and it stays competitive with ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout criteria costing three to fifty forward passes per unlabeled image. Experiments use the single-stage detector under which the compared criteria report their results, so that the selection decision is isolated from the strength of the detector.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a new active learning scoring criterion for object detection that uses supervised contrastive learning to create an embedding space where distance encodes class membership. The method scores unlabeled images based on how far detections lie from their predicted category region, weighted by confidence. It achieves better performance than class posterior while requiring only a single forward pass, unlike ensemble or Monte Carlo dropout methods that need multiple passes.
AI.motivation: Deploying deep object detectors in new settings is limited by annotation costs. Active learning aims to reduce these costs by selecting most informative images to label. Existing signals either use class posterior (cheap but poorly calibrated) or model disagreement (better but requires multiple inferences), making them expensive for large unlabeled pools.
AI.method: The method adds a supervised contrastive term to the training objective, shaping a per-object embedding space where distance encodes class membership. Unlabeled detections are scored by measuring how far they lie from the region occupied by their predicted category, weighted by their confidence. This requires only one forward pass of one network, with only 2.89M additional parameters (8.3% increase).
AI.result: On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO, the proposed method beats the class posterior of the same detector in every selection round, achieving up to 1.08% mAP50 improvement against run-to-run deviations of 0.02% to 0.18%. It remains competitive with ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout criteria that cost three to fifty forward passes per unlabeled image.
AI.conclusion: The proposed contrastive-based scoring criterion provides a richer signal than class posterior while maintaining the efficiency of single forward pass inference. It successfully bridges the gap between cheap but poorly calibrated posterior-based methods and expensive ensemble/disagreement-based methods, achieving competitive performance with significantly reduced computational cost.

title: PaGNet: A Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network for Multi-Target Corporate Tax Avoidance Proxy Forecasting
summary: Forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies from firm--year panel data is challenging because predictive signals are distributed across short firm histories and related targets, while screening-oriented use requires transparent model behavior. We propose PaGNet (Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network), a two-branch hybrid that combines a LightGBM branch using panel-temporal summaries with a Panel-MLP branch using attention-pooled temporal aggregation and shared-trunk multi-task learning. A per-target validation-optimal blender produces both the final prediction and a compact branch-reliance diagnostic without trainable fusion parameters. On the KoTaP panel of 1{,}754 Korean listed firms from 2011--2024, PaGNet is evaluated under a leakage-free, shared-hyperparameter protocol across four feature regimes. In the direct-proxy-lag-excluded FS1 regime and the tax-history-augmented FS2 regime, accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA) route stably to the LightGBM branch, where PaGNet raises explained variance over the strongest of six baselines by roughly $0.08$--$0.11$ on the primary split. GETR often leans toward the neural branch, while CETR exposes a validation--test branch-selection mismatch rather than a stable branch assignment. A panel-flatten control shows that most accrual gains come from observed multi-year base-panel values, with PaGNet's panel-aware representation adding a smaller but directionally consistent refinement. Rolling-origin analysis confirms stable accrual routing, bounds ETR diagnostics to split-specific behavior, and identifies a far-horizon split where supervised models underperform naive persistence. PaGNet is therefore best viewed not as a universally superior tabular learner, but as a proxy-aware panel model that combines competitive forecasting with explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting.

AI.tldr: PaGNet is a two-branch hybrid model combining LightGBM and neural network for forecasting corporate tax avoidance from panel data. It uses per-target validation-optimal blending to produce predictions and branch-reliance diagnostics without trainable fusion parameters.
AI.motivation: Forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies is challenging because predictive signals are distributed across short firm histories and related targets, while screening-oriented use requires transparent model behavior.
AI.method: PaGNet combines a LightGBM branch (using panel-temporal summaries) with a Panel-MLP branch (using attention-pooled temporal aggregation and shared-trunk multi-task learning). A per-target validation-optimal blender produces final predictions and branch-reliance diagnostics without trainable fusion parameters. Evaluation uses 1,754 Korean listed firms (2011-2024) under a leakage-free protocol across four feature regimes.
AI.result: For accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA), PaGNet increases explained variance by 0.08-0.11 over six baselines. Accrual targets route stably to the LightGBM branch. Most gains come from observed multi-year base-panel values, with panel-aware representation adding smaller refinement. Rolling-origin analysis confirms stable accrual routing and identifies a far-horizon split where supervised models underperform naive persistence.
AI.conclusion: PaGNet is best viewed as a proxy-aware panel model that combines competitive forecasting with explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting, not as a universally superior tabular learner. Different tax avoidance proxies show distinct branch routing patterns: accrual targets favor LightGBM, GETR leans toward neural branch, and CETR exhibits validation-test branch-selection mismatch.

title: Evaluating Financial Sentiment in the Age of AI
summary: Financial sentiment measures are widely used in empirical finance, but it remains unclear whether general-purpose large language models (LLMs) improve on existing finance-specific methods. This paper evaluates twelve sentiment models, including dictionary-based methods, finance-specific transformers, and open-source LLMs, using two criteria: linguistic validity and economic validity. We find that general-purpose LLMs achieve classification performance comparable to finance-specific transformer models without task-specific fine-tuning. However, higher classification accuracy does not translate into stronger economic relationships. Several models produce sentiment measures that are significantly associated with earnings surprises, but none is significantly associated with next-day stock returns. Model performance is strongest for announcements with large earnings beats or misses and substantially weaker for announcements with more moderate earnings surprises. These findings suggest that financial sentiment captures information about firms' economic performance but has limited ability to explain short-run market reactions

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates 12 financial sentiment models (dictionary-based, finance-specific transformers, and general-purpose LLMs) against two criteria: linguistic validity and economic validity. The key finding is that while LLMs perform comparably to finance-specific models in classification, this doesn't translate to better economic predictions.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the gap in understanding whether general-purpose LLMs improve upon existing finance-specific sentiment methods, given their widespread use in empirical finance.
AI.method: The study evaluates twelve sentiment models using two criteria: linguistic validity (classification performance) and economic validity (association with earnings surprises and stock returns).
AI.result: General-purpose LLMs achieve comparable classification performance to finance-specific transformers without fine-tuning. However, higher classification accuracy does not lead to stronger economic relationships. Several models produce sentiment significantly associated with earnings surprises, but none with next-day stock returns. Performance is strongest for large earnings beats/misses.
AI.conclusion: Financial sentiment captures information about firms' economic performance but has limited ability to explain short-run market reactions. The disconnect between linguistic and economic validity suggests that classification accuracy alone is insufficient for economic forecasting.

title: Generative Verification: Rethinking the Uncertainty Signal for Active Learning of Object Detection
summary: Nearly every acquisition function for active object detection shares one arrangement, in that the model being improved is also the model being interrogated. We depart from it. In generative verification an independent generative model re-derives the label of a detection from the pixels inside its predicted box, and the disagreement between the two becomes the acquisition signal. Two properties follow from the arrangement itself rather than from any tuning. A displaced box, a box on background and a correct box carrying the wrong label all yield a crop that fails verification, so the failure modes arrive already combined in one scalar and the hand-weighted classification and localization terms of existing criteria are no longer needed. And because the verifier never observes the detector confidence, confidently wrong detections score highest, although a self-derived signal reads them as uninteresting and they are the costliest to leave unlabeled. We build the verifier as a conditional diffusion model whose diffusion target is a label representation rather than an image. Its reverse process is stochastic, so repeated generations return a distribution whose concentration reports how firmly the evidence determines the label, where a classifier returns a single point estimate. On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO the signal outperforms output-uncertainty, feature-geometry, perturbation and ensemble criteria, gaining about one mAP50 point per round on MS-COCO, with its largest margins in the early rounds where confident detector errors are most common.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes "generative verification" for active object detection, where an independent conditional diffusion model verifies detections by re-deriving labels from cropped pixels. The disagreement between detector and verifier serves as the acquisition signal, outperforming existing methods by ~1 mAP50 point per round on MS-COCO, with biggest gains in early rounds.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the common assumption in active object detection that the same model serves both as the detector and the acquisition function scorer. The authors argue that this arrangement has limitations: 1) Hand-weighted classification and localization terms are needed, and 2) Confidently wrong detections are scored as uninteresting, making them costly to leave unlabeled.
AI.method: The authors propose generative verification using a conditional diffusion model as an independent verifier. The verifier re-derives labels from pixels inside predicted bounding boxes. Its reverse process is stochastic, generating a distribution whose concentration indicates how firmly the evidence determines the label. The acquisition signal is the disagreement between the detector and this independent verifier.
AI.result: The generative verification signal outperforms output-uncertainty, feature-geometry, perturbation, and ensemble criteria on PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO datasets, gaining approximately one mAP50 point per round on MS-COCO. The largest margins appear in early rounds where confident detector errors are most common.
AI.conclusion: The proposed generative verification method outperforms existing acquisition criteria (output-uncertainty, feature-geometry, perturbation, ensemble) on PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO, achieving approximately 1 mAP50 point gain per round on MS-COCO, with largest improvements in early rounds when confident detector errors are most prevalent.

title: Sequential Contextual Fit Predicts Human Behavioural and Neural Dynamics Across Domains
summary: Human perception, action and decision making unfold in sequences, but computational predictors are often domain-specific. This study computes and tests sequential contextual fit (SCF), an embedding-based measure of how well a current information state matches its recent context. The metric uses a simple recency-weighted similarity kernel and can be applied to words, sounds, visual scenes, affective states, choices, actions and neural representations. Across language processing, music-evoked emotion, a subset of audiovisual emotion EEG data, gambling decisions, human activity recognition and decision-related EEG, lower contextual fit predicted longer processing times, larger affective or behavioural transitions and stronger neural-state changes. These effects remained after controlling for established predictors including surprisal, reinforcement-learning prediction error, acoustic change, visual change and sensor change. SCF therefore provides a computational measurement layer for relating contextual compatibility to behavioural processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics.

AI.tldr: This study introduces Sequential Contextual Fit (SCF), an embedding-based measure evaluating how well current information matches its recent context. SCF uses a recency-weighted similarity kernel and can be applied across domains including words, sounds, visual scenes, affective states, choices, actions, and neural representations.
AI.motivation: Human perception, action and decision making occur sequentially, but existing computational predictors are domain-specific. There is a need for a universal measure that can capture contextual compatibility across different cognitive domains.
AI.method: The researchers computed SCF using a recency-weighted similarity kernel applied to various data types (words, sounds, visual scenes, affective states, choices, actions, neural representations). They tested SCF across six domains: language processing, music-evoked emotion, audiovisual emotion EEG, gambling decisions, human activity recognition, and decision-related EEG. They controlled for established predictors including surprisal, reinforcement-learning prediction error, acoustic change, visual change, and sensor change.
AI.result: Lower contextual fit (i.e., poorer match between current state and recent context) predicted: (1) longer processing times, (2) larger affective or behavioural transitions, and (3) stronger neural-state changes. These effects remained significant after controlling for established predictors.
AI.conclusion: Sequential Contextual Fit provides a computational measurement layer for relating contextual compatibility to behavioural processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics, serving as a domain-general measure applicable across multiple cognitive domains.

title: Towards a Unified Modality-Agnostic Multimodal Framework for Cognitive Workload Assessment
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: Cognitive workload reflects the mental effort required during task performance and is central to the design of adaptive human-machine systems. The use of biosignals to measure cognitive workload has been extensively researched and documented; however, studies examining the effects of combining heterogeneous biosignal modalities for this purpose remain limited. To provide insight into this area, we developed a unified, modality-agnostic, hierarchical Transformer-based architecture to process heterogeneous biosignal modalities within a single model. We use this framework in a pilot study evaluating all $31$ possible combinations of five modalities: Electrocardiogram (ECG), Electrodermal Activity (EDA), Respiration (RESP), Peripheral Oxygen Saturation (SpO$_2$), and Electroencephalogram (EEG), under leave-one-subject-out validation across three cognitively distinct tasks: abstract reasoning (IQ), arithmetic problem solving (MATH), and a game task (GAME). In this pilot setting, the results suggest that: (i) EEG is the strongest single modality, ranking highest in IQ, GAME, and the pooled ALL setting, where samples from all three tasks are combined; (ii) adding more modalities does not consistently improve performance; (iii) the full five-modality combination achieves the highest \textit{Average} score of $73.02%$ on IQ and $68.08%$ when the \textit{Average} scores are averaged over the four evaluation settings: IQ, MATH, GAME, and ALL; and (iv) the proposed method reduces model size by approximately $50%$ compared with late-fusion alternatives while maintaining a lower inference time.

AI.tldr: A unified Transformer-based architecture processes heterogeneous biosignal modalities (ECG, EDA, RESP, SpO2, EEG) for cognitive workload assessment. The pilot study evaluates all 31 modality combinations across three cognitive tasks (IQ, MATH, GAME) using leave-one-subject-out validation.
AI.motivation: Cognitive workload measurement is crucial for adaptive human-machine systems, but research on combining heterogeneous biosignal modalities remains limited. Existing methods typically use late-fusion approaches that are computationally heavy.
AI.method: A unified, modality-agnostic, hierarchical Transformer-based architecture processes multiple biosignal modalities within a single model. Evaluation uses leave-one-subject-out validation across three cognitively distinct tasks, testing all 31 possible combinations of five modalities.
AI.result: EEG emerges as the strongest single modality (highest in IQ, GAME, and pooled ALL). Adding more modalities does not consistently improve performance. The full five-modality combination achieves 73.02% on IQ and 68.08% average across all four evaluation settings. The method reduces model size by ~50% compared to late-fusion alternatives while maintaining lower inference time.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical Transformer architecture effectively fuses heterogeneous biosignal modalities for cognitive workload estimation, achieving competitive performance with significantly reduced model size and inference time. EEG alone is a strong predictor, and multi-modality fusion does not guarantee improved performance.

title: AI or Real: Detecting Partially Altered Videos Under Resource-Constrained Environments
summary: The proliferation of generative video models has shifted the practical detection threat from fully fabricated clips to partially manipulated footages. Although modern detectors achieve strong accuracy using foundation backbones of 400M+ parameters, their resource footprint precludes edge deployment. In this paper, we present a lightweight full-frame detector for partially manipulated AI-generated video, designed for deployment on edge hardware without face-detection preprocessing. The system distills a DINOv2-Base teacher into a frozen MobileNetV3-Small student through a pipeline that combines temperature-annealed soft-label transfer, attention-diversity regularization, frame-level supervision, and a residual feature adapter that conditions ImageNet features for artifact detection. We additionally target two failure modes specific to the partial-manipulation regime: false positives on legitimate scene cuts, addressed through within-video temporal hard negatives; and threshold-level miscalibration on the dominant pure-real class, addressed through calibration-aware sampling. Evaluation on a 55,393-sample spliced test set across fake-frame ratios from 6.2% to 31.2% demonstrates the student model closing 58% of the gap to the DINOv2-Base teacher (AUC 0.766) while running at 3.65 ms per 16-frame clip on RTX A4000 with a 150.4 MB checkpoint compatible with edge-device memory and latency budgets.

AI.tldr: A lightweight full-frame detector for partially manipulated AI-generated video that distills a DINOv2-Base teacher into a MobileNetV3-Small student, achieving 58% gap closure to the teacher while running at 3.65ms per 16-frame clip on edge hardware.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of generative video models has created a threat shift from fully fabricated clips to partially manipulated footage. While modern detectors achieve strong accuracy using large foundation models (400M+ parameters), their resource footprint prevents edge deployment. There is a need for lightweight detectors that can run on edge hardware without face-detection preprocessing.
AI.method: The system uses knowledge distillation with four key components: (1) temperature-annealed soft-label transfer, (2) attention-diversity regularization, (3) frame-level supervision, and (4) a residual feature adapter that conditions ImageNet features for artifact detection. Two specific failure modes are addressed: (1) false positives on legitimate scene cuts resolved through within-video temporal hard negatives, and (2) threshold-level miscalibration on the pure-real class addressed through calibration-aware sampling.
AI.result: Evaluation on a 55,393-sample spliced test set (fake-frame ratios 6.2%-31.2%) shows the student model achieves AUC of 0.766, closing 58% of the gap to the DINOv2-Base teacher. The model runs at 3.65 ms per 16-frame clip on RTX A4000 with a 150.4 MB checkpoint, suitable for edge-device memory and latency budgets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed distilled MobileNetV3-Small model successfully balances detection accuracy and computational efficiency for partially manipulated AI-generated video detection. It achieves significant compression (from 400M+ to a lightweight student) while retaining meaningful detection capability, enabling edge deployment for real-time video analysis without preprocessing requirements.

title: JointMatch: A Unified Heterogeneous Graph Neural Solver for Large-Scale Ride-Sharing Matching
summary: Ride-sharing platforms must continuously decide which open requests to bundle into shared trips and which idle vehicles should serve them. The dominant academic approach decomposes this into two sequential matching problems -- request pairing first, then vehicle assignment -- and applies a separate solver to each. This decomposition is convenient computationally but loses revenue and scales poorly because the first stage commits to ride bundles before the available vehicles are known. We propose JointMatch, a learning-based framework that handles request pairing and vehicle assignment together on a single graph. The graph is sparsified by spatial proximity so that its size grows linearly rather than quadratically with the number of vehicles and requests, and a graph neural network scores all candidate decisions in one forward pass. On the New York City Yellow Taxi data, the framework already exceeds both the classical Blossom heuristic and a faithfully-trained two-stage GNN baseline -- often by a wide margin -- and at city scale (fleet 10000) it runs more than $20\times$ faster per dispatch epoch than either. A supervised training stage closes most of the remaining revenue gap, and a policy-gradient fine-tune aligns the trained model with realised revenue.

AI.tldr: JointMatch is a learning-based framework that jointly handles request pairing and vehicle assignment in ride-sharing platforms on a single graph, outperforming traditional two-stage approaches in both revenue and speed at city scale.
AI.motivation: The dominant academic approach decomposes ride-sharing dispatch into two sequential problems (request pairing first, then vehicle assignment), which is computationally convenient but loses revenue and scales poorly because the first stage commits to ride bundles before knowing available vehicles.
AI.method: JointMatch uses a graph-based approach that handles both request pairing and vehicle assignment together. The graph is sparsified by spatial proximity so size grows linearly (not quadratically) with vehicles and requests. A graph neural network (GNN) scores all candidate decisions in one forward pass. Training involves supervised learning followed by policy-gradient fine-tuning.
AI.result: On NYC Yellow Taxi data, JointMatch exceeds both the classical Blossom heuristic and a two-stage GNN baseline, often by a wide margin. At city scale (10,000 vehicles), it runs more than 20× faster per dispatch epoch. A supervised training stage closes most of the remaining revenue gap, and policy-gradient fine-tuning aligns the model with realized revenue.
AI.conclusion: JointMatch demonstrates that joint optimization of request pairing and vehicle assignment significantly outperforms traditional decomposition approaches, achieving better revenue and substantially faster computation at scale, making it suitable for real-time ride-sharing dispatch systems.

title: Scene-Conditioned Relation Routing for urban cellular activity forecasting
comment: Accepted in IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC), 2026
summary: Urban cellular activity forecasting requires jointly modeling heterogeneous spatiotemporal signals, including SMS usage, mobile network traffic, and call activity. Existing methods often separate temporal modeling, spatial relation learning, and multi-signal prediction, relying on fixed graph structures or static multi-task learning schemes, which limits their adaptability to changing urban scenes. We propose SCRR-Net, a scene-conditioned spatial relation routing framework in which urban contextual information jointly controls spatial dependency selection and cross-task knowledge transfer. SCRR-Net includes a context encoder, a spatial graph expert routing module, a temporal Transformer encoder, and a task knowledge routing module. Experiments on the Milano and Trento datasets demonstrate that SCRR-Net consistently outperforms competing methods on SMS, network traffic, and call activity forecasting, while providing interpretable routing behaviors.

AI.tldr: SCRR-Net is a scene-conditioned spatial relation routing framework for urban cellular activity forecasting that jointly models heterogeneous spatiotemporal signals (SMS, network traffic, call activity) using context-aware routing mechanisms for spatial dependency selection and cross-task knowledge transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing methods separate temporal modeling, spatial relation learning, and multi-signal prediction, relying on fixed graph structures or static multi-task learning schemes. This limits adaptability to changing urban scenes, necessitating a unified framework where urban contextual information dynamically controls both spatial dependencies and knowledge transfer.
AI.method: SCRR-Net comprises four components: (1) Context encoder to extract urban contextual features; (2) Spatial graph expert routing module for dynamic spatial dependency selection; (3) Temporal Transformer encoder for temporal modeling; (4) Task knowledge routing module for cross-task knowledge transfer. Urban contextual information jointly controls both routing modules.
AI.result: Experiments on Milano and Trento datasets demonstrate that SCRR-Net consistently outperforms competing methods on SMS, network traffic, and call activity forecasting, while providing interpretable routing behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SCRR-Net successfully addresses the limitations of prior methods by introducing scene-conditioned dynamic routing, achieving superior forecasting performance across multiple cellular activity signals while maintaining interpretability.

title: CleanVideo: Adaptive Concept Erasure for Text-to-Video Diffusion Models
summary: Concept erasure aims to selectively eliminate undesired visual semantics from pre-trained generative models without compromising their general utility. Extending concept erasure from images to video is nontrivial. Target concepts emerge gradually and vary across frames and denoising steps. As a result, fixed interventions may miss the target or introduce blurring, jitter, and content distortion. We propose CleanVideo, a selective erasure framework that performs low-dimensional subspace intervention controlled by a tri-modal gating mechanism. By jointly processing spatiotemporal visual features, timestep signals, and textual semantics, CleanVideo determines where, when, and whether to intervene, steering erased content toward natural surrogate concepts when such surrogates can be clearly defined while preserving non-target content. Experiments on three video diffusion models show that CleanVideo effectively erases target concepts while maintaining visual fidelity and temporal coherence, outperforming existing baselines under frame-level and video-level evaluations and under concept-recovery attacks when the protected pipeline remains intact.

AI.tldr: CleanVideo is a framework for selectively erasing undesired concepts from video diffusion models using a tri-modal gating mechanism that determines where, when, and whether to intervene in the generation process, outperforming baselines while preserving visual fidelity and temporal coherence.
AI.motivation: Concept erasure from images to video is challenging because target concepts emerge gradually and vary across frames and denoising steps. Existing fixed interventions may miss targets or introduce artifacts like blurring, jitter, and content distortion.
AI.method: CleanVideo uses low-dimensional subspace intervention controlled by a tri-modal gating mechanism that jointly processes spatiotemporal visual features, timestep signals, and textual semantics to determine intervention points. It steers erased content toward natural surrogate concepts when definable while preserving non-target content.
AI.result: Experiments on three video diffusion models show CleanVideo effectively erases target concepts while maintaining visual fidelity and temporal coherence, outperforming existing baselines under frame-level and video-level evaluations and under concept-recovery attacks.
AI.conclusion: CleanVideo provides an effective solution for video concept erasure that balances target removal with content preservation across temporal dimensions, demonstrating robustness against concept-recovery attacks.

title: When AI Agents Commit: Cognitive Serializability Across Data, Evidence, Policy, and Authority
summary: Autonomous agents derive concrete mutations from database reads, retrieved evidence, policy, beliefs, and delegated authority. Those inputs may change while reasoning is in progress. Database isolation orders the submitted transaction; agentic transaction processing determines whether a proposal satisfies an executable contract. Neither guarantee establishes a common valid point for the mutation and its derivation inputs unless the contract represents the relevant predicates. Typed dependency tokens distinguish content integrity from applicability, and trusted mediation captures the values exposed to reasoning. Under strict Cognitive Serializability, committed effects admit a serial order and a logical event at which every value exposed to derivation is unchanged. The fences last until the runtime event that realizes the sealed durability domain. The weaker Effect-Compatible Cognitive Admission recertifies an effect against a simultaneously held current dependency vector and current policy without claiming to serialize the original stochastic derivation. TCT combines immutable versioned executable definitions, registry-derived authority plans, sealed envelopes, guard-first commit transactions, post-seal envelope- and witness-bound grants, co-committed receipts, idempotent grant finalization, and receipt-driven epistemic reconciliation. Complete registered footprints and a single growing phase induce an acyclic lock-point order over local guards and incompatible external reservations. The corresponding results give serializability conditions and an observational-equivalence boundary for zero-error soundness and positive progress. A falsification suite tests the implementation obligations: the prototype prevented all injected anomalies and added 3.22 ms mean commit overhead.

title: Subdomain-aware representation compression for pretrained image embeddings
summary: Dimensionality reduction is a well-known technique for improving space efficiency, typically applied uniformly across an entire dataset. This paper investigates the possibilities of using dimensionality reduction techniques for subdomain representation compression. We explore standard techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) in image domains. The results not only demonstrate the expected improvements in space and computation complexity crucial for edge-device ML applications but also show improvements in accuracy over direct full-embedding procedure. One possible explanation is that dimensionality reduction effectively extracts subdomain features. We also performed experiments to demonstrate transfer learning capabilities using the compressed representations.

AI.tldr: This paper explores applying dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA, LDA) specifically for subdomain representation compression rather than uniform application across entire datasets. The approach targets edge-device ML applications and demonstrates improvements in space efficiency, computation complexity, and accuracy compared to full-embedding approaches.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to improve space efficiency for edge-device ML applications by applying dimensionality reduction techniques to subdomain representation compression instead of uniform dimensionality reduction across entire datasets. The authors also investigate whether dimensionality reduction can effectively extract subdomain features.
AI.method: The paper explores standard dimensionality reduction techniques - Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) - applied to image domains for subdomain representation compression. Experiments were conducted to test transfer learning capabilities using the compressed representations.
AI.result: The results demonstrate: (1) Expected improvements in space and computation complexity, which are crucial for edge-device ML applications; (2) Improvements in accuracy over direct full-embedding procedure; (3) Transfer learning capabilities using the compressed representations. One explanation for the accuracy improvement is that dimensionality reduction effectively extracts subdomain features.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that applying dimensionality reduction techniques for subdomain representation compression is viable and beneficial. It not only addresses space and computational constraints for edge devices but also can improve accuracy, potentially due to effective feature extraction of subdomains. The demonstrated transfer learning capabilities further validate the approach.

title: Queries Knew More Than We Thought: Uncovering Latent Knowledge in Segmentation Models
summary: Modern segmenters often fail after the expensive computation has already been done: a useful mask is present among the model's query-conditioned candidates, but the deployed selection rule does not expose it. We study this output-selection bottleneck in frozen DETR-family models. A ground-truth-only oracle first shows substantial hidden headroom in already-computed mask proposals. This raises a simple question: How can we better use the masks a segmenter has already computed but does not expose? We then ask whether that headroom can be recovered without adding queries, generating new masks, rerunning the backbone, or updating weights. HYDRA is a small selector trained only on cached frozen outputs. At inference time, it scores the cached candidates against an explicit keep-baseline option and acts only when a held-out calibrated margin indicates the selected candidate is sufficiently better. Trained on training-split caches and calibrated on held-out data, HYDRA improves Mask2Former, MaskDINO, and OneFormer by up to +7.41 dataset mIoU points on ADE20k and COCO, and improves SAM 3 by +9.4 class-macro prompt-IoU points on average across eight domains while preserving useful predictions through calibration. Paired LoRA controls show that lightweight weight adaptation does not remove the bottleneck: exposed predictions are often flat or worse, while routing over the adapted candidates still recovers accuracy. Finally, we connect the effect to query specialization under bipartite matching and verify it in a controlled TinyDETR study. These results show that frozen segmenters should be evaluated not only by the masks they expose, but also by the useful candidates they suppress.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the "output-selection bottleneck" in frozen DETR-family segmentation models, where useful masks exist among computed candidates but are not exposed by the deployment selection rule. The authors propose HYDRA, a small selector trained on cached frozen outputs that scores candidates against a keep-baseline option using calibrated margins. The method achieves significant improvements: +7.41 mIoU on ADE20k/COCO for Mask2Former/MaskDINO/OneFormer, and +9.4 class-macro prompt-IoU for SAM across eight domains.
AI.motivation: Modern segmenters compute useful masks among query-conditioned candidates, but the deployed selection rule fails to expose them. This creates an "output-selection bottleneck" where expensive computation has already produced valid masks that are then suppressed. The key insight is that frozen segmenters should be evaluated not only by masks they expose, but also by useful candidates they suppress.
AI.method: The authors first use a ground-truth-only oracle to demonstrate substantial hidden headroom in already-computed mask proposals. They then propose HYDRA, a small selector trained only on cached frozen outputs. At inference time, HYDRA scores cached candidates against an explicit keep-baseline option and acts only when a held-out calibrated margin indicates the selected candidate is sufficiently better. The method requires no additional queries, new mask generation, backbone reruns, or weight updates.
AI.result: HYDRA improves Mask2Former, MaskDINO, and OneFormer by up to +7.41 dataset mIoU points on ADE20k and COCO. It improves SAM 3 by +9.4 class-macro prompt-IoU points on average across eight domains while preserving useful predictions through calibration. Paired LoRA controls demonstrate that lightweight weight adaptation does not remove the bottleneck—exposed predictions remain flat or worse, while routing over adapted candidates still recovers accuracy. The effect is connected to query specialization under bipartite matching and verified in a controlled TinyDETR study.
AI.conclusion: Frozen segmenters have significant hidden headroom in their computed mask proposals. The output-selection bottleneck can be recovered without adding queries, generating new masks, rerunning the backbone, or updating weights. Lightweight weight adaptation (LoRA) does not remove this bottleneck. The effect is linked to query specialization under bipartite matching. This work demonstrates that frozen segmenters should be evaluated not only by the masks they expose, but also by the useful candidates they suppress.

title: AI-Driven Real-Time Relay Optimisation in Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimise Graph Neural Networks
summary: Reliable and low-latency communication is a fundamental requirement for smart city services and Industry 4.0 applications enabled by NR-V2X networks. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) deployment and complex urban propagation conditions often prevent Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable connectivity. This paper proposes an AI-driven Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X systems. The vehicular network is modelled as a graph, where nodes represent CAVs and RSUs, and edges encode radio-link characteristics. An offline Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation provides optimal relay decisions used as supervision for training an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE). Extensive experiments on realistic urban datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves near-optimal connectivity performance, recovering up to 11.3% connectivity gain, while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude (up to 100 x speed-up) compared to MILP. The framework enables scalable and real-time network control, making it suitable for smart city and Industry 4.0 deployments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an AI-driven Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X networks. The approach models vehicular networks as graphs and trains an edge-aware GINE to select optimal relays, achieving near-optimal connectivity with up to 100x speed-up compared to traditional MILP methods.
AI.motivation: Reliable and low-latency communication is essential for smart city services and Industry 4.0 applications. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) deployment and complex urban propagation conditions often prevent Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable connectivity, creating a critical challenge for V2X networks.
AI.method: The vehicular network is modeled as a graph where nodes represent CAVs and RSUs, and edges encode radio-link characteristics. An offline Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation generates optimal relay decisions used as supervision for training an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE).
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves near-optimal connectivity performance, recovering up to 11.3% connectivity gain while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude (up to 100x speed-up) compared to MILP.
AI.conclusion: The L2O framework enables scalable and real-time network control, making it suitable for smart city and Industry 4.0 deployments where low-latency and reliable V2X communication is critical.

title: Explaining spatial information flow in short-term traffic forecasting models using a gated graph attention network
summary: Short-term traffic forecasting supports real-time monitoring and control of road networks, and graph attention networks (GAT) are the standard means of representing spatial dependence in these models. GAT layers are widely described as capturing the influence of neighbouring locations, but this is seldom verified, because the attention weights offered in support cannot be compared against any measured quantity. That leaves two questions open, how the model should be explained and which of its components are necessary. We address this by adding a gate to the GAT layer which learns, at every sensor and every time step, what share of a sensor's updated state is drawn from its neighbours rather than from itself. Regularising the gate withdraws neighbour information progressively and thereby provides a graded form of ablation. We apply the gated GAT to ST-MetaNet, whose encoder and decoder each place one GAT layer between two recurrent layers, and train it on one calendar year of records from 498 loop detectors on the strategic road network of England. The gate assigns a larger share of neighbour information to sensors carrying heavier traffic and follows the daily and weekly cycle of travel, consistent with adjacent locations being more strongly coupled when busy. Mild regularisation improves accuracy slightly, and accuracy declines at higher strengths as the penalty withdraws information the model needs. The encoder gate closes before the decoder gate, but direct ablation qualifies that ordering. Removing either GAT layer alone leaves accuracy at least as good as keeping both, whereas removing both degrades it substantially, so the two layers are largely redundant rather than either being indispensable. The gated GAT therefore yields a modest accuracy gain, an explanation of where and when spatial information flows, and evidence on which layers the architecture requires.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a gated GAT layer that learns what share of a sensor's updated state comes from neighboring locations versus itself. Applied to ST-MetaNet for short-term traffic forecasting on England's strategic road network (498 loop detectors), the method reveals when and where spatial information flows, and whether GAT layers are truly necessary. The gated approach provides a graded ablation mechanism and shows that GAT layers are largely redundant rather than indispensable.
AI.motivation: GAT layers are standard for modeling spatial dependence in traffic forecasting, but they cannot be verified against measured data because attention weights cannot be compared against any ground truth. Two key questions remain: how to explain the model's behavior and which components are actually necessary.
AI.method: The authors added a gate to the GAT layer that learns, at every sensor and time step, what share of a sensor's updated state comes from neighbors versus itself. Regularizing the gate withdraws neighbor information progressively, providing a graded ablation. They applied this gated GAT to ST-MetaNet (with encoder and decoder each having one GAT layer between two recurrent layers) and trained it on one calendar year of data from 498 loop detectors on England's strategic road network.
AI.result: The gate assigns larger neighbor information shares to sensors with heavier traffic and follows daily/weekly cycles, consistent with adjacent locations being more coupled when busy. Mild regularization slightly improves accuracy, while higher strengths degrade it. The encoder gate closes before the decoder gate, but direct ablation shows the two GAT layers are largely redundant—both can be removed individually without hurting accuracy, but removing both substantially degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: The gated GAT yields modest accuracy gains, explains where and when spatial information flows, and provides evidence that the two GAT layers in ST-MetaNet are largely redundant rather than indispensable. The approach offers both interpretability and a form of ablation analysis.

title: TinyCNN: A 193K-Parameter Network for On-Device Plant Disease Detection, with a Cross-Dataset Robustness Diagnosis
summary: Detecting crop disease early is central to sustainable agriculture and food security under United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger), and is especially urgent in resource-constrained regions where expert diagnosis is scarce but low-cost mobile devices are widespread. This paper presents TinyCNN, a lightweight convolutional neural network for on-device plant disease classification. TinyCNN uses depthwise separable convolution blocks and contains only 193,190 trainable parameters with 110.05M MACs for a 224x224 input image. On the 38-class PlantVillage benchmark, TinyCNN achieves 98.88% test accuracy and 98.03% macro-F1 while being approximately 58x smaller than ResNet18 and 11.8x smaller than a MobileNetV2 teacher, directly reducing the energy, memory, and cost footprint of inference in line with Green AI principles. The paper further analyzes vanilla knowledge distillation as a sustainable model-compression strategy; an ablation over alpha in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} and T in {2, 4} selects alpha=0.3, T=4, producing a distilled TinyCNN with 98.81% test accuracy. Finally, cross-dataset evaluation from PlantVillage to PlantDoc reveals a substantial robustness gap under real-world conditions, which a Grad-CAM analysis attributes to off-leaf, background-driven attention consistent with shortcut learning. TinyCNN is thus an energy-efficient, deployable building block for sustainable agricultural intelligence, while field robustness remains the key barrier to durable real-world impact.

AI.tldr: TinyCNN is a lightweight CNN (193K parameters, 110M MACs) for on-device plant disease classification, achieving 98.88% accuracy on PlantVillage dataset. Knowledge distillation from MobileNetV2 produces 98.81% accuracy. Cross-dataset evaluation reveals significant robustness gap attributed to shortcut learning via background-driven attention.
AI.motivation: Early crop disease detection is critical for sustainable agriculture and food security (UN SDG 2), particularly in resource-constrained regions where expert diagnosis is scarce but mobile devices are widespread. The need is for energy-efficient, deployable models that can run on low-cost devices.
AI.method: TinyCNN uses depthwise separable convolution blocks. The paper evaluates vanilla knowledge distillation with varying alpha (0.3, 0.5, 0.7) and temperature T (2, 4). Grad-CAM analysis is used to interpret model attention and understand robustness gaps.
AI.result: TinyCNN achieves 98.88% test accuracy and 98.03% macro-F1 on 38-class PlantVillage, being 58x smaller than ResNet18 and 11.8x smaller than MobileNetV2 teacher. Best distillation: alpha=0.3, T=4 yields 98.81% accuracy. Cross-dataset evaluation (PlantVillage to PlantDoc) reveals substantial robustness gap due to off-leaf, background-driven attention (shortcut learning).
AI.conclusion: TinyCNN is an energy-efficient, deployable model for sustainable agricultural intelligence. However, field robustness remains the key barrier to real-world impact, as models rely on background features rather than disease-specific patterns. Future work should focus on improving cross-domain generalization.

title: JEPA-WAM: Connecting Generated Visual Instructions to World Action Models through JEPA Latent Representations
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have demonstrated strong robotic manipulation capabilities by augmenting pretrained video generative models with action experts. However, current WAMs still show limited instruction-following ability when conditioned solely on text instructions. We argue that this limitation stems in part from a structural imbalance in robot-learning data: rich visual-action trajectories are often paired with sparse and repetitive language annotations, allowing policies to identify tasks from visual context and motion regularities rather than grounding the instruction itself. To address this limitation, we introduce JEPA-WAM, which augments each text instruction with a bank of stochastically generated visual instructions, providing diverse visual cues for instruction following. Specifically, JEPA-WAM uses an off-the-shelf text-to-image generator to sample multiple task-completion images conditioned on the text instruction, without training the generator. Although these generated images may differ from the current visual scene in appearance and layout, they remain semantically aligned with the instruction and serve as visual goal references. To focus on task-level semantics beyond appearance, we encode these references with a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. The resulting dense goal representations are compressed into compact goal tokens that condition both the video and action experts through cross-attention. We further construct a real-robot instruction-following benchmark covering in-distribution, out-of-distribution scene, and out-of-distribution instruction settings. On this benchmark, JEPA-WAM achieves success rates of 87.3%, 74.5%, and 80.9% in these three settings, outperforming π0 and Fast-WAM by at least 10.0, 27.3, and 14.5 percentage points, respectively.

AI.tldr: JEPA-WAM addresses limited instruction-following in World Action Models by augmenting text instructions with multiple AI-generated visual goal references, using V-JEPA 2.1 encoder for semantic representation, achieving 74-87% success rates on a new real-robot benchmark.
AI.motivation: Current WAMs show limited instruction-following ability when conditioned solely on text instructions. This stems from structural imbalance in robot-learning data: rich visual-action trajectories paired with sparse/repetitive language annotations, allowing policies to rely on visual context rather than grounding the instruction itself.
AI.method:
1) Use off-the-shelf text-to-image generator to sample multiple task-completion images conditioned on text instructions (without training the generator)
2) Encode generated images with frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to focus on task-level semantics beyond appearance
3) Compress dense goal representations into compact goal tokens
4) Condition both video and action experts through cross-attention using these goal tokens
AI.result: On a newly constructed real-robot instruction-following benchmark covering three settings (in-distribution, OOD scene, OOD instruction), JEPA-WAM achieves 87.3%, 74.5%, and 80.9% success rates respectively, outperforming π0 and Fast-WAM by at least 10.0, 27.3, and 14.5 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting text instructions with stochastically generated visual instructions and using V-JEPA encoder for semantic goal representation significantly improves instruction-following in robotic manipulation, particularly in out-of-distribution settings.

title: Is It Still Worth Training a Classical Model in the Era of LLMs? A Crossover Benchmark on Tabular Data
summary: Large language models can label a tabular row from a plain-English description with no training - a capability now shipping in mainstream spreadsheet tools such as Microsoft Copilot in Excel and Anthropic's Claude for Excel - raising a practical question for the many business prediction problems where labels are expensive: should you prompt a frozen LLM, or collect data and train a model - and if so, how much data? We quantify the answer with the labeled-data crossover N*, the training-set size at which a trained classical model's learning curve overtakes a frozen LLM's training-free (and therefore flat) error. Aggregating 126 independent student evaluations of small GPT models under eight prompting configurations across 18 tabular datasets, paired with authoritative power-law learning curves for six classical model families, we find that training wins fast: even given an oracle choice of its best prompt configuration, a trained classical model beats the small frozen LLM using no more labeled data than is already on hand in 86% of cases, and wins by the smallest labeled subset we evaluate in 40%, with the observed crossover at a median of ~6% of the training set. In-context few-shot examples do not behave like training - error versus shot count does not follow a power law - and the same protocol re-run by independent implementers varies with a coefficient of variation of 0.148. A controlled probe indicates the LLM depends on recognizable feature-name semantics, which plausibly makes our crossover a conservative estimate (we do not claim memorization). For a typical business table, the evidence is clear: collect a few hundred labels and train a gradient-boosted model.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies when to use frozen LLMs vs. training classical models for labeling tabular data. Introducing the "labeled-data crossover N*" (the training-set size where trained models beat frozen LLMs), the study finds trained models outperform small GPT models in 86% of cases, with a median crossover at only ~6% of the training set. Conclusion: for typical business tables, collect a few hundred labels and train a gradient-boosted model.
AI.motivation: Practical question for business prediction problems where labels are expensive: should you prompt a frozen LLM (no training required) or collect data and train a classical model? This decision has direct implications for mainstream spreadsheet tools now shipping LLM-based labeling (Microsoft Copilot in Excel, Anthropic's Claude for Excel).
AI.method: Aggregated 126 independent student evaluations of small GPT models under eight prompting configurations across 18 tabular datasets, paired with authoritative power-law learning curves for six classical model families. Also conducted a controlled probe to understand LLM dependencies on feature-name semantics.
AI.result: Even with oracle choice of best prompt configuration, a trained classical model beats the small frozen LLM in 86% of cases using no more labeled data than already on hand, and wins by the smallest labeled subset in 40% of cases.
