Observed crossover at a median of ~6% of the training set. In-context few-shot examples do not behave like training (error vs. shot count doesn't follow power law). Protocol re-run by independent implementers shows coefficient of variation of 0.148. LLM depends on recognizable feature-name semantics, making crossover likely a conservative estimate.
AI.conclusion: For a typical business table, the evidence is clear: collect a few hundred labels and train a gradient-boosted model. Training wins fast over frozen LLMs for tabular labeling tasks.

title: Not All Layers Are Equal: Dynamic Layer Routing for Reliable CLIP OOD Detection
summary:
Information aggregation across model layers are revealed to improve OOD detection. In contrast to crafting a method for layer-wise information aggregation in recent work, we investigate if layer selection is a learnable problem. In other words, we transpose the question from how to fuse layers to one asking which layers to trust for an input. Using a generalizable, weak, out of distribution context crafting approach for supervision, shown to be more effective than state of the art methods' mechanisms, we formulate learning a lightweight router to select a sparse, final-layer-anchored expert over CLIP's layer depth for OOD detection.
  Across three diverse benchmarks we demonstrate our learnable routing method dubbed Voyager improves OOD detection. On ImageNet-1K, Voyager achieves an average FPR@95 of 18.86, outperforming the strongest, comparable, prompt-learning method by 8.8 points. These gains persist across multiple supervision sources, including those used by existing state-of-the-art prompt-learning methods, demonstrating that, whilst our weak OOD supervision context is highly effective, the key advantage is realized from the learnable router component rather than the supervision source. Significantly, Voyager is highly practical; router learning takes approximately two minutes using less than 1 GB of memory, making it approximately 20x more efficient than current prompt-learning approaches.
  Anonymized Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Voyager/

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Voyager, a learnable routing method for OOD detection that selects trustworthy layers from CLIP's depth using a lightweight router, instead of manually aggregating layer information. It uses weak OOD context crafting for supervision and achieves state-of-the-art results with 20x efficiency improvement.
AI.motivation: Prior work focuses on crafting methods for layer-wise information aggregation. This paper transposes the question from "how to fuse layers" to "which layers to trust" for OOD detection, making layer selection a learnable problem.
AI.method:
1) Use a generalizable, weak OOD context crafting approach for supervision
2) Learn a lightweight router to select a sparse, final-layer-anchored expert over CLIP's layer depth
3) Router operates on layer selections rather than traditional fusion
AI.result:
1) On ImageNet-1K: achieves FPR@95 of 18.86
2) Outperforms strongest comparable prompt-learning method by 8.8 points
3) Gains persist across multiple supervision sources
4) Router learning takes ~2 minutes with <1 GB memory
5) Approximately 20x more efficient than current prompt-learning approaches
AI.conclusion: The key advantage comes from the learnable router component rather than the supervision source. Voyager provides a practical, efficient solution for OOD detection with strong performance across diverse benchmarks, while being highly efficient in terms of training time and memory usage.

title: AgentPProf: Semantic Profiler for Long Horizon AI Agents
summary: AI agents increasingly orchestrate long-running activities with users, tools, and system resources for days and weeks. To improve agent quality, safety, and cost efficiency, developers need to determine where failures happen, what triggers unsafe effects, and which tasks consume the most budget, then optimize those tasks. In systems software, profiling answers similar questions by aggregating resource consumption and attributing it to responsible code paths to identify hotspots. Yet existing agent observability tools focus on per-execution debugging and tracing rather than cross-run, long term profiling, making these questions difficult to answer at scale. Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging, but profiling agents is challenging: the responsible entities are task intent like diagnose authentication, compare branches rather than code paths, and lack stable identifiers for aggregation. We propose a semantic operation stack model that adapts profiling to agent trajectories. Uniform operations represent all activities, and operation stacks replace the runtime call stack, enabling hierarchical attribution at different granularities. We observe that an agent's task occupies a contiguous span and decomposes into subtasks, so we introduce recursive operation segmentation, which recursively splits trajectories at task boundaries. AgentPProf is a profiler that aggregates agent trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles, enabling flame graph visualization and analysis. AgentPProf reaches 0.764 $B^3$ F1 against human annotations on CodeTraceBench. On three problem-localization benchmarks, the profile raises MAP by up to 56%, demonstrating that it effectively attributes resources, locates problems, and helps optimize token cost at practical profiling cost. AgentPProf is available at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentsight.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AgentPProf, a profiler for AI agents that adapts software profiling techniques to agent trajectories using semantic operation stacks and recursive operation segmentation. It enables flame graph visualization and analysis for agent systems, achieving 0.764 B³ F1 on CodeTraceBench and improving MAP by up to 56% on problem-localization benchmarks.
AI.motivation: AI agents increasingly orchestrate long-running activities with users, tools, and system resources for days and weeks. Developers need to determine where failures happen, what triggers unsafe effects, and which tasks consume the most budget. Existing agent observability tools focus on per-execution debugging and tracing rather than cross-run, long-term profiling, making these questions difficult to answer at scale.
AI.method: The paper proposes a semantic operation stack model that adapts profiling to agent trajectories. Uniform operations represent all activities, and operation stacks replace the runtime call stack, enabling hierarchical attribution at different granularities. The paper introduces recursive operation segmentation, which recursively splits trajectories at task boundaries. AgentPProf aggregates agent trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles.
AI.result: AgentPProf reaches 0.764 B³ F1 against human annotations on CodeTraceBench. On three problem-localization benchmarks, the profile raises MAP by up to 56%, demonstrating that it effectively attributes resources, locates problems, and helps optimize token cost at practical profiling cost.
AI.conclusion: AgentPProf effectively attributes resources, locates problems, and helps optimize token cost at practical profiling cost. It is available at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentsight.

title: Accuracy Is Not Enough: A Cross-Architecture Audit of Demographic Bias in Deep Knowledge Tracing
summary: Deep knowledge tracing (DKT) models implicitly decide which students an adaptive system believes have mastered a skill, yet almost all evidence on their demographic fairness comes from Bayesian knowledge tracing; the deep models that power modern systems have received no comparable cross-architecture audit. We close this gap: four architectures (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) trained under three regimes (standard, reweighting, adversarial) on two public datasets with demographic metadata, Eedi (15.9M interactions) and OULAD (167k after preprocessing), evaluated with ABROCA, student-level bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests addressing recent critiques of fairness-metric instability. Three findings emerge. (i) Bias is real but context-dependent: every architecture shows a significant socioeconomic ABROCA on Eedi (0.018-0.023, $p<0.005$), with per-group AUC lower for economically disadvantaged students, while gender bias is significant on OULAD for three of four architectures after multiplicity correction yet negligible on Eedi. (ii) The most accurate architecture is the most biased: AKT gains about 4 AUC points from item-level Rasch embeddings and shows the largest socioeconomic ABROCA, exceeding every other architecture under a paired bootstrap ($p\leq0.002$); ablating only the Rasch embeddings removes the accuracy gain and the excess bias together. (iii) Standard mitigation is unreliable: reweighting and adversarial debiasing leave ABROCA essentially unchanged in every configuration that preserves accuracy, even though the adversary is pinned at chance at full reversal strength and a weak-strength positive control rules out a dead probe.

AI.tldr: This paper audits deep knowledge tracing models (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) for demographic fairness across two datasets (Eedi, OULAD). The study reveals that bias exists but is context-dependent, that more accurate models tend to be more biased, and that standard debiasing methods (reweighting, adversarial) fail to mitigate the bias effectively.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to close a research gap: while Bayesian knowledge tracing has been extensively studied for demographic fairness, the deep learning models that power modern adaptive learning systems have not received comparable cross-architecture audit. This is important because deep knowledge tracing models are widely deployed in educational systems and could perpetuate or amplify existing educational inequalities.
AI.method: The study trains four different deep knowledge tracing architectures (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) under three training regimes (standard, reweighting, adversarial) on two public datasets (Eedi with 15.9M interactions, OULAD with 167k interactions after preprocessing). Evaluation uses ABROCA (Area Between ROC Curves), student-level bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests to address fairness-metric instability critiques.
AI.result: Three key findings emerge: (i) Bias is real but context-dependent - significant socioeconomic ABROCA on Eedi (0.018-0.023, p<0.005) with lower per-group AUC for economically disadvantaged students; gender bias significant on OULAD for 3/4 architectures but negligible on Eedi. (ii) The most accurate architecture (AKT) shows the largest socioeconomic ABROCA; ablating Rasch embeddings removes both the accuracy gain and excess bias. (iii) Standard mitigation (reweighting, adversarial debiasing) leaves ABROCA essentially unchanged while preserving accuracy, even when adversary achieves chance performance at full reversal strength.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion indicates that deep knowledge tracing models exhibit real demographic bias that varies by context and architecture, that accuracy improvements may come at the cost of increased bias, and that current debiasing techniques are ineffective. This suggests the need for new approaches to ensure fairness in adaptive learning systems.

title: AgriScope: Pixel-Grounded Multimodal Understanding for Agricultural Images
summary: Agricultural image understanding requires fine-grained recognition of plant diseases, pests, crop structures, and botanical species under complex real-world conditions. Despite recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), existing models remain limited to text-only outputs and lack pixel-level visual grounding capabilities. In this work, we introduce AgriScope, a unified pixel-grounded multimodal framework for agricultural image understanding. AgriScope jointly supports image-level, region-level, and pixel-level understanding within a unified framework, enabling tasks such as grounded caption generation, referring expression segmentation, and multi-turn multimodal interaction for agricultural imagery. AgriScope integrates biologically specialized semantic representations with dense spatial grounding through biological-semantic encoding, dense spatial representations, and pixel decoding. To support large-scale grounded learning, we introduce AgriGround, a large-scale pixel-grounded agricultural multimodal instruction-tuning dataset containing over 500K images and 11M instruction-following samples spanning plant disease analysis, crop and weed identification, insect pest recognition, and fine-grained botanical understanding. AgriGround is constructed through a multi-stage automatic annotation pipeline that integrates multimodal caption generation, phrase-level grounding, segmentation mask generation, and task-oriented instruction synthesis to produce densely grounded supervision. Extensive experiments across multiple agricultural vision-language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of AgriScope in pixel-grounded multimodal understanding, establishing a strong benchmark for agricultural vision-language learning and visual grounding. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at (https://github.com/boudiafA/AgriScope)

AI.tldr: AgriScope is a unified pixel-grounded multimodal framework for agricultural image understanding that jointly supports image-level, region-level, and pixel-level understanding tasks. It integrates biological-semantic encoding with dense spatial grounding and is supported by AgriGround, a large-scale dataset with 500K images and 11M instruction-following samples.
AI.motivation: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are limited to text-only outputs and lack pixel-level visual grounding capabilities, which are essential for fine-grained recognition of plant diseases, pests, crop structures, and botanical species under complex real-world conditions in agricultural image understanding.
AI.method: AgriScope integrates biologically specialized semantic representations with dense spatial grounding through three key components: (1) biological-semantic encoding, (2) dense spatial representations, and (3) pixel decoding. The framework supports tasks including grounded caption generation, referring expression segmentation, and multi-turn multimodal interaction. Additionally, AgriGround dataset was constructed through a multi-stage automatic annotation pipeline integrating multimodal caption generation, phrase-level grounding, segmentation mask generation, and task-oriented instruction synthesis.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple agricultural vision-language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of AgriScope in pixel-grounded multimodal understanding, establishing a strong benchmark for agricultural vision-language learning and visual grounding.
AI.conclusion: AgriScope successfully provides unified pixel-grounded multimodal understanding for agricultural imagery, with the AgriGround dataset enabling large-scale grounded learning across plant disease analysis, crop and weed identification, insect pest recognition, and fine-grained botanical understanding tasks.

title: Diagnose, Recover, Certify: Task Readiness under Hidden Dynamics Changes
summary: A deployed control policy can conceal consequential dynamics changes: an actuator may lose effectiveness without affecting the current task when the policy rarely excites it, despite being critical for a future task that has not yet been specified. We introduce task readiness under dormant dynamics drift, a decision problem that unifies active change diagnosis and post-change control recovery under a limited, task-agnostic interaction budget. An agent must identify whether and where local dynamics have changed, use a small number of informative interactions to characterize the change before downstream task identity is revealed, and subsequently provide each candidate task with either a recovered policy and a calibrated lower bound on its achievable return or an abstention decision to a safe fallback. We propose Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport, an intervention-based Bayesian procedure that couples fault localization with estimation of actuator effectiveness through a shared matched-response representation, thereby preserving diagnostic reliability while converting localized evidence into recovery-relevant uncertainty. This uncertainty is propagated to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, enabling deployment decisions that explicitly trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use. We evaluate the resulting framework on a diverse suite of dormant-actuator benchmarks spanning multiple simulators, under a protocol that separates diagnosis from capability recovery, scores deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, and interaction cost as well as return, and identifies the fault regimes in which transported evidence is decisive.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses fault detection and policy recovery in control systems where actuator effectiveness can degrade without affecting the current task, but critical for future unspecified tasks. The authors propose a unified decision framework combining active change diagnosis with post-change control recovery under limited task-agnostic interactions.
AI.motivation: A deployed control policy can hide consequential dynamics changes: actuators may lose effectiveness without affecting the current task when the policy rarely excites it, yet this degradation is critical for future tasks. Existing approaches fail to handle this "dormant dynamics drift" problem where diagnosis must precede knowledge of downstream task requirements.
AI.method: The authors propose Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport (EG-MPT), an intervention-based Bayesian procedure that couples fault localization with actuator effectiveness estimation through a shared matched-response representation. This preserves diagnostic reliability while converting localized evidence into recovery-relevant uncertainty. The uncertainty is propagated to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, enabling deployment decisions that trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use.
AI.result: The framework was evaluated on a diverse suite of dormant-actuator benchmarks spanning multiple simulators. The evaluation protocol separates diagnosis from capability recovery and scores deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, interaction cost, and return, identifying fault regimes where transported evidence is decisive.
AI.conclusion: The proposed EG-MPT framework successfully unifies active change diagnosis and post-change control recovery under limited interaction budgets. It enables an agent to identify dynamics changes, characterize them with minimal informative interactions, and provide either a recovered policy with calibrated performance bounds or an abstention decision to a safe fallback, effectively handling dormant dynamics drift in control systems.

title: How Far Can Sub-3B Open Language Models Go in Zero-Shot Essay Scoring on an 8 GB Consumer GPU?
summary: Zero-shot essay scoring with large language models is usually demonstrated with proprietary API models, yet the settings where automated scoring is most needed, such as public schools grading thousands of essays under strict privacy rules, are often those where sending student writing to a third-party API is unacceptable. We ask how much capability survives when the model must be a sub-3B open model running fully locally in FP16, with a controlled study of four instruction-tuned models from two families (Qwen2.5 at 0.5B/1.5B/3B, SmolLM2 at 1.7B) on all eight ASAP-AES prompts on a single 8 GB consumer GPU, with bootstrap confidence intervals, Holm-corrected paired tests, and deployment-realistic variants of the key design choices. Three findings emerge. (i) Rubric-decomposed prompting beats holistic prompting for every model under batch min-max aggregation (though Qwen2.5-3B drops significantly on one prompt), and under mean aggregation two unrelated families land within 0.01 at the 1.5-1.7B scale. (ii) Mapping trait scores into the prompt range is fragile to grader calibration: one model compresses traits into a narrow low band (2-4 on 0-10) and naive mean aggregation collapses, while the min-max normalization of Multi-Trait Specialization repairs it (macro QWK 0.204 to 0.388) and stays within 0.03 when its statistics are frozen on 30 held-out essays. (iii) Signed error falls with essay length in eleven of twelve configurations, opposite to the verbosity bias reported for large LLM judges; normalized rubric decomposition largely flattens this slope for well-calibrated models. We anchor results honestly: the best local configuration (0.388) remains far below both the human inter-rater ceiling (0.769) and a length-only baseline (0.523), so we position sub-3B local models strictly for formative, human-supervised feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates zero-shot essay scoring using small open-source LLMs (sub-3B parameters) running locally on consumer hardware for privacy-sensitive educational settings. The study tests four models (Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B, SmolLM2 1.7B) on the ASAP-AES dataset, finding that rubric-decomposed prompting outperforms holistic approaches, and that score normalization (Multi-Trait Specialization) is critical for performance. However, the best QWK (0.388) remains below human inter-rater reliability (0.769) and a length-only baseline (0.523), positioning these models only for formative feedback.
AI.motivation: Address the practical need for automated essay scoring in settings where sending student data to third-party APIs is prohibited (e.g., public schools with strict privacy rules). The authors investigate whether small open-source models can perform this task locally on consumer hardware, as an alternative to proprietary API-based solutions.
AI.method: Controlled study comparing four instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5 at 0.5B/1.5B/3B, SmolLM2 at 1.7B) on all eight ASAP-AES prompts. Experiments run on a single 8GB consumer GPU in FP16. Statistical evaluation includes bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm-corrected paired tests. Tests multiple prompt engineering strategies (holistic vs. rubric-decomposed) and aggregation methods (mean vs. min-max normalization).
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Rubric-decomposed prompting consistently beats holistic prompting under min-max aggregation; Qwen2.5-1.5B and SmolLM2-1.7B achieve similar performance (~0.01 difference). (2) Score mapping is fragile - one model compresses scores into narrow range (2-4/10), causing mean aggregation to fail. Multi-Trait Specialization with min-max normalization improves macro QWK from 0.204 to 0.388 and remains stable with frozen statistics. (3) Signed error decreases with essay length in 11/12 configurations (opposite to large LLM verbosity bias), and normalized rubric decomposition flattens this relationship for well-calibrated models. Best local configuration achieves 0.388 QWK.
AI.conclusion: Sub-3B local models can perform zero-shot essay scoring but with limited accuracy (0.388 QWK), remaining significantly below human inter-rater ceiling (0.769) and a simple length-only baseline (0.523). These models should be positioned strictly for formative, human-supervised feedback rather than high-stakes automated grading. The study provides practical deployment guidance for resource-constrained educational settings.

title: FreqDINO++: A Frequency-Guided Multi-Task Routing Vision Foundation Model for Universal Ultrasound Analysis
summary: Ultrasound image analysis plays a crucial role in cancer screening and prenatal diagnosis, yet comprehensive assessment requires jointly addressing tasks such as lesion segmentation and benign-malignant classification. While recent vision foundation models have shown remarkable universal representations, unlocking their potential for ultrasound is bottlenecked by the considerable domain gap from natural images. Existing methods typically fine-tune heavy vision encoders for isolated tasks, incurring substantial computational overhead while overlooking the underlying commonalities across heterogeneous tasks. In this work, we propose FreqDINO++, a frequency-guided multi-task routing vision foundation model for universal ultrasound analysis. We first introduce a Multi-task Routing Adapter (MR-Adapter) to support parameter-efficient integration of task-common and task-specific knowledge, a Frequency-aware Feature Enhancer (F$^2$-Enhancer) is then designed to capture the rich multi-scale frequency characteristics of ultrasound images, and a Task-aligned Collaborative Decoder (TC-Decoder) is devised to promote collaboration between dense and global prediction tasks through global-local token interaction. Extensive experiments on large-scale multi-task and external single-task ultrasound benchmarks demonstrate that FreqDINO++ consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent foundation models across 27 diverse clinical task scenarios, while also showing promising generalization to unseen data. The code is at https://github.com/MingLang-FD/FreqDINO-Plus.

AI.tldr: FreqDINO++ is a frequency-guided multi-task routing vision foundation model for universal ultrasound analysis that addresses the domain gap between natural images and ultrasound images through task-specific adapters and decoders.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound image analysis requires addressing multiple tasks (lesion segmentation, benign-malignant classification), but existing methods face three key challenges: 1) significant domain gap between natural image foundation models and ultrasound images, 2) heavy computational overhead from fine-tuning large vision encoders for isolated tasks, and 3) overlooking commonalities across heterogeneous tasks.
AI.method: The proposed FreqDINO++ consists of three key components: 1) Multi-task Routing Adapter (MR-Adapter) for parameter-efficient integration of task-common and task-specific knowledge; 2) Frequency-aware Feature Enhancer (F²-Enhancer) to capture multi-scale frequency characteristics of ultrasound images; 3) Task-aligned Collaborative Decoder (TC-Decoder) to promote collaboration between dense and global prediction tasks through global-local token interaction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on large-scale multi-task and external single-task ultrasound benchmarks demonstrate that FreqDINO++ consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent foundation models across 27 diverse clinical task scenarios, while also showing promising generalization to unseen data.
AI.conclusion: FreqDINO++ successfully enables vision foundation models to work effectively on ultrasound images by addressing the domain gap through frequency-aware features and multi-task routing, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse clinical scenarios with parameter-efficient training.

title: NeuSOGA3D: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Explainable 3D Geometric Reconstruction
comment: Preprint. Community feedback and comments are welcome
summary:
Three-dimensional reconstruction from unorganized point clouds remains a challenging problem in computer vision, geometric modeling, and computer-aided design. While neural implicit methods achieve impressive reconstruction accuracy, geometry is typically encoded in latent representations that limit interpretability and reuse within engineering workflows.
  We present NeuSOGA3D (Neuro-Symbolic Geometric Abstraction in 3D), a hybrid framework that combines learned perceptual priors inherited from NeuSOGA with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning. The method projects point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, constructs symbolic implicit spline representations from the resulting observations, and fuses them through shape-preserving constructive solid geometry operations to generate a coarse visual hull. Additional geometric detail is recovered through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines.
  Unlike conventional neural implicit approaches, NeuSOGA3D progressively transforms observations into explicit symbolic entities, including control polygons, implicit spline fields, cross-sections, and volumetric lofts. Experiments on all forty categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark demonstrate the ability of the framework to recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations. The results highlight the potential of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning for explainable geometric intelligence.

AI.tldr: NeuSOGA3D is a hybrid neuro-symbolic framework for 3D reconstruction from unorganized point clouds that combines neural perceptual priors with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning. It projects point clouds onto orthographic planes, constructs symbolic implicit spline representations, and uses shape-preserving CSG operations to generate CAD-compatible geometric representations.
AI.motivation: Neural implicit methods for 3D reconstruction achieve high accuracy but encode geometry in latent representations that limit interpretability and reuse in engineering workflows. There is a need for methods that produce explicit, CAD-compatible geometric representations.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) projecting point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, (2) constructing symbolic implicit spline representations from observations, (3) fusing via shape-preserving constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations to generate a coarse visual hull, (4) recovering geometric detail through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines.
AI.result: Experiments on all 40 categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark demonstrate the framework's ability to recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations.
AI.conclusion: The approach highlights the potential of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning for explainable geometric intelligence, producing interpretable and reusable CAD models rather than black-box latent representations.

title: Improving Online Reinforcement Learning via Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation
summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms frequently exhibit poor sample efficiency and unstable learning dynamics, stemming from systematic critic estimation errors that are exacerbated by greedy policy updates. Existing behavior-prior reinforcement learning methods attempt to alleviate this issue by relying on offline pre-training to learn behavior models from fixed datasets and using policy priors to constrain online policy updates. However, the limited quality of offline datasets often hinders the ability to provide high-value policies that can effectively guide policy updates. The absence of expert trajectories significantly impairs online policy learning, leading to low sample efficiency and suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we depart from conventional behavior prior approaches and propose a Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation (B2PD) algorithm. B2PD leverages action-value priors to guide a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) in generating a high-value behavior support set. The resulting expert behavior priors are further distilled into the agent, effectively reducing inefficient exploration and enabling stable policy optimization, while establishing a bidirectional knowledge flow mechanism. Empirical evaluations on both state- and pixel-based tasks verify that B2PD substantially improves sample efficiency while maintaining stable policy optimization. More broadly, this work shows that enforcing high-quality behavioral support during online learning effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification, enabling structured behavior priors to guide policy updates in a principled and sample-efficient manner.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes B2PD (Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation), a novel reinforcement learning algorithm that addresses poor sample efficiency and unstable learning in online RL by using action-value priors to guide a CVAE in generating high-value behavior support sets, which are then distilled into the agent to reduce inefficient exploration and enable stable policy optimization.
AI.motivation: Online RL algorithms suffer from poor sample efficiency and unstable learning dynamics due to critic estimation errors exacerbated by greedy policy updates. Existing behavior-prior methods rely on offline pre-training with limited-quality datasets, lacking expert trajectories that impair online policy learning.
AI.method: B2PD leverages action-value priors to guide a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) in generating high-value behavior support sets. The resulting expert behavior priors are distilled into the agent, establishing a bidirectional knowledge flow mechanism to reduce inefficient exploration and enable stable policy optimization.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on both state- and pixel-based tasks demonstrate that B2PD substantially improves sample efficiency while maintaining stable policy optimization. The approach effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification through high-quality behavioral support during online learning.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing high-quality behavioral support during online learning effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification, enabling structured behavior priors to guide policy updates in a principled and sample-efficient manner.

title: Fast Cross-Strength Multi-Contrast Brain MRI Translation using Latent Bridge Matching
summary: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) acquired at different field strengths exhibits pronounced variation in noise, resolution, homogeneity, and contrast, which limits comparability across acquisition settings and complicates downstream analysis. We address this with a unified conditional model for controllable field-to-field synthesis, built on the framework of conditional latent bridge matching. Our single model achieves highly competitive results across the validation phase for all three tasks of the MRIxFields2026 challenge without task-specific architectures or training. We achieve fast generation with only a single inference step, producing all modality and field-strength combinations for $30$ axial slices in under $90$ seconds, as well as cross-modality-strength translation for a full volume in under $70$ seconds, on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU. We further provide extensive ablations regarding different components of our solution. Code: https://gitlab.com/siddharthsrivastava/mrixfields-2026

AI.tldr: A unified conditional model using conditional latent bridge matching for cross-field-strength MRI synthesis, achieving competitive results across all three MRIxFields2026 challenge tasks with a single model architecture.
AI.motivation: MRI images acquired at different field strengths (e.g., 1.5T, 3T, 7T) exhibit significant variations in noise, resolution, homogeneity, and contrast, limiting comparability across acquisition settings and complicating downstream analysis.
AI.method: A unified conditional model built on the framework of conditional latent bridge matching, enabling controllable field-to-field synthesis without task-specific architectures or training. The model uses single inference step generation.
AI.result: Achieved highly competitive results across all three validation tasks of the MRIxFields2026 challenge. Fast generation: 30 axial slices in under 90 seconds; cross-modality-strength translation for full volume in under 70 seconds on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU.
AI.conclusion: The proposed conditional latent bridge matching framework provides an effective unified solution for multi-field MRI synthesis, achieving strong performance across diverse tasks while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation: From Natural-Language Traffic Rules to PROLOG
comment: In Proceedings of the International Workshop on Translating Natural Legal Language into Formal Representations (NLL2FR 2025)
summary: Traffic regulations are written for human interpretation and therefore rely on shared background knowledge and flexible phrasing, which inherently introduce ambiguity, context dependence, and semantic underspecification. These linguistic characteristics conflict with the precision required by computational reasoning engines such as Prolog, which demand explicit logical structure. This study evaluates two baseline translation approaches, Natural Language to Prolog ($NL\rightarrow Prolog$) and Logical English to Prolog ($LE\rightarrow Prolog$), and introduces a new reasoning-guided translation framework called Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation ($S4L\rightarrow Prolog$). The proposed S4L framework performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt, enabling direct translation of raw traffic rules into executable logic without human intervention. A benchmark consisting of twenty real-world traffic rules was used to evaluate each approach in terms of syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness. $S4L\rightarrow Prolog$ achieves the highest accuracy, correctly formalizing 75 percent of the rules, while $NL\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 60 percent and $LE\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 55 percent. Qualitative analysis further shows that S4L captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure more reliably than the baselines. These results demonstrate that structured reasoning prompts can substantially improve the reliability of natural-language-to-logic translation for legal and safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of translating ambiguous human-written traffic regulations into precise Prolog logic for computational reasoning. It proposes S4L (Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation), a framework that performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a guided prompt. Evaluated on 20 real-world traffic rules, S4L achieves 75% accuracy, outperforming NL→Prolog (60%) and LE→Prolog (55%) in syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness.
AI.motivation: Traffic regulations are written for human interpretation with flexible phrasing, introducing ambiguity and context dependence. This conflicts with computational reasoning engines like Prolog that require explicit logical structure. The study aims to improve automatic translation of legal text into executable logic without human intervention.
AI.method: The study evaluates three translation approaches: (1) NL→Prolog - direct natural language to Prolog; (2) LE→Prolog - Logical English to Prolog; (3) S4L→Prolog - a new four-stage framework performing semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt. A benchmark of 20 real-world traffic rules was used to assess syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness.
AI.result: S4L→Prolog achieves 75% accuracy, correctly formalizing 15 out of 20 traffic rules. NL→Prolog reaches 60% (12/20), and LE→Prolog reaches 55% (11/20). Qualitative analysis shows S4L captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure more reliably than baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: Structured reasoning prompts (S4L framework) can substantially improve the reliability of natural-language-to-logic translation for legal and safety-critical applications. The four-stage approach within a guided prompt enables direct translation of raw traffic rules into executable logic without human intervention.

title: Placement Is Free, Composition Is Not: The Latin Square as a Provably-Balanced Construction for Heterogeneous Sequence-Mixer Stacks
summary: Since GPT, most Transformers have repeated the same attention mechanism at every layer. Yet this design is largely a convention rather than a tested conclusion. When multiple sequence mixers are combined in one stack, improvements may arise from mechanism choice, placement, or both, making causal attribution difficult. We introduce Aether-7B-5Attn, a 6.59B-parameter mixture-of-experts model ($\approx$2.98B active) whose 49 layers contain seven sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged as a $7\times7$ Latin square. Because each mechanism appears exactly once in every row and column, the design guarantees balanced exposure across depth while eliminating placement confounds. To evaluate this principle, we build a parameter-matched proxy with four mechanisms arranged as a $4\times4$ Latin square over sixteen layers, matched to 700.9M parameters and trained with eight seeds per arm. The results reveal a clear dissociation. Rearranging a distributed heterogeneous stack into a balanced periodic cycle changes validation loss by only 0.16\%, indicating that exact placement has little effect. In contrast, clustering the same mechanisms into contiguous depth bands incurs a 0.59\% penalty, while replacing the heterogeneous stack with a homogeneous one incurs a 1.68\% penalty. These results indicate that performance depends primarily on heterogeneous composition distributed across depth rather than on any particular permutation. We confirm this finding at 2.16$\times$ larger scale (1.514B parameters), where the homogeneous-stack penalty increases to 2.63\% and removing the SSM-family mechanism produces a 3.20\% degradation. We further report per-mechanism cost profiles, English and Korean evaluations, and a causal-safety audit of all 49 layers. We release model weights, training recipes, training code, logs, and architecture source code.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether Transformer architectures need uniform attention mechanisms at every layer, or if heterogeneous mixture of sequence mixers distributed across depth improves performance. The authors introduce Aether-7B-5Attn, a 6.59B MoE model with 49 layers containing seven sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged in a 7×7 Latin square to ensure balanced exposure across depth. Experiments using a 700.9M parameter proxy model with 8 seeds per arm reveal that placement has minimal effect (0.16%), while clustering mechanisms into contiguous bands incurs 0.59% penalty and using homogeneous stack incurs 1.68% penalty. These findings indicate that heterogeneous composition across depth matters more than specific arrangement.
AI.motivation: The Transformer architecture has conventionally used the same attention mechanism at every layer, but this design choice has not been rigorously tested. The authors seek to determine whether performance gains come from mechanism choice, placement, or both, and to isolate these factors through controlled experiments.
AI.method: The authors designed a 7×7 Latin square arrangement of seven sequence-mixing mechanisms across 49 layers, ensuring each mechanism appears exactly once in every row and column to guarantee balanced exposure while eliminating placement confounds. They built a parameter-matched 700.9M proxy model with four mechanisms in a 4×4 Latin square over 16 layers, trained with eight seeds per arm. Experiments compared: (1) balanced periodic cycle, (2) clustered mechanisms in contiguous depth bands, and (3) homogeneous stack. They also conducted a 2.16× scale replication (1.514B parameters) and evaluated English/Korean tasks plus safety audit.
AI.result: Rearranging a distributed heterogeneous stack into a balanced periodic cycle changed validation loss by only 0.16%, indicating minimal placement effect. Clustering mechanisms into contiguous depth bands incurred a 0.59% penalty. Replacing with a homogeneous stack incurred 1.68% penalty. At larger scale (1.514B parameters), homogeneous penalty increased to 2.63%, and removing the SSM-family mechanism caused 3.20% degradation. The model also demonstrated favorable English/Korean evaluations and passed causal-safety audit.
AI.conclusion: Performance depends primarily on heterogeneous composition of sequence-mixing mechanisms distributed across depth, rather than any particular permutation or placement. The exact arrangement matters little, but having a diverse set of mechanisms across layers is crucial for optimal performance.

title: EliGSiR: Continual RGB-D Mapping with Gaussian Splatting under Bounded Compute
summary: Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting assumes a closed set of observations and long optimization schedules. Continual RGB-D mapping in contrast poses the problem that new observations arrive online, while previously reconstructed regions must be preserved. We present EliGSiR (Evidence-guided Load-adaptive Incremental Gaussian Splatting with Image Replay), a continual Gaussian mapper that controls how the available optimization budget is used as the reconstruction evolves. Map-Guided View Scheduling filters redundant incoming views and reconsiders retained views according to the current state of the map. Load-Adaptive Fidelity adjusts supervision resolution to the current mapping load instead of following a fixed resolution schedule. Targeted Geometry Growth separates depth supervision from Gaussian creation and adds geometric capacity only where repeated RGB-D observations indicate missing or misplaced structure. Together, these mechanisms adapt which views are optimized, how much image detail is used, and where the representation grows while mapping remains active. We evaluate EliGSiR on Replica, TUM RGB-D, ScanNet++, and real RGB-D sensor sequences, considering both the final reconstruction and the map available throughout acquisition. On TUM RGB-D fr3/long_office_household, EliGSiR reaches 21.52 dB with the same ground-truth mapping poses used by the controlled baselines, compared with 19.42 dB for SplaTAM. In the tracked-pose comparison, EliGSiR with live ORB-SLAM3 poses reaches 23.02 dB in 155.5 s, compared with 20.10 dB in 230.9 s for CaRtGS using its native tracker. We further evaluate reconstruction throughout acquisition and show how EliGSiR adaptive view scheduling, supervision fidelity, and geometry growth improve the use of the available mapping budget.

AI.tldr: EliGSiR is a continual Gaussian Splatting mapper that handles online RGB-D observations while preserving previously reconstructed regions. It uses three adaptive mechanisms: Map-Guided View Scheduling (filters redundant views), Load-Adaptive Fidelity (adjusts supervision resolution), and Targeted Geometry Growth (adds geometry capacity where needed). It outperforms baselines like SplaTAM and CaRtGS on Replica, TUM RGB-D, ScanNet++ datasets.
AI.motivation: Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting assumes closed-set observations and long optimization schedules, making it unsuitable for continual RGB-D mapping where new observations arrive online while previously reconstructed regions must be preserved. The problem is to effectively allocate limited optimization budget as reconstruction evolves.
AI.method: EliGSiR introduces three key mechanisms: (1) Map-Guided View Scheduling - filters redundant incoming views and reconsiders retained views based on current map state; (2) Load-Adaptive Fidelity - adjusts supervision resolution to current mapping load instead of fixed schedules; (3) Targeted Geometry Growth - separates depth supervision from Gaussian creation and adds geometric capacity only where repeated RGB-D observations indicate missing/misplaced structure.
AI.result: On TUM RGB-D fr3/long_office_household: EliGSiR achieves 21.52 dB (vs 19.42 dB for SplaTAM) with ground-truth poses. With live ORB-SLAM3 poses: 23.02 dB in 155.5s (vs 20.10 dB in 230.9s for CaRtGS). The method shows adaptive view scheduling, supervision fidelity, and geometry growth improve mapping budget utilization throughout acquisition.
AI.conclusion: EliGSiR successfully enables continual 3D Gaussian Splatting by dynamically adapting view optimization, supervision detail, and geometry growth. It achieves higher quality reconstructions with faster processing times compared to existing methods, demonstrating effective allocation of optimization budget in online mapping scenarios.

title: A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support
comment: Workshop on Qualitative Reasoning 2026 at IJCAI (35th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
summary: Spatial reasoning abilities correlate strongly with performance in STEM fields. Games offer a compelling medium for training these critical skills in developing children who have a natural proclivity for play. However, to facilitate human-like tutoring and player guidance, these games require an AI agent capable of making commonsense inferences from spatial events. Qualitative reasoning (QR) models appear to be a suitable framework for these application domains. As these models reason in symbolic representations, they can seamlessly translate game states into interpretable feedback for human-like player guidance. This paper introduces a hybrid qualitative model designed for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game that requires constructing multi-level bridges to connect two avatars stationed on separate towers. The game poses a challenge for the player, who must make platforms stable, plan their path, and ensure they use all the provided blocks. To handle the precise physics required by the domain, we integrate a mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to guide our qualitative solver. Our work facilitates spatial skill training in Camelot Jr. and contributes to the development of human-centric, explainable game-playing agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a hybrid qualitative reasoning model for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game designed to train spatial reasoning skills in children. The model integrates mathematical center-of-mass stability logic with qualitative reasoning to enable AI agents to provide human-like tutoring and explainable feedback.
AI.motivation: Spatial reasoning abilities strongly correlate with STEM performance. Games offer an engaging medium for training these skills in children, but require AI agents capable of making commonsense inferences from spatial events to provide effective tutoring and player guidance.
AI.method: The researchers developed a hybrid qualitative model that combines symbolic qualitative reasoning with mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to handle the precise physics required for block-puzzle scenarios in Camelot Jr.
AI.result: The model enables interpretable feedback generation for player guidance in a game requiring multi-level bridge construction, platform stability planning, and path planning under constraint satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: This work contributes to human-centric, explainable game-playing agents and facilitates spatial skill training through integrated qualitative reasoning and physics-based stability analysis.

title: Labeled Incidence Structures for Native Transformer Modeling of Text, Knowledge Graphs, and Hypergraphs
summary:
Text, knowledge graphs, and hypergraphs all have elements that play distinct roles within relation instances, structure that is lost when data is flattened into token sequences. We introduce labeled incidence structures (LIS), a uniform representation that encodes each endpoint as $(x_d, s, e)$: content $x_d$, a role or slot $s$, and the relation instance $e$ in which that role appears. Because every data type maps to the same $(x_d, s, e)$ representation without flattening, a single standard transformer can process them all natively, structural differences are carried entirely by the operators, not the architecture.
  LIS assigns a structural address to each endpoint by composing a slot operator and an instance operator, $A(s,e) = R_s R_e$. We characterize when this factorization gives every token a unique, path-independent address. When it does, the natural operator comparing endpoint $j$ to endpoint $i$ is the relative transport $P_{j\to i} = A_i^{-1} A_j$, which gives attention a role- and relation-aware inductive bias without imposing an arbitrary sequence order.
  Additive encodings of the form "position term plus relation term" can miss information that depends jointly on $s$ and $e$. We prove this in a controlled example family: when the journey operator is approximated by the sum of a position-only term and a relation-only term, the approximation cannot capture how position and relation combine, only their separate effects.
  We also analyze persistent knowledge repositories. Identifiers tied to storage locations make models sensitive to storage order, while freely learned identifiers can become harder to control as the repository size $M$ grows relative to the sample size $n$. Computing relation-instance operators from content avoids this storage-order issue and yields a capacity bound independent of $M$, under fixed architectural and Lipschitz assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Labeled Incidence Structures (LIS), a unified representation framework that encodes endpoints as (content, role, relation instance) tuples, enabling standard transformers to process text, knowledge graphs, and hypergraphs natively without flattening. It characterizes when this representation yields unique path-independent addresses, proposes the relative transport operator for role- and relation-aware attention, proves limitations of additive encodings, and analyzes capacity bounds for persistent knowledge repositories.
AI.motivation: Current approaches flatten structured data (text, knowledge graphs, hypergraphs) into token sequences, losing critical information about the distinct roles elements play within relation instances. This loss of structural information is a fundamental limitation.
AI.method: The paper uses operator-based representations: structural addresses via A(s,e) = R_s R_e (composition of slot and instance operators), relative transport P_{j→i} = A_i^{-1}A_j for endpoint comparison, and mathematical analysis to prove limitations of additive encodings and derive capacity bounds for knowledge repositories.
AI.result: The paper characterizes conditions for unique path-independent addresses, proves that additive encodings cannot capture joint position-relation dependencies, and shows that computing relation-instance operators from content avoids storage-order sensitivity while yielding a capacity bound independent of repository size M.
AI.conclusion: LIS provides a uniform representation that preserves structural information across data types, enabling a single standard transformer to process diverse structured data. The relative transport operator gives attention a role- and relation-aware inductive bias without arbitrary sequence ordering. The approach resolves storage-order issues in knowledge repositories while maintaining bounded capacity.

title: MM-Future: Multi-Mode Joint World-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving involves coupled decision-making and scene evolution under multi-mode uncertainty. To capture this coupling and uncertainty, we introduce MM-Future, a world-action model that generates multiple paired scene-action hypotheses and models bidirectional interaction within each pair. Each hypothesis is initialized from a structured action prior and an independent future scene source, which are then co-evolved through a modality-aware diffusion Transformer. To support efficient multi-mode rollout, MM-Future compresses multi-view video into planning-oriented representations, dubbed MM-Tokens. Finally, a future-conditioned proposal scorer ranks trajectory candidates by shared history context and their paired predicted future. On NAVSIM navtest, MM-Future achieves 94.0 PDMS and 91.5 EPDMS, while attaining a 32.3 HD-Score in zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show consistent improvements over both single-mode and action-only variants, validating the benefit of multi-mode joint world-action modeling.

AI.tldr: MM-Future is a world-action model for autonomous driving that generates multiple paired scene-action hypotheses to capture coupling and uncertainty between decision-making and scene evolution. It uses a modality-aware diffusion Transformer to co-evolve structured action priors with future scene sources, compressed into MM-Tokens for efficient multi-mode rollout.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving involves coupled decision-making and scene evolution under multi-mode uncertainty. Existing methods fail to capture this bidirectional coupling and uncertainty effectively.
AI.method: MM-Future introduces: (1) Multiple paired scene-action hypotheses initialized from structured action prior and independent future scene source; (2) Modality-aware diffusion Transformer for co-evolution within each pair; (3) MM-Tokens - planning-oriented representations compressing multi-view video; (4) Future-conditioned proposal scorer ranking trajectory candidates by shared history context and predicted future.
AI.result: On NAVSIM navtest: 94.0 PDMS and 91.5 EPDMS. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM: 32.3 HD-Score. Ablations show consistent improvements over single-mode and action-only variants.
AI.conclusion: Multi-mode joint world-action modeling provides significant benefits for autonomous driving, validating the importance of capturing bidirectional interaction between decision-making and scene evolution under uncertainty.

title: Generating Heterogeneous 3D Geological Microstructures from 2D Images via a Stable Diffusion-Adversarial Model
summary:
Characterizing the physical properties of clay and cementitious materials matters across many fields, from materials science to geological waste disposal. Property simulation typically calls for 3D imaging, which is expensive, not always accessible, and technically limited for certain materials. Recent progress in deep generative models offers a way around this, reconstructing 3D volumes from the more easily acquired 2D images.
  Among GAN-based methods for 3D microstructure generation, SliceGAN has shown strong results for homogeneous isotropic and anisotropic systems. It struggles, however, to capture the finer detail of more complex heterogeneous microstructures, which motivates alternative generative frameworks.
  We introduce a hybrid approach that draws on the stability and generation quality of denoising diffusion models. Since no 3D ground truth is available, we replace the standard denoising loss with an adversarial loss, which yields a stable training process in our experiments. We show that the resulting model generates microstructures of varying complexity with minimal slice artefacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.

AI.tldr: A hybrid denoising diffusion model with adversarial loss generates 3D microstructures of clay and cementitious materials from 2D images, overcoming limitations of SliceGAN for complex heterogeneous systems.
AI.motivation: 3D imaging for microstructure simulation is expensive and limited; GAN-based methods like SliceGAN struggle with complex heterogeneous microstructures. A more capable generative framework is needed.
AI.method: Hybrid approach combining denoising diffusion models with adversarial loss (replacing standard denoising loss due to lack of 3D ground truth) to generate 3D microstructures from 2D images.
AI.result: The model generates microstructures of varying complexity with minimal slice artifacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid diffusion-adversarial approach successfully captures fine details of complex heterogeneous microstructures that previous GAN-based methods could not.

title: Personalising a Cross-User Surface Electromyography Encoder Under a Small Calibration Budget
summary: A myoelectric interface needs calibration from the user before it will function. Earlier work has treated calibration as a quantity, but has not asked the question of what a device should do with the calibration repetitions once they have been collected. This paper views personalizing the cross-user encoder as a design decision with a cost. Four alternative approaches to using exactly the same labeled repetitions were tested from a single cross-user encoder per held-out subject. Prototypical adaptation, linear probes, scaled fine-tuning and full fine-tuning were tested at every budget up to the maximum each database allows, five repetitions on DB1 and four on DB2 and DB5. Comparing four ways to spend a small calibration budget across 77 subjects, full fine-tuning is the most accurate at every budget, consistently enough that there is no exception among subsets of subjects. The result which impacts how one might make an engineering decision however is that a gradient free prototypical rule recovers 52 to 78 per cent of its benefit with no optimiser and no per-user copy of the weights, which makes personalisation something a worn device can do at donning time. The widespread intuition that a good representation only needs a fresh classifier is incorrect here. How well each method may perform relative to a per-user classifier that would be fitted by a clinic will depend on the specific database.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates four approaches to personalize a cross-user myoelectric interface using a limited calibration budget (4-5 repetitions per subject). Full fine-tuning consistently outperforms other methods, but a gradient-free prototypical rule can recover 52-78% of the benefit without requiring an optimizer or per-user weight copies, enabling on-device personalization at donning time.
AI.motivation: Previous work treated calibration as merely a quantity without considering what to do with the collected calibration repetitions. This study treats personalizing the cross-user encoder as a design decision with an associated cost.
AI.method: Four alternative approaches were tested using exactly the same labeled repetitions from a single cross-user encoder per held-out subject: prototypical adaptation, linear probes, scaled fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. Experiments were conducted across 77 subjects with budgets up to 5 repetitions (DB1) and 4 repetitions (DB2 and DB5).
AI.result: Full fine-tuning achieved the highest accuracy at every budget level, with no exceptions across all subject subsets. A gradient-free prototypical rule recovered 52 to 78 percent of its benefit without requiring an optimizer or per-user copy of the weights.
AI.conclusion: The widespread intuition that a good representation only needs a fresh classifier is incorrect for this task. The performance relative to a per-user classifier fitted by a clinic depends on the specific database. The gradient-free approach enables on-device personalization at donning time.

title: Compact Vision Models for Iris Presentation Attack Detection under Presentation Attack Instrument Shift and Environmental Degradation
comment: Accepted at BIOSIG 2026. This preprint includes minor nomenclature and editorial corrections clarifying the project-specific Patch-ABMIL and Compact-TransMIL variants
summary: Iris presentation attack detection (PAD) is security-critical when a subsystem that appears reliable during development encounters presentation attack instruments (PAIs) or acquisition conditions absent from validation data. We benchmark three compact scratch-trained computer-vision models, each with at most approximately 0.26 million trainable parameters, on the Notre Dame subset of LivDet-Iris 2017 under PAI-driven domain shift and environmental degradation. All models are trained without external pretraining or data augmentation and evaluated over five seeds. A validation-selected threshold is transferred unchanged to the known-attack, unknown-attack, corrupted, and pooled test partitions. From known to unknown attack presentations, Attack Presentation Classification Error Rate (APCER) increases by 17.11-30.47 percentage points and Detection Equal Error Rate (D-EER) increases by 7.38-12.73 percentage points. At the validation-selected threshold, ZACH-ViT obtains the lowest unknown-attack APCER (47.69 +/- 4.84%) and D-EER (38.87 +/- 0.93%), while Compact-TransMIL obtains the lowest Bona Fide Presentation Classification Error Rate (BPCER). ZACH-ViT also gives the lowest unknown-attack BPCER at an APCER limit of 10% (81.29 +/- 1.95%). The high absolute errors show that the comparative advantage of the best compact model does not constitute deployment readiness under unknown PAIs.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks three compact scratch-trained computer vision models (≤0.26M parameters) for iris presentation attack detection (PAD) on LivDet-Iris 2017. Under unknown attack presentations, models show significant performance degradation with APCER increases of 17-30 percentage points, indicating none are deployment-ready despite comparative advantages.
AI.motivation: Iris PAD systems that appear reliable during development may fail when encountering presentation attack instruments (PAIs) or acquisition conditions absent from validation data. This work addresses the need to benchmark compact models under domain shift and environmental degradation to assess real-world deployment viability.
AI.method: Three compact scratch-trained computer vision models (≤0.26M parameters) were benchmarked on the Notre Dame subset of LivDet-Iris 2017. Models were trained without external pretraining or data augmentation and evaluated over five seeds. A validation-selected threshold was transferred unchanged to known-attack, unknown-attack, corrupted, and pooled test partitions.
AI.result: From known to unknown attack presentations, APCER increases by 17.11-30.47 percentage points and D-EER increases by 7.38-12.73 percentage points. ZACH-ViT achieves lowest unknown-attack APCER (47.69 ± 4.84%) and D-EER (38.87 ± 0.93%). Compact-TransMIL achieves lowest BPCER. ZACH-ViT achieves lowest unknown-attack BPCER at 10% APCER limit (81.29 ± 1.95%).
AI.conclusion: The high absolute errors demonstrate that the comparative advantage of the best compact model (ZACH-ViT) does not constitute deployment readiness under unknown PAIs. Significant performance degradation occurs when models face unseen attack types, highlighting the challenge of generalizing iris PAD systems to real-world deployment scenarios.

title: The Organization of Inference: Information, Resource Constraints, and AI Production
summary: The economic value of inference depends on how capacity and task information are distributed across stages of AI production. We study these organizational margins using controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks. In two matched resource panels, direct execution records the same success rate of 59.6 percent at logical-token ceilings of 12,000 and 24,000, while success under information-constrained planning rises from 36.2 to 51.2 percent. The planning disadvantage narrows by 15.0 percentage points (95 percent task-cluster bootstrap interval: 4.2 to 25.8). A strict read-only planning campaign varies whether the planner sees the task issue. At 12,000 tokens, issue access raises success by about 16 percentage points over issue-hidden planning. Compared with direct execution, task-informed planning is about 10 points lower at 12,000 tokens; at 24,000 tokens, it shows a 29.6-point advantage. In the resource panels, direct execution uses substantially less than either ceiling, while the planning workflow's binding rate falls from 46.2 to 0.8 percent and downstream execution accounts for 89.9 percent of the increase in total use. Scale determines the capacity available to a system; workflow and information structure shape the productive value

AI.tldr: This paper studies how organizing AI inference across different production stages (planning vs. execution) affects economic value, using controlled experiments on software engineering tasks. Key findings: direct execution maintains constant success (59.6%) across token limits, while planning improves with more capacity (36.2% → 51.2%). At 24K tokens, task-informed planning outperforms direct execution by 29.6 points.
AI.motivation: The research addresses how capacity and task information should be distributed across AI production stages to maximize economic value. This organizational question has implications for AI system design and resource allocation.
AI.method: Controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks. Two matched resource panels tested direct execution vs. information-constrained planning at 12,000 and 24,000 token ceilings. Additional experiments varied whether planners had access to task issues.
AI.result: Direct execution achieved 59.6% success at both token limits. Planning success improved from 36.2% to 51.2% (15.0pp narrowing, 95% CI: 4.2-25.8). Issue access improved planning by ~16pp at 12K tokens. Task-informed planning was ~10pp lower than direct execution at 12K but 29.6pp higher at 24K. Planning's binding rate dropped from 46.2% to 0.8%; downstream execution accounted for 89.9% of total use increase.
AI.conclusion: Scale determines available capacity, while workflow and information structure determine productive value. The optimal allocation depends on resource constraints—planning outperforms direct execution at higher token limits but underperforms at lower limits.

title: Intact-to-Amputee Transfer in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding: Training Source and Calibration Budget
summary: A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A systematic review of 1077 studies quantifies where the evidence is thin: amputees appear in about one in six. Here a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder is carried to eleven transradial amputees on a protocol matched to its intact-limb training data. Zero-shot cross-population transfer fails outright: the encoder requires labeled data from the new user before it begins decoding, and it then exceeds the per-user classifier a clinic would fit by 0.190 macro F1 at three repetitions and for every subject in the cohort. Given three labelled repetitions it reaches 0.779 macro-F1 against 0.589 for the per-user pipeline. Training on forty intact subjects produces better transfers to a new amputee than training on ten other amputees, and combining the two produces better transfers than either individually. The prediction pre-registered for this study, which extends the encoder's baseline-strength account with the premise that amputee EMG is less separable, holds true only after a few repetitions become available and after enriching the source pool with additional amputees. At a single repetition, and at every budget under a source matched to the intact-limb comparison, it fails. Thus, it locates the boundary of the proposed account.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of transferring myoelectric pattern recognition models across different users, specifically from intact-limb users to transradial amputees. The study trains an encoder on intact subjects and tests it on 11 amputees, finding that zero-shot transfer fails, but with few labeled repetitions (3), the pre-trained encoder outperforms per-user classifiers (0.779 vs 0.589 macro-F1). Training on intact subjects transfers better to amputees than training on other amputees, and combining both is optimal.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the limited generalizability of myoelectric pattern recognition systems across users, particularly the lack of data from amputees in training (only ~1 in 6 studies include amputees). The goal is to develop a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder that can reduce the need for extensive labeled calibration data from new users.
AI.method: A montage-agnostic cross-user encoder was trained on 40 intact-limb subjects and transferred to 11 transradial amputees. The study compared: (1) zero-shot transfer, (2) few-shot transfer with varying labeled repetitions (1-3), and (3) different source pool configurations (intact only, amputee only, combined). The encoder was compared against a per-user classifier baseline.
AI.result: Zero-shot transfer failed completely. With 3 labeled repetitions, the encoder achieved 0.779 macro-F1 vs 0.589 for per-user pipeline (+0.190). Training on 40 intact subjects transferred better to new amputees than training on 10 amputees. Combining both datasets produced the best transfer performance. The hypothesis that amputee EMG is less separable held true only after a few repetitions and with enriched amputee source data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed account (that amputee EMG is less separable) has clear boundaries: it only works after a few labeled repetitions become available and after enriching the source pool with additional amputees. At a single repetition and under source-matched conditions, the approach fails. This locates the practical boundary of the baseline-strength account and suggests that while transfer learning helps, some user-specific calibration remains necessary.

title: TouchSight: Bare-Handed Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Video via Generative Visual Augmentation
summary: Tactile signals provide direct contact and force measurements that are essential for understanding physical interactions and enabling dexterous robotic manipulation. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection reliant on intrusive, costly, and restrictive instrumentation. We present TouchSight, a monocular egocentric vision framework for dense full-hand contact force prediction that leverages 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and extensive hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand real-world scenarios, we construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data in which generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations against new backgrounds while preserving the original measured tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos, outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and improves consistently as glove supervision scales. These results demonstrate that dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time.

AI.tldr: TouchSight is a monocular egocentric vision framework that predicts dense full-hand contact force from video, using 500 hours of pressure-glove data and a synthetic bare-hand dataset (TwinTouch-20H) to bridge the gloved-to-bare-hand domain gap.
AI.motivation: Tactile sensing requires intrusive, costly instrumentation, making large-scale data collection restrictive. This paper aims to recover dense tactile signals from egocentric vision alone, eliminating the need for tactile instrumentation at capture time.
AI.method: 1) Collect 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings with hand-object interaction data 2) Generate TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data using generative video models to re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations while preserving tactile labels 3) Train TouchSight to predict dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos
AI.result: TouchSight outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and shows consistent improvement as glove supervision scales.
AI.conclusion: Dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone without tactile instrumentation at capture time, enabling large-scale tactile data collection through vision alone.

title: SkillAA: Attribution-Guided Skill-Graph Updating with Targeted Validation and Rollback
summary: External skills provide domain procedures without parameter updates, but existing methods often edit skills directly from failed rollouts without structured routing from an observed failure to an editable location; existing skill graphs also underuse semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for skill retrieval, targeted updating, and scoped validation. We introduce SkillAA (Skill Abductive Attribution), a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen language models. It represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph, allowing the same structure to support skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. SkillAA contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, updates only the selected local structure, and uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment. With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA reaches 81.5%, 66.7%, and 91.2% on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, respectively, and attains the highest observed mean in every main setting. These results support the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation.

AI.tldr: SkillAA is a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen language models that uses a unified graph representation to support skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. It contrasts successful and failed executions to route repairs to specific graph objects, with Local and Big Gates screening candidate changes before commitment.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for external skills (providing domain procedures without parameter updates) have two key limitations: 1) They edit skills directly from failed rollouts without structured routing from observed failure to editable location; 2) Existing skill graphs underuse semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for skill retrieval, targeted updating, and scoped validation.
AI.method: SkillAA introduces three key innovations: 1) A unified graph representing skill applicability, execution, and composition that supports skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation; 2) Contrasting successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects; 3) Using Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment.
AI.result: With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA achieves 81.5% on SearchQA, 66.7% on LiveMath, and 91.2% on DocVQA, attaining the highest observed mean in every main setting.
AI.conclusion: The results support the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation for skill optimization in frozen language models. The structured approach to routing repairs and validating updates is effective.

title: A Learning Algorithm for Threshold Boolean Networks with Prescribed Fixed Points
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, to be published in 20th International Meeting, CIBB 2025, Revised Selected Papers
summary: We present a learning algorithm for inferring threshold Boolean networks (TBNs) with a prescribed set of fixed points. The proposed method employs a custom differentiable loss function that jointly enforces fixed point preservation, penalizes spurious attractors, encourages binary outputs, and promotes sparsity through L1 regularization. Applied to the FOS-GRN model of Arabidopsis thaliana, the approach achieved perfect reconstruction (i.e., all 10 desired fixed points and no spurious ones) in 5 out of 30 independent runs, recovering on average 8.53 $\pm$ 0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. In contrast, standard methods such as the Perceptron and Logistic Regression recovered up to 10 fixed points but introduced between 8 and 31 spurious ones.
