An additional analysis varying the sparsity coefficient ($λ$) confirmed that the method's performance and the structural properties of the inferred networks remain robust within a practical range (up to 0.01) of regularization strengths. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of the proposed algorithm in capturing meaningful network dynamics under prescribed dynamical constraints.

AI.tldr: A learning algorithm using a custom differentiable loss function to infer threshold Boolean networks (TBNs) with prescribed fixed points, applied to Arabidopsis thaliana gene regulatory network modeling.
AI.motivation: Inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) with specific dynamical behaviors (fixed points) is challenging. Standard methods like Perceptron and Logistic Regression produce spurious attractors, making accurate network reconstruction difficult.
AI.method: Custom differentiable loss function combining: (1) fixed point preservation, (2) spurious attractor penalty, (3) binary output encouragement, and (4) L1 regularization for sparsity. Applied to FOS-GRN model of Arabidopsis thaliana.
AI.result: Achieved perfect reconstruction (10 fixed points, 0 spurious) in 5/30 runs; average 8.53 ± 0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. Standard methods yielded 10 fixed points but 8-31 spurious ones. Performance robust for λ up to 0.01.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm effectively captures network dynamics under prescribed dynamical constraints, outperforming Perceptron and Logistic Regression in eliminating spurious attractors while maintaining stability across regularization strengths.

title: WeVisDoc: From Coverage to Capability for Robust End-to-End Document Parsing
summary: Document parsing converts document images into structured content and requires reliable performance across diverse layouts and acquisition conditions. Yet training corpora are biased toward common document types and clean digital pages, while expanding coverage alone does not specify how to address a parser's remaining weaknesses. We present WeVisDoc, a two-stage data-centric framework for robust end-to-end document parsing. Stage I broadens semantic, structural, and appearance coverage through heterogeneous data and structure-preserving degradation synthesis. Stage II uses a held-out probe to measure the Stage I parser's residual errors within fixed visual-structural clusters. These diagnostics guide targeted data construction and reallocation of the target-token budget. WeVisDoc-4B achieves an Overall score of 95.38 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and a mean Overall score of 75.54 across the three PureDocBench tracks, ranking first among the compared end-to-end parsers in all four settings. Compared with Stage I, Stage II improves Overall scores for the 2B and 4B models on both benchmarks, with larger gains on the degraded PureDocBench tracks, including a 4.03-point gain for the 4B model on the Real Degraded track.

AI.tldr: WeVisDoc is a two-stage data-centric framework for robust end-to-end document parsing that addresses training data bias toward common document types and clean digital pages. It combines heterogeneous data with structure-preserving degradation synthesis in Stage I, then uses a held-out probe to diagnose residual errors and guide targeted data construction in Stage II.
AI.motivation: Training corpora for document parsing are biased toward common document types and clean digital pages. Expanding coverage alone does not specify how to address a parser's remaining weaknesses, requiring a systematic approach to identify and fix specific failure modes.
AI.method: Stage I broadens semantic, structural, and appearance coverage through heterogeneous data and structure-preserving degradation synthesis. Stage II uses a held-out probe to measure the Stage I parser's residual errors within fixed visual-structural clusters, with diagnostics guiding targeted data construction and reallocation of the target-token budget.
AI.result: WeVisDoc-4B achieves an Overall score of 95.38 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and a mean Overall score of 75.54 across three PureDocBench tracks, ranking first among compared end-to-end parsers in all four settings. Stage II improves Overall scores for 2B and 4B models on both benchmarks, with larger gains on degraded PureDocBench tracks, including a 4.03-point gain for the 4B model on the Real Degraded track.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage data-centric approach WeVisDoc significantly improves document parsing robustness across diverse layouts and acquisition conditions, with the diagnostic-guided Stage II providing substantial improvements especially on degraded document benchmarks.

title: How Do Agent Harnesses Create Value? Planning Information and Release Control in Stateful LLM Agents
summary: Agent harnesses supply planning guidance, organize execution, and check completion. We study how these components affect success, erroneous acceptance, and cost in two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot in $τ^2$-bench. The primary comparison pairs prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) with shuffled policy text matched in word count (Sham), isolating the contribution of guidance content. Across 265 matched cells, Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90\% task-clustered bootstrap interval, 1.15--13.36 points), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. A read-only terminal verifier rejects 61\% of Retail oracle-invalid episodes while withholding 17\% of correct ones, at less than one cent of additional cost per episode. Which component matters more depends on the loss assigned to erroneous acceptance: at low liability the planning gain dominates; at high liability the verifier's avoided false passes dominate---and a standalone verifier captures nearly all the false-pass benefit of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how three components of agent systems—supply planning guidance, execution organization, and completion checking—affect success rates, erroneous acceptance, and cost. Through two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot, the research compares prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) against shuffled policy text (Sham) to isolate guidance content's contribution. Results show Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points, with gains in higher-complexity tasks. A read-only terminal verifier rejects 61% of invalid episodes at minimal cost. The relative importance of planning vs. verification depends on the liability assigned to erroneous acceptance.
AI.motivation: The research aims to understand how different components of agent systems (planning guidance, execution organization, and completion checking) contribute to task success, and to isolate the specific contribution of guidance content by comparing prewritten plans against sham controls.
AI.method: Two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot in τ²-bench, comparing Fixed (prewritten task-specific plans) with Sham (shuffled policy text matched in word count) across 265 matched cells. A read-only terminal verifier was also tested.
AI.result: Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90% CI: 1.15-13.36 points), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. The verifier rejects 61% of invalid episodes while withholding 17% of correct ones, at less than one cent additional cost per episode. At low liability, planning gains dominate; at high liability, verifier benefits dominate.
AI.conclusion: The component that matters most depends on the loss assigned to erroneous acceptance. A standalone verifier can capture nearly all false-pass benefits of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost, particularly in high-liability scenarios.

title: Improving Generalization and Robustness in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation
summary: Current offline reinforcement learning (ORL) algorithms tend to overfit the training dataset and exhibit poor in-distribution generalization and robustness performance when deployed to real environments, thus compromising their effectiveness. Existing methods typically enhance in-distribution generalization and robustness by leveraging regularization techniques widely used in computer vision. However, due to the high sensitivity of low-level physical signals to distributional shifts, these methods still suffer from notable limitations in in-distribution generalization and robustness, making it difficult to achieve stable performance in complex environments. To address this issue, we theoretically analyze the error bounds of the behavior policy and action-value function trained with random episode interpolation, revealing that the error scales positively correlated with the distance between states. Based on this insight, we propose a method called $\bf{B}$oundary-$\bf{A}$ware $\bf{D}$ata $\bf{A}$ugmentation (BADA), which leverages neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries, enabling the generation of synthetic data that more faithfully preserves the original data distribution. We first conduct qualitative studies in a toy environment, showing that BADA generates mixed samples that preserve desirable policy smoothness while accurately reconstructing multimodal value distributions. Extensive experiments on limited offline datasets further demonstrate that BADA attains state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the overfitting and poor in-distribution generalization problem in offline reinforcement learning (ORL) by proposing Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation (BADA). The method uses neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries, generating synthetic data that preserves the original data distribution better than existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Current ORL algorithms tend to overfit the training dataset and exhibit poor in-distribution generalization and robustness when deployed to real environments. Existing methods using regularization techniques from computer vision still suffer from notable limitations due to the high sensitivity of low-level physical signals to distributional shifts.
AI.method: The paper theoretically analyzes error bounds of behavior policy and action-value function trained with random episode interpolation, revealing that error scales positively correlated with the distance between states. Based on this insight, BADA leverages neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries, enabling generation of synthetic data that more faithfully preserves the original data distribution.
AI.result: Qualitative studies in a toy environment show that BADA generates mixed samples that preserve desirable policy smoothness while accurately reconstructing multimodal value distributions. Extensive experiments on limited offline datasets further demonstrate that BADA attains state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: BADA provides a principled approach to improving in-distribution generalization and robustness in ORL by using boundary-aware data augmentation. The theoretical analysis connecting error bounds to state distance provides a solid foundation for the method, and the experimental results validate its effectiveness across various benchmarks.

title: When Do Language-Grounded Explanations Help? A Graph-Bottleneck for Farm Monitoring Interpretable Sheep Facial Pain
summary: Automated pain recognition from facial expression could make continuous welfare assessment practical in sheep, but adoption depends on trust: a stockperson cannot act on a score that arrives without justification. We ground a model in the Sheep Pain Facial Expression Scale (SPFES) by letting each detected facial region attend over text embeddings of the clinical descriptors and then test whether the resulting explanations mean anything. They do not. Ablating an entire descriptor changes the predicted logit by about $10^{-4}$, and the most-attended cue agrees with the predicted pain level in only $32.6\%$ of regions, although the attention maps, the learned gate, and the generated text all proposed otherwise. We therefore remove the appearance bypass with a concept bottleneck whose classifier reads only SPFES concept scores, supervised by per-region state annotations that image-level pipelines discard. This costs $0.05$--$0.10$ in Cohen's $κ$ but yields concepts that are demonstrably learned: minority pain-indicating states are recovered at $3.5$--$8.3\times$ their base rates, and the ear and eye severity orderings emerge without severity supervision. Removing the supervision alone leaves $κ$ unchanged while concept accuracy falls to $0.109$, showing that architectural necessity does not imply semantic validity. We also show that pooled concept accuracy is misleading under clinical imbalance and provide a cross-validated, protocol-matched benchmark of seven methods on this dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses trust issues in automated sheep pain recognition by testing whether attention-based explanations align with actual pain predictions, finding they do not. The authors then propose a concept bottleneck model that uses SPFES (Sheep Pain Facial Expression Scale) concept scores with per-region supervision, achieving good concept learning despite modest accuracy trade-offs.
AI.motivation: The core motivation is trust: automated pain recognition systems for sheep are useless if stockpeople cannot understand or verify the scores. The authors question whether attention mechanisms in deep learning models actually provide meaningful explanations, and whether architectural choices imply semantic validity.
AI.method:
1) Built an attention-based model where facial regions attend over text embeddings of SPFES clinical descriptors
2) Tested explanatory power through ablation (removing descriptors) and alignment analysis (does attention match predicted pain?)
3) Replaced with a concept bottleneck model using only SPFES concept scores, supervised by per-region state annotations
4) Provided cross-validated benchmark of seven methods on the dataset
AI.result:
1) Attention explanations are not meaningful: ablating descriptors changes predicted logit by only ~10^-4, and most-attended cues agree with predicted pain level in only 32.6% of regions
2) Concept bottleneck costs 0.05-0.10 in Cohen's κ but achieves meaningful concept learning: minority pain states recovered at 3.5-8.3× base rates, ear and eye severity orderings emerge without supervision
3) Without supervision, κ unchanged but concept accuracy drops to 0.109, showing architectural necessity ≠ semantic validity
4) Pooled concept accuracy is misleading under clinical imbalance
AI.conclusion: Attention-based explanations in pain recognition models are not trustworthy. Concept bottleneck models, while slightly less accurate, provide demonstrably learned concepts that could enable meaningful human oversight. The paper also highlights the importance of proper evaluation metrics under class imbalance and provides a rigorous benchmark for future work.

title: SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/NVlabs/SoL-Pi . Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/SoL-Pi/
summary: As coding agents move from supervised code completion to unattended, around-the-clock exploration, their work expands from isolated predictions into long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback. Token efficiency therefore becomes important for scaling recursive self-improvement. We take an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across increasingly numerous and diverse environments for harness rollouts. At this scale, the process yields reusable improvements that transfer beyond their development setting, moving automated harness discovery toward production-level outcomes. Four mechanisms survive selection and form SoL-Pi, spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading. On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. In other words, estimated hourly savings are \$8.75-\$13.50 relative to native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and \$4.36-\$5.71 relative to Pi.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SoL-Pi, a system of four mechanisms for token-efficient scaling of auto-research loops in coding agents. It achieves comparable performance to Pi on EdgeBench while reducing token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API costs by about one third.
AI.motivation: As coding agents evolve from supervised code completion to unattended, continuous exploration, they generate long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback. Token efficiency becomes critical for scaling recursive self-improvement (RSI). The goal is to reduce token traffic and API costs while maintaining performance across diverse environments.
AI.method: The authors use an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across increasingly numerous and diverse environments. Four mechanisms survive selection, forming SoL-Pi: (1) action execution, (2) context compaction, (3) observation handling, and (4) delegated reading. The system is evaluated on the 51-task EdgeBench benchmark using GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 models.
AI.result: SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. Estimated hourly savings are $8.75-$13.50 relative to native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and $4.36-$5.71 relative to Pi. The process yields reusable improvements that transfer beyond their development setting.
AI.conclusion: The four mechanisms spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading form an effective system (SoL-Pi) for token-efficient scaling. This approach moves automated harness discovery toward production-level outcomes by achieving significant cost reductions while maintaining comparable performance. The reusable improvements transfer across different development settings.

title: Cross-Architecture Foundation-Model Distillation for Edge Flood Segmentation
comment: Main paper (17 pages) with supplementary material (11 pages). Submitted to IEEE JSTARS, Special Section on Generalist-Specialist Model Synergy for Remote Sensing: Theories, Methods, and Applications
summary: Geospatial foundation models can provide strong flood-segmentation performance, but their size limits deployment on memory-constrained edge hardware. We distill a 300-million-parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher, fine-tuned on the 252 manually labeled Sen1Floods11 training scenes, into a 0.7-million-parameter EfficientViT-B0 student. The teacher supervises additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery, allowing the student training set to grow without new manual annotations. At the matched budget of 252 scenes, teacher-supervised training is competitive with direct training and improves STURM-Flood performance across tested configurations; a geometry-matched control shows that label source alone does not explain the difference. Scaling the teacher-supervised pool to 2,500 scenes narrows the remaining student--teacher gap: the float student reaches 0.787 water intersection over union on the Sen1Floods11 test split against 0.822 for the teacher, matches the teacher on STURM-Flood under our evaluation protocol, and remains below it on WorldFloods-v2. After activation replacement and quantization-aware training, the student runs as a 1.5-megabyte 8-bit integer (INT8) TensorRT engine on a Jetson Xavier NX at 5.57 milliseconds of graphics processing unit (GPU) compute per 512-by-512 image, with approximately 14 megabytes of runtime device memory. A fixed modified normalized difference water index (MNDWI) threshold is competitive with both models on the two clean external benchmarks, so we interpret those benchmarks as generalization tests rather than as evidence of learned-model superiority over a spectral rule. The results support the conclusion: foundation-model supervision can amplify a fixed manual annotation budget into a substantially larger training set and yield a compact, deployable edge model.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a knowledge distillation approach that transfers flood segmentation knowledge from a 300M parameter geospatial foundation model (Prithvi-EO-2.0) to a compact 0.7M parameter EfficientViT-B0 model, using unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery to expand the training data without manual annotations. The resulting student model achieves 0.787 IoU on Sen1Floods11 test, runs at 5.57ms on Jetson Xavier NX with only 14MB memory, demonstrating that foundation model supervision can amplify limited manual annotation budgets into deployable edge models.
AI.motivation: Geospatial foundation models provide strong flood segmentation but are too large for memory-constrained edge hardware deployment. The authors aim to create a compact model suitable for edge deployment while maintaining performance through teacher-supervised training on expanded unlabeled data.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) Distilling a 300M parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher (fine-tuned on 252 Sen1Floods11 scenes) into a 0.7M parameter EfficientViT-B0 student; (2) Using the teacher to supervise additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery, expanding the training set without manual annotations; (3) Scaling the teacher-supervised pool from 252 to 2,500 scenes; (4) Applying activation replacement and quantization-aware training for edge deployment.
AI.result: At 252 scenes, teacher-supervised training improves STURM-Flood performance. Scaling to 2,500 scenes: student achieves 0.787 water IoU on Sen1Floods11 (teacher: 0.822), matches teacher on STURM-Flood, but remains below on WorldFloods-v2. The quantized 1.5MB INT8 model runs at 5.57ms on Jetson Xavier NX with ~14MB memory. A fixed MNDWI threshold competes with learned models on clean benchmarks, suggesting those benchmarks test generalization rather than model superiority over spectral rules.
AI.conclusion: Foundation-model supervision can amplify a fixed manual annotation budget into a substantially larger training set and yield a compact, deployable edge model. The student achieves competitive performance while being small enough for edge deployment, with inference at 5.57ms and only 14MB memory consumption.

title: FreqCondNorm: Towards Cross-domain Predictive Maintenance through a Frequency-Conditioned Transformer Foundation Model
summary: Deep learning predictive maintenance models suffer from poor transferability across machines and operating conditions, especially when labelled data are scarce and signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz). We propose FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture that introduces a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series within a single model. The architecture is pretrained on five public predictive maintenance datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling. On fault diagnosis, the model achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 pp over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, demonstrating strong transfer across sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life prediction, suggesting a mismatch between pretraining and RUL objectives that warrants future investigation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture with FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization to address poor transferability in deep learning predictive maintenance models across machines and operating conditions with signals spanning 1 Hz to ~100 kHz. The model is pretrained on five public datasets using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning, achieving 99.2% accuracy on CWRU fault diagnosis and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, but fails to improve remaining useful life prediction.
AI.motivation: Deep learning predictive maintenance models suffer from poor transferability across machines and operating conditions, especially when labeled data are scarce and signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz). This heterogeneity in time-series data limits the practical deployment of such models.
AI.method: The authors propose FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture that introduces a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series within a single model. The architecture is pretrained on five public predictive maintenance datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling.
AI.result: On fault diagnosis, the model achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 percentage points over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, demonstrating strong transfer across sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life (RUL) prediction.
AI.conclusion: The FreqCondNorm architecture demonstrates strong transfer learning capabilities across different sampling frequencies for fault diagnosis tasks. However, the approach does not improve RUL prediction, suggesting a mismatch between pretraining and RUL objectives that warrants future investigation.

title: Hypernetwork-Parameterized Spatially Adaptive Neural Operators for PDE Learning
summary: Spatially heterogeneous partial differential equations (PDEs) exhibit location-dependent dynamics arising from variations in geometry and physical coefficients. Existing neural operators improve localized modeling through multiscale features, attention mechanisms, or domain decomposition, yet their update rules often remain spatially shared. Hypernetwork-based methods adapt parameters across PDE instances but typically generate only one global parameterization per instance. Consequently, shared operators may underfit boundaries and high-gradient regions, with these localized errors accumulating during autoregressive rollout. We propose a spatially adaptive neural operator (SANO), which replaces this spatially shared parameterization with a spatially continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters. SANO uses Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. A Hyper-Neural Element (HNE) mechanism interpolates these codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators while allowing their update rules to vary across space, and partition-of-unity weights assemble the overlapping local predictions. Experiments on one-, two-, and three-dimensional PDEs and two perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks show that SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural-operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines.

AI.tldr: SANO proposes a spatially adaptive neural operator that replaces spatially shared parameterization with a continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters, using Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes.
AI.motivation: Existing neural operators use spatially shared update rules, and hypernetwork-based methods generate only one global parameterization per instance. This leads to underfitting at boundaries and high-gradient regions, with localized errors accumulating during autoregressive rollout.
AI.method: SANO uses Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. A Hyper-Neural Element (HNE) mechanism interpolates these codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators while allowing update rules to vary across space. Partition-of-unity weights assemble overlapping local predictions.
AI.result: SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural-operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines on 1D, 2D, and 3D PDEs and two perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The spatially continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters enables SANO to better capture localized dynamics at boundaries and high-gradient regions, addressing the key limitation of spatially shared parameterization in existing neural operators.

title: SenseFuse: Label-Free Fusion of Image and Shape Encoders for Open-Vocabulary 3D Instance Segmentation
summary: Open-vocabulary scene understanding is fundamental for robotics, laying the groundwork for spatial reasoning and object manipulation. While closed-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation heavily leverages 3D shape information, state-of-the-art open-vocabulary methods remain predominantly restricted to 2D image features or image-distilled representations during mask labeling. In this paper, we propose SenseFuse, a label-free fusion method that balances 2D image and 3D shape encoders for robust open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation, refining only the mask-labeling stage of existing pipelines. We reveal that 2D image and 3D shape encoders exhibit largely disjoint failure patterns and rarely share identical wrong labels, whereas two 2D image encoders frequently repeat the same errors. This distinct behavior makes the 2D and 3D pair inherently complementary. We introduce an adaptive mechanism that selects a scene-level fusion weight to maximize a label-free sensitivity measure, estimated directly from a single scene's unlabeled proposals in milliseconds. SenseFuse improves labeling accuracy in every evaluated setting across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++, recovering 67-100% (median 93%) of the gain achievable with an oracle weight, and it raises instance AP in 21 of 22 reported settings. Code is available at https://github.com/hanes1207/SenseFuse.

AI.tldr: SenseFuse is a label-free fusion method for open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation that combines 2D image and 3D shape encoders. It uses an adaptive mechanism to select fusion weights based on a label-free sensitivity measure, improving labeling accuracy across multiple datasets while requiring no additional supervision.
AI.motivation: Current open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation methods rely predominantly on 2D image features, neglecting valuable 3D shape information. The authors discovered that 2D and 3D encoders have largely complementary failure patterns, making them inherently suitable for fusion, whereas two 2D encoders tend to repeat similar errors.
AI.method: SenseFuse introduces an adaptive mechanism that selects scene-level fusion weights to maximize a label-free sensitivity measure. This measure is estimated directly from a single scene's unlabeled proposals in milliseconds, requiring no ground truth labels. The method refines only the mask-labeling stage of existing pipelines.
AI.result: SenseFuse improves labeling accuracy in every evaluated setting across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++. It recovers 67-100% (median 93%) of the gain achievable with an oracle weight, and raises instance AP in 21 of 22 reported settings.
AI.conclusion: The fusion of 2D image and 3D shape encoders through adaptive, label-free weight selection is highly effective for open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation. The complementary nature of 2D and 3D encoders enables robust performance across diverse scenes and datasets, with minimal computational overhead (estimation in milliseconds).

title: Refuse, Decompose, Refresh: A Claim-Safe Protocol for Closed-Loop AI Evaluation
comment: 8 pages, 0 figures, 3 tables. The reproducibility artifact is linked in the paper
summary: An AI evaluation can be perfectly reproducible and still support the wrong claim. This risk is acute in closed-loop systems: policy determines visited states, observable components, and which failures leave a measurable trace. We propose a claim-safe protocol with three actions. Refuse: abstain when a clean reference stream or matched runtime comparison lacks support. Decompose: report protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses separately rather than as one PASS/FAIL label. Refresh: treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate and recompute a reference map, not as fault evidence. We instantiate the protocol in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development and heldout seeds. The preregistered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows. Only 55/72 regime-component units were reference-admitted and 54/55 remained runtime-admitted, making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 represented components, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: across 540 unit-arm rows nested in 20 component clusters, the cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference was 0.1264 nats per row, with a 95% component-cluster interval of [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log shows why "null" must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across three regimes, while only the middle regime matched the frozen detector reference. Rather than a universal threshold, we contribute an executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical flaw in AI evaluation: reproducible evaluations can still support incorrect claims, especially in closed-loop systems where policy behavior affects what can be observed and measured. The authors propose a "claim-safe protocol" with three actions—Refuse (abstain when reference support lacks), Decompose (report components separately rather than as PASS/FAIL), and Refresh (treat distribution shifts as recomputation requests rather than faults). They validate this in a simulator with 24 policy components, showing that only 55/72 regime-component units passed reference admission, and stable false admission was 0/20 with a 95% upper bound of 0.1391.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that even perfectly reproducible AI evaluations can support wrong claims. This is particularly dangerous in closed-loop systems (like autonomous vehicles or RL agents) where the policy determines which states are visited, what can be observed, and which failures leave traces. Existing evaluation methods lack a framework to ensure claims are actually supported by observable evidence.
AI.method: The authors instantiate their protocol in an aggregate-only simulator with: 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development/heldout seeds. The pre-registered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows. They use statistical measures including negative-log-likelihood differences and confidence intervals, and apply a "frozen 0.20 rule" for calibration.
AI.result: Only 55/72 regime-component units achieved reference admission, and 54/55 remained runtime-admitted—making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 represented components (one-sided exact 95% upper bound = 0.1391). Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: 0.1264 nats per row difference (95% CI: [0.0593, 0.1918]). The drift log showed clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across regimes, with only the middle regime matching the frozen detector reference.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose an "executable contract" linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims rather than a universal threshold. The key insight is that "null" must be reference-relative—meaningful evaluation requires treating distribution-shift alarms as requests to recompute reference maps, not as fault evidence. This provides a rigorous framework for making claim-safe evaluations in AI systems, particularly for high-stakes closed-loop applications.

title: ZeroHAT: Behavior-Conditioned Zero-Shot Human Activity Trace Generation
summary: Human activity traces record individuals' timestamped visits to points of interest and are essential for applications such as mobility prediction and urban simulation. However, accessing large-scale HATs is challenging due to high collection costs and privacy concerns. Synthetic HAT generation offers a promising way to make such data available and has attracted growing interest from both industry and academia. Although many efforts have been devoted to this topic, most of them rely on real data from a region to generate synthetic data for the same region, which is infeasible for the many regions where real HATs are unavailable. To fill this gap, we propose ZeroHAT, a behavior-conditioned framework that generates synthetic HATs for a target region in a zero-shot manner by transferring behavioral patterns learned from real HATs in source regions and adapting them with publicly available contextual information about the target region. ZeroHAT has three key novel components: (i) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor; (ii) a cross-region behavioral cloning module; and (iii) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module. We evaluate ZeroHAT on a ten-city benchmark, where extensive experiments show that ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions.

AI.tldr: ZeroHAT is a zero-shot framework that generates synthetic human activity traces for target regions by transferring behavioral patterns from source regions and adapting them with publicly available contextual information, without requiring any real data from the target region.
AI.motivation: Real human activity traces (HATs) are difficult to access due to high collection costs and privacy concerns. While synthetic HAT generation offers a solution, existing methods require real data from the target region, making them infeasible for regions without available real HATs. This creates a significant gap for many regions where real data is unavailable.
AI.method: ZeroHAT proposes a three-component framework: (1) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor to capture behavioral patterns; (2) a cross-region behavioral cloning module to transfer patterns from source regions; and (3) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module to adapt patterns using publicly available contextual information about the target region.
AI.result: ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions on a ten-city benchmark.
AI.conclusion: ZeroHAT successfully enables synthetic HAT generation for regions without real data, addressing a critical gap in the field. The framework demonstrates significant improvements in both downstream utility and fidelity compared to existing baselines, making it valuable for applications like mobility prediction and urban simulation where real data is unavailable.

title: Grounded Product Understanding in Livestream Videos
summary: E-commerce livestreams have emerged as an important channel for presenting products to online consumers, containing multiple products whose information is scattered in different moments. This poses significant challenges for downstream product understanding applications, such as product-centric livestream clipping, where models need to identify the product and its relevant segments for information gathering. However, existing benchmarks for general product understanding typically evaluate product retrieval and temporal localization in isolation, leaving the critical correspondence between product identity and temporal evidence largely unassessed. To address this limitation, we introduce GPUB, a large-scale benchmark comprising 3,000 livestream instances with quality-controlled multi-moment temporal annotations and a catalog of over 31K fashion products. GPUB supports three evaluation tasks: the main task Grounded Product Understanding (GPrU) requires jointly identifying the target product and localizing its supporting moments from a livestream video and a candidate product set; Product Retrieval and Product Moment Localization serve as two complementary subtasks. Evaluation of existing multimodal models shows that GPrU remains highly challenging, with the best-performing baseline achieving only 10.13% Pair mAP@.3. To narrow the performance gap, we further develop UniPro, a unified product understanding model that derives product-aligned and temporally structured representations from shared multimodal encoding, improving Pair mAP@.3 to 21.53% while achieving 37.23% Joint R@1@.3 on GPrU.

AI.tldr: GPUB is a large-scale benchmark for evaluating product understanding in e-commerce livestreams, addressing the gap where existing benchmarks evaluate product retrieval and temporal localization in isolation. It supports three tasks, with the main task being Grounded Product Understanding (GPrU) that requires jointly identifying products and localizing their supporting moments. The best baseline achieves only 10.13% Pair mAP@.3, while the proposed UniPro model achieves 21.53% Pair mAP@.3.
AI.motivation: E-commerce livestreams contain multiple products at different moments, creating challenges for downstream applications like product-centric livestream clipping. Existing benchmarks fail to assess the correspondence between product identity and temporal evidence, leaving a critical gap in evaluating product understanding.
AI.method: The researchers created GPUB, a benchmark with 3,000 livestream instances, quality-controlled multi-moment temporal annotations, and a catalog of over 31K fashion products. They also developed UniPro, a unified product understanding model that derives product-aligned and temporally structured representations from shared multimodal encoding.
AI.result: GPrU remains highly challenging - the best-performing baseline achieves only 10.13% Pair mAP@.3. UniPro improves performance to 21.53% Pair mAP@.3 and achieves 37.23% Joint R@1@.3 on GPrU.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark addresses a critical gap in e-commerce livestream product understanding. While significant progress has been made with UniPro, there's still substantial room for improvement as current models achieve relatively low accuracy on this joint task.

title: Language-model groups overstate consensus when replaying human deliberation on a reasoning task
comment: 37 pages, 4 figures. Preregistration: https://osf.io/5jp7s . Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21318346
summary: Full-consensus rates are often treated as indicators of collective cognition, yet depend on how participation and final states are operationalized. We replayed 100 held-out human Wason groups with matched large language model (LLM) agent groups, seeding one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer and scoring agents and people with the same code. Across human scoring definitions, estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0%; about one fifth of participants never posted, whereas agents almost always did. Agent groups remained more consensual in two post-unblinding sensitivity analyses: the submit-based comparison (n = 98) yielded gaps of 34.0 and 43.9 percentage points for chat and reasoning modes, and the participation-matched comparison (n = 45) yielded gaps of 34.1 and 44.4 points. These complementary routes reduced different measurement asymmetries yet converged within 0.5 percentage points. The gap persisted without early stopping and under a reparameterization removing the memorizable answer; reasoning-mode groups then agreed nearly unanimously, mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups were biased estimators of the human group-outcome distribution in this setting. These analyses provide a scoring-explicit basis for assessing simulated-group estimates of human deliberative outcomes.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether full-consensus rates in large language model (LLM) agent groups can serve as indicators of human collective cognition, using the Wason selection task. The study replayed 100 human groups with matched LLM agent groups and found that consensus rates vary dramatically (24-57%) depending on operationalization. Agent groups showed 34-44 percentage points higher consensus than human groups, even persisting under reparameterization. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and reasoning-mode agents often reached near-unanimous agreement on incorrect answers.
AI.motivation: Full-consensus rates are often used as indicators of collective cognition, but depend heavily on how participation and final states are defined. The researchers wanted to test whether LLM agent groups could serve as proxies for human deliberative outcomes, and to provide a scoring-explicit framework for assessing such simulated-group estimates.
AI.method: The researchers replayed 100 held-out human Wason groups with matched LLM agent groups. They seeded one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer and scored both agents and humans with the same code. They conducted multiple sensitivity analyses: submit-based comparison (n=98), participation-matched comparison (n=45), analyses without early stopping, and reparameterization removing the memorizable answer.
AI.result: Human consensus estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0% depending on scoring definitions. About 20% of human participants never posted, while agents almost always did. Agent groups remained more consensual: chat mode showed 34.0-34.1 point gaps, reasoning mode showed 43.9-44.4 point gaps. The gap persisted without early stopping. Under reparameterization, reasoning-mode groups agreed nearly unanimously but mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups were biased estimators of human group-outcome distribution.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent groups should not be used as proxies for human deliberative outcomes in collective cognition research. The study provides a scoring-explicit framework for assessing simulated-group estimates, showing that consensus rates in agent groups are not reliable indicators of human collective cognition and may systematically mislead researchers about human group outcomes.

title: EviRec: Continual Evidence Learning for Dual Cold-Start POI Recommendation
summary: Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation is a core task in location-based services, yet most existing methods assume a fixed user population and POI catalog. Through a large-scale data-driven analysis of 10 U.S. cities, we identify substantial POI churn, user turnover, category drift, and decay in static POI memory, motivating the study of continual dual cold-start POI recommendation. To address this setting, we propose EviRec, a continual evidence-learning framework that estimates how much historical evidence should be trusted separately for each candidate POI. EviRec scores each visible candidate from three complementary views: a matching view based on the user's recent mobility profile, a transition-memory view that captures repeated mobility routines, and a lifecycle view that reflects candidate maturity. Because a near-zero transition score may indicate either irrelevance or insufficient observation, EviRec qualifies the evidence using each candidate's observation state and applies a reliability gate to adaptively route between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence. We evaluate EviRec on a full-year, five-city POI check-in dataset containing more than 30,000 users and 684,200 trajectories. Experimental results show that EviRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with the largest gains concentrated on cold-start queries. In particular, EviRec improves NDCG@10 by 20.4\% on Dual-New cases over the strongest baseline. In-depth analyses further confirm that these gains arise primarily from candidate-specific reliability gating while largely preserving previously learned mobility routines.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a novel problem in POI recommendation: continual dual cold-start recommendation, where both users and POIs are continuously changing. The authors propose EviRec, a framework that estimates trust in historical evidence for each candidate POI using three complementary views (matching, transition-memory, lifecycle) and a reliability gating mechanism. Experiments on a large-scale dataset show significant improvements, especially on cold-start cases.
AI.motivation: Existing POI recommendation methods assume a fixed user population and POI catalog, which doesn't reflect real-world dynamics. Through large-scale data analysis of 10 U.S. cities, the authors identify four key phenomena: POI churn (POIs open/close), user turnover, category drift, and decay in static POI memory. These motivate the study of continual dual cold-start POI recommendation.
AI.method: EviRec is a continual evidence-learning framework that estimates trustworthiness of historical evidence for each candidate POI separately. It scores visible candidates from three complementary views: (1) Matching view based on user's recent mobility profile, (2) Transition-memory view capturing repeated mobility routines, and (3) Lifecycle view reflecting candidate maturity. A key innovation is the reliability gate that uses observation state to adaptively route between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence when transition scores are near-zero.
AI.result: Evaluated on a full-year, five-city dataset with 30,000+ users and 684,200 trajectories. EviRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The largest gains are on cold-start queries, with NDCG@10 improved by 20.4% on Dual-New cases over the strongest baseline. In-depth analyses confirm the gains arise from candidate-specific reliability gating while preserving previously learned mobility routines.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully addresses the overlooked problem of continual dual cold-start in POI recommendation. The three-view approach with reliability gating effectively handles the dynamic nature of users and POIs. The significant improvement on cold-start cases (20.4% NDCG@10 gain) demonstrates the framework's effectiveness in handling new users and new POIs simultaneously.

title: Automated Goldsmith's Mark Retrieval in Silverware
comment: Accepted at the VISART workshop, ECCV 2026. 18 pages, 8 figures, 1 table
summary: For art historians, goldsmith marks play a critical role in the identification and dating of artifacts. In practice, experts must manually compare a query mark against hundreds of documented examples, a process that is both tedious and highly dependent on specialist knowledge. To address this, we present an AI-assisted retrieval pipeline that combines mark localization with metric-learning fine-tuning across three backbone architectures: an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, a supervised ViT-S/16, and a self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14. We conduct a systematic evaluation of cropping strategies, where we measure the impact of no cropping, manual ground-truth cropping, and learned detection-based cropping, and assess their interaction with each backbone. Our strongest configuration, DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with manual crop and metric-learning fine-tuning, achieves an mAP of 62.63% and a Top-1 accuracy of 73.74%. Our experiments show that self-supervised pretraining and mark localization are the two most impactful factors, with learned cropping recovering the majority of the gain from manual cropping without requiring ground-truth annotations at inference time. To enable reproducibility and adoption in the digital humanities, we release our manually annotated dataset and codebase, and deploy the system via a public web interface.

AI.tldr: An AI-assisted retrieval system for goldsmith mark identification that combines mark localization with metric-learning fine-tuning across three backbone architectures (ResNet-50, supervised ViT-S/16, and self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14), evaluating three cropping strategies. The best configuration achieves 62.63% mAP and 73.74% Top-1 accuracy.
AI.motivation: Art historians manually compare query marks against hundreds of documented examples for identification and dating, which is tedious and highly dependent on specialist knowledge. An automated system was needed to assist experts in this task.
AI.method: Developed an AI-assisted retrieval pipeline combining mark localization with metric-learning fine-tuning. Systematically evaluated three backbone architectures (ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, supervised ViT-S/16, and self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14) with three cropping strategies (no cropping, manual ground-truth cropping, and learned detection-based cropping), assessing their interactions.
AI.result: The strongest configuration (DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with manual crop and metric-learning fine-tuning) achieved 62.63% mAP and 73.74% Top-1 accuracy. Self-supervised pretraining and mark localization were the two most impactful factors. Learned cropping recovered most of the gain from manual cropping without requiring ground-truth annotations at inference time.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining (DINOv2) and mark localization are critical for goldsmith mark retrieval. The learned cropping approach effectively substitutes manual cropping in production. The system is publicly deployed for digital humanities applications, with released dataset and codebase for reproducibility.

title: Limits of Confidence in Diffusion
summary: Discrete diffusion, including remasking and uniform-state samplers, generate a sequence by writing multiple token positions per step, drawing each from a per-position distribution and choosing which positions to write from those same distributions. For domains of general interest (pixels, phonemes, or words) there are inherent dependencies between tokens. We show that a step matches the training distribution only when the positions it writes are conditionally independent given the tokens already fixed, that no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and that per-position distributions do not determine whether a group is dependent: two joint distributions can have identical per-position marginals while differing in which combinations of values occur. On ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task whose joint distribution is available in closed form, we verify that every group of two or more undetermined positions a confidence ranking writes is dependent, and measure the generated distribution to be $29\times$ the sampling-noise floor total variation while per-sample metrics are $1.0$.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes discrete diffusion models (remasking and uniform-state samplers) and identifies a fundamental limitation: these methods cannot correctly generate dependent token groups because they use per-position distributions that assume conditional independence. The authors prove theoretically that no product of per-position distributions can match dependent groups, and demonstrate empirically on a synthetic task (ScanAndAdd) that the generated distribution deviates significantly from the target (29× noise floor).
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand why discrete diffusion models struggle with generating realistic sequences in domains like images, speech, or text where tokens have inherent dependencies. The authors investigate whether multi-token per-step generation can preserve the training distribution when tokens are dependent.
AI.method: The authors use theoretical analysis to prove that per-position distributions cannot match dependent joint distributions, and empirically validate this on ScanAndAdd - a synthetic task with closed-form known joint distribution. They measure the generated distribution using total variation distance and per-sample metrics.
AI.result: The key results are: (1) theoretically, no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and per-position marginals don't determine dependency; (2) empirically on ScanAndAdd, every group of 2+ undetermined positions is dependent, the generated distribution is 29× the sampling-noise floor total variation, while per-sample metrics show 1.0.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that discrete diffusion models with per-position distributions fundamentally cannot correctly generate dependent token groups, representing a significant limitation for applications in pixels, phonemes, or words where dependencies are inherent.

title: Sharp Reconstruction Bounds for Autoencoders Using the Same Forward Map
summary: We study reconstruction in autoencoders that apply the same forward map before and after setting the observed coordinates to zero. For equal odd input and hidden dimensions $d\geq 3$, among orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms whose Jacobian singular values lie in $[m,M]$, we show that the least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is $\max\{1-M(M-m)/2,0\}$, with affine maps attaining this sharp bound at every prescribed depth. A translated radial rotation can nevertheless reconstruct any prescribed ball exactly with singular values arbitrarily close to one, motivating additional conditions for a finite-data bound. We test this prediction on a 798,452-point terrestrial LiDAR forest scan. At input scale $0.05$, the mean theoretical bound is $0.155$, about $84\%$ of the mean normalized training error $0.185$ across four spatial regions, two depths, and three seeds. At this scale, adding one hidden coordinate reduces the mean reconstruction error below $6\times10^{-6}$.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes reconstruction error bounds in autoencoders that apply zero-masking (setting observed coordinates to zero) before and after a forward map. It provides sharp theoretical bounds for reconstruction-derivative error under constraints on Jacobian singular values, validates these bounds on large-scale LiDAR forest data, and shows that additional hidden coordinates can dramatically reduce reconstruction error.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand the theoretical limits of reconstruction in autoencoders under specific architectural constraints (zero-masking). The authors seek to establish bounds on reconstruction error that depend on the Jacobian singular values of the underlying diffeomorphism, and to test whether these theoretical predictions hold in practice on real-world data.
AI.method: The authors use mathematical analysis involving orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms with bounded Jacobian singular values in [m, M]. They derive analytical bounds for the least uniform reconstruction-derivative error and compare these with empirical measurements on a 798,452-point terrestrial LiDAR forest scan, testing across four spatial regions, two depths, and three random seeds.
AI.result: The theoretical bound for reconstruction-derivative error is max{1-M(M-m)/2,0}, with affine maps achieving this bound. At input scale 0.05, the mean theoretical bound is 0.155, which is approximately 84% of the mean normalized training error (0.185). Adding one hidden coordinate reduces mean reconstruction error to below 6×10⁻⁶.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical predictions align reasonably well with empirical results (84% of training error). The authors note that a translated radial rotation can achieve exact reconstruction with singular values close to one, motivating the need for additional conditions to derive finite-data bounds. The dramatic improvement with additional hidden coordinates suggests that depth and hidden dimension are critical for achieving low reconstruction error.

title: A Dual-Stream Regulated Reconstruction and Segmentation Network with Hierarchical Artifact-Prior Modeling for Ultra-Low-Field Pediatric Neuroimaging
summary: Automated quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation of multiple structures in $0.064\,\mathrm{T}$ ultra-low-field pediatric MRI are limited by a low signal-to-noise ratio, weak anatomical boundaries, and frequent artifacts. We present a unified framework for the LISA 2026 Challenge that performs all three tasks together within one inference pipeline. A network with two coupled streams, built on a 3D U-Net, first reconstructs an enhanced uLF volume and then combines the original and enhanced images for subcortical segmentation. To improve boundary stability, we add an auxiliary class covering brain tissue outside the target structures, derived from whole brain masks. A head conditioned on an artifact graph predicts the seven artifact ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features. We address the scarcity of dense annotations using diffeomorphic registration from atlas to target for label propagation and to regularize anatomical reconstruction. We report validation results across all three tasks.

AI.tldr: A unified framework for automated quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation of multiple structures in 0.064T ultra-low-field pediatric MRI, addressing challenges of low SNR, weak boundaries, and artifacts through a 3D U-Net-based dual-stream network with auxiliary classes and diffeomorphic registration.
AI.motivation: Ultra-low-field (0.064T) pediatric MRI suffers from low signal-to-noise ratio, weak anatomical boundaries, and frequent artifacts, limiting automated quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation capabilities. The LISA 2026 Challenge requires a unified approach for all three tasks within a single inference pipeline.
AI.method: A dual-stream 3D U-Net architecture: (1) First stream reconstructs enhanced uLF volumes; (2) Second stream combines original and enhanced images for subcortical segmentation with an auxiliary class covering brain tissue outside target structures; (3) Artifact prediction head conditioned on artifact graph predicts seven ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features; (4) Diffeomorphic registration from atlas to target for label propagation and anatomical reconstruction regularization.
AI.result: Validation results across all three tasks (quality assessment, enhancement, segmentation) are reported, demonstrating the framework's capability to handle the challenging uLF pediatric MRI data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified framework successfully integrates quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation into a single inference pipeline for 0.064T ultra-low-field pediatric MRI, effectively addressing the challenges of low SNR, weak boundaries, and artifacts through innovative architectural designs and registration-based regularization.

title: PAA: The Probabilistic Allen Algebra: A Generative and Complete Probabilistic Extension of Allen's Interval Relations
summary: Allen's interval algebra is a qualitative calculus for temporal relations, but its thirteen base relations are crisp predicates over exact interval boundaries. This is inadequate for temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories, where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain and expressions such as "just before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning. We develop the probabilistic Allen algebra (PAA): a generative and complete extension in which relation probabilities are derived from distributions over interval boundaries rather than assigned as scores. Time points are Gaussian; intervals have Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. Every relation is a boundary-ordering predicate in one common probability space: point-point relations reduce to error functions, and point-interval and interval-interval relations to multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations (meets, starts, finishes, equals) receive positive measure through a tolerance band, and under a single tolerance the thirteen relations form a true partition that recovers crisp Allen as the tolerance vanishes. The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it: coarse predicates such as precedence, overlap, and containment are unions of leaves whose probabilities are leaf sums, and this hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points and thirteen relations reduce to five and then three. Each relation further decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the spirit of CIDOC CRM. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions such as "shortly before" from contact relations. All results are Monte-Carlo validated and shipped as an open, tested Python package.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Probabilistic Allen Algebra (PAA), an extension of Allen's interval algebra that handles uncertainty in temporal relations by modeling intervals with Gaussian distributions. Rather than crisp predicates, PAA derives relation probabilities from distributions over interval boundaries, enabling handling of vague temporal expressions like "just before" or "roughly during."
AI.motivation: Allen's interval algebra provides thirteen crisp base relations for temporal reasoning, but this is inadequate for real-world temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain. Expressions like "shortly before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning that cannot be captured by binary predicates.
AI.method: The method involves modeling time points as Gaussian distributions and intervals as having Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. Every relation is modeled as a boundary-ordering predicate in a common probability space: point-point relations use error functions, while point-interval and interval-interval relations use multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations receive positive measure through a tolerance band, and under a single tolerance the thirteen relations form a true partition that recovers crisp Allen algebra as tolerance vanishes.
AI.result: The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it: coarse predicates (precedence, overlap, containment) are unions of leaves whose probabilities are leaf sums. The hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points, reducing thirteen relations to five and then to three. Each relation further decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the spirit of CIDOC CRM. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions like "shortly before" from contact relations. All results are Monte-Carlo validated.
AI.conclusion: The Probabilistic Allen Algebra provides a complete, generative extension of Allen's interval algebra that handles uncertainty in temporal relations. It successfully models graded temporal expressions and provides a principled probabilistic framework that recovers crisp Allen algebra as a special case. The results are validated and shipped as an open, tested Python package.

title: COMPASS: Ordered Clustered Routing at 100K Scale
summary: Large-scale routing often requires visiting clusters of nodes in a prescribed order, giving rise to the Ordered Clustered Traveling Salesman Problem (OCTSP). Optimizing each cluster independently seems natural, but misses non-local dependencies. We introduce the COMPASS algorithm for OCTSP, which combines search with learning-accelerated routing by orchestrating parallel sub-solvers. COMPASS has no quality ceiling and its solutions keep improving with compute. It exploits the clustered structure, and can reach exact solutions in time exponential in cluster size rather than instance size. Empirically, COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods. Unlike common large-scale routing solvers, COMPASS consumes general distance matrices and is not limited to coordinate inputs. We demonstrate scaling to 100K synthetic nodes and to 28.5K real e-commerce nodes. To our knowledge, the latter is the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, 9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks.

AI.tldr: COMPASS is an algorithm for the Ordered Clustered Traveling Salesman Problem (OCTSP) that combines search with learning-accelerated routing through parallel sub-solvers. It handles general distance matrices (not just coordinates), scales to 100K+ nodes, and achieves the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances (28.5K e-commerce nodes, 9x beyond prior ATSP benchmarks).
AI.motivation: Large-scale routing often requires visiting clusters of nodes in prescribed order (OCTSP). Existing methods that optimize each cluster independently miss non-local dependencies, limiting solution quality. There was a need for a solver that can exploit clustered structure while handling general distance matrices and scaling to real-world problem sizes.
AI.method: COMPASS orchestrates parallel sub-solvers that combine search with learning-accelerated routing. It exploits the clustered structure of the problem and can reach exact solutions in time exponential in cluster size rather than instance size. Unlike common large-scale routing solvers, it accepts general distance matrices rather than being limited to coordinate inputs.
AI.result: COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods. It scales to 100K synthetic nodes and 28.5K real e-commerce nodes. To the authors' knowledge, the 28.5K node solution represents the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, achieving 9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: COMPASS provides a powerful approach to OCTSP with no quality ceiling—solutions keep improving with compute. Its ability to handle general distance matrices and scale to tens of thousands of nodes makes it suitable for real-world e-commerce logistics applications. The method bridges the gap between exact solutions (exponential in cluster size) and practical large-scale routing problems.

title: DocAttriBench: Benchmarking Answer Grounding in Document Visual Question Answering
summary: Answer grounding in document visual question answering remains an open challenge: most benchmarks lack grounding annotations or provide limited-quality labels, while constructing grounded datasets still requires costly manual effort. We introduce DocAttriBench (DAB), a large-scale benchmark for fine-grained, element-level source attribution in Document VQA, grounding answers to specific layout elements such as text blocks, tables, and images. To build DAB, we propose a Mask-based Perplexity-Derived Attribution method (MAPPET) that combines document layout and language modeling to identify the most informative element for each answer. MAPPET measures the increase in perplexity after masking candidate elements and attributes the answer to the element contributing most to model confidence. Applying MAPPET to multiple existing Document VQA datasets yields DAB, with 237k documents and 296k question-answer pairs with element-level grounding. We benchmark grounding-capable multimodal LLMs on DAB, evaluating answer accuracy, attribution accuracy, and overall answer quality. Results show that while larger models generally achieve higher answer accuracy, even the strongest models often fail to localize the supporting elements. DAB provides a scalable benchmark for developing grounded, verifiable, and trustworthy Document VQA models. Dataset and code are available at https://aimagelab.github.io/DocAttriBench/.

AI.tldr: DocAttriBench (DAB) is a large-scale benchmark for element-level source attribution in Document VQA, built using a novel MAPPET method that uses perplexity changes to automatically ground answers to specific layout elements (text blocks, tables, images). The benchmark contains 237k documents and 296k QA pairs, revealing that while larger models achieve higher answer accuracy, they often fail to localize supporting elements.
AI.motivation: Answer grounding in Document VQA remains challenging: existing benchmarks lack grounding annotations or provide limited-quality labels, and constructing grounded datasets requires costly manual effort. There is a need for a scalable benchmark for developing grounded, verifiable, and trustworthy Document VQA models.
AI.method: The paper proposes MAPPET (Mask-based Perplexity-Derived Attribution method) which combines document layout and language modeling. It measures the increase in perplexity after masking candidate elements and attributes the answer to the element contributing most to model confidence. This method is applied to multiple existing Document VQA datasets to generate DAB.
AI.result: Benchmarking grounding-capable multimodal LLMs on DAB shows that while larger models generally achieve higher answer accuracy, even the strongest models often fail to localize the supporting elements. The evaluation covers answer accuracy, attribution accuracy, and overall answer quality.
AI.conclusion: DAB provides a scalable benchmark for developing grounded, verifiable, and trustworthy Document VQA models. The MAPPET method enables automatic generation of element-level grounding annotations at scale, addressing the annotation bottleneck in document VQA research.

title: Ownership in AI-Assisted Everyday Tasks
summary: When does work done with AI still feel like ours? As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, we must examine what happens to our sense of ownership and contribution when a machine shares in producing what we make. We report an exploratory qualitative survey in which participants were asked to describe two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. We find that felt ownership depends on the process of collaboration: people disown work when they merely approve AI's suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can also extend to settings where people own the vision for a project but not the execution; respondents reported high ownership on tasks they could not have completed without AI. Loss of personal voice and a lack of comprehension of the output both erode ownership. Finally, willingness to disclose AI use is often decoupled from actual pride or ownership, and instead shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure. We propose several research directions as a result of these findings to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

AI.tldr: This paper explores when AI-assisted work still feels like "ours" by examining people's sense of ownership and contribution in human-AI collaboration. Through qualitative surveys, researchers found that felt ownership depends on the collaboration process—people retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite, but disown work when they merely approve AI suggestions. Ownership can extend to vision-driven work even without execution involvement. Key erosion factors include loss of personal voice and lack of comprehension. Willingness to disclose AI use is shaped by community norms rather than actual ownership feelings.
AI.motivation: As AI becomes integrated into everyday tasks, there is a need to understand what happens to people's sense of ownership and contribution when machines share in producing what we make. This research addresses the psychological and social implications of human-AI collaboration on authorship and personal agency.
AI.method: An exploratory qualitative survey was conducted where participants described two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. The study analyzed the differences in collaboration processes between these two scenarios.
AI.result: Felt ownership depends on the process of collaboration. People disown work when they merely approve AI's suggestions but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can extend to settings where people own the vision but not the execution. Loss of personal voice and lack of comprehension erode ownership. Willingness to disclose AI use is decoupled from actual pride/ownership and is shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure.
AI.conclusion: The research proposes several directions for future research to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives, highlighting the importance of designing AI systems that enhance human agency rather than diminish it.

title: Minimax-Optimal Online Contract Design with Unrestricted Bounded Contracts
summary: We study repeated contract design when a principal observes outcomes but not the actions that generate them. The principal may use any bounded outcome-contingent payment vector, and the agent's best response can make expected profit discontinuous in those payments. For every fixed number $m\ge2$ of outcomes, the minimax regret over $T$ rounds is of order $T^{m/(m+1)}$, up to logarithmic factors. The upper bound allows arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity, without smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions. Its key is an effective-dimension reduction that the benchmark can be normalized even when fixed tie-breaking is not shift invariant, after which revealed preference yields a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates. A learning policy built on a Lipschitz parametrization of this map attains the rate using only observed outcome categories. The lower-bound construction accounts for how incentive losses accumulate across outcome dimensions. It shows that each additional contractible outcome creates a precise and unavoidable increase in the worst-case cost of learning.

AI.tldr: This paper studies repeated contract design where a principal observes outcomes but not the underlying actions. It establishes that the minimax regret over T rounds scales as T^(m/(m+1)) for m≥2 outcomes, and proves this rate is optimal by showing each additional outcome dimension necessarily increases the worst-case learning cost.
AI.motivation: The problem arises because the principal may use any bounded outcome-contingent payment vector, but the agent's best response can make expected profit discontinuous in those payments. This creates a challenging learning problem where the principal must learn optimal contracts despite this discontinuity and without observing the agent's actions.
AI.method: The key methodological contributions include: (1) an effective-dimension reduction technique that normalizes the benchmark even without shift-invariant tie-breaking; (2) revealed preference analysis yielding a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates; (3) a learning policy built on Lipschitz parametrization of this map that achieves the T^(m/(m+1)) rate using only observed outcome categories. The lower bound accounts for incentive losses accumulating across outcome dimensions.
AI.result: The minimax regret over T rounds is Θ(T^(m/(m+1))) (up to logarithmic factors) for every fixed number m≥2 of outcomes. This rate is achieved by a learning policy that works with arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity, without requiring smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The learning complexity is fundamentally tied to the number of outcome dimensions—each additional contractible outcome creates a precise and unavoidable increase in the worst-case cost of learning. This establishes a tight bound on the learnability of repeated contract design under moral hazard.

title: RawSLAM: Online HDR Gaussian SLAM from Linear Radiance
