summary: Current dense visual SLAM systems rely almost exclusively on 8-bit tonemapped Low Dynamic Range (LDR) inputs, limiting their robustness in extreme lighting where shadows and highlights trigger tracking drift and mapping collapse. Conversely, existing raw and High Dynamic Range (HDR) reconstruction pipelines operate strictly offline. They depend on Structure-from-Motion preprocessing and are not suited for large inter-frame motion. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first online Gaussian SLAM framework that tracks and maps directly on single-exposure 16-bit linear HDR imagery. Our method rests on three core components: an architecture-agnostic HDR Gaussian Splatting module featuring an MLP-free logarithmic parameterization of Gaussian color features; a Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective; and structure-guided spatial gradient weighting. Combined, these components allow our approach to outperform a direct HDR adaptation of MonoGS in both trajectory and reconstruction accuracy, while rendering natively in linear scene radiance for post-rendering processing. The same formulation runs unchanged on standard 8-bit inputs, roughly halving the MonoGS baseline error. Furthermore, our HDR Gaussian module transfers seamlessly to SplaTAM, Gaussian SLAM, and DROID-W, eliminating all tracking failures these systems suffer on challenging illumination sequences. To enable this research, we introduce RawSLAM: a dataset of 10 real-world indoor sequences featuring 16-bit RAW imagery, aligned depth, IMU measurements, and external OptiTrack poses. Code and dataset will be made publicly available soon.

AI.tldr: First online Gaussian SLAM framework that processes single-exposure 16-bit linear HDR imagery directly, eliminating the need for offline processing. Uses three core components: MLP-free logarithmic parameterization for Gaussian color features, Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective, and structure-guided spatial gradient weighting.
AI.motivation: Current dense visual SLAM systems rely on 8-bit LDR inputs, causing tracking drift and mapping collapse in extreme lighting. Existing HDR reconstruction pipelines operate offline and require Structure-from-Motion preprocessing, making them unsuitable for large inter-frame motion.
AI.method: Three core components: (1) Architecture-agnostic HDR Gaussian Splatting module with MLP-free logarithmic parameterization of Gaussian color features; (2) Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective; (3) Structure-guided spatial gradient weighting. Works on both 16-bit HDR and standard 8-bit inputs.
AI.result: Outperforms direct HDR adaptation of MonoGS in trajectory and reconstruction accuracy. On 8-bit inputs, roughly halves MonoGS baseline error. Successfully transfers to SplaTAM, Gaussian SLAM, and DROID-W, eliminating tracking failures on challenging illumination sequences.
AI.conclusion: First online HDR Gaussian SLAM system that enables robust tracking and mapping in extreme lighting conditions. The method is architecture-agnostic and can be applied to multiple existing SLAM systems, with a new dataset (RawSLAM) provided for benchmarking.

title: Deep Noir: Autonomous Steering Discovery via Architectural Chronometry in Transformer Models
summary: Activation steering modifies LLM behavior at inference time, but identifying where and how strongly to steer remains manual. We introduce Deep Noir, a framework that uses Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously discover optimal steering parameters. Across three scales (1B x 3, 2-3B x 2, and 7-9B x 4), our engine achieves 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam at 1B (standard deviation 4.7; 39 runs), with gains increasing to 21 to 42 percentage points at 7-9B across four architectures. On SST-2 sentiment, it achieves a 13.1 percentage-point improvement with zero code changes. Mechanistic grounding enables automated discovery of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. On sentiment, RepE without head masking fails to improve over baseline, while Deep Noir improves all models (p less than 0.01). We further show that steering creates a predictable prompt-injection attack surface whose vulnerability increases monotonically with steering magnitude. This finding is relevant to agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

AI.tldr: Deep Noir is an automated framework for discovering optimal activation steering parameters in LLMs using Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution, eliminating manual tuning. It achieves 16.7-42 percentage-point improvements across multiple model scales and tasks, while also revealing a security vulnerability where steering increases susceptibility to prompt-injection attacks.
AI.motivation: Activation steering modifies LLM behavior at inference time, but identifying where (which layers/heads) and how strongly to steer remains a manual, trial-and-error process. This limits the practical deployment of steering techniques.
AI.method: The framework combines two key techniques: (1) Logit Lens convergence - to identify where model representations converge across different inputs, and (2) causal head-level attribution - to determine which attention heads are causally responsible for steering effects. This enables autonomous discovery of optimal steering parameters across model scales (1B, 2-3B, 7-9B) and four architectures.
AI.result:
- 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam detection at 1B scale (SD 4.7, 39 runs)
- 21-42 percentage-point gains at 7-9B scale across four architectures
- 13.1 percentage-point improvement on SST-2 sentiment with zero code changes
- Statistically significant improvement over baseline on all models (p < 0.01)
- Outperforms RepE (Representation Engineering) without head masking, which fails to improve over baseline
AI.conclusion: Deep Noir enables automated, mechanistic grounding of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. However, steering introduces a predictable prompt-injection attack surface that increases monotonically with steering magnitude, which is a security concern for agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

title: Learning Principal-Agent Contracts for Equitable Smallholder Carbon Farming under Moral Hazard and Adverse Selection
summary: Agricultural soils are a major untapped carbon sink. Carbon farming is emerging as a promising practice for tapping this potential. Smallholder farmers, who dominate agriculture across South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, are key to scaling climate mitigation via carbon farming. It is ironic that real-world carbon programs largely fail to reach them. We study this important gap through the lens of contract design. An aggregator offers a single pooled contract to a heterogeneous population of smallholder farmers who have private adoption costs (adverse selection) and exert unobserved effort (moral hazard), with agronomic outcomes evolving over multiple seasons. We formulate this evolving contracting problem as a POMDP and use reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic profit-maximising contract. We analyse the performance of the aggregator under various conditions. We find that a profit-maximising aggregator does not merely inherit the exclusion of smallholders, it amplifies it. On large farms the aggregator realises 87.7% of achievable adoption, against only 8.2% on smallholdings. Per-hectare Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) costs fall as farm size rises, and the aggregator's pooling contract compounds this gradient rather than offsetting it. A counterfactual that makes MRV costs purely area-proportional eliminates this disparity. Our results and simulation can guide contract and policy design that opens carbon income to smallholders while enabling agricultural soils to contribute to climate mitigation at scale.

AI.tldr: This paper examines why carbon farming programs fail to reach smallholder farmers in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, using contract design theory and reinforcement learning. The study finds that aggregators amplify rather than reduce exclusion of smallholders, with 87.7% adoption on large farms versus only 8.2% on smallholdings, primarily due to per-hectare MRV costs that disadvantage smaller farms.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the irony that while smallholder farmers are key to scaling climate mitigation through carbon farming, real-world carbon programs largely fail to reach them. The authors seek to understand this gap through the lens of contract design.
AI.method: The authors formulate the contracting problem as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and use reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic profit-maximizing contract. They analyze the aggregator's performance under various conditions, including a counterfactual with area-proportional MRV costs.
AI.result: A profit-maximizing aggregator amplifies exclusion of smallholders: 87.7% adoption on large farms vs 8.2% on smallholdings. Per-hectare MRV costs fall as farm size rises, and the pooling contract compounds this gradient. A counterfactual with purely area-proportional MRV costs eliminates this disparity.
AI.conclusion: Results suggest that contract and policy design can open carbon income to smallholders while enabling agricultural soils to contribute to climate mitigation at scale. Making MRV costs area-proportional could eliminate the disparity in adoption rates.

title: PhGS: Post-Hoc Pruning and Refinement of Single-View Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Reconstructions
summary: Recent single-view feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) generation predicts a fixed number of Gaussians per camera ray, introducing severe spatial redundancy. Most existing compaction strategies target multi-view setups to exploit cross-view consistency and are incompatible with single-image models. Instead of retraining the base feed-forward network to directly output compact representations, our insight is to keep the base models frozen and apply post-hoc pruning and recurrent refinement to the generated Gaussians. Consequently, we propose a backbone-agnostic compaction pipeline for single-view feed-forward 3DGS that couples an importance-score-based pruning mechanism with a trainable, lightweight recurrent refinement module, which iteratively updates the surviving primitives to restore image quality. Our results demonstrate seamless integration with existing baselines while preserving novel-view rendering fidelity and achieving high memory reduction. Furthermore, our method supports flexible inference-time keep ratios for application needs.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses spatial redundancy in single-view feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting by proposing a backbone-agnostic compaction pipeline that combines importance-score-based pruning with a trainable recurrent refinement module, achieving memory reduction while preserving rendering quality.
AI.motivation: Single-view feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models predict a fixed number of Gaussians per camera ray, which introduces severe spatial redundancy. Existing compaction strategies are designed for multi-view setups and exploit cross-view consistency, making them incompatible with single-image models. The authors seek a solution that doesn't require retraining the base feed-forward network.
AI.method: The proposed method is a post-hoc compaction pipeline consisting of two components: (1) an importance-score-based pruning mechanism that identifies and removes redundant Gaussians, and (2) a lightweight trainable recurrent refinement module that iteratively updates the surviving primitives to restore image quality. The base models remain frozen during this process, and the approach is designed to be backbone-agnostic.
AI.result: The method demonstrates seamless integration with existing baselines while preserving novel-view rendering fidelity and achieving high memory reduction. It also supports flexible inference-time keep ratios to accommodate different application needs.
AI.conclusion: This work provides an effective, generalizable solution for compacting single-view 3DGS representations without retraining base models. The combination of pruning and recurrent refinement successfully balances memory efficiency with rendering quality, offering flexibility through adjustable keep ratios.

title: The Bias of Nonlinear Two-Time-scale Stochastic Approximation under Constant Step-Sizes
summary: Two-timescale stochastic approximation (TTSA) is a fundamental tool for analyzing coupled iterative algorithms in reinforcement learning, optimization, and stochastic control. However, finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale schemes remain difficult to obtain, especially under constant step-sizes. In this paper, we study nonlinear TTSA with step-sizes $α\ggβ$. Under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions, we upper bound the mean-squared error and the bias of both iterates around their limiting equilibria. Our bounds scale as $O(α+β^2/α^2)$, which we prove to be tight when $β\leα^{3/2}$. The analysis separates the contributions of initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking error, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling, thereby clarifying the origin of the $β^2/α^2$ term. Our results reveal qualitative differences from the linear TTSA setting previously studied, showing that nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects that are absent in the linear case.

AI.tldr: This paper provides finite-time error bounds for nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation (TTSA) under constant step-sizes, with the fast timescale step-size α much larger than the slow timescale step-size β. The bounds are O(α + β²/α²) and are tight when β ≤ α^(3/2).
AI.motivation: Finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale schemes remain difficult to obtain, especially under constant step-sizes. This is important because TTSA is a fundamental tool for analyzing coupled iterative algorithms in reinforcement learning, optimization, and stochastic control.
AI.method: The analysis uses standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions. It separates the contributions of four factors: initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking error, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling.
AI.result: The mean-squared error and bias of both iterates around their limiting equilibria are bounded. The bounds scale as O(α + β²/α²), which is proved tight when β ≤ α^(3/2). The analysis reveals qualitative differences from linear TTSA, showing nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects absent in the linear case.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear dynamics in TTSA introduce additional finite-time effects that are not present in linear settings. The β²/α² term arises from timescale coupling, and the results clarify the origin of this term through the separated analysis of contributing factors.

title: Refinement Is Inherently Editable: Training-Free Prompt-to-Prompt Image Editing with Generative Refinement Network
summary: Text-guided image editing must introduce the requested changes while preserving unrelated source content. Diffusion-based editors rely on spatial controls whose inaccuracies can leave edits incomplete or alter unrelated regions. Causal autoregressive editors face a further constraint: their fixed decoding order limits revision of earlier decisions. We introduce RefineEdit, a training-free prompt-to-prompt image editing framework built on a Generative Refinement Network. Our key idea is to couple edit localization with content generation through the global refinement of binary image codes, allowing editing evidence to be reassessed as the image evolves. RefineEdit initializes an editing branch from an intermediate source state, reusing the emerging layout. We compare the probabilities assigned by the two branches to the same source-sampled bits, using their signed differences to select editable positions and bits. Selected bits follow editing refinement, while the remaining bits copy the evolving source state. To stabilize editing across refinement steps, adaptive spatial freezing limits unnecessary mask expansion, while finite bit locking keeps recently selected bits editable. The framework requires no additional training, external masks, or attention control. Across nine editing categories of PIE-Bench, RefineEdit achieves the best background-preservation scores in PSNR, LPIPS, MSE and SSIM, together with the highest whole-image and edited-region CLIP scores among the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: RefineEdit is a training-free text-guided image editing framework that couples edit localization with content generation through global refinement of binary image codes. It uses two branches (source and editing) to compare probabilities for editable bits, with adaptive spatial freezing and finite bit locking to stabilize editing across steps.
AI.motivation: Text-guided image editing faces challenges: diffusion-based editors with spatial controls can leave edits incomplete or alter unrelated regions, while causal autoregressive editors have fixed decoding order that limits revision of earlier decisions. The goal is to preserve unrelated source content while introducing requested changes accurately.
AI.method: RefineEdit uses a Generative Refinement Network that: (1) initializes an editing branch from an intermediate source state, reusing the emerging layout; (2) compares probabilities from two branches to same source-sampled bits, using signed differences to select editable positions and bits; (3) selected bits follow editing refinement while remaining bits copy evolving source state; (4) adaptive spatial freezing limits mask expansion; (5) finite bit locking keeps recently selected bits editable. Requires no additional training, external masks, or attention control.
AI.result: On PIE-Bench across nine editing categories, RefineEdit achieves: best background-preservation scores in PSNR, LPIPS, MSE, and SSIM; highest whole-image and edited-region CLIP scores among evaluated methods.
AI.conclusion: RefineEdit provides an effective training-free solution for text-guided image editing that better preserves background content while accurately applying edits, outperforming existing methods on multiple metrics.

title: RAFT: A Stateful Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track
summary: Effective troubleshooting agents in enterprise customer support depend on retrieving actionable guidance from similar historical cases, yet existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat support cases as static documents and overlook their multi-stage, stateful nature. We introduce RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents), a stateful RAG framework that abstracts each closed historical case into a directed chain of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level, surfacing cases whose intermediate states match the active case and returning the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state; an optional case-level graph links cases through a configurable similarity representation. We evaluate this retrieval layer directly, which, unlike evaluating a full agent system, requires no production deployment. Because public multi-stage troubleshooting data is extremely rare, we pair a synthetic benchmark built from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation with real Apache Jira issues carrying human-created duplicate labels. RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline; the Jira results provide directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories. We release our benchmark, implementation, and the Apache Jira evaluation set.

AI.tldr: RAFT is a stateful RAG framework for troubleshooting agents that retrieves at the entry level from case timelines rather than treating cases as static documents, improving case retrieval accuracy across all stages of case progress compared to vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems treat support cases as static documents, missing their multi-stage, stateful nature. This limits the ability to retrieve actionable guidance from similar historical cases at different stages of troubleshooting.
AI.method: RAFT abstracts closed historical cases into directed chains of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level. It surfaces cases whose intermediate states match the active case and returns the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state. An optional case-level graph links cases through configurable similarity representation. Evaluation uses a synthetic benchmark from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation paired with real Apache Jira issues with human-created duplicate labels.
AI.result: RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline. Jira results provide directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories.
AI.conclusion: RAFT represents a novel approach to stateful RAG for troubleshooting that captures the temporal dynamics of support cases. The framework releases its benchmark, implementation, and Apache Jira evaluation set for further research.

title: SCGFM-ART: Amortized Relational Transport for Structure-Centric Graph Foundation Models
summary: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable representations across severely heterogeneous graph domains. However, severe domain shifts in topology, graph scale, and feature semantics impede the construction of a unified, domain-agnostic representation space. To address this, we propose SCGFM-ART, a structure-centric GFM framework that aligns arbitrary graphs onto a shared relational atlas via Amortized Relational Transport (ART). The relational atlas serves as a universal coordinate system defined by a finite set of relational landmarks (bases), while ART directly predicts reusable, end-to-end graph-to-base transport plans, bypassing costly runtime Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations. Under this formulation, SCGFM-ART decomposes a graph into a unified representation: globally via its relational response coordinates relative to the atlas, and locally via its node-to-role structural correspondences. These correspondences project disparate node attributes into a canonical role space, resolving structural and semantic heterogeneity within a singular alignment interface. Rigorously modeling graphs and atlas bases as finite measured relational spaces, we establish coordinate fidelity bounds, prove stability under predicted transport plans, and derive an amortized coverage bound that guarantees our learning objective tightly surrogates ideal relational coverage. Benchmarked across 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks, SCGFM-ART achieves state-of-the-art transferability, securing superior average ranks of 2.29 and 1.14, respectively. Topological perturbation analyses demonstrate that node-role transport retains fine-grained structural nuances beyond global coordinates. On real-world benchmarks, the amortized formulation yields 44.2 to 85.1 times faster frozen target-domain inference by avoiding iterative alignment at test time.

AI.tldr: SCGFM-ART is a structure-centric graph foundation model that aligns arbitrary graphs onto a shared relational atlas using Amortized Relational Transport (ART). It decomposes graphs into global relational response coordinates and local node-to-role structural correspondences, enabling transfer learning across heterogeneous graph domains without costly runtime optimization.
AI.motivation: Graph foundation models face severe challenges when learning transferable representations across heterogeneous domains due to domain shifts in topology, graph scale, and feature semantics. Existing methods rely on costly runtime Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations for graph alignment.
AI.method: The proposed SCGFM-ART framework uses Amortized Relational Transport (ART) to directly predict reusable, end-to-end graph-to-base transport plans. It constructs a universal coordinate system (relational atlas) defined by finite relational landmarks (bases), and decomposes graphs into: (1) global relational response coordinates relative to the atlas, and (2) local node-to-role structural correspondences that project node attributes into a canonical role space. The method models graphs and atlas bases as finite measured relational spaces.
AI.result: Evaluated on 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks, SCGFM-ART achieves state-of-the-art transferability with superior average ranks of 2.29 and 1.14 respectively. Topological perturbation analyses show node-role transport retains fine-grained structural nuances. The amortized formulation yields 44.2 to 85.1 times faster frozen target-domain inference by avoiding iterative alignment at test time.
AI.conclusion: SCGFM-ART successfully addresses cross-domain graph representation learning by providing a unified alignment interface that resolves structural and semantic heterogeneity. The theoretical guarantees (coordinate fidelity bounds, stability, amortized coverage bound) ensure learning objectives tightly surrogate ideal relational coverage, while the amortized approach enables efficient inference.

title: PROVIA: Procedure State Tracking for Online Mistake Detection in Egocentric Videos
summary: An assistant watching egocentric video should notice a mistake from past frames alone, before the next step begins, and keep working once the person recovers. A mistake changes the state of the work, so every later step has to be read against what was done rather than against the plan. The first-mistake protocol that current online methods report on cuts each recording at its first mistake, so a fixed-time rule that never looks at the video is right on every case. We evaluate on complete trials, where mistakes and recoveries arise naturally, under a validation false-alarm budget and against controls that use timing alone. PROVIA keeps two records apart: a factual state, a learned summary of the steps each actor performed, mistakes included, and the accepted progress, an exact posterior over the state of an automaton induced from correct demonstrations by Bayesian state merging and over the execution status of each actor. Procedure-state transitions occur only in the correct-status branch; the mistake and correction branches retain the source state. A sequential test turns the per-frame mistake probability into alarms. With one filter and one optimization rule, PROVIA ranks mistakes best among the evaluated controlled baselines on CaptainCook4D, IndustReal, HoloAssist and IMPACT-ego. At a validation budget of 0.1 false alarms per minute it recalls .154 against .128 on CaptainCook4D and .034 against .015 on HoloAssist, where it leads at every budget. The pipeline runs at 58-70 frames per second. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/PROVIA.

AI.tldr: PROVIA is a computer vision system for egocentric video that detects mistakes from past frames before the next step begins, using Bayesian state merging and a sequential test to convert per-frame mistake probabilities into alarms. It outperforms baselines on four datasets at 58-70 fps.
AI.motivation: Current methods use a "first-mistake protocol" that cuts recordings at the first mistake, making a fixed-time rule always correct. However, in real scenarios with complete trials containing natural mistakes and recoveries, a more sophisticated approach is needed to detect mistakes while respecting a false-alarm budget.
AI.method: PROVIA maintains two separate records: (1) a factual state - a learned summary of steps each actor performed including mistakes, and (2) accepted progress - an exact posterior over automaton state induced from correct demonstrations via Bayesian state merging. Procedure-state transitions occur only in the correct-status branch, while mistake and correction branches retain the source state. A sequential test converts per-frame mistake probability into alarms.
AI.result: PROVIA ranks best among controlled baselines on CaptainCook4D, IndustReal, HoloAssist, and IMPACT-ego. At a validation budget of 0.1 false alarms per minute, it achieves recall of .154 vs .128 on CaptainCook4D and .034 vs .015 on HoloAssist, leading at every budget. The pipeline runs at 58-70 frames per second.
AI.conclusion: PROVIA successfully detects mistakes in egocentric video by maintaining separate factual and progress states, enabling continued monitoring after mistakes and recoveries. It outperforms timing-only controls and other baselines while maintaining real-time performance.

title: Seismic Site Response Prediction from Sparse Observations Using Finite-Element-Pretrained Latent Dynamics
summary: Numerical site-response predictions often deviate from observations, yet correcting these discrepancies is difficult because records are limited in both sensor coverage and number of events. This study proposes the Transfer-Enabled Forced Latent Autoencoder for Response Equations (FLARE-T) to improve these predictions by learning and calibrating low-dimensional latent dynamics that connect the base acceleration input to acceleration outputs at multiple depths. FLARE-T learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations. It then trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into the learned coordinates and uses limited records to calibrate the dynamics within them. A short response window initializes each prediction, while the complete base motion drives the response. The framework was evaluated using a layered-soil centrifuge test and the Lotung field vertical array. Test-set results show that FLARE-T improved multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration response spectra relative to the original finite-element models, reducing errors at every evaluated sensor for motions of different intensities and, at Lotung, for both horizontal components. Two Lotung source models with different constitutive parameters achieved comparable test-set accuracy, indicating reduced dependence on precise prior calibration. FLARE-T therefore provides a data-efficient means of combining dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve future site-response predictions.

AI.tldr: FLARE-T is a deep learning framework that improves numerical site-response predictions by learning low-dimensional latent dynamics from dense finite-element simulations and calibrating them with limited field records. It was validated on a centrifuge test and Lotung vertical array, showing improved acceleration histories and response spectra across multiple sensors and motion intensities.
AI.motivation: Numerical site-response predictions often deviate from observations, but correcting these discrepancies is challenging due to limited records in both sensor coverage and number of events. There is a need to combine dense numerical simulations with limited field observations to improve prediction accuracy.
AI.method: FLARE-T learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations. It trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into learned coordinates and uses limited records to calibrate the dynamics. Each prediction is initialized with a short response window, while the complete base motion drives the response.
AI.result: FLARE-T improved multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration response spectra relative to original finite-element models. It reduced errors at every evaluated sensor for motions of different intensities and both horizontal components at Lotung. Two different constitutive parameter models achieved comparable accuracy, indicating reduced dependence on precise prior calibration.
AI.conclusion: FLARE-T provides a data-efficient method for combining dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve site-response predictions. It successfully reduces prediction errors and shows reduced sensitivity to constitutive model parameters.

title: Earth Surface Immune System for Rapid Monitoring of Unknown Anomalies
summary: Earth surface anomalies, driven by escalating climate change, and expanding human activities, are increasing in both frequency and diversity, yet their limited historical data and unpredictability make them fundamentally different from conventional remote sensing targets. Existing methods address specific anomaly categories or stop at localization, leaving a gap between detection and actionable information. Here we present ESIA, an Earth Surface Immune System whose architecture is constrained by three principles from the biological immune system, refined over millions of years against equally diverse and uncertain threats. A non-specific innate immune stage treats anomalies as unobserved changes in time-series satellite imagery, generating binary localization maps at 14.51 km2/s without assuming any anomaly category, surpassing the strongest general baseline by 37% in F1. A specific adaptive immune stage applies negative selection to filter text prompts and matches surviving prompts with localized image patches through a multi-modal foundation model, enabling open-vocabulary recognition of unknown anomaly attributes including category, affected area, and damage severity, with recognition F1 exceeding 80%. A mutation mechanism tunes minimal embeddings at test time, adapting to each scene in 3.26s using a single reference image pair. We validate ESIA on a global-scale dataset covering 19,801.60 km2 across six anomaly categories, comparing against 22 models, and further apply it to quantify degraded farmland in the Dnipro Delta following the Kakhovka Dam collapse and assess burn severity from 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles. This unprecedented flexibility in handling unknown anomalies opens new avenues for real-time disaster response and environmental surveillance.

AI.tldr: ESIA (Earth Surface Immune System) is a novel framework for detecting and recognizing earth surface anomalies using principles inspired by the biological immune system. It combines a non-specific innate immune stage for localization with a specific adaptive immune stage for open-vocabulary recognition of unknown anomaly attributes.
AI.motivation: Earth surface anomalies driven by climate change and human activities are increasing in frequency and diversity, but existing methods have limited scope—they either address specific anomaly categories or only perform localization without providing actionable information. There is a gap between detection and comprehensive anomaly understanding.
AI.method: The architecture is constrained by three principles from the biological immune system: (1) Non-specific innate immune stage treats anomalies as unobserved changes in time-series satellite imagery, generating binary localization maps at 14.51 km²/s without assuming any anomaly category; (2) Specific adaptive immune stage applies negative selection to filter text prompts and matches surviving prompts with localized image patches through a multi-modal foundation model for open-vocabulary recognition; (3) Mutation mechanism tunes minimal embeddings at test time, adapting to each scene in 3.26s using a single reference image pair.
AI.result: The non-specific innate stage surpasses the strongest general baseline by 37% in F1. The specific adaptive stage achieves recognition F1 exceeding 80% for unknown anomaly attributes including category, affected area, and damage severity. Validated on a global-scale dataset covering 19,801.60 km² across six anomaly categories against 22 models. Successfully applied to quantify degraded farmland in the Dnipro Delta following the Kakhovka Dam collapse and assess burn severity from the 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles.
AI.conclusion: ESIA demonstrates unprecedented flexibility in handling unknown anomalies by combining biological immune system principles with multi-modal foundation models. This opens new avenues for real-time disaster response and environmental surveillance, enabling rapid detection and comprehensive analysis of diverse earth surface anomalies without prior category specification.

title: Training Neural Networks to Approach the Optimum Bayes Estimator in Dense Multi-Emitter Localization
summary: We train neural networks on synthesized frames to approach the optimum Bayes estimator for dense emitter localization. The result justifies the future work on training neural networks to achieve high-throughput large-FOV super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM.

AI.tldr: The paper trains neural networks on synthesized frames to approximate the Bayes optimal estimator for dense emitter localization in single molecule localization microscopy (SMLM), with applications toward high-throughput large-FOV super-resolution imaging.
AI.motivation: Dense emitter localization in SMLM is challenging because traditional methods struggle with high emitter densities while maintaining high spatial and temporal resolution. The goal is to achieve large-field-of-view (FOV) super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM.
AI.method: Neural networks are trained on synthesized frames to approach the optimum Bayes estimator for dense emitter localization.
AI.result: The neural network approach successfully approximates the Bayes optimal estimator for dense emitter localization.
AI.conclusion: The results justify future work on training neural networks to achieve high-throughput large-FOV super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM, paving the way for advanced super-resolution microscopy applications.

title: FunArt: Decoding Functional Structure and Articulation from Generative 3D Latents
summary: To operate effectively in human environments, robots must identify articulated objects, segment their movable and interactive parts, and estimate their kinematic models. Existing articulated scene representations typically recover kinematics from observed interactions, while methods operating on static scans often decouple articulation from functional interactive elements. We present FunArt, a framework that constructs articulation-aware functional 3D scene graphs from posed RGB-D observations captured in a single static configuration. FunArt reconstructs object instances, converts their fused geometry directly into the O-Voxel representation of TRELLIS.2, and exploits its frozen, sparse-compression VAE as a structural prior. A lightweight query-based decoder combines compact object-level latents with dense, surface-aligned features to jointly segment movable parts and functional interactive elements while estimating motion type, axis, origin, and range. On the Articulate3D dataset, FunArt achieves state-of-the-art performance across movable-part segmentation, articulation estimation, and functional-element segmentation, both with and without ground-truth object input. In the end-to-end setting, it outperforms the strongest baselines by 1.5 AP_{50} points for movable parts, 2.8 AP_{50} points under joint origin-and-axis constraints, and 6.7 AP_{50} points for functional elements. These results demonstrate that generative 3D latents encode actionable structural cues that can initialize robotic perception and planning before physical interaction.

AI.tldr: FunArt is a framework that constructs articulation-aware functional 3D scene graphs from single static RGB-D observations, using generative 3D latents (O-Voxel from TRELLIS.2) to jointly segment movable parts and functional interactive elements while estimating motion parameters (type, axis, origin, range).
AI.motivation: Existing methods either recover kinematics from observed interactions or decouple articulation from functional elements in static scans. Robots need to perceive articulated objects before physical interaction in human environments.
AI.method: FunArt reconstructs object instances, converts fused geometry into O-Voxel representation, exploits frozen sparse-compression VAE as structural prior, and uses a lightweight query-based decoder combining object-level latents with surface-aligned features for joint segmentation and estimation.
AI.result: On Articulate3D, FunArt achieves state-of-the-art. End-to-end: +1.5 AP50 (movable parts), +2.8 AP50 (origin-and-axis constraints), +6.7 AP50 (functional elements). Works with and without ground-truth object input.
AI.conclusion: Generative 3D latents encode actionable structural cues that can initialize robotic perception and planning before physical interaction.

title: Deep Learning-Based Classification of Cognitive and Resting States Using Electroencephalography Signals
summary: The categorization of cognitive and resting states derived from electroencephalography (EEG) signals is crucial for comprehending fluctuations in brain activity linked to various mental states. EEG provides a non-intrusive approach for documenting brain function in both resting and task-oriented cognitive conditions, whilst deep learning techniques enable the automatic extraction of significant patterns from intricate EEG data. This study presents a deep learning framework to distinguish between resting and cognitive states through EEG records. The proposed framework integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) stacked with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for the extraction of features from EEG signals. Time-frequency analysis is conducted to explore the salient aspects of signals, and the derived features are then assessed utilizing conventional deep learning and machine learning classifiers, including the suggested 2D-Net architecture. The proposed approach and feature extraction strategy outperform the evaluated comparative methods, achieving accuracies of 83.177% for resting-versus-mathematical task classification, 76.107% for resting-versus-memory task classification, and 83.432% for resting-versus-music task classification. The findings illustrate the efficacy of integrating signal processing with deep learning methodologies to discriminate resting from cognitive states utilizing EEG signals.

AI.tldr: This study proposes a deep learning framework combining CNN and GRU to classify resting vs cognitive states (mathematical, memory, and music tasks) from EEG signals, achieving accuracies of 83.177%, 76.107%, and 83.432% respectively.
AI.motivation: The categorization of cognitive and resting states from EEG signals is crucial for understanding brain activity fluctuations linked to various mental states, as EEG provides a non-intrusive method for documenting brain function in both resting and task-oriented cognitive conditions.
AI.method: The proposed framework integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) stacked with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for feature extraction from EEG signals. Time-frequency analysis is conducted to explore salient aspects of signals, and derived features are evaluated using conventional deep learning and machine learning classifiers, including the suggested 2D-Net architecture.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieved accuracies of 83.177% for resting-versus-mathematical task classification, 76.107% for resting-versus-memory task classification, and 83.432% for resting-versus-music task classification, outperforming comparative methods.
AI.conclusion: The findings illustrate the efficacy of integrating signal processing with deep learning methodologies to discriminate resting from cognitive states using EEG signals.

title: Should This Case Be Adapted? Prediction Fragmentation Controls Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Episodic test-time adaptation resets a frozen segmenter to source weights $M_0$ on each case and adapts for a fixed step count. A fixed horizon conflates a cohort-level question, how far to adapt, with an irreducibly per-case one, whether this case should be adapted at all. Cohort means hide that decision: on cross-vendor cardiac MRI the mean $Δ$Dice from adaptation is statistically indistinguishable from zero while 58.7% of cases are individually made worse. We quantify this harm as harmful accepted area (HA), the harmful fraction of the edited area a controller deploys. Held-out tuning gives a stronger baseline than a fixed horizon, but the budget it selects transfers on neither of the two main medical benchmarks, and no global budget can condition on the case. We show that prediction fragmentation---the disagreement geometry between $M_0$ and the adapted mask $M_k$---predicts HA with no labels or extra backward passes at decision time, comparably on three benchmarks (Spearman $ρ$ 0.50--0.60), at a quarter of gradient-norm's latency. A case-level router built on it cuts HA from 0.228 to 0.139 on a benchmark that took no part in its design, with the design frozen and only cut-points recalibrated there. On the cardiac benchmark the design was selected on, the router cuts HA from 0.129 to 0.013 at matched Dice and 1.10 deployed updates, against the retrospective-best budget found post hoc on evaluation labels, and reduces that 58.7% to 20.0%, an upper bound we quantify. Where the retained cases are not net-helped (as on prostate), the router still cuts HA but concedes accuracy, a boundary we report. Thresholds are fit once on a labeled split disjoint from evaluation; decisions use no labels or gradients. The template ports across architecture and domain (nnU-Net$\to$SegFormer, Cityscapes$\to$ACDC) with coordinate, thresholds and per-bucket actions instantiated per domain.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that episodic test-time adaptation harms a majority of individual cases (58.7% on cross-vendor cardiac MRI) despite appearing neutral at the cohort level, and proposes using prediction fragmentation as a label-free, per-case router to selectively apply adaptation, significantly reducing harmful accepted area across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a critical issue in episodic test-time adaptation: fixed adaptation horizons cannot condition on individual cases, leading to adaptation harming 58.7% of cases on cross-vendor cardiac MRI while mean ΔDice appears near zero. Current solutions like held-out tuning budgets fail to transfer across domains, necessitating a per-case decision mechanism.
AI.method: The authors propose using prediction fragmentation (disagreement geometry between source weights M₀ and adapted mask M_k) as a routing signal to decide per-case whether to accept adaptation, without requiring labels or gradients at decision time. They also compare against fixed horizon and held-out tuning baselines, and evaluate on three benchmarks: cross-vendor cardiac MRI, prostate, and Cityscapes→ACDC domain shift.
AI.result: Prediction fragmentation predicts HA with Spearman ρ 0.50-0.60 across three benchmarks, at 1/4 the latency of gradient-norm. The router reduces HA from 0.228 to 0.139 on an independent benchmark, and from 0.129 to 0.013 on the design benchmark (cardiac), while reducing cases worsened from 58.7% to 20.0%. The method transfers across architectures (nnU-Net→SegFormer) and domains (Cityscapes→ACDC), though it trades accuracy for reduced harm on prostate data.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces prediction fragmentation as a case-level router to decide whether to apply test-time adaptation, achieving significant HA reduction (0.129→0.013 on cardiac, 58.7%→20.0% cases worsened) without labels or gradients at decision time. The method transfers across architectures (nnU-Net→SegFormer) and domains (Cityscapes→ACDC), though it trades accuracy for safety on prostate data.

title: Distributionally Robust Federated Learning with Multi-Source Data
summary: Federated learning trains a shared model from private client data. In practice, data-generating distributions may differ, and the true mixture across clients is often unknown, making the underlying group distribution difficult to specify. Existing approaches address cross-client mixture uncertainty by optimizing against the worst-case mixture, yet assume accurate client-wise distribution estimates. However, these estimates can be unreliable when based on finite samples. To handle both cross-client mixture uncertainty and within-client distributional ambiguity, we construct a global ambiguity set as the union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets. The construction allows client-specific ambiguity radii and admits a client-wise separable reformulation. Leveraging this structure, we establish a high-probability out-of-sample performance guarantee. We further develop a federated algorithm for a penalty-based reformulation and prove its convergence under milder regularity conditions. Simulations validate the algorithm's effectiveness.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses distributionally robust federated learning by constructing a global ambiguity set as the union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets, enabling client-specific ambiguity handling and achieving high-probability out-of-sample performance guarantees with a convergent federated algorithm.
AI.motivation: In federated learning, data-generating distributions differ across clients and the true mixture is often unknown. Existing approaches handle cross-client mixture uncertainty by optimizing against worst-case mixtures but assume accurate client-wise distribution estimates, which can be unreliable with finite samples.
AI.method: The paper constructs a global ambiguity set as the union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets, allowing client-specific ambiguity radii. This formulation admits a client-wise separable reformulation, enabling development of a penalty-based federated algorithm with convergence guarantees under milder regularity conditions.
AI.result: The proposed approach establishes a high-probability out-of-sample performance guarantee and proves convergence of the federated algorithm under milder regularity conditions. Simulations validate the algorithm's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The method successfully handles both cross-client mixture uncertainty and within-client distributional ambiguity in federated learning, providing robust performance guarantees with theoretical convergence properties.

title: FlowSGS: Improving Flow Matching Priors for Inverse Imaging with Stochastic Interpolants
summary: Flow matching has emerged as the state-of-the-art generative model and has been used for plug-and-play (PnP) priors to solve inverse problems in computational imaging. However, existing flow-based inverse solvers assume linear forward models and/or make simplifying approximations in posterior sampling. To circumvent these problems, we introduce FlowSGS, a flow-based posterior sampling method using Split Gibbs Sampling (SGS) to decompose the posterior into a likelihood step and a prior step. Specifically, we sample from the likelihood step using Langevin dynamics and leverage the Stochastic Interpolants (SI) framework to integrate a pretrained flow model into the prior step. We provide a form for the prior step that uses SI's reverse-time SDE, and show connections to previous PnP methods. Moreover, with the aid of the flow prior's straight probability paths and a novel timestep correction technique for the reverse-time SDE, FlowSGS requires fewer network evaluations in its prior step than plug-and-play diffusion samplers. Our experiments show state-of-the-art performance on a range of inverse problems. For the first time, we provide an experiment on a nonlinear inverse problem (Fourier phase retrieval) for flow-based inverse solvers.

AI.tldr: FlowSGS introduces a flow-based posterior sampling method using Split Gibbs Sampling to handle inverse problems in computational imaging, outperforming existing flow-based solvers and achieving state-of-the-art results, including the first flow-based approach on nonlinear inverse problems.
AI.motivation: Existing flow-based inverse solvers assume linear forward models and/or make simplifying approximations in posterior sampling, limiting their applicability to real-world computational imaging problems.
AI.method: FlowSGS uses Split Gibbs Sampling (SGS) to decompose the posterior into likelihood and prior steps. The likelihood step employs Langevin dynamics, while the prior step integrates a pretrained flow model via the Stochastic Interpolants framework using a reverse-time SDE with a novel timestep correction technique.
AI.result: FlowSGS achieves state-of-the-art performance on a range of inverse problems and requires fewer network evaluations than plug-and-play diffusion samplers. It is the first flow-based inverse solver to handle nonlinear inverse problems (Fourier phase retrieval).
AI.conclusion: FlowSGS successfully extends flow-based inverse solvers to handle nonlinear forward models through a principled Bayesian decomposition, demonstrating superior performance and efficiency compared to existing methods.

title: Radio Frequency Detection and Classification of Microplastics in Water
summary: Micro- and nano-plastic particles (MPs/NPs) are ubiquitous environmental contaminants whose increasing abundance and potential health impacts have created an urgent need for rapid, label-free detection methods. As particle size decreases to the low-micrometer range, conventional optical and spectroscopic techniques become increasingly challenging because of limited throughput and/or complex sample preparation. In this work, we present a machine learning (ML)-assisted radio-frequency (RF) dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) platform for the label-free detection and classification of MPs. Eight types of $ 10 $ μm nominal-diameter MP particles suspended in deionized (DI) water were characterized at four frequencies spanning $ 0.2\text{-}9\text{ GHz} $. The measured alterations in RF scattering parameters (S-parameters), referenced to the carrier medium, were used to train supervised ML models for material classification, including the identification of MPs in mixed samples and saline-water environments. For eight MP classes suspended in DI water, the proposed method achieved macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall values exceeding $ 0.71 $. Furthermore, PET classification performance was largely maintained in saline carrier media containing $3.3\% $ and $ 6.6\% $ sea salt. These results demonstrate the feasibility of ML-assisted RF DiSC for rapid, single-particle MP classification in aqueous environments. Future work will focus on improving classification performance through enhanced RF calibration, increased spectral coverage, larger training datasets, and validation using environmentally aged and biologically contaminated microplastics.

AI.tldr: A machine learning-assisted radio-frequency (RF) dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) platform is developed for label-free detection and classification of 8 types of 10 μm microplastic particles. Using RF scattering parameters (S-parameters) measured across 0.2-9 GHz, the system achieves macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall exceeding 0.71 in deionized water, with maintained performance in saline environments containing up to 6.6% sea salt.
AI.motivation: The increasing abundance of micro- and nano-plastic particles (MPs/NPs) as environmental contaminants creates an urgent need for rapid, label-free detection methods. Conventional optical and spectroscopic techniques become challenging as particle size decreases to the low-micrometer range due to limited throughput and complex sample preparation requirements.
AI.method: RF dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) platform combined with supervised machine learning models. Eight types of 10 μm nominal-diameter MP particles suspended in deionized water were characterized at four frequencies spanning 0.2-9 GHz. The measured alterations in RF scattering parameters (S-parameters), referenced to the carrier medium, were used to train ML models for material classification, including identification of MPs in mixed samples and saline-water environments.
AI.result: For eight MP classes suspended in DI water, the proposed method achieved macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall values exceeding 0.71. PET classification performance was largely maintained in saline carrier media containing 3.3% and 6.6% sea salt.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates the feasibility of ML-assisted RF DiSC for rapid, single-particle MP classification in aqueous environments. Future work will focus on improving classification performance through enhanced RF calibration, increased spectral coverage, larger training datasets, and validation using environmentally aged and biologically contaminated microplastics.

title: ERCPMP-Gx: Endoscopic Image and Video Dataset for Morphological, Histopathological, and Genomic Characterization of Colorectal Polyposis
summary: Hereditary polyposis syndromes can be precursor lesions to colorectal cancer and are associated with a broad spectrum of extracolonic tumors. Early identification and accurate classification of these syndromes are essential for timely diagnosis, individualized patient management, and targeted surveillance strategies for affected families. However, public endoscopic datasets are largely organized around the individual sporadic polyp, and none links the polyposis phenotype to histopathology and germline findings at the patient level. Here, we present ERCPMP-Gx, an endoscopic, histopathological, and genomic dataset developed to support the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the recognition, characterization, and classification of colorectal polyposis. Most procedures were performed using the Olympus EVIS X1 system with white-light endoscopy (WLE), narrow-band imaging (NBI), magnifying NBI (M-NBI), and NBI with near focus modes, yielding 160 images and accompanying video clips. Approximately eighty percent of cases represent clinically and/or genetically confirmed hereditary polyposis syndromes (PG), including familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS), and ganglioneuroma syndrome (GNS), while the remaining twenty percent comprise non-hereditary polyps and polyp-mimicking lesions with overlapping morphological features (Non-PG), included to support differential classification. Each released record is linked, where available, to standardized endoscopic annotations, representative histopathology, and clinically reported germline findings, forming an AI-ready, patient-level annotation framework. The dataset is publicly accessible at Mendeley (https://doi.org/10.17632/nzyfc544bx.2). For the latest updates and further information, readers are referred to the DataBioX website: https://databiox.com.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ERCPMP-Gx, a novel multimodal dataset combining endoscopic images, histopathology, and germline genomic data for AI-based detection and classification of hereditary colorectal polyposis syndromes. The dataset contains 160 images/video clips from procedures using the Olympus EVIS X1 system with multiple imaging modes (WLE, NBI, M-NBI, near focus). Approximately 80% represent confirmed hereditary polyposis syndromes (FAP, PJS, JPS, GNS), while 20% are non-hereditary mimics. Each record is linked to endoscopic annotations, histopathology, and germline findings, forming a patient-level AI-ready framework.
AI.motivation: Hereditary polyposis syndromes are precancerous lesions associated with colorectal and extracolonic tumors. Early identification and accurate classification are critical for patient management and family surveillance. However, existing public endoscopic datasets focus on individual sporadic polyps rather than the polyposis phenotype linked to histopathology and germline findings at the patient level. This gap阻碍s AI development for recognizing and classifying these hereditary syndromes.
AI.method: The dataset was constructed using the Olympus EVIS X1 endoscopy system with multiple imaging modalities: white-light endoscopy (WLE), narrow-band imaging (NBI), magnifying NBI (M-NBI), and NBI with near focus. The dataset comprises 160 images and accompanying video clips. Approximately 80% represent clinically and/or genetically confirmed hereditary polyposis syndromes (familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis syndrome, and ganglioneuroma syndrome), while 20% include non-hereditary polyps and polyp-mimicking lesions for differential classification. Each record is linked to standardized endoscopic annotations, representative histopathology, and clinically reported germline findings.
AI.result: ERCPMP-Gx is established as a publicly accessible, AI-ready dataset at Mendeley (DOI: 10.17632/nzyfc544bx.2), featuring patient-level annotations that integrate endoscopic imaging, histopathology, and germline genomic data. The dataset supports differential classification between hereditary polyposis syndromes and non-hereditary mimics.
AI.conclusion: ERCPMP-Gx addresses a critical gap in medical imaging datasets by providing a patient-level, multimodal dataset for AI development in hereditary colorectal polyposis recognition, characterization, and classification. This resource enables development of AI systems to support early diagnosis and targeted surveillance for affected families.

title: When EOS Tokens Disagree: Understanding Length Inflation in On-Policy Distillation
comment: 30 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, code available at https://github.com/UNCSciML/opd-eos
summary: We study length inflation in on-policy distillation (OPD), where student responses can become excessively long and even exhaust the generation budget. We identify \emph{termination-token mismatch} between base students and post-trained teachers as an important source of this behavior. Across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma, the two models can place their stopping probability on different EOS tokens, even when their declared stopping sets are identical. This mismatch can suppress the student's preferred termination action without reliably transferring the teacher-preferred alternative. We show that aligning the decoding stopping set alone is insufficient, while treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action substantially mitigates mismatch-induced length inflation across all three model families. To further understand how termination behavior evolves over training, we study OPD across different K2-Horizon training stages. This stage-wise analysis shows that termination preferences can shift substantially during training, while also revealing a distinct length inflation late in the OPD run that persists beyond termination alignment. Together, these results identify termination mismatch as an important, but not exhaustive, source of OPD length dynamics. We release an implementation incorporating the proposed termination-handling corrections.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies termination-token mismatch between base students and post-trained teachers as a key source of length inflation in on-policy distillation (OPD), where student responses become excessively long. The authors show that aligning decoding stopping sets is insufficient, but treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action substantially mitigates this issue across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma model families.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a critical problem in on-policy distillation where student responses can become excessively long, even exhausting the generation budget. The motivation was to understand why this length inflation occurs and identify its root causes.
AI.method: The authors analyzed termination behavior across three model families (Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma), studied how stopping probabilities are placed on different EOS tokens despite identical declared stopping sets, and conducted stage-wise analysis of OPD across different K2-Horizon training stages to understand how termination preferences evolve.
AI.result: The key findings are: (1) termination-token mismatch between base students and post-trained teachers suppresses the student's preferred termination action without reliably transferring the teacher-preferred alternative; (2) aligning the decoding stopping set alone is insufficient; (3) treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action substantially mitigates mismatch-induced length inflation; (4) termination preferences shift substantially during training; (5) a distinct length inflation late in the OPD run persists beyond termination alignment.
AI.conclusion: Termination mismatch is an important but not exhaustive source of OPD length dynamics. The proposed termination-handling corrections effectively mitigate the mismatch-induced length inflation, but other sources of length inflation remain to be addressed.

title: Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing
summary: Professional design requires any-color control: the ability to specify an object's target color with any 24-bit hex value for image generation and editing. Prior work has explored color generation, editing, and colorization, but often relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference procedures. Advances in large language models offer a simpler starting point: even compact models can associate hex values with color semantics. We present Paint-Anything, which learns a shared hex-prompt interface for generation and editing through object-level color supervision. We develop a data pipeline that constructs Paint-500K from real images through object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. Since shadows make real-image labels only approximate colors, we complement this supervision with pure-color anchors whose pixels exactly match their paired hex values. These anchors are used only at high-noise timesteps, leaving low-noise training to natural images. We further introduce Any Color Benchmark (ACBench), comprising ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit, to measure object-level hex color fidelity across both tasks. On FLUX.2-4B, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit scores by 85.3% and 28.3%, respectively, relative to the base model, with ablations supporting the training recipe. It also achieves the highest average CompColor score among the compared methods.

AI.tldr: Paint-Anything introduces a hex-prompt interface enabling any 24-bit color specification for both image generation and editing, using object-level color supervision with a constructed dataset (Paint-500K) and pure-color anchors. The method achieves significant improvements on the Any Color Benchmark (ACBench) over FLUX.2-4B base model.
AI.motivation: Professional design requires precise any-color control (specifying any 24-bit hex value), but prior work relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference. Large language models offer a simpler starting point as they can associate hex values with color semantics.
AI.method: 1) Data pipeline constructing Paint-500K from real images via object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. 2) Pure-color anchors (pixels exactly matching hex values) complement real-image labels (affected by shadows) - used only at high-noise timesteps. 3) Shared hex-prompt interface for both generation and editing tasks.
AI.result: On FLUX.2-4B: ACBench-T2I score improved by 85.3%, ACBench-Edit score improved by 28.3% relative to base model. Achieved highest average CompColor score among compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Paint-Anything successfully enables any-color control through a hex-prompt interface, with the training recipe (combining real images with pure-color anchors at appropriate timesteps) validated by ablations. The ACBench benchmark provides proper evaluation for object-level hex color fidelity.

title: Parallelism, critical windows, and separations among diffusion language models
summary:
A popular selling point of diffusion large language models (dLLMs) is their capacity for parallelism: the ability to generate sequences of text far more efficiently than autoregressive models, which require one forward pass per token. Yet among the many competing paradigms for dLLMs, from masked to uniform to Gaussian diffusion, principled understanding of how these different proposals compare in parallelism remains limited. In this work, we initiate a fine-grained comparison of the capacity for parallelism among these three leading approaches and prove the following:
  - Uniform and Gaussian diffusion can sample in a number of forward passes which scales with the dual total correlation of the underlying distribution, a measure of intrinsic complexity which can be much smaller than the context length. Previously, it was only known how to achieve this using masked diffusion.
  - For a certain family of random empirical measures, we show that $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{d})$ forward passes are necessary and sufficient to sample using uniform or Gaussian diffusion, yet there exist approximate score oracles for which $\widetildeΩ(d)$ forward passes are needed for masked diffusion. This establishes the first provable separation in parallelism between the three prevailing dLLM paradigms.
  Contrary to popular intuition that masked diffusions are harder to parallelize because they must commit to token values, the latter separation instead comes from the fact that the critical windows in masked diffusion sampling are asymptotically narrower than those in uniform and Gaussian diffusion sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a theoretical comparison of parallelism capabilities across three major diffusion large language model (dLLM) paradigms: masked, uniform, and Gaussian diffusion. It proves that uniform and Gaussian diffusion can achieve better parallelism scaling than previously known, depending on the dual total correlation of the underlying distribution. Additionally, it establishes the first provable separation between these paradigms, showing that masked diffusion actually requires more forward passes than uniform/Gaussian diffusion for certain distributions, contrary to popular intuition.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the limited principled understanding of how different dLLM paradigms compare in parallelism, despite parallelism being a major selling point for diffusion-based text generation. The authors aim to provide rigorous theoretical comparisons between masked, uniform, and Gaussian diffusion approaches.
AI.method: The methodology involves theoretical analysis using information-theoretic measures, particularly dual total correlation, and complexity bounds. The authors prove theoretical results about the number of forward passes needed for sampling under each paradigm, using techniques from probability theory and information theory.
AI.result: The key results include: (1) Uniform and Gaussian diffusion can sample using forward passes scaling with dual total correlation, which can be much smaller than context length; (2) For certain random empirical measures, Θ(√d) forward passes are necessary and sufficient for uniform/Gaussian diffusion, while masked diffusion requires Ω(d) forward passes with certain oracles; (3) This establishes the first provable separation between the three paradigms.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion challenges the popular intuition that masked diffusion is harder to parallelize due to token commitment. Instead, the narrower critical windows in masked diffusion sampling actually create the parallelism disadvantage compared to uniform and Gaussian diffusion approaches.

title: FAMOS: Feed-Forward 3D Articulation Modeling from Sparse Observations
summary: Modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views is challenging because each observation reveals only partial geometry and motion evidence. Most feed-forward methods infer articulation from a single observation and therefore rely heavily on learned category-level shape priors. We present FAMOS, a feed-forward model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds. Our model jointly reasons over multiple observations and naturally supports a variable number of inputs, including a single view. To aggregate articulation cues across observations, we introduce a Multi-state Articulation Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention. We further propose an observed articulation span objective that supervises the motion range each part exhibits across the input observations, encouraging the model to leverage the full observation set. To overcome the limited scale and diversity of existing datasets, we introduce a procedural data generator that synthesizes self-annotated assets during training. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K demonstrate consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines. Project page: https://kevinqu7.github.io/famos

AI.tldr: FAMOS is a feed-forward model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from sparse, unordered partial point clouds of articulated objects, using a Multi-state Articulation Transformer to aggregate articulation cues across multiple observations.
AI.motivation: Modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views is challenging because each observation reveals only partial geometry and motion evidence. Existing feed-forward methods rely heavily on learned category-level shape priors since they infer articulation from a single observation.
AI.method: FAMOS introduces a Multi-state Articulation Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention to jointly reason over multiple observations (supporting variable number of inputs including single view). It uses an observed articulation span objective to supervise motion range across observations. A procedural data generator is proposed to overcome limited dataset scale and diversity.
AI.result: Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K demonstrate consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: FAMOS successfully leverages multiple observations to predict articulation parameters, outperforming existing methods through its transformer architecture and novel supervision objective.

title: Mitigating Retaliatory Algorithmic Collusion in Repeated Games
summary: Reinforcement learning agents trained to maximize their own reward in repeated interactions can converge to supra-competitive outcomes resembling explicit collusion, without communication or shared design. Existing mitigation approaches are largely tied to specific economic settings, like two-sided platforms and auctions, leaving open how to design interventions for general repeated games. We address this gap by formalizing the connection between empirical observations from prior work on Q-learning collusion and classical theory of Simple Penal Codes (SPCs). We show any non-trivial SPC induces a quantifiable conditional dependence in agents' policies, detectable via the total variation distance between an agent's action distributions across cooperation and defection histories. Building on this connection, we propose CURB (Collusion Unwinding via Reward shaping and Belief injection), a reward-shaping framework that penalizes this Total Variation (TV) distance signal during Q-learning and is guaranteed to convert any SPC fixed point of the dynamics into a trivial one, thus precluding collusive equilibria sustained by punishment threats. Empirically, CURB substantially reduces collusion by Q-learning agents in both Bertrand and Cournot Competition Repeated Games. We further demonstrate that CURB extends to deep Q-network agents in Bertrand competition, suggesting the mechanism generalizes beyond tabular Q-learning.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses how reinforcement learning agents can converge to collusive outcomes without explicit communication, and proposes CURB, a reward-shaping framework that detects and prevents such collusion by penalizing conditional policy dependence, converting collusive equilibria into competitive ones.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows Q-learning agents can achieve supra-competitive (collusive) outcomes in repeated games without communication. Existing mitigation approaches are tailored to specific settings (two-sided platforms, auctions), lacking a general solution for repeated games.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the connection between Q-learning collusion and Simple Penal Codes (SPCs) from classical theory. It proposes detecting collusion via total variation (TV) distance between agent action distributions across cooperation vs. defection histories. CURB is introduced as a reward-shaping framework that penalizes this TV distance signal during Q-learning.
AI.result: CURB is proven to convert any non-trivial SPC fixed point into a trivial one, eliminating collusive equilibria. Empirically, it substantially reduces collusion in both Bertrand and Cournot repeated games, and extends to deep Q-network agents in Bertrand competition.
AI.conclusion: The connection between empirical collusion observations and SPC theory provides a general detection and intervention mechanism. CURB offers a broadly applicable solution for preventing learned collusion in repeated games, even with deep reinforcement learning agents.

title: CrystalMO-TuRBO: Multi-Objective Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for High-precision Joint Crystal Structure Refinement
summary: Crystal structure refinement is a fundamental inverse problem in materials characterization, where structural parameters are optimized to reproduce experimental diffraction data. Conventional approaches, such as least-squares and likelihood-based optimization, rely on local search and often struggle with non-convex, noisy, and highly correlated parameter landscapes, particularly when integrating multiple diffraction modalities. Joint refinement of X-ray and neutron data is especially challenging due to their complementary but competing sensitivities, which are typically combined through scalarized objectives requiring manual weighting and leading to suboptimal solutions. We propose CrystalMO-TuRBO, a multi-objective trust region Bayesian optimization architecture for joint crystal structure refinement. The method models X-ray and neutron discrepancies as separate objectives and transforms the problem into a normalized maximization setting. A two-phase optimization strategy is introduced: Phase 1 performs global exploration using parallel trust-region Bayesian optimization across multiple scalarizations to identify promising regions of the parameter space, while Phase 2 conducts localized refinement within a shrinking region to achieve high-precision solutions. This design explicitly separates global search from fine-grained optimization, addressing the unique accuracy requirements of refinement tasks. We evaluate the proposed method on experimentally collected X-ray and neutron diffraction data from single-crystal Ho2Ti2O7. Results demonstrate improved convergence, robustness, and parameter precision compared to classical refinement methods and Bayesian optimization baselines on refinement of a single-crystal pyrochlore material system.

AI.tldr: CrystalMO-TuRBO is a multi-objective Bayesian optimization framework for joint X-ray and neutron crystal structure refinement. It uses a two-phase approach: global exploration via parallel trust-region BO across multiple scalarizations, followed by localized refinement in a shrinking region.
