Tested on Ho2Ti2O7, it shows improved convergence, robustness, and precision over classical and baseline BO methods.
AI.motivation: Conventional crystal structure refinement struggles with non-convex, noisy, and highly correlated parameter landscapes, especially when integrating multiple diffraction modalities. Joint X-ray and neutron refinement is particularly challenging due to their complementary but competing sensitivities, typically combined through manual weighting that leads to suboptimal solutions.
AI.method: CrystalMO-TuRBO models X-ray and neutron discrepancies as separate objectives and transforms the problem into normalized maximization. The two-phase strategy includes: (1) Phase 1 - global exploration using parallel trust-region Bayesian optimization across multiple scalarizations to identify promising regions; (2) Phase 2 - localized refinement within a shrinking region for high-precision solutions.
AI.result: Evaluated on experimentally collected single-crystal Ho2Ti2O7 data, the method demonstrates improved convergence, robustness, and parameter precision compared to classical refinement methods and Bayesian optimization baselines.
AI.conclusion: The explicit separation of global search from fine-grained optimization effectively addresses the accuracy requirements of crystal structure refinement. This approach provides a robust solution for multi-modal diffraction data integration without manual weighting.

title: Can 4D Foundation Models Remember?
summary: Perceiving and remembering the visual world is fundamental to navigating and interacting with our environment. Current 4D foundation models, such as camera-controllable video models or 4D reconstruction models, can perceive and reconstruct dynamic environments, but how well they remember what they have perceived remains an open question. Existing benchmarks largely rely on pixel-level metrics and lack ground truth for objects once they leave the field of view, making them unable to evaluate visual memory in an object-centric manner against references. To fill this gap, we introduce PersistBench, a dataset and metric suite that leverages 360° videos as omniscient ground truth and proposes three evaluation aspects: object permanence, motion continuity, and appearance preservation. Evaluating various models across diverse categories reveals that current models can only maintain short-term consistency that degrades significantly once objects leave the field of view. Our findings highlight the gap between current model capabilities and robust visual memory ("seeing is not remembering"), providing guidance for future development of 4D foundation models. Dataset and code are available on the project page: https://guangzhaohe.com/persistbench.

AI.tldr: PersistBench introduces a benchmark for evaluating visual memory in 4D foundation models, using 360° videos as omniscient ground truth to assess object permanence, motion continuity, and appearance preservation when objects leave the field of view.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for 4D foundation models (camera-controllable video models or 4D reconstruction models) rely on pixel-level metrics and lack ground truth for objects once they leave the field of view, making it impossible to evaluate visual memory in an object-centric manner.
AI.method: The authors propose PersistBench, a dataset and metric suite leveraging 360° videos as omniscient ground truth, with three evaluation aspects: object permanence, motion continuity, and appearance preservation.
AI.result: Evaluating various models across diverse categories reveals that current models can only maintain short-term consistency that degrades significantly once objects leave the field of view.
AI.conclusion: Current 4D foundation models have a significant gap between perceiving and remembering - "seeing is not remembering". The findings provide guidance for future development of 4D foundation models with robust visual memory.

title: Recursive Quantum Long Short-Term Memory for Stable Short-Horizon Temperature Forecasting
summary: Quantum long short-term memory (QLSTM) models extend recurrent sequence learning with variational quantum circuits, but their optimization behavior can vary substantially across random initializations and temporal contexts. This paper evaluates a recursive QLSTM architecture against a standard QLSTM for one-step-ahead prediction of daily minimum and maximum temperature. Using daily weather observations from Toronto and identical training settings, we compare convergence, predictive accuracy, and generalization across input windows of 8, 16, and 32 days over 20 random seeds. The recursive model consistently reaches a near-optimal test loss earlier, reduces mean absolute error and root mean squared error, and exhibits a smaller generalization gap. These results indicate that recursive quantum feature transformations can improve stability and out-of-sample performance for compact hybrid quantum--classical temporal models.

AI.tldr: This paper compares a recursive QLSTM architecture against a standard QLSTM for temperature prediction tasks, demonstrating that the recursive approach achieves better convergence, accuracy, and generalization.
AI.motivation: Quantum LSTM models extend recurrent sequence learning with variational quantum circuits, but their optimization behavior varies across random initializations and temporal contexts. The authors aim to address this instability through a recursive architecture.
AI.method: The study evaluates both architectures on one-step-ahead prediction of daily minimum and maximum temperature using Toronto weather data. Experiments use identical training settings across 20 random seeds and input windows of 8, 16, and 32 days.
AI.result: The recursive QLSTM consistently reaches near-optimal test loss earlier, reduces mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE), and exhibits a smaller generalization gap compared to the standard QLSTM.
AI.conclusion: Recursive quantum feature transformations can improve stability and out-of-sample performance for compact hybrid quantum-classical temporal models.

title: COIN-GP: Cooperative Online Learning in Networked Distributed Systems with Partial Measurements via Gaussian Process Regression
summary: In this paper, we tackle the problem of jointly estimating the system states and partially unknown dynamics within distributed sensor-equipped networks, particularly in scenarios where only partial state observations are available. To address this issue, we propose an observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework incorporating online distributed Gaussian Process (GP) regression, which enables accurate estimation despite incomplete in measurements and deficient GP models. In addition, a novel data collection strategy is introduced, with theoretical conditions ensuring feasible data acquisition. Moreover, we also derive an error upper bound encompassing state estimation and model estimation, leveraging the deterministic error bounds of GPs. Empirical simulations demonstrate the superiority of our approach compared to existing distributed GP-based methods.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses joint estimation of system states and partially unknown dynamics in distributed sensor networks with partial state observations, using an observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework with online distributed Gaussian Process regression.
AI.motivation: Distributed sensor networks often face challenges with incomplete measurements and deficient models when estimating system states and unknown dynamics. Existing methods struggle with partial state observations, necessitating a new approach that can handle these limitations effectively.
AI.method: The authors propose an observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework incorporating online distributed Gaussian Process (GP) regression. A novel data collection strategy is introduced with theoretical conditions ensuring feasible data acquisition. Error bounds encompassing both state estimation and model estimation are derived using deterministic GP error bounds.
AI.result: The approach provides an error upper bound for both state and model estimation. Empirical simulations demonstrate superior performance compared to existing distributed GP-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework with online distributed GP regression effectively handles joint state and unknown dynamics estimation in distributed sensor networks with partial observations, outperforming existing methods.

title: Multi-center Medical Data Mining with FL-Net - A One-stop Shop for Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning enables collaborative training without sharing patient-level data, but most studies remain simulations. Based on five requirements derived from the literature, we analyzed 14 FL frameworks and found that none fully satisfied these requirements. We present FL-Net, a novel federated clinical research framework to fulfill all requirements. It integrates modular data harmonization, data discovery, disclosure control, securely built versioned FL-Net-Tools and containerized federated workflow execution into a persistent network. It enables the re-use of harmonized data and workflows across studies. FL-Net's end-to-end capabilities were evaluated through harmonization, cross-study patient discovery across MIMIC and US-130, and reproducible, audited federated workflows with up to 50 concurrent clients. FL-Net is being developed within the dAIbetes and Microb-AI-ome EU projects and will cover over 800,000 patients across 10 hospitals in 9 countries covering longitudinal and single point in time data, FL-Net provides a practical foundation for interoperable, reproducible, and privacy-preserving multicenter clinical research.

AI.tldr: FL-Net is a novel federated clinical research framework designed to enable privacy-preserving collaborative training without sharing patient-level data. It addresses the gap that no existing FL framework (among 14 analyzed) fully satisfies five literature-derived requirements. The framework integrates modular data harmonization, data discovery, disclosure control, versioned FL-Net-Tools, and containerized workflow execution into a persistent network, supporting reusable harmonized data and workflows across studies.
AI.motivation: Federated learning enables collaborative training without sharing patient-level data, but most studies remain simulations. The authors identified five requirements from literature that no existing FL framework fully satisfies, necessitating the development of a comprehensive solution for practical multicenter clinical research.
AI.method: The authors derived five requirements from literature and analyzed 14 existing FL frameworks against these requirements. They developed FL-Net, which integrates: (1) modular data harmonization, (2) data discovery, (3) disclosure control, (4) securely built versioned FL-Net-Tools, and (5) containerized federated workflow execution in a persistent network. Evaluation was conducted through harmonization tasks, cross-study patient discovery across MIMIC and US-130 datasets, and reproducible, audited federated workflows with up to 50 concurrent clients.
AI.result: FL-Net successfully satisfies all five requirements. It was evaluated through harmonization, cross-study patient discovery (MIMIC and US-130), and reproducible audited federated workflows supporting up to 50 concurrent clients. The framework is being deployed in the dAIbetes and Microb-AI-ome EU projects, covering over 800,000 patients across 10 hospitals in 9 countries with both longitudinal and single point in time data.
AI.conclusion: FL-Net provides a practical foundation for interoperable, reproducible, and privacy-preserving multicenter clinical research. It addresses the gap between simulation-based FL studies and real-world deployment by offering end-to-end capabilities including data harmonization, discovery, disclosure control, and secure workflow execution. The framework's deployment across multiple EU projects with extensive patient data demonstrates its viability for large-scale federated clinical research.

title: Epidemiological Causal Graph Identification: Challenges, Identifiability and Algorithms
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, accepted at the 60th Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems, and Computers 2026
summary: Causal discovery from observational data is fundamental to statistics and machine learning, yet determining causal direction without interventions necessitates structural assumptions. Existing identifiability research primarily focuses on continuous variables under additive noise models, often neglecting mixed datasets containing ordinal scales, counts, and continuous measurements. This paper investigates causal discovery in Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) where nodes follow either an ordinal distribution (via an ordered logit model) or a regular one-parameter exponential family distribution. We prove that the edge direction between an ordinal and an exponential family node is distributionally identifiable for generic parameter values. Our findings generalize previous Ordinal-Poisson results to the broader exponential family. Computationally, we introduce a score-based exhaustive search and a masked continuous optimization framework using DAGMA for larger graphs. Numerical results validate the theory, recovering edge orientations within a Markov equivalence class that are unidentifiable under classical structural equation models.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses causal discovery in mixed datasets containing ordinal, count, and continuous variables. The authors prove that edge direction between ordinal and exponential family nodes is distributionally identifiable, generalizing previous Ordinal-Poisson results. They propose computational frameworks (exhaustive search and DAGMA-based optimization) that successfully recover edge orientations within Markov equivalence classes that classical SEMs cannot identify.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery research primarily focuses on continuous variables under additive noise models, neglecting mixed datasets containing ordinal scales, counts, and continuous measurements. This gap limits the applicability of causal discovery methods to real-world data where variables often have different types (ordinal, count, continuous).
AI.method: Theoretical: The authors investigate causal discovery in Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) where nodes follow either ordinal distribution (via ordered logit model) or one-parameter exponential family distribution. They prove distributional identifiability of edge direction between ordinal and exponential family nodes for generic parameter values. Computational: A score-based exhaustive search and a masked continuous optimization framework using DAGMA are introduced for larger graphs.
AI.result: The edge direction between an ordinal and an exponential family node is distributionally identifiable for generic parameter values. This generalizes previous Ordinal-Poisson results to the broader exponential family. Numerical experiments validate the theory, successfully recovering edge orientations within a Markov equivalence class that are unidentifiable under classical structural equation models.
AI.conclusion: This work extends causal discovery methodology to handle mixed data types (ordinal and exponential family distributions), providing both theoretical identifiability guarantees and practical computational algorithms. The proposed methods can recover causal directions that classical approaches cannot determine, significantly broadening the applicability of causal discovery to real-world mixed datasets.

title: RISC-V and machine learning: a survey
summary: The intersection of open-source processor architectures and machine learning is driving the demand for customizable, efficient, and accessible hardware. This survey examines the state of the RISC-V ISA in machine learning applications, analyzing current capabilities, challenges, and future directions based on recent research. The analysis covers academic and commercial implementations, software frameworks, and real-world applications. The RISC-V machine learning ecosystem is evaluated, from instruction set extensions and core implementations to compiler optimizations and deployment strategies. Key contributions include a unified taxonomy of RISC-V ML implementations, a comparative analysis of performance and design trade-offs, an evaluation of software toolchain maturity, and the identification of emerging trends in instruction set extensions and specialized accelerators. Findings reveal progress in energy efficiency, specialized instruction development, and framework integration, while highlighting challenges in standardization, verification complexity, and ecosystem fragmentation. The analysis proposes four research directions to address current limitations: specialized neural processing extensions, adaptive and modular processor architectures, security frameworks, and energy-efficient multi-domain architectures. These directions provide a roadmap for advancing RISC-V as a foundational platform for next-generation machine learning systems.

AI.tldr: A survey paper examining how RISC-V ISA is being used in machine learning applications, covering implementations, software frameworks, and real-world applications, with analysis of current capabilities, challenges, and future research directions.
AI.motivation: The intersection of open-source processor architectures and machine learning is creating demand for customizable, efficient, and accessible hardware. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of RISC-V's role in ML.
AI.method: The paper analyzes academic and commercial implementations, evaluates the RISC-V ML ecosystem through instruction set extensions, core implementations, compiler optimizations, and deployment strategies. It provides a unified taxonomy, comparative analysis of performance and design trade-offs, and evaluation of software toolchain maturity.
AI.result: Findings show progress in energy efficiency, specialized instruction development, and framework integration. However, challenges remain in standardization, verification complexity, and ecosystem fragmentation.
AI.conclusion: Four research directions are proposed: (1) specialized neural processing extensions, (2) adaptive and modular processor architectures, (3) security frameworks, and (4) energy-efficient multi-domain architectures. These provide a roadmap for advancing RISC-V as a platform for next-generation ML systems.

title: Don't Mask the Environment: Observation Supervision Changes How Agents Explore Under RL
summary: Agent trajectories record what an agent does and what happens next. Yet standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) applies loss only to agent-authored action tokens, using environment observations as context but not as prediction targets. We ask whether this convention provides the best initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. We introduce ActObs, which also supervises the observation tokens already present in each trajectory. Although deployed agents never generate observations, learning to predict them encourages the policy to model action consequences without adding data, parameters, sequence tokens, or forward passes. The methods perform similarly after SFT but diverge after GRPO. On Qwen3-4B, GRPO from ActObs achieves higher pass@k at every evaluated sampling budget than its action-only counterpart on Terminal-Bench 2.0. On Qwen3-8B, it trades some pass@1 reliability for higher pass@k (+3.4 pp at pass@16) and solves more distinct tasks. The advantage extends to cross-domain code editing on aider-polyglot (+4.2 pp at pass@1 at 4B), whose tasks are unseen during SFT and RL. ActObs retains more entropy during RL while requiring less policy movement, leaving the final policy closer to its SFT initialization. Our analysis traces this difference to SFT: action and observation gradients rapidly become orthogonal, while action-only training leaves a large residual observation gradient and degrades environment prediction below the base model. Joint supervision prevents this one-sided specialization, preserving consequence prediction and preparing the policy for downstream exploration.

AI.tldr: ActObs proposes supervising observation tokens alongside action tokens during SFT, enabling better downstream RL performance without additional data or parameters. The method preserves consequence prediction capabilities and leads to higher pass@k scores on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and aider-polyglot benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard SFT only applies loss to action tokens, treating observations as context but not prediction targets. The authors question whether this convention provides optimal initialization for subsequent RL, as it may cause one-sided specialization that degrades the model's ability to predict action consequences.
AI.method: ActObs extends standard SFT by also supervising observation tokens already present in each trajectory. This encourages the policy to model action consequences without adding data, parameters, sequence tokens, or forward passes. The method is then evaluated with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) for downstream RL.
AI.result: On Qwen3-4B, GRPO from ActObs achieves higher pass@k at every evaluated sampling budget on Terminal-Bench 2.0. On Qwen3-8B, it shows +3.4 pp at pass@16. Cross-domain generalization on aider-polyglot shows +4.2 pp at pass@1 (4B). ActObs retains more entropy during RL while requiring less policy movement, leaving the final policy closer to its SFT initialization.
AI.conclusion: Joint supervision of actions and observations during SFT prevents the one-sided specialization seen in action-only training, preserving consequence prediction capabilities and preparing the policy better for downstream exploration. The key insight is that action and observation gradients rapidly become orthogonal in action-only training, degrading environment prediction below the base model.

title: Video DeltaNet: A Video-Native Hybrid Attention for Livestream Video Generation
summary: Video diffusion models repeatedly process long spatiotemporal token sequences during denoising, making attention a major computational bottleneck. Linear attention offers an appealing alternative and has been widely adopted in recent large language models, but directly applying it to video models often fails to preserve the fine-grained interactions required for high-quality generation. We present Video DeltaNet (VDN), which combines local Softmax attention with bidirectional linear memory for long-range video context. Its linear branch introduces Video Delta Attention (VDA), which updates memory once per frame by jointly incorporating its spatial tokens. Separate output projections and learnable gates calibrate the two branches, while a staged teacher-alignment recipe progressively introduces the new pathway into pretrained models. We instantiate VDN on MiniMax H3, applying the hybrid to video-to-video interactions while retaining Softmax for interactions involving text or audio. With eight-step distillation and an optimized SGLang serving stack, VDN-H3 completes DiT denoising for a 14.3-second, 768p video in 6.70 seconds on eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs, corresponding to a 14.5x speedup over the 50-step dense H3 baseline on the same GPU count.

AI.tldr: Video DeltaNet (VDN) is a hybrid attention mechanism that combines local Softmax attention with bidirectional linear memory (Video Delta Attention) to accelerate video diffusion models. It achieves 14.5x speedup over baseline while maintaining high-quality generation.
AI.motivation: Video diffusion models suffer from excessive computational cost when processing long spatiotemporal token sequences during denoising, making standard attention a major bottleneck. Linear attention offers efficiency but fails to preserve fine-grained interactions needed for high-quality video generation when directly applied.
AI.method: VDN introduces Video Delta Attention (VDA) in its linear branch, which updates memory once per frame by jointly incorporating spatial tokens. The method uses separate output projections and learnable gates to calibrate both branches, and employs a staged teacher-alignment recipe to progressively introduce the new pathway into pretrained models. Applied to MiniMax H3: hybrid attention for video-to-video interactions while retaining Softmax for text/audio interactions.
AI.result: With eight-step distillation and optimized SGLang serving stack, VDN-H3 completes DiT denoising for a 14.3-second, 768p video in 6.70 seconds on eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs, achieving a 14.5x speedup over the 50-step dense H3 baseline.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid approach successfully combines the efficiency of linear attention for long-range video context with the precision of Softmax attention for text/audio interactions, enabling practical high-quality video generation with significant computational savings.

title: Calibrated RF-Fingerprinting Under Interference With Heterogeneous Transmission Protocols
summary: Radio Frequency(RF)-Fingerprinting is a spectrum monitoring technique that identifies specific transmitters based on hardware impairments imprinted within the emitted signal. Although widely researched, studies almost exclusively consider scenarios where only one transmitter is emitting at a time, limiting real world applicability. In this work, we further the study of RF-Fingerprinting by considering co-channel interference, with multiple emitted signals interfering with each other, overlapping in time and frequency. Specifically, we formulate this problem as a multi-label classification problem and employ a 1D convolutional neural network (CNN). Furthermore, the models are calibrated such that the confidence thresholds for the label probabilities are derived, with guarantees on the upper bound on the average number of False Negatives, providing a degree of confidence in not missing a true spectrum policy violation. The proposed method is validated using real world data from the POWDER 5G testbed on devices transmitting 802.11a(Wi-Fi), 4G LTE, and 5G NR waveforms. The results show accuracy as high as 97% and as low as 73% after calibration depending on channel conditions. Also calibrating for various average false negatives upper bounds achieves micro recall scores of approximately (1 - calibrated false negatives) with the calibration robust to out-of-distribution interference, demonstrating the potential of the proposed method in a realistic high contention wireless environment

AI.tldr: This paper addresses RF-Fingerprinting in realistic multi-transmitter scenarios with co-channel interference, formulating it as a multi-label classification problem using 1D CNN, with confidence calibration to bound false negatives.
AI.motivation: Previous RF-Fingerprinting research only considers single-transmitter scenarios, which lacks real-world applicability. This work aims to address co-channel interference where multiple signals overlap in time and frequency.
AI.method:
1. Formulated the problem as multi-label classification
2. Employed 1D convolutional neural network (CNN)
3. Implemented confidence calibration to derive thresholds with guarantees on upper bound of average False Negatives
AI.result: Accuracy ranges from 73% to 97% depending on channel conditions. Calibration achieves micro recall scores approximately equal to (1 - calibrated false negatives), robust to out-of-distribution interference.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method demonstrates potential for spectrum monitoring in realistic high-contention wireless environments, validated on real-world data from POWDER 5G testbed with 802.11a, 4G LTE, and 5G NR waveforms.

title: PosteriorBench: From Point Estimates to Posterior Matching in Evaluating Generative Inverse Solvers
comment: 32 pages, 10 figures, 21 tables; the code is available at https://github.com/neuraloperator/PosteriorBench
summary: Generative models are increasingly used to solve scientific inverse problems, but existing evaluations still focus primarily on whether a method can produce a single plausible reconstruction. This is insufficient for ill-posed problems, where multiple solutions may be consistent with the same sparse or noisy observations. In these settings, a method can achieve strong pointwise accuracy while still failing to capture the true posterior through mode collapse, overconfident uncertainty, or averaging incompatible solutions. We introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for evaluating the distributional accuracy of generative inverse solvers. PosteriorBench evaluates four physics-based inverse problems: Darcy flow inversion, Poisson source recovery, carbon capture and storage, and light transport material inference. For each task, we construct high-fidelity reference posteriors using computationally heavy but established procedures such as rejection sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo, enabling direct assessment of whether solvers recover the full set of solutions rather than the single best sample. We pair these references with a five-metric posterior evaluation suite: posterior-mean error, posterior-standard-deviation error, maximum mean discrepancy, sliced Wasserstein distance, and radially averaged power-spectrum error. These metrics assess pointwise accuracy, marginal uncertainty, distributional alignment, and global frequency fidelity. The benchmark spans sparse sensing, low-resolution observations, nonlinear forward models, varying noise levels, and multimodal priors, with a unified pipeline for distribution matching and uncertainty quantification. Our experiments reveal substantial distribution-matching gaps across current solvers, while showing that neural operators improve resolution robustness, and guidance weights and generation noise are key to posterior-variance calibration.

AI.tldr: PosteriorBench is a benchmark for evaluating the distributional accuracy of generative inverse solvers in scientific inverse problems, addressing the limitation that existing evaluations focus only on single reconstruction quality rather than posterior distribution accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of generative models for inverse problems focus on single plausible reconstructions, which is insufficient for ill-posed problems where multiple solutions exist. A method can achieve strong pointwise accuracy while failing to capture the true posterior through mode collapse, overconfident uncertainty, or averaging incompatible solutions.
AI.method: Construct high-fidelity reference posteriors using computationally heavy but established procedures (rejection sampling and MCMC) for four physics-based inverse problems: Darcy flow inversion, Poisson source recovery, carbon capture and storage, and light transport material inference. Evaluate using five metrics: posterior-mean error, posterior-standard-deviation error, Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), sliced Wasserstein distance, and radially averaged power-spectrum error.
AI.result: Experiments reveal substantial distribution-matching gaps across current solvers. Neural operators improve resolution robustness. Guidance weights and generation noise are key to posterior-variance calibration.
AI.conclusion: PosteriorBench provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating distributional accuracy of generative inverse solvers, covering sparse sensing, low-resolution observations, nonlinear forward models, varying noise levels, and multimodal priors. The benchmark reveals significant room for improvement in current solvers' ability to capture true posterior distributions.

title: Score Centering Stabilizes Off-policy Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models is notoriously sensitive to small differences between training and inference engines, often referred to as the training-inference mismatch (TIM). However, completely eliminating TIM is impractical, as it would come at a major cost to rollout efficiency. In this paper, we show that the instability of RL under TIM is primarily caused by drift: a persistent bias between training and inference engines that accumulates with every training step. We derive an additive "score centering" correction term that stabilizes RL under TIM by canceling drift. When training models from 0.6B to 30B parameters, score centering alone matches or outperforms methods based on importance sampling under quantization, with the gap growing as the mismatch becomes more severe. Because the correction is additive, score centering also composes with importance sampling -- their composition outperforms pure importance-sampling baselines in our staleness experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses training-inference mismatch (TIM) in reinforcement learning for large language models by introducing an additive "score centering" correction term that cancels drift between training and inference engines.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning of LLMs is sensitive to small differences between training and inference engines (TIM), which causes instability. Completely eliminating TIM is impractical due to rollout efficiency costs. The instability is caused by drift - a persistent bias that accumulates with each training step.
AI.method: The authors derive an additive "score centering" correction term that stabilizes RL under TIM by canceling drift. This is a simple additive modification that corrects for the bias between training and inference engines.
AI.result: Score centering alone matches or outperforms importance sampling methods under quantization across models from 0.6B to 30B parameters, with the gap increasing as mismatch becomes more severe. Score centering also composes with importance sampling, outperforming pure importance-sampling baselines in staleness experiments.
AI.conclusion: Score centering is an effective, simple solution to stabilize RL training under training-inference mismatch. It works across model scales, handles severe mismatches well, and can be combined with importance sampling for additional benefits.
